exp.0:1:
It says that on the third day after David returned to Ziklag, a man came from Saul's camp. He had his clothes torn and dirt on his head, signs of mourning and grief in that time. When he came before David, he bowed down to the ground and paid him homage, as one would before someone in authority.

The narrator is the one telling this. David had just defeated the Amalekites and did not yet know what had happened in Israel's battle against the Philistines. This man arrives with news of Saul's death. His gesture of reverence suggests that he already saw David as the future king. Later in the chapter, his account will have important consequences, and the Bible does not make clear whether everything he said was true.

Today we can learn to receive hard news calmly, asking questions and listening before we react. It is also wise to examine carefully what we are told, especially when the person speaking might have interests of their own.
exp.0:3:
Here David urgently asks what happened in the battle, and the messenger answers with three hard pieces of news: Israel's army fled, many soldiers died, and King Saul and his son Jonathan also died.

David was in Ziklag, waiting for news of Israel's war against the Philistines. The man speaking has come from the battlefield, with torn clothes and dirt on his head, signs of mourning. Later it becomes clear that his account includes details that do not match 1 Samuel 31, so his version is doubtful.

When difficult news arrives, it is wise to ask calmly and seek the truth before reacting. We can also ask God for wisdom to listen, to feel the pain honestly, and not to be carried away by the first thing we hear.
exp.0:4:
Here David asks a direct question of a young man who arrived with news from the battle. He does not simply accept what he hears; he wants to know how he can be sure that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead.

David is in Ziklag, where he has returned after defeating the Amalekites. The young man arrives running from the Israelite camp, and his report brings the hardest blow: the king is dead, and Jonathan, David's friend, as well. David's question does not come from coldness but from a wish to verify the facts. Later, the young man will tell a story that the Bible does not confirm, and for that reason people debate whether he was telling the truth.

For today: when you receive serious news, do not let yourself be carried away by emotion or by rumors. Ask calmly, seek clarity, and trust God while you wait.
exp.0:5:
Here the young man answers David's question and tells how he came upon Saul. He says that he happened by chance upon mount Gilboa and saw Saul leaning on his spear, while the enemy chariots and horsemen came closer behind him. The young man who speaks is an Amalekite who arrived at David's camp with the news of Israel's defeat. David asks him how he knows that Saul and Jonathan died. His account presents Saul wounded and pursued. Later he says he killed him, but 1 Samuel 31 tells that Saul threw himself upon his own sword. For this reason many believe this young man invented part of his story to win David's favor. The Bible does not state this with complete clarity.

Today, before believing a piece of news or taking advantage of it, it is wise to ask how we know it and what interests the person telling it has. The truth matters more than convenience.
exp.0:7:
This verse is part of the account of a young man who comes to David after the battle of Gilboa. It says that Saul asked him who he was, and he answered that he was an Amalekite. The word "Amalekite" means that he belonged to the people of Amalek.

The one speaking is this young man, who arrives at David's camp with the news of Saul's death. His account is hard to confirm: 1 Samuel 31 tells of Saul's death in a different way, and many think the young man exaggerated or made up his part to win David's favor. Others believe something else may have happened. The Bible does not settle the question completely.

For today: let us not seek advantage through half-truths or by taking advantage of another's misfortune. God sees the heart, and honesty is worth more than any reward we hope to gain through deceit.
exp.0:9:
A young Amalekite tells David that he killed Saul, the king who was wounded in battle. He says he did it because Saul was not going to survive his fall. As proof, he brings the crown and the armlet, which is a bracelet the king used to wear. He hands them to David, whom he calls "my lord."

This messenger is the one speaking, and he hopes to receive a reward from David. His account differs from chapter 31 of 1 Samuel, where Saul takes his own life. Many think the young man invented or embellished the story to win David's favor. Others believe that Saul, already wounded, may indeed have asked him for help. The Bible does not make this clear. David, however, does not celebrate: he weeps.

Today we can learn not to take advantage of another person's misfortune for our own benefit. And, like David, we can respect and grieve the fall of others, even of those who have wronged us.
exp.0:10:
David heard the news of Saul's death, took hold of his clothes and tore them. The men who were with him did the same. "Took hold" means grabbed firmly, and "tore" means ripped them apart.

A young Amalekite had just arrived at David's camp carrying Saul's crown and armlet (a bracelet). He said he had killed Saul at the request of the wounded king. His account differs from 1 Samuel 31, where Saul takes his own life; many believe the young man lied to win David's favor. Tearing one's clothes was a way of expressing deep grief in that culture. David wept even though Saul had pursued him.

For today: learn from David not to rejoice at the fall of someone who harmed you. Let your heart feel sorrow and seek God in those moments.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that David and his men wept, mourned, and did not eat until evening. They did this for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel. The phrase "by the sword" means in battle, as the verse itself says they had fallen in war. To fast means to go without food as a sign of grief.

Here the narrator speaks. A young Amalekite came saying that he had killed Saul, and he brought Saul's crown and his armband. His account does not fully agree with 1 Samuel 31, so he probably lied to win David's favor. David did not rejoice at the death of his pursuer; instead he was filled with sorrow.

For today: let us learn to mourn with honesty, even for those who have wronged us. Grief over a loss does not have to be mixed with resentment or celebration. We can ask God for a compassionate heart, one that suffers with his people and does not rejoice in the downfall of others.
exp.0:12:
David asked the young man who brought him the news of Saul's death: "Where are you from?" The young man answered that he was the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.

David and his men had just wept, torn their clothes, and fasted for Saul, Jonathan, and the people of God. This young man claimed he had killed Saul, believing he would receive a reward. David asks about his origin because he wants to understand who he is and what he was doing there. That he was a foreigner and an Amalekite, a longtime enemy of Israel, highlights that he had no excuse for laying a hand on the Lord's anointed. The Bible presents this young man's account in a way that some scholars see as true and others see as exaggerated.

For today: respect the authority God allows, and do not rejoice at the fall of others, even if it was to your advantage. Weep with those who suffer, and do not seek advantage from their pain.
exp.0:13:
Here David asks the young Amalekite how he was not afraid to lift his hand against King Saul. The word "anointed" refers to someone set apart by God with oil to be king. "Lord" is the name of God.

David speaks after receiving the news of Saul's death. That young man said he had killed him, hoping for a reward. But David, who had spared Saul's life even when Saul was pursuing him, does not celebrate the news: he grieves and fasts. For David, the king was still someone placed by God. (The young man's account differs from 1 Samuel 31, where Saul takes his own life; we do not know whether the young man lied or exaggerated.)

For today: respect what God values, even when someone has harmed you. Do not rejoice at the fall of others or seek advantage from it.
exp.0:14:
David ordered one of his young soldiers to come near and strike down the Amalekite, and the man struck him so that he died. The explanation of "young men" is that they were the young soldiers who served David.

David speaks here after receiving the news of Saul's death. This foreign Amalekite claimed to have killed him, perhaps hoping for a reward. Another account of Saul's death appears in 1 Samuel 31, where Saul takes his own life; for this reason many believe the man was lying, though this cannot be stated with certainty. David judges him by his own words.

For today: David respected the authority that God had placed over him, even when Saul was his enemy. We can learn not to rejoice in the fall of someone who has harmed us, nor to take advantage of another's misfortune, and to take seriously the weight of our words.
exp.0:19:
He says that the news of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan should not be told in Gath or announced in the streets of Ashkelon, two Philistine cities. That way the Philistine women would not rejoice or celebrate.

David speaks in a lament, a funeral song, after Israel's defeat on Mount Gilboa, where Saul and his son Jonathan died. David feels grief and does not want Israel's enemies to mock. Although Saul had hunted him, David mourns him with respect.

For today: when someone who hurt us falls or suffers, we are not called to rejoice or to speak of their fall with mockery. We can honor the good that was in that person, mourn with sincerity, and guard the good name of others.
exp.0:20:
David speaks to the mountains of Gilboa as though they were people. He wishes that no dew or rain would fall on them, and that they would not yield fields for offerings. The shield lay cast down on the ground there, and the final phrase can be understood in two ways: as if Saul had never been anointed king, or as if his shield had never been anointed with oil.

David sings this lament after the death of Saul and Jonathan in battle against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not celebrate his death. He mourns the fallen king and his friend, and he wants Israel to remember them with respect.

For today: when someone who wronged us fails or dies, we can avoid mockery and resentment. It is possible to grieve sincerely, to acknowledge the good that was there, and to leave the final judgment in God's hands.
exp.0:23:
This verse calls the women of Israel to weep for King Saul. It reminds them that, during his reign, he gave them clothing of scarlet (a bright red cloth, very valuable) and gold ornaments for their garments. It speaks of a time of abundance and celebration.

David speaks in a song of mourning for the death of Saul and Jonathan in battle. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not rejoice at his death. He highlights the good the people received during that reign and honors the fallen king. Scholars see here a tone of public tribute.

For today: even when someone has done us harm, we can recognize the good they did and avoid rejoicing in their fall. Honoring with truth and respect is also a way of loving.
exp.0:24:
This verse is a lament. David expresses his grief because strong and brave men died in the middle of battle. He mentions Jonathan in a special way, saying that he was slain on the heights, that is, on the hills or high places where he fell. The "mighty" are the warriors, and "fallen" means that they died.

David speaks in a funeral song. Saul and his son Jonathan had just died fighting against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not celebrate his death, but mourns the king and, above all, his friend Jonathan, with whom he shared a very deep friendship.

For today: when someone dies or we feel the pain of a loss, we can grieve honestly, without hiding our sorrow. We can also honor the good that was in other people, even if the relationship was difficult, and thank God for faithful friends.
exp.1:2:
This verse tells us that David did not go to Hebron alone. He also brought the men who had stayed with him during his years of flight, each one with his family. They settled in the towns around Hebron.

This is the narrator's account, following the death of Saul. David asked God what to do and obeyed his answer: go up to Hebron, in the territory of Judah. Those men had been loyal to him while he was being hunted. Soon after, the men of Judah anointed him king over their tribe. Hebron thus became the center of a new beginning.

For today: when God opens a new stage for us, we do not live it alone. Let us care for and thank those who walked with us in hard times, and seek God's guidance before taking each step.
exp.1:3:
To anoint meant pouring oil on someone to mark him as chosen for an office. Then they told David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul.

This is a historical account. Saul had died in battle, and David, who had already been anointed in private years earlier by Samuel, now receives public recognition from his own tribe. The news about the men of Jabesh-gilead leads David to respond with gratitude, as is seen later. His reign over all Israel would come later.

For today: David did not rush to take all the power, but accepted what God opened up for him step by step. He also valued an act of kindness toward someone who had died. We can learn to wait for God's timing and to recognize with gratitude the good that others do.
exp.1:9:
Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. The verse also says that only the tribe of Judah followed David, that is, it supported him as king.

The narrator of the book describes how the people were divided after Saul's death. Abner, the commander of the army, set Ish-bosheth up as king to keep power in Saul's family. David's seven years and a half in Hebron suggest there was a period of waiting before he reigned over all Israel. Scholars explain the difference from Ish-bosheth's two years in several ways, and it is not certain which explanation is best.

Today we can learn to trust God's timing. Sometimes promises take a long time to arrive, and others rush ahead with human plans. To wait with faith and integrity, without forcing our way, is also a way of obeying.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that David ruled in Hebron for seven years and a half. During that time he reigned only over the tribe of Judah, his own house.

The narrator of the book, who keeps track of the time, is the one speaking. Meanwhile, Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, ruled over the rest of Israel. The book does not explain why there is a difference in the years: some think Ish-bosheth took time to be established, or that there were years of war and transition. This is a point that is not entirely clear. What we can see is that the kingdom was divided and that conflict would soon come.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often does so with patience. David was anointed, yet he waited years to reign over all of Israel. If you are waiting, remain faithful where you are.
exp.1:11:
This verse tells us that Abner, the son of Ner, marched out from Mahanaim toward Gibeon. The servants of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, marched with him. "Servants" here means the men in his service, probably soldiers. The phrase "One day" simply marks the moment in the story when this march began.

The narrator describes a time when Israel was divided. Ish-bosheth ruled over Israel, and only Judah followed David in Hebron. Abner was the commander of Saul's army and supported Ish-bosheth. His march toward Gibeon prepares the encounter with Joab and David's men. The text does not say clearly what his exact purpose was; some think he sought to affirm the power of Ish-bosheth.

For today: when there are divisions, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are seeking God's will or only defending our own side. Let us ask him for wisdom to pursue peace.
exp.1:12:
It says that Joab, David's nephew and commander of his army, went out with David's men and met Abner and the men of Ish-bosheth by the pool of Gibeon. They sat down, or stopped facing each other, some on one side of the pool and the others on the other side.

The narrator describes how the conflict between the two sides began. Judah was following David in Hebron, and the rest of Israel was following Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army, came to Gibeon, and Joab went out to meet him. Here there is still no fighting, only two groups separated by a pool and a growing tension.

For today: many great quarrels begin with situations that seem small. Before we take our places on opposite sides, let us ask God for wisdom to seek peace and not to feed pride.
exp.1:18:
He says that Asahel pursued Abner without turning aside even a little. The phrase we must avoid is the one meaning neither to the right nor to the left, so in plain terms it means he did not turn to the right hand or to the left. Asahel was going after him in a straight line, determined.

This happens after a fierce battle between David's men and those of Israel, who were defeated. Asahel, brother of Joab and Abishai, was very swift. The narrator tells us that he went straight after Abner, the commander of the enemy army. Later Abner warns him to stop, but Asahel does not heed him. The text does not explain his reasons; we may suppose ambition or bravery, but that is only an interpretation.

Persistence is good, but we need to ask where we are going. Before pursuing a goal with determination, it is wise to pray, to listen to counsel, and to know whether God is guiding us. Sometimes stopping in time is wisdom.
exp.1:21:
Abner, commander of Saul's army, warns Asahel once more to stop chasing him. He asks why he should have to strike him down to the ground, and he asks how he could show his face to Joab, Asahel's brother, if he did. The warning is plain: keep following, and Abner will have to defend himself with deadly force.

After a battle between the men of Saul and the men of David, Asahel, who was very swift, was pursuing Abner. Abner did not want to kill him, since he knew that would bring revenge from Joab. But Asahel paid no attention, and the account shows how pride and stubbornness can end in tragedy.

For today: when someone warns you wisely, listen in time. Sometimes the insistence on getting our own way costs us more than we expect. Humility keeps us from dangerous paths.
exp.1:22:
He says that Asahel would not stop chasing Abner, and Abner struck him with the back end of his spear (the metal tip at the bottom, used to plant the spear in the ground). The blow was so hard that it went clear through him, and Asahel died right there. Those who were passing by stopped, probably out of sorrow and shock at seeing his body.

This is part of the war between the army of Judah, with David, and the army of Israel, with Abner, who supported the house of Saul. Asahel, brother of Joab, was chasing Abner. Abner warned him twice to turn aside, because he did not want to kill him or get into trouble with Joab.

For today: when a wise person gives us a clear warning, it is wise to listen. Stubbornness and pride can lead us to lose more than we imagine.
exp.1:23:
This verse tells us that Joab and his brother Abishai did not stop and kept pursuing Abner. When they came to a hill called Ammah, near Giah and along the road through the wilderness of Gibeon, the sun was already going down. The word "hill" here means a small rise or knoll. The exact location of that place is not known.

Here the narrator speaks. Asahel, brother of Joab, had been killed by Abner after ignoring his warnings. Now Joab wants revenge. This happens during the war between the followers of Saul and the followers of David.

For today: the desire for revenge can keep us going after someone without thinking about the consequences. Before reacting in anger, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek peace, as Abner later asked.
exp.1:25:
Abner calls out to Joab with three questions: Will the sword keep devouring forever? Don't you know that in the end it will only bring bitterness? How long will it be before you tell your people to stop chasing their own brothers? Abner shouted, which means he called out loudly, and in the end means at last.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army, and Joab was the commander of David's army. After a very bloody battle between the two forces, Abner was fleeing and Joab was pursuing him. As evening was falling, Abner asked that they stop, because both sides belonged to the same people. Joab answered him and then blew the horn to call off the pursuit.

Today, when a conflict with someone close to us drags on, it is worth asking where it is leading us. We can be the ones who say enough before bitterness grows, seeking peace and not merely winning the argument.
exp.1:27:
Joab sounds the horn, which was a military signal, and all his men come to a halt. They no longer chase the soldiers of Israel who were following Abner, and the battle ends for that day.

After a hard fight between the men of David (Judah) and those of Ishbosheth (Israel), Abner called out to Joab to stop killing his own brothers. Joab agreed and gave the order to stop. It was a ceasefire, although the conflict between the two houses continued afterward. The passage shows the sadness of a war between brothers.

Today, knowing when to stop in time is a kind of wisdom. When an argument within the family, the church, or the workplace only leaves wounds, it is wise to listen to the one who asks for peace and to stop. Let us ask God for humility to hold back before bitterness grows.
exp.1:28:
This verse tells us that Abner and his men fled all through the night. They crossed the plain (the flat valley land along the Jordan), crossed the Jordan River, and went through the region called Bithron. In the end they reached Mahanaim, on the other side of the river. It is not known for certain where Bithron was; we only understand that it was a part of the route.

Here the narrator is speaking. There had been a battle between David's men and those of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. Abner had asked Joab to stop pursuing them, and Joab sounded the horn to halt the fighting. Abner used the chance to escape during the night.

For today: conflicts that drag on leave death and wounds behind. Knowing when to stop in time, listening to a call for peace, and not continuing to fight out of pride can prevent much pain in family, work, or church.
exp.1:29:
This verse tells what happened after the battle. Joab stopped chasing Abner, came back, and gathered the whole army to count the losses. On David's side, nineteen men were missing, besides Asahel. "Servants" here means David's soldiers, and "were missing" means they had died.

The narrator of the book describes the end of a civil war between David's followers, in Judah, and those of Abner, who supported the house of Saul. Asahel, Joab's brother, had pursued Abner, and Abner killed him. That is why his name appears separately, since his death would have consequences later on.

For today: fights between brothers leave real losses and people who do not come back. Before feeding a conflict, think about the human cost. Seek peace and reconciliation while there is still time.
exp.1:31:
It says that Joab and his men marched through the whole night and came to Hebron when the day was already breaking.

The account has no character who speaks; it is the narrator who tells the story. The battle between David's men and Abner's men had just taken place, in which Asahel, Joab's brother, died. After burying him in Bethlehem, the group continued on their way to Hebron, where David was. Perhaps Joab and his men were tired and in mourning, but they did not stop.

There are days when we carry losses and weariness, and still we must go on with our responsibilities. When you walk through a difficult night, take the next step in faith, trusting that God is with you and that the dawn will come.
exp.2:0:
The explanation says there was a long war between the followers of Saul and those of David. Over time, David grew stronger, while Saul's family grew weaker. "House" here means family and supporters, not just a building. The phrase "grew stronger and stronger" means he gained strength and support.

The author of the book is not identified; it is a historical account. Saul had died, and David was reigning only over Judah from Hebron, while Saul's son Ish-bosheth had the support of the other tribes. This verse summarizes years of conflict before David was accepted as king over all Israel. The verses that follow list the sons born to him in Hebron.

For today: sometimes God's promises are not fulfilled overnight. David had to wait and go through conflicts. If you are in a long season of waiting or difficulty, remain faithful and trust that God is working slowly, even if you don't notice it every day.
exp.2:1:
This verse begins a list of the sons who were born to David while he was living in Hebron. The word "firstborn" means the eldest son, the first one born.

The narrator presents this list in the middle of the account of the long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. While David ruled over Judah alone, his family was growing and his position was becoming secure. The list also prepares the reader for the painful family conflicts that would come later, since Amnon and Absalom will be the main figures in them.

For today: God can bless a life and yet wounds still remain within a family. Let us care for our homes with prayer, a good example, and attentiveness, for the fruits of our decisions are seen over time.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues the list of the sons born to David in Hebron. The second was Chileab, son of Abigail, who had been the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. The third was Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.

The writer of the book presents details about David's family while his household grows stronger and Saul's house declines. Many believe that marrying the daughter of a foreign king was a political alliance, though the text does not explain this. The Bible records these marriages without approving of them, and later Absalom will cause great trouble.

For today: God fulfills his plans even through imperfect people, but our family decisions leave lasting marks. Care for your home with prayer, wisdom, and faithfulness.
exp.2:3:
This verse continues the list of the sons born to David in Hebron. Here appear the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith, and the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital. The names of the mothers are given because David had several wives, and each son is identified by his mother.

The author of the book recounts, as in a family record, what happened while David reigned alone over Judah, in Hebron. Meanwhile, the house of Saul and the house of David were at war. This list shows that David's family was growing and becoming stronger. It also reveals that having many wives would bring conflicts, as the Bible tells later on. Adonijah, for example, later tried to make himself king.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that seem unimportant. Care for your home with prayer and wisdom, because the decisions you make today affect the family for years.
exp.2:4:
This verse ends the list of the six sons born to David in Hebron. The sixth was Ithream, the son of Eglah, one of his wives.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book who presents a family summary. David was reigning in Hebron over Judah, while the house of Saul was still in dispute with him. The list shows that his household was growing, though it also reveals a family with several wives, something that would later bring conflict. Very little is known about Eglah.

For today: God works through real and sometimes imperfect stories. Care for your home with prayer and wisdom, and trust that God can guide even what is full of weakness.
exp.2:7:
Abner becomes very angry at Ish-bosheth's question. He asks with irony, "Am I a dog's head, a worthless man working for the enemy?" He says he has been loyal to Saul's family and did not hand Ish-bosheth over to David. Yet now Ish-bosheth accuses him of this woman's offense.

Abner, the commander of the army, speaks to King Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. Ish-bosheth had accused him of taking Rizpah, one of Saul's concubines, which could be seen as a claim to the throne. The text does not say whether Abner did so; he is offended by the accusation and breaks with Ish-bosheth.

For today: when you are corrected or accused, examine your heart before reacting in anger. A wounded pride can lead us to decisions that cause great harm. Ask God for humility and calm.
exp.2:13:
David sends messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, who was ruling over Israel, and demands that he return his wife Michal to him. David recalls that he won her by paying a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, the proof Saul asked for as the price of marrying her.

David speaks from a position of strength: Abner, the commander of Ish-bosheth's army, has just offered him an alliance to unite all of Israel under his command. David makes the return of Michal, his first wife, whom Saul had given to another man, the condition for this.

Interpreters debate whether David acted out of love, out of legitimate right, or out of political advantage, since he was Saul's son-in-law. The Bible does not make this clear, and the text also shows the grief of Paltiel, who followed her weeping.

For today: claiming what is rightfully ours does not excuse us from seeing the pain of others. As we pursue what belongs to us, let us take care in how we treat those who are affected.
exp.2:14:
This verse tells how Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, sent for Michal and took her away from her husband Paltiel, son of Laish. Paltiel was her husband at that time.

The narrator describes one step in the political agreement between David and Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army. David demanded that his first wife, Michal, be returned to him before he would negotiate. Ish-bosheth, weak before Abner, complied. Saul had given Michal to Paltiel earlier (1 Samuel 25:44). The text does not explain her feelings, but it shows Paltiel's grief, since he followed her weeping.

The decisions of the powerful, even political ones, can wound ordinary people. Today we can ask God for sensitivity to treat with compassion those who suffer the consequences of decisions made by others, and to comfort them.
exp.2:18:
This verse tells how Abner, the commander of Saul's army, also spoke with the tribe of Benjamin. Then he went to Hebron to report to David what the elders of Israel and the whole house of Benjamin had decided.

Abner was switching sides. After Saul's death, he had supported Saul's son Ish-bosheth, but now he wanted to bring Israel together under David. Benjamin was Saul's tribe, so its support was very important. Abner said that God had promised that David would deliver Israel. His personal motives are not spelled out here, and the text shows a mix of reasons.

For today: when God has already shown the way, it is wise to listen patiently to others and to seek unity, without forcing our own will on them.
exp.2:20:
Abner tells David that he will set out to gather all of Israel to the king, who is David, so that they may make a covenant with him. In this way David would reign over everyone, as he desired.

Abner had been commander of Saul's army and had supported Saul's house. After fighting with Ish-bosheth, he turned to David. He had already spoken with the leaders of Israel and of Benjamin. David received him with a feast and let him go in peace, a sign of good will. What follows shows that Joab was not present and that the story would become complicated.

For today: when seeking peace with someone, it is wise to go about it calmly and with good will, as David did. Even so, one must act with wisdom, because not everyone responds the same way to reconciliation.
exp.2:21:
This verse tells how David's men and Joab returned from a raid carrying a large amount of plunder. But Abner was no longer in Hebron, because David had sent him away and he had gone off in peace.

The narrator is describing what happened while Joab, the commander of David's army, was away. Abner, who had earlier been commander of Saul's army, had come to offer that all Israel would join David. David welcomed him with a feast and let him go safely. The text sets up Joab's reaction, which will come in anger. The Bible later says that Joab killed Abner, and here we can see that David acted in good faith.

For today: when someone seeks peace, let us receive them with honesty and without deceit. We should also be careful that resentment does not lead us to destroy what God may be healing.
exp.2:28:
The explanation says that David asks that the punishment for the death of Abner fall on Joab and his family. It mentions five hardships: an illness with a discharge (a bodily discharge that left the person unclean), leprosy (a skin disease), a person who leans on a staff (perhaps from disability or weakness), death by the sword, and lacking bread (poverty).

It speaks of David, now king in Hebron. Joab treacherously killed Abner, who had come in peace to unite the people under David. Joab said he was avenging his brother Asahel, but he did it through deceit. David publicly distances himself and asks that the guilt rest on Joab. It is a curse, not a certain prophecy; the Bible does not say it was fulfilled to the letter.

For today: personal revenge destroys, and peace is kept through honesty. When we are wronged, let us leave justice in God's hands and not use deception to settle accounts.
exp.2:29:
This verse explains why Abner died. Joab and his brother Abishai killed him in revenge, because Abner had killed their brother Asahel during the battle at Gibeon. The word "and" here only joins the sentence to what came before.

The narrator of the book gives us the reason behind the crime. Abner had made peace with David, and Joab murdered him treacherously in Hebron (v. 27). Earlier, Abner had killed Asahel, though he did it while defending himself from Asahel's pursuit (2 Samuel 2:18-23). For this reason David distances himself from the deed, curses the house of Joab, and publicly mourns Abner.

Today, resentment can lead us to harm others and to justify ourselves with excuses. If someone has wounded us, let us ask God for help to forgive and to leave justice in his hands, instead of taking revenge.
exp.2:30:
Here David orders Joab and all the people who were with him to tear their clothes, put on rough mourning clothes, and weep openly before Abner's body. The "sackcloth" is the coarse cloth worn as a sign of grief. The "bier" is the stretcher or coffin on which the dead man was carried. David himself walked behind it, showing respect.

David speaks as king of Judah. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had come to offer him peace, and Joab killed him out of revenge. By having Joab take part in the mourning, David makes it clear before all the people that he did not agree with that crime. Many understand that he also wanted to prevent further division and violence in the nation.

For today: when there is injustice, silence is not enough. We must reject evil clearly and humbly, and seek peace and truth without letting ourselves be carried away by revenge.
exp.2:33:
This verse is part of David's lament for Abner. It tells us that Abner did not die like a prisoner, with his hands tied and his feet in chains. He died the way a man falls at the hands of wicked people, that is, betrayed and murdered. When the people heard this, they all wept again.

David speaks at Abner's funeral. Abner was the commander of Saul's army. Joab had killed him treacherously in Hebron, partly out of personal revenge. David wanted everyone to know that he had taken no part in that death. That is why he mourns him publicly, and the people recognize his sincerity.

For today: when someone suffers injustice, it is not enough to stay silent or look the other way. We can honor the victims with clear and truthful words and with compassion, and live in a way that shows our actions reject violence.
exp.2:37:
Here David speaks to his servants about the death of Abner. He asks them whether they do not realize that a man of importance and great worth had fallen that day in Israel. The word "prince" here means a leader or chief, and "fallen" in this verse means that he died.

David is the one speaking. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had come to help him unite the tribes under his reign, but Joab, commander of David's army, killed him out of revenge. David grieves publicly and wants everyone to know that he had no part in that crime. The people understood it this way. Moreover, David acknowledges that his power is still fragile and that Joab and his brother are hard to control.

For today: let us learn to recognize the worth of people and to lament injustice, even when it is uncomfortable. Also, when something wrong happens near us, let us act with honesty and allow God to be the final judge.
exp.3:1:
This verse introduces two men: Baanah and Rechab, brothers, sons of Rimmon, from the town of Beeroth. They were captains of companies, that is, leaders of groups of soldiers who served Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul. It is clarified that Beeroth was counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin, the same tribe as Saul.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, preparing the account. Israel was very weak: Abner, the commander of the army, had died, and Saul's son had lost heart. These two captains appear just before they do something serious, which the text will recount immediately. Why they acted as they did, the passage does not explain here.

For today: holding a position or being close to someone does not guarantee a faithful heart. Let us ask God for integrity, especially when we see others growing weak and the temptation to take advantage appears.
exp.3:3:
This verse tells that Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who was five years old and lame in his feet. When the news came that Saul and Jonathan had died, his nurse picked him up and fled in fear. In her hurry, the boy fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.

The narrator pauses the story of the murder of Ish-bosheth, another son of Saul, to introduce Mephibosheth. With Saul and Jonathan dead, the house of Saul was losing its power, and a young heir was in danger. Later, David will show him kindness for the sake of Jonathan.

For today: sometimes our lives are marked by accidents or tragedies we did not choose. But God does not define us by those wounds. You can trust that He cares for the vulnerable and can bring kindness, even after pain.
exp.3:4:
This verse tells how Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon from the town of Beeroth, went to the house of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul. They arrived at the hottest time of the day, when he was resting in his room.

The author of the book tells the events as a narrator. Ish-bosheth was ruling over Israel after Saul's death, and David was ruling over Judah. These two brothers were captains serving Ish-bosheth, and they were planning to kill him, most likely to win David's favor. The narrator makes it clear that this was a betrayal, and later David punishes the murderers.

For today: let us not justify wrongdoing with the excuse that it suits us. God does not need our schemes or our disloyalty to carry out his plans. Let us seek to move forward with integrity, even when it seems slower.
exp.3:10:
David is outraged by a serious crime: two men killed an innocent man, in his own house and while he was sleeping. David asks, with force, whether he should not hold them accountable for that blood. Holding them accountable for that death means making them answerable for it, and removing them from the earth means putting them to death. Young soldiers are what is meant here.

David speaks to Rechab and Baanah, who murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, and brought his head to him expecting a reward. David had already punished another man who claimed to have killed Saul. He wants to make it clear that he does not rejoice in the violence or profit from it. What follows, the execution and the mutilation of the bodies, was a harsh practice of that time; the text reports it without asking us to imitate it.

Today: let us not seek to gain advantage through unjust means, nor expect applause for doing wrong. God values justice and innocent life. Let us trust in Him and act with integrity.
exp.3:11:
It says that David ordered his young soldiers to execute the two men who had killed Ish-bosheth. Then they cut off their hands and feet and hanged them up beside the pool at Hebron, in full view of everyone. Ish-bosheth's head, by contrast, was buried with honor in the tomb of Abner.

Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, ruled over part of Israel. Two of his captains murdered him while he slept and brought his head to David, expecting a reward. David, who had previously punished the man who announced Saul's death, condemned them for killing an innocent man. Their punishment was public and very severe, which was common in that era.

For today: God is not pleased to achieve good ends through unjust means. Let us seek justice without taking advantage of another's wrong, and honor the truth even when no one rewards us for it.
exp.4:1:
Here the leaders of Israel's tribes tell David that even earlier, while Saul was king, it was he who led the army out to battle and brought it back home. They also remember that God promised he would be the shepherd of his people and their ruler, that is, their governor and leader.

The tribes of Israel speak here, gathered in Hebron. Saul had already died, and David was ruling over Judah alone. Now they acknowledge his leadership and ask that he reign over all of them. They base their decision on two things: what they saw in him and what God had said.

For today: God often prepares people in hidden places before giving them greater responsibility. Be faithful where you are, serve with humility, and trust that God opens doors in his time. And if you lead, remember that caring for others is part of your calling.
exp.4:2:
This verse tells how the leaders of Israel went to see David in Hebron. There David made an agreement with them, in the presence of God, and they anointed him as king over all Israel. The "elders" are the heads and representatives of the tribes. A "covenant" is a formal commitment between both parties. "Anointed" means they poured oil on his head, a sign that he was set apart to rule.

The one acting here is the people, through their leaders. After Saul's death, David already reigned alone over Judah. Now the other tribes recognize that he is one of their own, that he had already led them in battle, and that God had chosen him to shepherd his people.

For today: whoever leads should take up their role with clear commitments and with humility before God, knowing that their authority is a service and not a privilege.
exp.4:4:
This verse sums up how long David ruled. First he reigned seven years and six months in Hebron, and over the tribe of Judah only. Then he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem, already over all Israel and Judah. Together they add up to the forty years of the verse before. The name Jerusalem refers to the city of Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book gives a brief summary before telling of the capture of Jerusalem. The elders of Israel had just anointed David as king in Hebron. This closed a time of division and began a united kingdom. The text shows that this process was long and not immediate.

For today: God keeps his promises, but often with patience. David waited years before reigning over the whole people. If you are waiting for something from God today, be faithful in the place where you are now, as David was in Hebron.
exp.4:8:
David settled down to live in the stronghold he had just captured in Jerusalem. He gave it the name "City of David" and began building all around it, from Millo inward. Millo seems to have been an area of earthworks or fill, though its exact nature is not known.

The passage is a historical narrative. David was already king over all Israel and needed a central, well-defended capital. The Jebusites had considered the city impregnable. By taking it and strengthening it, David made it the political and, later, religious center of the nation. The next verse says that God was with him.

For today: David did not only win a battle; he also committed himself to building and caring for what he had won. We can learn not to be satisfied with an achievement, but to build steadily on what God entrusts to us: family, work, the church, and to do so depending on Him.
exp.4:9:
David kept growing stronger and greater, and the Lord God of hosts was with him. The phrase about David growing and increasing refers to his power, his kingdom and his influence advancing little by little. The title of God as Lord God of hosts presents him as the Lord of all power. The phrase about God being with David means that God accompanied him and supported him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had just taken Jerusalem, which had been a fortress of the Jebusites, and he made it his capital. The text explains the cause of his growth: it was not only his skill, but the presence of God. Shortly afterward, Hiram, king of Tyre, sent him help, and David understood that God had confirmed him as king.

For today: if you are moving forward in your work, your family, or your service, do not forget that the true support is God. Seek his company first, and thank him for every achievement.
exp.4:10:
This verse tells that Hiram, king of Tyre, sent David messengers, cedar wood, carpenters, and stonemasons (workers who shape stone). They built David's palace.

The narrator describes how David was becoming established in Jerusalem, his new capital. That a foreign king supported him shows that his kingdom was recognized. The next verse explains the meaning: David understood that God had confirmed him as king for the sake of his people. Some see here the hand of God using a non-believer to help.

For today: God can give us help through unexpected means, even through people who do not share our faith. Let us receive with gratitude whatever comes, and, like David, remember that every achievement comes from God and should serve others, not only ourselves.
exp.4:11:
David realized something important: God himself had established him as king over Israel. The idea of being established means that God had firmly set him in his place. God had also raised up his kingdom, and David understood that this was not only for his own sake, but for the sake of his people Israel.

Here the narrator of the book is telling us what David came to understand. David had just conquered Jerusalem and was growing in power. Hiram, king of Tyre, sent him materials and workers to build his house. The text stresses that all this success came from God, not only from David's own effort.

For today: if God gives you a place of influence, at work, in your family, or in your church, remember that it is not meant only for your own benefit. Ask him to help you use it to serve and bless others.
exp.4:12:
The explanation says that David, now settled in Jerusalem after leaving Hebron, took more wives and concubines, and that he had more sons and daughters. Concubines were women of a lower rank than a wife, but they were part of the king's household.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not David. Just before this, the text says that God had confirmed him as king and that his kingdom was growing. Then his sons born in Jerusalem are listed, including Solomon. The text only reports the facts; it neither approves nor condemns them. However, the Law asked that the king not multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), and this set the stage for family problems later on.

For today: when God blesses us with success or power, we should take care with our decisions and obey his Word. Blessings do not protect us from mistakes.
exp.4:15:
This verse finishes a list of sons born to David in Jerusalem. Four more names appear here: Japhia, Elisama, Eliada, and Eliphelet. They are all men's names, and the list continues the one begun in the previous verse, with Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon.

The account is by the author of the book, who is not identified. It tells how David, now king over all Israel, settled in Jerusalem. The list shows that his reign was becoming established and that his family was growing. It has also been noted that, in that period, having many wives was common among kings, though the Bible does not present this as an ideal. Immediately after, the attacks of the Philistines follow.

For today: God pays attention to people, even to those who are hardly mentioned. Remember that your life and your name matter to Him, and serve faithfully even when no one applauds you.
exp.4:16:
The explanation says that when the Philistines learned that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they went out, all of them, to look for him. David heard about it and went down to the stronghold, which here is a protected place, probably a refuge in the mountainous area. It is not certain exactly what it was, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

The narrator describes what follows David's coronation in Hebron over all the tribes. While David reigned only over Judah, the Philistines did not see him as a great threat. Now that Israel was united under a single king, they saw him as a danger and reacted at once.

When God gives us a responsibility or an advance, opposition sometimes comes with it too. David did not act on impulse: he took refuge and, according to the passage that follows, sought God's counsel before fighting. Before you decide, ask God in prayer.
exp.4:17:
The explanation says that the Philistines came in large groups and spread out across the valley of Rephaim, an area near Jerusalem. The word spread out in the verse means that they scattered over the land and took possession of it.

The account is told by the narrator of the book. David had just been anointed king over all Israel, and the Philistines, who had previously tolerated him, now saw him as a threat and came up to attack him. David withdrew to the stronghold. Scholars debate exactly which stronghold that was. What matters next is that David did not act on impulse but sought the Lord's counsel.

For today: when a great problem comes, before reacting, ask God in prayer and seek his guidance in the Bible. He can give you clear direction.
exp.4:22:
It says that David asked God what to do in the face of the new Philistine attack. God answered him that he should not go up straight at them, but should go around and confront them from the side of the trees, which were mulberry trees or poplars (scholars are not sure which).

The Philistines had already been defeated once, but they came back to the valley of Rephaim. David did not assume he would repeat the same tactic. The one speaking is God, who answers David, now king of Israel, when David seeks his direction before fighting.

For today: even though God has helped us before in a similar situation, it is wise to ask him again. He does not always guide us the same way. Praying and waiting for his direction at each new stage keeps us from relying only on habit or on our own experience.
exp.4:23:
It says that David was to wait for a sign: a loud sound, like footsteps or wind, in the tops of the mulberry trees (a kind of tree). When he heard it, he was to move, because the Lord would go out ahead of him to defeat the Philistine army. A loud sound means a very powerful noise. Here, to strike means to attack or to win in battle.

The one speaking is God, who answers David after David asked him for guidance. The Philistines had attacked again in the valley of Rephaim. This time God did not give him the same instruction as before: he told him to go around the enemy and wait for the sign. Some think the sound was a divine intervention; the text does not explain exactly what it was.

For today: before acting, ask God and wait for his direction, even if you have already lived through a similar situation. What worked yesterday may not be today's plan. Trusting means obeying at the moment he indicates.
exp.5:1:
David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale of Judah, to bring up from there the ark of God. The ark was a sacred chest over which the name of the Lord of hosts was called, the One who dwells between the cherubim, that is, figures of angels that were on the lid of the ark.

The narrator tells what David did as king. He had just gathered thirty thousand chosen men. He wanted to bring the ark, the symbol of God's presence, to the center of his kingdom. Baale of Judah is usually identified with Kiriath-jearim, although the text does not explain this here.

For today: David sought to make God the center of his nation's life. We can ask ourselves whether, in our homes and our decisions, we give God first place. But we must also seek Him with reverence and obedience, as He directs, not only with good intentions.
exp.5:3:
This verse tells us that the ark of God was brought out of the house of Abinadab, in Gibeah (a high place, a hill). While they were carrying it, Ahio, the son of Abinadab, walked in front of the ark, and his brother Uzzah went with him, guiding the cart.

The text does not say who is speaking; it is the narrator of the book, who tells how David wanted to bring the ark to Jerusalem. The ark represented God's presence among his people, and David wanted it at the center of Israel's life. However, the law said that the ark was to be carried on the shoulders of the Levites, not on a cart. The account thus prepares the way for what happens next.

For today: wanting to honor God is good, but it is also wise to ask how he wants to be honored. Seek his Word, not only your good intention.
exp.5:5:
It says that when they came to the threshing floor of Nachon (a flat place where grain was threshed), the oxen pulling the cart stumbled or shook it. Uzzah, one of those driving the cart, reached out his hand and took hold of the ark of God so that it would not fall.

It is part of the account in the book of Samuel. David was bringing the ark to Jerusalem with music and joy. But the law said the ark was to be carried by the Levites with poles, and that it was not to be touched (Numbers 4:15). Here it was riding on a new cart, as the Philistines had done. The text that follows speaks of rashness. Some see in this a lack of care in the way God was being honored.

For today: God deserves to be honored with sincerity and also according to his Word. Good intentions do not replace obedience. Let us ask him for humility to learn how he wants to be worshipped.
exp.5:6:
God became angry with Uzzah and struck him down right there for his reckless and disrespectful act. Uzzah died beside the ark. The word for the anger that burned against him denotes a fierce, intense anger, and the act itself was carried out without the proper reverence due to God.

The narrator tells us that David was bringing the ark to Jerusalem amid music and celebration. The oxen pulling the cart stumbled, and Uzzah reached out and touched the ark. The Law said that the ark was to be carried with poles, and that no one should touch it (Numbers 4:15). Here it had been transported on a cart. Many think Uzzah wanted to help, but the text does not explain every detail.

Good intentions do not replace obedience. Let us draw near to God with love, but also with reverence, seeking to do things as He directs.
exp.5:10:
The ark of God stayed for three months in the house of Obed-edom, a man described as the Gittite, which is usually understood to mean he came from Gath. During that time, the Lord blessed Obed-edom and all his family. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "blessed" means that he gave him his favor.

The account is told by the author of the book. David had been frightened because Uzzah died when he touched the ark, so he did not dare to bring it to Jerusalem and left it in that house. The text does not explain what the blessing consisted of, but the report to David shows that it was evident.

For today: the presence of God is not something we should fear, but something to receive with respect and reverence. When we give him an honest place in our home and in our lives, we can expect his care, even if it does not always come in the way we imagine.
exp.5:12:
It says that when the men carrying the ark of God had gone six steps, David offered an ox and a well-fed ram as a sacrifice. The verse does not make clear whether the sacrifice was made every six steps or only at the beginning; it has been understood both ways.

The narrator tells of David's second attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem. Earlier, a man named Uzzah died when he touched it, and the ark stayed for three months at the house of Obed-edom, where God blessed the household. Now David moves it with more care and with joy, beginning with offerings.

For today: before we move forward in something important, we put God first with humility and gratitude. We can pray and acknowledge his place before taking each step, not only once we are already on our way.
exp.5:13:
The verse says that David danced or leaped with all his strength before God, holding nothing back. He was wearing a "linen ephod," a simple garment like an apron or short tunic that the priests used. He was not dressed as a king, but as an ordinary worshiper.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Samuel. David is bringing the ark of God, the symbol of the divine presence, to Jerusalem, the city of David. Earlier, the ark had been in the house of Obed-edom, and there God blessed him. Now all Israel celebrates with sacrifices, trumpets, and shouts of joy. Later, Michal, his wife, despises him for this.

Today we can worship God with sincerity and devotion, without worrying too much about what others think. Our gratitude to God deserves to be expressed from the heart, even if someone does not understand it.
exp.5:14:
This verse tells how David and all the people of Israel brought up the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem, with shouts of joy and the blast of the trumpet. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence with his people. The shouting, meaning very great joy expressed aloud, is what the verse describes.

It is the narrator of the book who describes the scene. Before this, the ark had been far from the center of Israel's life for many years, and an earlier attempt to bring it up ended badly, with the death of Uzzah. Now David moves it with sacrifices and reverence. Soon after, Michal despises him for the way he celebrates, which shows that not everyone understood that joy.

For today: worshiping God can include sincere and visible joy. We do not need to measure our worship by what others think, but offer it with a grateful and reverent heart.
exp.5:16:
It says that the Israelites brought the ark of the Lord and set it in the prepared place, inside a tent that David had put up for it. Then David offered sacrifices: the "burnt offerings" were offerings that were burned whole for God, and the "peace offerings" were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving, from which the meal was also shared.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The ark represented God's presence with his people. Earlier, an attempt to bring it had ended in tragedy (2 Samuel 6:1-11). Now David brings it with joy and worship. The texts do not say that this tent was the tabernacle of Moses, so it is better not to claim that.

For today: before making plans or celebrating, we put God at the center. David gave him a place and thanked him with offerings. We can begin the day, the week, or a project by giving thanks and seeking his presence with reverence and joy.
exp.5:17:
It says that David, after finishing offering the sacrifices, blessed the people. The "burnt offerings" were offerings that were completely burned in honor of God. The "peace offerings" were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving, of which a portion was shared in a meal.

The "Lord of hosts" is a name for God that emphasizes his power and his authority over all things.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had just brought the ark of God to Jerusalem with great joy. As king, he also played the role of spiritual guide: he worshiped God and then blessed the people in God's name, not in his own. Right after this, it is told that he gave food to everyone.

For today: when God blesses us, it is not meant to be kept only for ourselves. We can thank him from the heart and then share what we have received with others, through kind words, help, and generosity.
exp.5:20:
David answered Michal that everything he did was "before the Lord," meaning to honor God and not to impress people. He reminds her that God chose him, and not Saul or his family, to be prince, or leader, over Israel. That is why he says he will keep dancing with joy before the Lord.

David speaks after bringing the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem amid festivities and praise. Michal, Saul's daughter, criticized him with contempt because he showed himself without his royal dignity, dressed simply. Interpreters debate how much was exposed, but the point is his humility. David defends his worship and his calling.

Today, do not let criticism or what people will say keep you from worshiping God with sincerity. If your heart is directed toward Him, His approval is worth more than that of others.
exp.6:10:
This verse says that God gave his people rest from the time he set judges over Israel, and that now he will also give David rest from all his enemies. Then God announces to him that he himself will make a house for him, that is, a family and a dynasty, not a building.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple for the Lord, but God answers that it will be he who establishes David's house. He reminds David that he has always been with him and promises stability for Israel. This promise is known as the Davidic covenant, and Christians see it fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: before doing great things for God, remember what he has already done for you. Rest in his faithfulness and serve with gratitude, not with anxiety.
exp.6:18:
David tells God that what he had already given him seemed like a lot, but now God goes further and makes him a promise for the future of his family. "House" here means descendants or dynasty. "Servant" is how David refers to himself, with humility. The last question is hard to translate. It may mean that God does not treat David the way a man would, or that this promise reaches to all of humanity. Scholars understand it in several ways.

David speaks in prayer, after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: his kingdom and his family would endure. David sits before the Lord, amazed that God has chosen him.

For today: when God blesses you, respond as David did, with humility and gratitude, recognizing that everything comes from his grace and not from your merits.
exp.6:25:
This verse is part of a prayer. David asks that God's name be honored forever, and that people will recognize that the Lord of hosts, that is, the God of all power, is truly God over Israel. He also asks that his family remain firm before God.

David speaks after God, through the prophet Nathan, promised him a lasting line and kingdom. David does not begin by asking for honor for himself, but responds with humility and asks God to fulfill what he has already said. Many Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when you ask something of God, try to make your greatest desire that his name be honored. Trust his promises and pray based on what he has already said in his Word.
exp.7:3:
David captured a thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers from the enemy army. He "hamstrung" the horses of the chariots, that is, he cut the tendons of their legs so they could neither run nor serve in war. He left only a hundred chariots.

The narrator of the book recounts David's victories over Hadadezer, king of Zobah. God had commanded that the king of Israel not multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). For this reason many think David kept only a few chariots out of obedience, though the text does not explain this. The figures in this passage differ slightly from 1 Chronicles 18:4.

For today: do not put your trust in what you have, whether money, strength, or resources. Use what God gives you with wisdom, and trust that He cares for you, as He cared for David.
exp.7:4:
The Syrians of Damascus (also called Arameans) came to help Hadadezer, king of Zobah, a kingdom north of Israel. David struck them, that is, defeated them in battle, and twenty-two thousand men died. The figure points to a very great victory.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, whose author is not known for certain. He tells how David was expanding his kingdom and how God sustained him. The Syrians entered the war to defend their ally, but they were defeated. Afterward they were made subject to David and paid him tribute. The next passage summarizes it this way: "The LORD preserved David wherever he went."

For today: when you face pressures that seem greater than you are, remember that God cares for those He calls. Trust in Him and do your part with courage, without using this passage to justify violence.
exp.7:5:
It says that David placed garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers stationed in place, in the region of Syria whose capital was Damascus. The Syrians were made subject to David as servants and had to pay him tribute, which was a kind of tax imposed on a conquered people. Then the text sums up: "And the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went," that is, the Lord protected him and sustained him wherever he went.

The passage is a historical account, not a speech. The narrator tells how David extended his kingdom after defeating Hadadezer and the Syrians of Damascus who came to help him. By saying that the Lord preserved him, the author implies that his victories were not only military strength, but that God was sustaining him.

For today: we can thank God for his care in every place and stage of life, whether it is a new job, a move, or a difficult challenge. His protection does not depend on where we are, and that encourages us to trust in him.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that David set apart for God the vessels of silver, gold, and bronze that Toi had sent him. He also set apart the silver and gold he had taken from the nations he had conquered. To "dedicate" means to set something apart for sacred use. The LORD, the name of God, is the one to whom these things were given. "Subdued" means brought under control or defeated.

The account comes from the narrator of Samuel. It tells how Toi, king of Hamath, was glad that David had defeated Hadadezer, his enemy, and sent gifts to him through his son. David did not keep this wealth for himself but dedicated it to God. The text does not explain the exact use of these things, though many think they were kept for worship and for the future temple.

For today: what we achieve or receive is not only for ourselves. We can recognize God as the source of everything and ask him how to use our possessions, successes, and talents to honor him and help others.
exp.7:13:
It says that David placed garrisons, that is, groups of soldiers keeping watch, throughout the territory of Edom. The Edomites (called the Edomites in this version) were brought under subjection and served him. At the end, the text sums up that the Lord kept, that is, protected and sustained, David wherever he went.

This is the account of the book's narrator, who summarizes David's military victories over several neighboring peoples. It comes right after mentioning the defeat of the Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The author wants to show that the kingdom was established, and he credits the success not only to David's strength but to God's protection. Edom was a neighbor of Israel, and its subjection is understood as part of that advance.

For today: our efforts and plans matter, but true security comes from God. We can work responsibly and, at the same time, thank him for caring for us in every place we go, at home, at work, or on the road.
exp.7:15:
This verse names two officials of King David. Joab, son of Zeruiah, was the commander of the army, that is, the head of the soldiers. Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder, who kept the records and handled the affairs of the kingdom. Some understand him as the king's chronicler or spokesman; the Hebrew allows for several translations.

The narrator of the book lists the main people responsible for David's government. It comes after the king's victories and after the statement that he reigned with right and justice. It shows that the kingdom did not depend on a single man, but on an orderly structure.

For today: doing things well almost always requires teamwork. Recognize and value those who serve alongside you in your family, church, or work, and faithfully carry out the task God has given you.
exp.7:16:
This verse names three men in David's government. Zadok and Ahimelech were priests, that is, those in charge of worship and of offering the sacrifices. Seraiah was the scribe, the one who kept the records and wrote the documents of the kingdom. Some scholars note that the name "Ahimelech son of Abiathar" could appear in another form in other passages, where Abiathar is called the son of Ahimelech, and there is no single certain explanation for this.

The text is the narrator's account of how David organized his kingdom, now firmly established. After his victories, the list shows an orderly government, with those responsible for war, justice, worship, and administration.

For today: God values order and the service of each person in their place. Whether you care for others, teach, keep records, or serve quietly, your task matters. Faithfully carry out what has been entrusted to you.
exp.8:0:
Here David asks a question: is there anyone left from the family of King Saul to whom he can show kindness? "Kindness" here means faithful, loyal treatment, not just forgiveness. And he would do it for Jonathan's sake, that is, in honor of his friend.

David is speaking as the king of Israel now. Saul, his predecessor, had died, and Jonathan, Saul's son, had made a covenant of friendship with David. Normally, a new king might see the family of the previous king as a threat, but David looks for someone to bless. The following text shows that he does so because of the promise he made to Jonathan.

For today: keep your promises and show kindness without expecting anything in return. Ask yourself: whom can I bless today, even if they cannot repay me?
exp.8:6:
David tells Mefibosheth not to be afraid. He promises him kindness (the word here means gentle and generous treatment) for the sake of Jonathan, his father. He will also give back to him the lands of Saul, his grandfather (in that time "father" could refer to an ancestor), and invites him to eat at the king's table always.

David speaks as king now. Earlier he had made a covenant of friendship with Jonathan, and he wants to keep that promise to Jonathan's family. Mefibosheth was Jonathan's son, lived hidden in Lodebar, and had a disability in his feet. As Saul's grandson, he could fear that the new king would harm him. David, on the other hand, shows him a favor he did not deserve.

For today: just as David honored a promise and reached out to someone who had nothing to offer in return, we can keep our word and show kindness to those who cannot repay us. Many Christians see in this a reflection of God's grace.
exp.8:8:
Here King David sends for Ziba, who had been Saul's servant. He tells him that everything that belonged to Saul and his family has now been given to your master's grandson, that is, to Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson.

David speaks as king, and he does so because of the promise of kindness he had made to Jonathan, the friend who had shown him loyalty. Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, was in a fragile situation. David returns the lands to him and invites him to always eat at his table. Ziba and his family are to work those lands to support him.

For today: keeping a promise and helping someone who is at a disadvantage is a concrete way of showing God's love. Think of someone to whom you owe support or remembrance, and do something simple for that person today.
exp.8:10:
Ziba tells King David that he will do everything the king has commanded. Then it is made clear that Mephibosheth will eat at the king's table, treated as if he were one of the king's own sons.

David speaks with Ziba, a former servant of Saul. David had promised his friend Jonathan that he would look after Jonathan's family. For that reason he gave back Saul's lands to Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, who was lame in both feet. David not only provides for him materially, but gives him a place at his own table, which was a great honor and a sign of acceptance.

God treats us with that same grace: he gives us a place at his table even though we do not deserve it. Today we can imitate David by keeping our promises and welcoming with dignity those who feel weak, forgotten, or without a place.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that Mephibosheth had a young son named Micha. It also says that all of Ziba's household, that is, his sons and his servants, were placed at the service of Mephibosheth. Servants are those who work for another person, and to dwell means to live in a place.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David, because of his covenant of friendship with Jonathan, sought someone from the house of Saul to show kindness to. He found Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, and returned to him the lands of his family. Ziba and his household were to work those lands. Micha is mentioned because Jonathan's family would continue. Later Micha will have descendants (1 Chronicles 8:35).

For today: keep the promises you have made, even when time has passed. Think of someone to whom you can show kindness without expecting anything in return, as God does with us.
exp.9:2:
This verse shows the officials of Ammon speaking to their new king, Hanun. They tell him not to think that David is honoring his father by sending "comforters," meaning people who come alongside those who are grieving. In their view, David has really sent these men to search out the city, that is, to spy on it and then destroy it.

It is the Ammonite princes who speak, as counselors to the king. Hanun had just lost his father and was new to the throne. David wanted to return a kindness that Hanun's father had shown him earlier. The Bible does not say whether the princes were sincere or had other interests, but their suspicion led Hanun to humiliate the messengers.

For today: before assuming bad intentions in someone who shows kindness, it is wise to ask questions and listen calmly. Suspicion without evidence can damage relationships and bring painful consequences.
exp.9:9:
This verse tells us that Joab, commander of Israel's army, placed the rest of his soldiers under the command of his brother Abishai. He charged him with arranging them in battle formation to face the Ammonites.

Joab is the one acting here, and the text narrates it. The Ammonites had hired Syrian troops, and Joab found himself surrounded: enemies in front of him and behind him. So he divided his forces. He took the best soldiers to face the Syrians, while Abishai was left in charge of the rest against Ammon. Afterward they agreed to help each other.

For today: when we face pressure from several sides, we do not have to carry everything alone. Joab organized, shared out responsibilities, and trusted his brother. We can do the same with family, church, or work: ask for help, offer support, and do our part with effort, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.9:10:
Joab speaks to his brother Abishai. He tells him that if the Syrians prove stronger than he is, Abishai will come to help him; and if the Ammonites prove stronger than Abishai, Joab will come to help him.

Joab is the commander of Israel's army. The Ammonites and the Syrians had surrounded them, with enemies in front and behind. Joab divided the troops: he faced the Syrians with the best soldiers, and Abishai faced the Ammonites. This agreement to help one another gave them security in the midst of great danger.

For today: no one should face difficult struggles alone. In the family, the church, or at work, we can agree to support one another, and also ask for help without shame when we feel weak. Joab, moreover, entrusted the outcome to God.
exp.9:12:
This verse tells us that Joab, the commander of Israel's army, advanced with his soldiers to fight against the Syrians, and they ran away. The Syrians are the Arameans.

The context is a war against the Ammonites, who had hired the Syrians as allies. Joab found himself surrounded and divided his troops: he would face the Syrians, and his brother Abishai would face the Ammonites. Before the battle he encouraged everyone with words of courage and confidence that God would decide the outcome. After that, the Syrians fled.

For today: do your part with diligence, work as a team, and leave the outcome in God's hands. We must be brave, remembering that He has the final word.
exp.9:17:
The Syrians (Arameans) fled before Israel. David defeated the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen (soldiers on horseback). He also struck Shobach, the captain of their army, and he died there.

The narrator tells of the war that began when the Ammonites humiliated David's messengers. They hired the Syrians, and David went out to face them. In 1 Chronicles 19:18 the numbers are different, and this is explained in several ways: copying errors, or different ways of counting. What is clear is the total defeat of the Syrians.

For today: when a conflict grows out of pride or out of backing a mistaken cause, it ends up costing a high price. Let us seek peace in time, and not ally ourselves with someone who persists in doing wrong.
exp.9:18:
The allied kings who served Hadadezer saw that they had lost to Israel. So they made peace with David and came under his rule. After this, the Syrians no longer wanted to help the Ammonites.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Ammonites had insulted David's messengers, and they looked for Aramean allies to fight. David went out with his army and defeated them. The text shows how that alliance ended: it was broken by the defeat. Some scholars see here the fulfillment of God's promises to protect Israel, although the passage does not say it in those words.

For today: alliances built on pride or on doing harm fall apart when difficulty comes. It is wise to seek peace and to lean on what is just and firm, trusting God more than human strength.
exp.10:2:
This verse tells how David sent to ask who the woman he had seen was. He was given her name, her father's name, and her husband's name: Bath-sheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite. The people who answered him made it clear that she was a married woman.
