The narrator describes David in Jerusalem while his army was at war. He is the king and gives the orders; his servants only report. The answer works as a warning, because David already knew she had a husband. Even so, he went ahead. The text does not justify this, and later God confronts him for it.

For today: when a temptation appears before us, the first step matters. If we already know something is wrong, we should not keep investigating or drawing closer; better to stop, flee, and ask God or someone we trust for help.
exp.10:9:
Some people told David that Uriah had not gone home. Then David asked him why he had not gone down to rest, since he had just come back from a long journey.

David wants to hide his sin with Bathsheba, who is pregnant. Her husband Uriah was at war, and David called him back so he would sleep with his wife and it would seem the child was his. But Uriah did not go home; he stayed with the king's servants. David, surprised, asks him to account for himself, without admitting his real reason.

Today, this scene reminds us that covering one mistake with more deceit only makes it worse. While David pretended to show interest, Uriah showed loyalty and self-sacrifice. If we have failed, the best thing is to come to God with sincerity and repent, as David later did in Psalm 51.
exp.10:11:
David asked Uriah to stay in Jerusalem one more day, and said that the next day he would send him back to the war. Uriah obeyed and stayed that day and the next.

David speaks with Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers. David had taken Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and she was pregnant. To cover up his sin, he wanted Uriah to sleep with his wife so that it would appear the child was his. But Uriah, out of loyalty to his companions in battle, refused to enjoy his own house. So David extends his stay, hoping he would change his mind.

For today: when we hide a sin, we tend to invent more plans and even deceptions. It is better to confess in time and ask God for forgiveness, who forgives the sincere heart.
exp.10:12:
This verse tells how David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him, and made him drink until he was drunk. Even so, Uriah went out in the evening and slept on his bed among the king's servants, without going home.

David had sent for Uriah from the front of the war so that he would go home and sleep with his wife Bathsheba, in order to hide the fact that she was pregnant by David. Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refused. Then David tried another way out through the wine, but that did not work either. The text does not say that David planned every detail of this, but his intention is clear: to cover up his sin.

For today: when we fail, the answer is not to hide the mistake with more deception, because that only makes it bigger. It is to confess in time and seek God's forgiveness.
exp.10:15:
Joab, the commander of David's army, was besieging the enemy city. There he placed Uriah in the spot where he knew the strongest men of the enemy were fighting. The word "besieged" in the verse means that he surrounded the city in order to attack it.

The narrator describes how David's plan is carried out. David had committed adultery with Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and he wanted to cover it up. When that failed, he sent an order by letter that Uriah should be killed in battle. Joab obeyed, even though it was an unjust command. Later, God sends the prophet Nathan to rebuke David.

A hidden sin often leads to another, worse one. If we have failed, the best thing is to confess it quickly to God and repair the harm, without concealing it. Moreover, obeying an authority does not free us from responsibility when we are asked to do wrong.
exp.10:16:
The explanation says that the men of the besieged city (Rabbah) came out to fight against Joab. In the battle several of David's soldiers died, and among them was Uriah the Hittite.

The narrator reports the result of the plan David had ordered in secret. David had committed adultery with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and wanted to hide his sin. Joab, the commander of the army, placed Uriah where the fighting was most dangerous. Other men died as well, so the maneuver cost more lives than Uriah's alone.

For today: a hidden sin often leads to worse ones and harms more people. Instead of covering up our failures, it is better to confess them to God promptly and seek repentance, as David did afterward (Psalm 51).
exp.10:17:
This verse says that Joab sent a messenger to David to tell him everything that had happened in the battle. The phrase about the affairs of the war means the matters or news of the fighting.

Joab was the commander of David's army. He was besieging the city of Rabbah. David had ordered him, in writing, to place Uriah in the most dangerous position so that he would die and thus cover up his sin with Bathsheba. Now Joab gives his report, but he had already arranged how he would deliver the news of Uriah's death.

For today: a report can be true in its facts yet be used in the service of something wrong. Let us ask God for courage not to take part in cover-ups, and to live with integrity even when someone in authority pressures us.
exp.10:18:
Joab gives an order to the messenger he will send to David. He tells him that, once he has finished telling the king everything that happened in the battle, he must be ready for what comes next.

The one speaking is Joab, the commander of David's army. He was besieging the city of Rabbah. David had ordered him to place Uriah in a dangerous spot so that he would die, and Joab carried it out. Now Joab carefully prepares the report, thinking about how the king will react. The Bible shows a hidden plan here, and it does not approve of it: later the text says that what was done displeased the Lord.

For today: when someone arranges words to hide an injustice, the sin grows. It is better to speak with truth and not help cover up evil, even when it costs us.
exp.10:19:
This verse is part of the instructions Joab gives to a messenger. He tells him that if King David becomes angry and asks why the soldiers went so near the city walls, the messenger should remind him that people inside the city usually shoot things down at attackers from above. The word "shoot" in the verse means throw or fire things, as arrows or stones.

Joab speaks after having attacked the city of Rabbah. Earlier, David had ordered him to put Uriah at the front of the battle so that he would die, and Joab carried out the order. Now he prepares the message to anticipate the king's reaction. In the end, the news of Uriah's death was meant to calm David.

For today: when an unjust decision leads us to hide the truth or to prepare excuses, it is better to stop and change course. God prefers a sincere and repentant heart over explanations, however well put together.
exp.10:24:
Here David tells the messenger to tell Joab, his commander, not to be troubled by the losses in the battle. He says the sword kills one as well as another, so Joab should press the attack against the city until he takes it, and encourage him.

David speaks with the messenger who brought the news from Rabbah. Earlier he had arranged for Uriah to be placed at the front so that he would die, and so hide his sin with Bathsheba. That is why his reply sounds calm, almost cold. The text goes on to say that this displeased the LORD.

For today: when we have done something wrong, it is tempting to use soft words to cover it. God sees what lies behind them. It is better to confess quickly, as David did later, and to seek his forgiveness.
exp.10:25:
This verse tells that Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, learned that her husband had died and mourned for him. Mourned here means she expressed her grief and lived through the period of mourning, which was a custom of the time. The phrase about her husband having died is simply the verse's statement that he was already dead when she heard the news.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Uriah died in the war, but David had ordered that he be left without support in the battle to hide his sin with Bathsheba. The text shows her grief and then makes clear that God saw what David had done and was not pleased.

For today: our hidden decisions can cause real pain to other people. If we have failed, let us not hide the wrong; let us go to God with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and try to correct whatever harm we can.
exp.11:0:
It says that God sent the prophet Nathan to speak with King David. Nathan begins to tell him a story: in a certain city there lived two men, one rich and the other poor.

Before this moment, David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and had ordered the death of her husband Uriah. Nathan speaks on God's behalf. Instead of accusing him directly, he uses a parable, that is, a story that carries a lesson. In this way David could judge the case honestly, without becoming defensive.

For today: it is sometimes easy to see injustice in others and not in ourselves. We can ask God to show us our faults with humility, and to receive with gratitude those who correct us with love and truth.
exp.11:1:
This verse says that the rich man in the story had a great many sheep and cattle. He owned large flocks and herds, so he lacked nothing. The phrase prepares the contrast with the poor man, who had only one little ewe lamb.

Here the prophet Nathan speaks, sent by God to David. David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and had had her husband Uriah killed. Nathan does not accuse him to his face, but tells a parable so that David himself will recognize his sin. The rich man represents David, who had many wives and yet took another man's wife.

For today: when we have much, it is easy to want more at the expense of others. Let us ask God for a grateful and honest heart, one that cares for what others have instead of taking it away.
exp.11:2:
This verse describes the poor man in the story. He had only one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and raised himself. The lamb grew up alongside his children, ate from his own food, drank from his own cup, and lay in his arms. He treated her as a daughter.

Here the prophet Nathan, sent by God to David, speaks. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed. Nathan does not accuse him to his face, but tells this parable so that David will recognize the seriousness of his sin for himself.

For today: God sees what is precious to others, even when it seems small in our eyes. We can ask ourselves whether we are abusing our position or power, and take tender care of what others love.
exp.11:3:
He says that a visitor came to the house of a rich man. The rich man had many sheep and cattle, but he did not want to prepare any of his own to feed the traveler. Instead, he took the poor man's one little ewe lamb and cooked it for his guest. The words that describe cooking and preparing the meal simply mean preparing food. The traveler is the one who came to visit.

The one speaking is the prophet Nathan, sent by God to King David. Nathan tells this story as a parable. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and had arranged for Uriah to be killed. Nathan does not accuse him directly, but uses the story so that David can see his own sin.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I judge the faults of others harshly, but am I soft on my own? Let us ask God for humility to hear correction, and let us take care of what others have, without abusing our power or advantage.
exp.11:9:
God tells David that the sword will never leave his family. The reason is that David "despised" him, that is, he gave no weight to God and showed him no respect, and he took Uriah the Hittite's wife to make her his own. "Sword" speaks of violence and death within his household.

The one speaking is the prophet Nathan, sent by the LORD. David had taken Bathsheba and then ordered her husband Uriah killed in battle to hide his sin. God reminds him of everything he had given him, and that is why his wrong was so serious. The consequences he announces are seen afterward in the history of David's family.

For today: sin leaves its marks, even though God forgives. If we have failed, we can come to God with sincerity, hiding nothing, and accept his correction. And if today we have everything, let us remember to thank him and not treat his word lightly.
exp.11:14:
This verse tells that Nathan the prophet went back to his house after delivering God's message. Then the Lord struck the child, that is, made him fall sick, and the baby became very ill. The verse says the child was born to Uriah's wife, who is Bathsheba.

Nathan had just confronted David about his adultery with Bathsheba and about having Uriah killed. David acknowledged his sin and God forgave him, but the consequences followed. Interpreters explain in different ways why the child died; the Bible does not go into more detail beyond what it says here.

For today: God truly forgives when we repent, but some consequences of our decisions can remain. This invites us to take sin seriously, to come to God quickly with humility, and to trust in his mercy even in pain.
exp.11:15:
In this verse we are told that David, when the son he had with Bathsheba fell ill, sought God with all his heart. "Pleaded" means he begged or asked earnestly and persistently. The verse says he went apart from the people and shut himself away alone. He fasted, took no food, and spent the night lying on the ground, showing grief and humility.

The narrator of the book describes what happened after the prophet Nathan confronted David about his sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. Nathan told him that the child would die. David did not defend himself or grow angry; he cried out to God, hoping that He would have mercy. The Bible does not fully explain why God acted this way, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when we fail or suffer, we can come to God with sincerity and humility, without excuses, trusting that He hears us, even though He does not always answer as we wish.
exp.11:17:
The explanation tells us that the child of David and Bathsheba died on the seventh day. The servants were afraid to give him the news. They thought: if, while the child was alive, David would not listen to us, what would he not do now that the child is dead?

Here the servants speak among themselves. David had sinned with Bathsheba, and the prophet Nathan had announced that the child would die. David fasted and pleaded with God for seven days, hoping that God would show mercy. The servants saw his grief was so deep that they feared making it worse. Shortly afterward, David worshiped God.

For today: when we have to give bad news to someone who is suffering, let us do it with tenderness and without fear of the truth. And when we ourselves suffer, we can cry out to God with sincerity and then, after that, accept his will and keep worshiping him.
exp.11:19:
David got up from the ground, where he had been lying face down, and he washed, put oil on himself, and changed his clothes. Then he went to the house of the Lord, that is, to the place of worship, and he worshipped. After that he went back to his own house, asked for food, they served it to him, and he ate. Putting oil on oneself was a sign of cleanliness and joy, and changing clothes is simply putting on different ones.

This is part of the story of David after his sin with Bathsheba. God had announced that the child of the two of them would die. David fasted and pleaded for seven days so that God would have mercy. When he learned that the child had died, he stopped his extreme mourning. The narrator shows his faith: he accepted God's decision and first worshipped him.

For today: when a loss comes, we can weep and pray sincerely, but we can also draw near to God, accept what we cannot change, and take care of our bodies and our lives again.
exp.11:21:
Here David explains why he was fasting and weeping while his son was sick. He said, "Who knows whether God will be gracious to me?" That is, he had no certainty, but he had hope that God would change the outcome and the child would live.

David speaks with his servants, who did not understand his change after the child's death. This son was born from his sin with Bathsheba, and God had announced it through the prophet Nathan. David pleaded for as long as there was hope. When the child died, he accepted God's will, worshiped, and went on.

For today: we can pray with persistence and sincerity, even though we do not know how God will respond. And when an answer comes that is different from what we asked for, we can worship, trust God, and receive strength to keep living.
exp.11:27:
Here Joab tells David to gather the rest of the army, set up camp in front of the city of Rabbah, and take it himself. The reason is that if Joab takes it, the city would carry his name and not the king's.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. He was besieging Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and had already taken the part of the city that supplied its water, which left Rabbah nearly defenseless. Joab could have claimed the credit, but he preferred that the final victory belong to David, who was the king. Some see here sincere loyalty; others, also a political gesture. The text does not make this clear.

For today: learn not to always seek applause. Do your work well and, when possible, let others receive the recognition. In the end, all true glory belongs to God.
exp.11:28:
It says that David gathered all the people together, meaning the army that was not yet in the battle, and went to attack the city of Rabbah, capital of the Ammonites. He fought against it and took it.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joab, the commander of the army, had already taken the main part of the city, known as the city of waters. But he asked David to come himself, so that the final victory would be credited to the king and not to Joab. This happens after David's sin with Bathsheba, and the war was still going on at that time.

Today we can learn from Joab's attitude: doing our work well without seeking all the recognition. It is also good to give credit to whom it is due, working together as a team with humility.
exp.12:1:
He says that Amnon was so distressed over Tamar, his half-sister, that he even fell sick. She was a virgin, and for that reason it seemed hard to him to do anything to her, that is, to bring about what he desired. What Amnon calls love is in fact an obsessive desire, which he himself sees as something he seeks to obtain.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. He tells how a tragedy begins within David's family. Tamar was David's daughter and Absalom's sister. After this desire will come a deception and a terrible abuse. The text does not justify Amnon; it shows how unchecked desire can lead to evil.

For today: when a desire takes control of you and steals your peace, do not feed it or look for advice that justifies it. Bring it to God and to a wise person, and learn always to respect the dignity of others.
exp.12:3:
Jonadab, Amnon's friend, noticed that the prince looked thinner and weaker every day. He asked him directly what was wrong. Amnon answered that he loved Tamar, his brother Absalom's sister.

The speaker is Jonadab, described as a very crafty man and Amnon's cousin. Amnon was suffering over Tamar, who was in fact his half-sister. What he calls love here is a desire that later leads to a serious abuse. Jonadab does not restrain him; instead he gives him a deceitful plan. The account shows how a wrong desire and bad advice can bring down a family.

For today: when a desire consumes you, tell it to someone wise and faithful, not to someone who will only give you clever advice. Seek out the one who draws you close to God and to what is right.
exp.12:4:
Jonadab tells Amnon to lie down and pretend to be sick. When King David comes to visit him, Amnon is to ask that his sister Tamar come, prepare food right there, and serve it to him from her own hand.

Jonadab, Amnon's cousin, is described in the text as very crafty. Amnon had become obsessed with Tamar, his half-sister. Jonadab does not encourage him to seek what is right, but proposes a deception so that he can be alone with her. What follows in the story is a grave tragedy of abuse and violence.

For today: let us be careful about whom we listen to. A clever friend may give us advice that seems ingenious but leads us into wrongdoing. Let us seek counselors who love truth and justice, and ask God for wisdom to reject deception.
exp.12:5:
This verse tells how Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When King David came to see him, Amnon asked that his sister Tamar come to his house and prepare two cakes, small loaves or flat cakes, so that he could eat them from her hand.

Amnon is speaking with his father, King David. He is following the advice of his cousin Jonadab. His real desire was to be alone with Tamar, his half-sister, whom he wanted in an unjust way. The sickness was a deception, and David, suspecting nothing, agreed. What follows in the account is a painful tragedy.

For today: lies often dress themselves up as necessity or affection. If something has to be hidden through deception, that is a warning sign. Let us strive to live with honesty, and to watch carefully over those who are under our responsibility.
exp.12:7:
She went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took flour, kneaded it, and made small cakes (little fried cakes or rolls) in front of him, and prepared them so they were ready to eat.

The narrator recounts a key moment in a painful story. Amnon, the son of David, pretended to be sick so that he could be alone with Tamar, his half-sister. David, not knowing what Amnon was plotting, sent her to care for him. Tamar acts with obedience and goodwill, not imagining the deception. What follows is a serious abuse against her.

For today: the Bible does not hide evil or wickedness that disguises itself as need. We should look after the vulnerable, pay close attention when something seems wrong, and protect those who serve in good faith, so they are not left exposed to people who could harm them.
exp.12:9:
Amnon asks Tamar to bring the food into the chamber, that is, into his private room, so that he can eat from her hand. Tamar takes the cakes, which were small fried loaves she had prepared, and brings them to her brother.

It is Amnon, the son of King David, who is pretending to be sick. Tamar was his half-sister, and she obeys, thinking she is helping someone who is ill. But Amnon had already sent everyone out of the house, and what follows shows that his plan was to harm her. Thus a request that seems simple hid a cruel deception.

For today: not everyone who asks for a favor has good intentions. Let us learn to be prudent, to listen to our inner unease, and to seek help from trusted people. And if anyone has suffered abuse, the blame is never theirs; it is good to seek support and justice.
exp.12:10:
Here the account tells that Tamar brings Amnon the food she prepared, and he seizes her forcefully and asks her to lie with him. "Took hold of her" means that he restrained her by force. Calling her "my sister" makes the act more serious, because she was his half-sister, a daughter of the same father, David.

Amnon pretended to be sick and sent all the servants out so he could be alone with her. Tamar had come at the command of King David, suspecting nothing, only to care for her brother. She protests, asks him not to dishonor her, and proposes speaking with the king. Amnon acts with deceit and abuse of power.

For today: the Bible does not stay silent about abuse; it calls it by its name. If someone pressures you or isolates you to harm you, it is not your fault. Seek help and trusted people. If you are a leader or a family member, protect the vulnerable.
exp.12:14:
It says that after abusing his half-sister Tamar, Amnon felt a hatred for her stronger than the "love" he had claimed to have. The phrase about him hating her right away means that he hated her immediately.

Amnon, David's son, speaks. He had pretended to be sick so he could be alone with Tamar, and he forced her, even though she begged him not to. What he felt was not true love but selfish desire. Once he had satisfied it, his sin and shame were exposed, and he blamed her with his contempt. Tamar protests that sending her away is an even greater wrong.

For today: true love cares for and respects people; it does not use them and then discard them. If someone has suffered abuse, the fault is not theirs, and seeking help and protection is right. And if we feel desires that harm others, we must stop and ask God and wise people for help.
exp.12:18:
Tamar puts ashes on her head, tears the robe of many colors she was wearing, and, with her hands on her head, goes away crying out. The ashes and the torn clothing were signs of mourning and deep grief.

Here the storyteller speaks. Tamar has just been assaulted by her half-brother Amnon, who then threw her out of his house with contempt. Her robe was the garment proper to the king's unmarried daughters, so in tearing it she shows that something very precious has been taken from her. Her cry is a public complaint about the wrong she has suffered, not an expression of shame on her own part.

Today, this passage teaches us to take seriously the pain of someone who has suffered abuse. Let us listen without hurrying to silence the person, as happened to Tamar, and accompany her in seeking help and justice. God sees the wounded.
exp.12:19:
Absalom asks Tamar whether Amnon was with her, meaning whether he abused her. He tells her to keep quiet, that he is her brother, and not to take this so much to heart.

Absalom, Tamar's brother, is the one speaking. She has just been violated by her half-brother Amnon and sent away with contempt, and she left weeping with the signs of mourning. Absalom seems to want to handle the matter in silence. Later it becomes clear that he did not forget it: he kept hatred against Amnon. The Bible does not explain in detail his reasons for telling her to be quiet.

For today: when someone suffers abuse, they should be listened to, believed, and accompanied, not asked to keep quiet. Silence protects the guilty and leaves the victim more wounded. God is near to those who are broken in heart.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that King David became very angry when he learned what had happened.

The narrator tells us that Amnon, David's son, had abused his half-sister Tamar. David hears of it and is outraged, but the text does not say that he did anything about it. Some ancient manuscripts, such as the Greek version and the Qumran scrolls, add that he did not want to grieve Amnon because he was his firstborn. That phrase does not appear in the traditional Hebrew text, so it is mentioned with caution. Absalom, Tamar's full brother, keeps a silent hatred.

For today: feeling anger at injustice is right, but it is not enough. God calls us to act with wisdom and courage to protect the one who was harmed, to listen to them, and to seek justice, without staying silent.
exp.12:22:
It says that two years passed after what Amnon did to Tamar. Absalom held a sheep-shearing festival at Baal-hazor, near Ephraim, and invited all the king's sons. The shearers are the men who cut the wool from the sheep, a time of year that was usually marked with food and joy.

This is part of the story of David's family. Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David was angry, but the Bible does not say that he did anything about it. Absalom said nothing, but he kept his hatred. The text does not explain his whole plan here, but the invitation seems to be an opportunity carefully prepared. Later we will see that he had a dark purpose.

For today: silent resentment does not disappear with time; it can grow. If something has hurt you, bring it to God and seek healthy help, before bitterness makes the decisions for you (Hebrews 12:15).
exp.12:26:
It says that Absalom pressed his father, King David, so hard that he finally let Amnon and all the king's other sons go with him. Absalom asked for this with a hidden plan.

Absalom was holding the sheep-shearing feast. Two years earlier, Amnon had dishonored Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom had been holding a grudge. David suspected nothing and gave in to the pressure. The verses that follow show that the whole thing was a trap to kill Amnon. The text does not say why David gave in; it only shows him trusting his son.

For today: kind insistence is not always sincere. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern intentions. And if we feel resentment, let us hand it over to God in time, before it leads us to do harm.
exp.12:27:
Absalom ordered his servants to wait for the moment when Amnon is cheerful from the wine. When he gives the signal, they are to kill him. He tells them not to be afraid, because he takes the responsibility upon himself.

Absalom speaks at the feast of his sheep-shearing. Two years earlier, Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David did not punish him. Absalom held a grudge and planned this revenge through deception, inviting the king and then Amnon.

For today: pain and injustice, if we keep them locked inside, can turn into revenge and bring about more death. Let us bring our wound before God, seek justice by honest ways, and not let resentment grow in secret.
exp.12:29:
This verse tells that, while the king's sons were still fleeing along the road, a false report reached David: that Absalom had killed all his sons and that not one of them was left.

The narrator describes what happened after Absalom had Amnon killed at a feast, a deed he ordered as an act of revenge. In the panic, people brought David an exaggerated account. Later, Jonadab makes clear that only Amnon had died. The cause went back years earlier: Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister.

For today: when we receive bad news, it is wise to pause and confirm the facts before reacting. Fear tends to make things seem larger than they are. We can bring our distress to God and ask him for calm so that we may act with wisdom.
exp.12:30:
This verse tells how David, on hearing the report that all his sons had been killed, got up, tore his clothes, and threw himself to the ground. His servants also tore their clothes and stood beside him. The word for these attendants can be understood as servants or aides, and tearing one's clothes was a visible way of showing deep grief.

The narrator describes the king's reaction to a false rumor. Absalom had ordered the killing of his brother Amnon because of what Amnon had done to their sister Tamar. In the middle of that turmoil came the exaggerated news that all the king's sons had died. Shortly afterward, Jonadab makes clear that only Amnon had been killed.

Today we can learn not to be carried away by rumors. Before reacting with fear or despair, it is wise to confirm the facts and bring our anguish to God calmly, seeking sensible counsel.
exp.12:34:
Jonadab says to King David: "Look, the king's sons are coming, just as I told you." That is, the princes arrive alive, and their arrival confirms what Jonadab had announced: that only Amnon had died.

Jonadab was David's nephew and a friend of Amnon. Absalom had ordered Amnon killed for having dishonored his sister Tamar. First came the rumor that all the king's sons had died, and Jonadab calmed David. When the sons appear, it is shown that he was right, but the king's grief does not go away, and Absalom flees.

For today: before reacting to a rumor, wait for the facts. And remember that being right does not remove the pain of the consequences. We can avoid much anguish if we seek the truth with calm and wisdom.
exp.12:36:
But Absalom fled and went to Talmai, son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day.

It is not entirely clear whether David was mourning for Amnon, who was dead, or for Absalom, who was far away. Many think it was for both.

The account tells that Absalom had his brother Amnon killed because of what Amnon had done to Tamar, Absalom's sister. Then he fled to Geshur, the land of his maternal grandfather. The narrator shows David's grief as a father and as a king, in a family wounded by sin and violence.

When a family is broken, the pain is real and it is not always resolved quickly. Bring your sadness to God and seek reconciliation with patience, without letting revenge make the decision.
exp.13:1:
Joab sends to Tekoa and brings back a clever woman, that is, a woman skilled and wise in speaking. He asks her to pretend to be in mourning: to put on mourning clothes, not to perfume herself with oil, and to look like a woman who has been grieving a dead person for a long time. Putting on mourning means dressing and behaving like someone who is in mourning. Anointing with oil was a way of using oil as a cosmetic.

Joab sees that King David misses his son Absalom, who had been sent away into exile for killing his brother Amnon. Joab prepares a made-up story to move the king's heart. The Bible does not clearly state all of his reasons; some think he wanted to help David, and others think he was also looking out for his own advantage.

Today, this passage invites us to seek reconciliation, but with honesty. A good goal does not justify deception. Let us work to restore relationships with truth and love.
exp.13:2:
Joab tells the woman from Tekoa to come before King David and speak to him in a certain way. In other words, he gives her the script: Joab put the words in her mouth, meaning he told her exactly what to say.

The narrator explains that Joab, the commander of David's army, noticed that the king missed his son Absalom, who had been banished for killing his brother Amnon. Joab prepared this woman to tell a made-up story and so lead the king to accept Absalom's return. Interpreters disagree about whether Joab acted for the good of the kingdom, out of compassion, or for his own advantage.

For today: before we speak to influence others, let us examine our intentions. Seeking reconciliation is good, but we must pursue it with sincerity and truth, without manipulating anyone.
exp.13:5:
This verse tells a story that the woman presents to King David. She says she had two sons, who fought in the field, and since there was no one nearby to separate them, one struck the other and killed him.

The woman is from Tekoa. Joab sent her and taught her what to say, so that David would see her situation as a parallel to his own: Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and was living in exile. The story was not real but a prepared account meant to move the king's heart.

For today: God invites us to look at family conflicts with mercy and truth. Before we judge harshly, let us ask whether we seek justice with compassion, and whether we are willing to help reconcile what is broken.
exp.13:6:
This woman tells the king that her whole family has turned against her. They demand that she hand over the son who killed his brother, so that they can kill him too and take the inheritance. She says that would put out the one spark left to her, that is, her last hope. Her husband would have no name or remnant, meaning no family name and no descendants on the earth.

She is a woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab, the commander of David's army. She tells a story, perhaps invented, to move the king's heart. The purpose was for David to reconsider his attitude toward his son Absalom, who had killed his brother Amnon and was in exile.

For today: justice matters, but so does mercy. Before judging someone harshly, let us ask whether we can act with compassion, seeking to restore and not only to punish.
exp.13:13:
It says that we all must die, like water spilled on the ground that can never be gathered up again. But God does not take pleasure in taking people's lives; rather, he looks for ways so that the one who has gone away from him is not kept apart forever.

A wise woman from Tekoa speaks, sent by Joab, according to the account. She tells King David a story about his son to lead him to think about Absalom, who was banished for having killed his brother Amnon. She suggests that David should seek a way to bring him back.

For today: God seeks the return of the one who has gone away. If someone has turned away from you or from God, do not give up; pray and look for a path of reconciliation, with wisdom and patience.
exp.13:17:
In this passage, King David, after listening to the woman, asks her to be completely honest and not to hold anything back from what he is going to ask her. She replies that the king may speak.

Here David speaks with a woman from Tekoa. She had told a sad story about her sons, but Joab, the commander of the army, had sent her and told her what to say. David suspects there is something behind all of that, and that is why he asks for frankness. The following scene confirms that Joab planned the account to lead the king to be reconciled with his son Absalom.

For today: truth told simply helps to resolve problems. When we seek advice or correct something, it is good to speak with honesty and listen with humility, without hiding what is important.
exp.13:18:
David asks the woman from Tekoa whether Joab is behind everything she has told him. She swears by his life, saying that none can turn to the right hand or to the left from anything the king has said, meaning there is no way to avoid his question. She admits that Joab sent her and put all these words in her mouth.

Joab, the commander of the army, wanted David to bring back his son Absalom, who had been banished for killing his brother Amnon. Joab used this woman to tell an invented story and lead the king to see his own situation. David realized the plan.

For today: when someone shows us a truth through a story or advice, let us listen with humility and honesty. And before deciding something important, let us ask ourselves whether we are seeking justice and reconciliation with wisdom.
exp.13:21:
Joab falls to the ground with his face toward the earth, and shows respect to the king. He blesses him, that is, he wishes him well and gives him honor. Then he says that now he knows David regards him with favor, because the king has granted his request. The phrase about finding favor in the king's eyes means being looked upon kindly and receiving a benefit. The phrase about bowing down means that he bent low out of respect.

Joab, the commander of David's army, speaks. He had arranged for the woman from Tekoa to tell the king a story and move him to allow Absalom to return, since Absalom had been sent away for killing his brother Amnon. David agrees, though afterward he keeps Absalom at a distance from his presence. Joab rejoices because he has achieved what he was seeking.

For today: reconciliation requires truth and wisdom, not just good intentions. Before trying to settle a conflict, let us ask God to guide us to act with honesty, patience, and love.
exp.13:22:
So Joab got up and went to Geshur, the place where Absalom had been living since he fled. There he took Absalom and brought him back to Jerusalem.

Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and had been in exile for three years. Joab, the commander of David's army, arranged for a wise woman from Tekoa to prepare a story that would persuade the king to let him come back. David agreed, though with reservations, as seen in the fact that he would not see him. Commentators debate what Joab's true motives were.

For today: returning to the house is not the same as being reconciled. If a relationship is broken, it is not enough to stay at a distance; it takes sincere forgiveness, honest conversation, and truth. Let us ask God for the courage to take that step.
exp.13:24:
This verse says that in all Israel there was no one so admired for his beauty as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, he had no flaw. The phrase about being greatly praised means that he was very highly admired.

The narrator of the book pauses to describe Absalom. Joab had just brought him back to Jerusalem, but King David did not want to see him. This description sets up what follows: a very attractive and popular man who would later rebel against his father. The Bible does not say that his beauty was wrong, but it also does not show that it reflected a good heart.

Today we can remember that appearance draws attention, but it does not reveal character. God looks at the heart. Let us ask him to help us value people, and ourselves, for humility, honesty and love, and not only for what can be seen on the outside.
exp.13:26:
Absalom had three sons and one daughter, named Tamar, who was a beautiful woman. Here no one is speaking. The narrator of the book keeps describing Absalom. Earlier he drew attention to Absalom's good looks and his hair. Now he turns to Absalom's family. Some readers believe Tamar was named after her aunt, Absalom's sister, who had suffered such a wrong in 2 Samuel 13. That is possible, but the text does not say so. Then we are told that Absalom stayed away from the king.

For today: beauty and fame draw attention, but they cannot take the place of a humble heart. Let us ask God to care for our character more than our image.
exp.13:28:
Absalom sent for Joab, asking him to speak to King David on his behalf. But Joab would not come. Absalom sent again a second time, and Joab again refused.

Absalom had returned to Jerusalem, but David did not want to see him. He had been without seeing the king for two years, because he had killed his brother Amnon. Joab, the commander of the army, had helped bring him back. Now Absalom wanted to be received by the king again. The text does not explain why Joab did not come; it could have been caution, or a wish to avoid more conflict with David.

For today: when we seek reconciliation, pressure and impatience can do more harm. Absalom ignored Joab's silence and ended up resorting to violence. Let us rather seek peace with humility, patience, and prayer.
exp.13:31:
Absalom tells Joab that he had sent for him so that Joab could carry a message to the king. Absalom wanted Joab to ask the king: "Why have I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there." Absalom asks to see the king's face, and says that if there is wrongdoing in him, the king may put him to death.

Absalom speaks after murdering his brother Amnon and fleeing to Geshur. He has already returned to Jerusalem, but David does not want to see him. Joab ignored his messages, so Absalom had Joab's fields set on fire to get his attention. That shows his impatience and his impulsive character.

For today: reconciliation needs truth and humility, not pressure or manipulation. Absalom wanted to be forgiven, but he used force. If there is a broken relationship in your life, seek to speak with sincerity, acknowledge your own responsibility, and trust that God will guide you.
exp.13:32:
This verse tells how Joab went to King David and reported what Absalom had said. Then David called for his son, and Absalom came and bowed himself down to the ground before the king. Then the king kissed him. The phrase about bowing himself on his face to the ground means that he prostrated himself as a sign of respect, and the kiss shows that David was receiving him back.

Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled to Geshur. After returning to Jerusalem, David would not see him for two years. Absalom even had Joab's fields set on fire so that Joab would come to see him. After Joab interceded, father and son met. The Bible does not detail what each of them felt, and the account later shows that Absalom would rebel.

For today: reconciliation begins with a concrete step, but a kiss is not enough if the heart is still unhealed. Let us seek forgiveness with sincerity and truth.
exp.14:1:
Verse 2 tells how Absalom would get up early and stand beside the road that led to the city gate. When anyone came with a lawsuit (a legal problem) to be judged by the king, Absalom would call him over and ask what city he was from. The man would answer that he was from one of the tribes of Israel.

The narrator of the book tells us this. Absalom, the son of King David, was building up his image with chariots, horses, and guards. The city gate was the place where cases were heard. The verses that follow show his purpose: to win the affection of the people so that he could take the throne from his father.

For today: let us make sure our kindness is sincere. Let us be wary of anyone who flatters to gain power, and let us also examine our own motives when we serve.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that Absalom kept up his habit with every Israelite who came before the king to ask for justice. Through those friendly gestures and words, he was winning the people over, that is, gaining their loyalty little by little.

The narrator describes how Absalom, son of King David, was preparing a rebellion. He would stand by the road, listen to those who came with their disputes, agree with them, and tell them that the king would not give them a hearing. He showed them closeness, embraced them, and kissed them. In this way he gained their goodwill while weakening their trust in David. The passage suggests that his affection was a strategy for gaining power.

For today: let us be wary of anyone who flatters us only to gain something. And let us examine our own dealings with others, so that our kindness is sincere and not a tool for using people.
exp.14:9:
Absalom sends secret messengers to all the tribes of Israel.

The narrator describes how Absalom organizes a rebellion against his father, King David. He had asked permission to go to Hebron on the pretext of fulfilling a vow to God, but in reality he was preparing a coup d'état. Hebron was an important city in Judah, where David himself had been proclaimed king. Many followed him without knowing what was really happening.

Today we learn that religious appearances can hide crooked motives. Before following anyone, it is wise to examine their intentions. And when we use God's name, let us do so with sincerity, not to achieve our own ends.
exp.14:10:
The explanation says that two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom because he had invited them. They went with simple hearts, meaning with good faith and no bad intentions, and they knew nothing, that is, they did not realize that Absalom was preparing a rebellion against his father David.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Absalom asked the king for permission to go to Hebron, saying he was going to fulfill a vow by means of a sacrifice. In reality he planned to proclaim himself king. He invited respected people to give his plan an appearance of legitimacy, and they were used without realizing it.

For today: good intentions are not enough; it is wise to ask where we are being led before following someone or supporting a cause. Let us ask God for wisdom, inform ourselves well, and think about who is inviting us and for what purpose, so that we do not lend our name to something we do not understand.
exp.14:11:
Absalom sends for Ahithophel from his city, Giloh, one of David's counsellors. He does this while he is offering sacrifices. The conspiracy was strong, because more and more people kept joining Absalom.

The narrator describes how Absalom prepares his rebellion against his father David. He uses the sacrifices to appear devout, and he draws in a highly respected counsellor. Some understand that Ahithophel had personal motives, since the Bible links him with a family from Giloh, but the text does not explain this with certainty. The two hundred guests went along without knowing anything.

Today we can learn not to be impressed by a religious appearance. Before supporting someone, it is wise to ask about their motives and their fruit. And if we have been hurt or deceived, God remains our refuge.
exp.14:12:
This verse tells us that someone came with news for King David. He told him that most of the people of Israel were supporting Absalom, his son. The phrase "the hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom" means that the loyalty and affection of the people had turned toward Absalom.

The one speaking is an unnamed messenger. Absalom had prepared a rebellion with great patience, winning the people over, and now the conspiracy was growing. David, on hearing this, decides to leave Jerusalem to protect the city and his people.

For today: popularity can change very quickly, so let us not place our security in the approval of people. When we face losses or betrayals, let us seek God with humility and act with wisdom, without clinging to pride.
exp.14:14:
The servants of David answer him that they are ready to do whatever the king decides. What remains is a promise of total loyalty, with no conditions attached.

David has just received word that his son Absalom has won the hearts of the people and is coming against him. David decides to flee from Jerusalem to avoid a massacre in the city. The ones speaking are the servants who were with him, and their answer shows that they remain faithful just when the king is weak and the situation seems lost.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are loyal only when everything goes well or also in difficult times. In the same way, our willingness toward Christ, our King, is tested when following him costs something. Let us ask God for a firm and faithful heart in hardship.
exp.14:17:
This verse describes David leaving Jerusalem. All his servants go at his side, along with the Cherethites and the Pelethites, who were guards or soldiers loyal to him. Six hundred men from Gath also go before the king; they had come on foot from that Philistine city.

The narrator recounts the moment when David flees Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. David leaves with his people to avoid a battle in the city. It is a time of humiliation and pain. The following verses show that the leader of these men from Gath is Ittai, a foreigner, to whom David gives freedom to return. This shows his considerate treatment of those who serve him.

For today: loyalty is tested in difficult times. We can ask ourselves whether we stand with others when they go through a crisis, and also whether, like David, we treat with respect and kindness those who follow us.
exp.14:20:
Ittai answers the king with an oath: "As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives". He says that, whether it means death or life, he will be wherever the king is. "Servant" here means someone who puts himself at the king's service.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ittai is from Gath, a foreigner who had arrived not long before with his men. David, out of kindness, offers to let him stay so as not to expose him to danger. But Ittai speaks with total loyalty, even when the future is uncertain and everything seems lost.

Today it teaches us what loyalty is when it does not depend on circumstances. We may ask ourselves whether we follow Christ only when things go well, or also in difficult moments. Whoever remains faithful in trial shows a true love.
exp.14:22:
This verse tells us that all the people of the region were weeping loudly as King David and his followers left Jerusalem. They crossed the brook Kidron, a stream east of the city, and continued along the road that leads to the wilderness. A brook like this is a stream that flows strongly, especially in times of rain.

The narrator describes David's flight. His son Absalom had rebelled against him, and David left the city with his servants and his loyal followers, such as Ittai. Later, David asks that the ark be brought back to Jerusalem and leaves his future in God's hands.

For today: when we go through times of loss or betrayal, we can weep honestly and, at the same time, keep trusting. David did not cling to what he had, but placed his situation in God's hands.
exp.14:24:
Here King David tells the priest Zadok to carry the ark of God back into the city of Jerusalem. David says that if the Lord looks on him with favor, the Lord will one day bring him back and let him see the ark again, along with the place where God dwells.

David is fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. The Levites had brought out the ark to accompany him, but David does not want to use it as a good-luck charm or to tie God to his cause. He prefers to leave his future in God's hands.

For today: when we go through a crisis, let us not try to manipulate God to get what we want. We can ask him sincerely and, at the same time, trust that his will is good, even when we do not yet see the outcome.
exp.14:28:
What it says: Zadok and Abiathar, the two priests, returned to Jerusalem carrying the ark of God, and they stayed there. "Returned" means they carried it back, and "stayed there" means they remained in the city.

Context: The author of the book is the one telling the story. David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. The priests had brought out the ark to accompany him, but David asked them to take it back and to send him news of what happened. He did not want to use the ark as a charm to secure his victory, but to leave his future in God's hands. Besides this, the priests and their sons could help him as informants.

For today: When we go through a crisis, let us not try to manipulate God or secure a result in our own way. We can act with wisdom and at the same time humbly trust that He will decide what is best.
exp.14:29:
David went up weeping along the slope of the Mount of Olives. He walked with his head covered and his feet bare, signs of mourning and humiliation. All the people who were with him did the same: they covered their heads and went up weeping.

The account is told by the narrator of Samuel. David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled and took away the support of many people. David leaves the ark in the city, trusting that God will decide his fate. His weeping shows grief over his son's betrayal. Some believe it also reflects repentance for his own past failures, but the text does not state this directly.

For today: when pain comes, there is no need to pretend to be strong. David wept, humbled himself, and kept going toward the place of worship, trusting God. We can weep before God and support one another through trials.
exp.14:30:
Someone tells David that Ahithophel, his trusted counselor, is among those who have joined Absalom's rebellion. David answers with a short prayer: he asks the Lord (the name of God in the Old Testament) to turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness, that is, to make it senseless and useless.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. He goes weeping, with his head covered and barefoot, signs of mourning and humility. Ahithophel was known for giving very wise advice, so his betrayal was a heavy blow. David does not make a plan for revenge; first he prays. Shortly afterward Hushai appears, who will help counter that advice. The Bible does not say exactly how the prayer and Hushai's arrival are connected, but the account puts them together.

When a betrayal or a problem that overwhelms you comes, first bring your concern to God in a simple and sincere prayer, and then act with confidence that he can guide things.
exp.14:31:
The account says that David came to the top of the mountain, where he used to worship God, and there Hushai met him. Hushai was a man from the region of the Archites. Hushai came with his coat torn and earth on his head, old signs of mourning and deep grief.

The narrator tells us that David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. David goes along weeping, and he even learns that his counselor Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy. Hushai arrives loyal and grieving, and David will see in him an answer to his prayer against the counsel of Ahithophel.

Even in the midst of sorrow and betrayal, David stops to worship. When everything falls apart, we can turn to God in prayer, and He can send us help in unexpected ways.
exp.14:34:
Here David tells Hushai that he will not be alone in Jerusalem. The priests Zadok and Abiathar will be there too. Whatever Hushai hears in the king's house, he must report to them.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled and took the support of the people from him. Hushai, his faithful friend, wants to go with him, but David asks him to return and pretend to serve Absalom. In this way he will be able to undo the counsel of Ahithophel, who had gone over to Absalom's side. The priests and their sons would be the secret channel for sending news to David.

Today we see that God often works through loyal people who serve where they are, even when the place is not comfortable. Ask yourself: where has God placed me to be faithful, and how can I support, with wisdom and honesty, those who need help?
exp.14:35:
He says that the sons of the two priests, Ahimaaz (son of Zadok) and Jonathan (son of Abiathar), are with them in Jerusalem. David explains to Hushai that through these young men they will send him word of everything they hear.

David speaks with Hushai, his faithful friend. Absalom, David's son, had rebelled, and David was fleeing Jerusalem. Hushai was to return to the city, pretend loyalty to Absalom, and help defeat the counsel of Ahithophel. The priests and their sons would be the secret channel for passing along information. The Bible here shows David's plan, and later the account says that God determined to defeat Ahithophel's counsel.

For today: in difficult times, let us not act alone. Let us pray and seek faithful and trustworthy people who will help us with wisdom, truth, and good counsel.
exp.14:36:
This verse says that Hushai, David's friend, came into the city of Jerusalem, and that at nearly the same time Absalom also came into it. The word "friend" here indicates a close counselor who was loyal to the king. The narrator simply reports their arrivals.

David was fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. Before leaving, David asked Hushai to return and pretend to serve Absalom, in order to frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel and send word through the priests Zadok and Abiathar. The narrator thus marks the moment when David's plan is set in motion: Hushai is already inside, just as Absalom takes the city.

For today: when we go through difficult situations, God may have loyal people placed in the right spot. We can pray with confidence and also be, for others, faithful friends who serve with courage and wisdom when they are most needed.
exp.15:1:
King David asks Ziba what he means by all he has brought. Ziba explains that the donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for those who grow faint in the wilderness, that is, in the open, empty countryside.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth, arrives with supplies just when David is in trouble. Then he accuses his master of wanting the throne, and David believes him and gives him everything. The Bible later shows that Ziba may have been lying, although the text lets us see this only with some caution.

For today: helping someone who is suffering is beautiful, but we must make sure our generosity is sincere. And when we hear accusations against others, it is wise to wait and find out before we judge.
exp.15:3:
Here King David tells Ziba that everything that belonged to Mephibosheth will now be his. Ziba bows down and asks that he may continue to find favor in the king's sight.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled. Ziba, a servant of the house of Saul, arrives with provisions and accuses Mephibosheth of wanting the throne. David decides quickly, without hearing Mephibosheth. Later, in chapter 19, Mephibosheth gives a different account, and the Bible does not make everything that happened fully clear. For this reason, this story shows a hasty decision.

For today: before judging or making an important decision, especially in moments of pain or pressure, it is wise to listen to all sides. Asking God for wisdom helps us not to act only on what we are told.
exp.15:4:
It says that King David came to a place called Bahurim, which was near Jerusalem. There a man from the family of Saul, named Shimei, son of Gera, came out to meet him. This man was cursing David, that is, speaking words of hatred and ill fortune toward him.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts how David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled. David was hurt, tired, and humiliated. Shimei took advantage of that moment of weakness to vent his resentment, since he belonged to the family of the previous king, Saul. Because the text gives no further details here, we only see his anger and his attack.

When we are going through a trial, sometimes people come along who criticize us or wound us even more. This passage invites us to keep our calm, not to answer with anger, and to place our situation in God's hands, who sees everything with justice.
exp.15:10:
Here David tells Abishai and his servants that his own son, Absalom, born from him, is seeking his life. So is it any surprise that a Benjamite, Shimei, curses him? David asks them to let him alone, because the Lord has bidden him.

David flees from Jerusalem because Absalom rebelled against him. On the way, Shimei, from the family of Saul, insults him and throws stones at him. Abishai wants to kill him, but David stops him. His words about God can be understood in several ways: he probably recognizes that God allows this humiliation, without saying that God approves of Shimei's wickedness.

For today: when we are criticized or treated badly, there is no need to respond with anger right away. We can pause, examine our hearts, and place our pain in God's hands, trusting that he sees.
exp.15:11:
The explanation says that David hopes God will see his suffering, that is, his pain and humiliation. With the word "perhaps" he does not affirm with certainty, but leaves the door open to God's mercy. He hopes that God will give him something good in return for the curses he is receiving today.

David speaks while fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. Along the way, Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, insults him and throws stones at him. Abishai wants to kill him, but David stops him. We do not know whether God really sent Shimei; David interprets it this way and responds with humility, without seeking revenge.

When someone offends us or life hurts us, we can avoid revenge and place our pain before God. He sees what we suffer, and we can wait on his goodness without demanding how or when he will respond.
exp.15:12:
This verse tells how David and his men continued on their way while Shimei followed them along the side of the hill, keeping some distance from them. He walked alongside, hurling curses at them, throwing stones at them, and kicking up dust. Scattering dust was a gesture of contempt and mockery.

Here the narrator describes David's flight from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, takes the moment to insult him. Abishai wanted to punish him, but David stopped him. He said that perhaps God was permitting that curse and that perhaps God would look upon his affliction and repay him with good. The Bible does not fully explain what David was thinking; it only shows his humility.

For today: when someone attacks us with unjust words, we do not have to respond at once in anger. We can keep silent, examine our hearts, and trust that God sees our affliction.
exp.15:13:
King David and all the people who were with him arrived very tired at their destination, and there they stopped to rest. Some scholars believe the Hebrew word could also be the name of a place, but the general sense is the same.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who tells the story. David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled against him. On the way, Shimei cursed him and threw stones at him, but David endured the insult and hoped that God would see his affliction.

After sorrows and humiliations, the body and the heart need rest. If you are worn out, do not blame yourself for stopping. Resting is a way of trusting that God cares for you and can give you new strength.
exp.15:14:
This verse tells how Absalom and all the men of Israel entered Jerusalem. Ahithophel was with him.

The narrator describes the moment when David flees the city because his son Absalom rebelled and seized power. While David moves forward tired and humiliated, Absalom enters as the new king. Ahithophel, who had been David's counselor, is now on Absalom's side. Shortly afterward it will be shown that Hushai, David's friend, steps into the story to help him in secret.

For today: difficult situations can make it seem that others are winning and that God is silent. Even so, He keeps working. When you feel weary or betrayed, do not act out of bitterness; trust that God cares for you and still directs the story.
exp.15:17:
Hushai answers Absalom with carefully chosen words: "No, I will be of the one whom the Lord, and this people, and all the men of Israel choose, and with him I will abide." The explanation below is translated into plain English.

Hushai is a friend of David, and David sent him to Jerusalem to defeat Absalom's counsel, since Absalom had rebelled. Absalom suspects his loyalty. Hushai does not clearly say whom God has chosen, so his words sound like support for Absalom, though they can be understood in another way. Commentators debate how much cunning and how much real loyalty to David is present here.

For today: our most important loyalty is to what God has chosen, not to what is fashionable. But truth is not defended by deception. Let us ask God for wisdom to be faithful and honest in our words.
exp.16:4:
Absalom asks that Hushai the Archite also be called, so that they may hear what he has to say. The phrase "the Archite" indicates that he was from the region of the Archites.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David and had already received the counsel of Ahithophel, which seemed good to him. Hushai, on the other hand, was a friend of David and pretended to support Absalom. The Bible shows that God allowed Hushai's counsel to prevail (2 Samuel 17:14). Absalom did not know that he was listening to someone with another purpose.

Asking for another opinion can be wise, but we also need discernment. Before deciding, let us seek sincere counsel, pray, and compare everything with the Word of God, not only with what sounds good.
exp.16:7:
Hushai tells Absalom that David and his men are very brave warriors, and that right now they are full of anger and grief, like a bear that has lost her cubs. He also reminds him that David is a man of war with a great deal of experience, and that he will not spend the night together with the common people in the camp.

Hushai, David's friend, speaks here while pretending to take Absalom's side. His real purpose was to defeat Ahithophel's advice, which proposed attacking David at once. Hushai wanted to buy time so that David could organize his forces and cross the Jordan. The text presents this as part of God's protection over David.

Today we can learn that wisdom and good counsel matter a great deal. Before deciding something important, it is wise to think carefully, listen closely, and pray, because a hasty decision can turn out to be very costly.
exp.16:19:
It says that Absalom's men came to the woman's house in Bahurim and asked about Ahimaaz and Jonathan. She answered that they had already crossed the ford of the waters, that is, the shallow place in the stream or river. The soldiers searched and did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem empty-handed.

The two young men were carrying a secret message for David, who was fleeing from Absalom. They were hiding in a well, and the woman protected them with her answer. The text does not judge her or explain her decision; it only shows that her action saved the message and, with it, the lives of David and his people.

God often works through ordinary people who never appear in the headlines. Today we can ask ourselves what opportunity we have to protect someone vulnerable or to help with courage. Still, let us pray for wisdom to act with integrity, for this account does not teach that lying is always right.
exp.16:20:
It says that when Absalom's servants had left, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed out of the well where they had been hiding. They went at once to tell King David. They urged him to get up and cross the river quickly, because Ahithophel had advised an attack on him.

The writer then explains how David was saved. Absalom had rebelled, and David was fleeing. Ahimaaz and Jonathan were David's secret messengers. A woman hid them in a well and tricked the pursuers. Now they carry out their mission of warning the king.

Today we can learn that God often takes care of his people through ordinary people who act with courage and speed. If God puts it on your heart to help or warn someone, do it promptly, and trust that he can use your small obedience.
exp.16:22:
He says that Ahithophel, when he saw that Absalom had not followed his counsel, saddled his donkey (the word he used means putting the saddle on it), and went back home to his house in his city. There he put his household affairs in order, then hanged himself and died. They buried him in the tomb of his father.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Ahithophel had been David's counselor and joined Absalom's rebellion. His advice was to attack David immediately, but Hushai, sent by David, succeeded in persuading Absalom to reject it. Ahithophel probably understood that the rebellion was lost and that he would be remembered as a traitor. The Bible only reports the event, without approving it.

For today: when wounded pride or fear crushes us, let us not make final decisions alone. Let us seek help, talk with someone we trust, and bring our pain before God, who gives hope.
exp.16:23:
This verse tells of two movements at the same time. David arrives at Mahanaim, a city east of the Jordan, and there he finds a place to take refuge. Absalom, his son, also crosses the Jordan, but with the whole army of Israel to pursue him.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, without speaking in the first person. David flees because Absalom rebelled and wanted to take the throne from him. A counselor of David, Hushai, had given Absalom a plan that gave David time to escape. That is why David arrived safely.

For today: when you feel pursued or surrounded by problems, remember that God can give you a refuge and time to catch your breath, even when everything seems against you. Trust, and seek that safe place.
exp.16:24:
Absalom put Amasa in charge of the army in place of Joab. The text explains who Amasa was: the son of Ithra, a man of Israel who went in to Abigail, meaning he took her as his wife. She was the sister of Zeruiah, the mother of Joab. So Amasa and Joab were cousins.

The narrator of the book explains this appointment while Absalom prepares for war against his father David. Joab remained loyal to David, so Absalom needed a new military leader, and he chose a relative. Some manuscripts and other passages give different details about Ithra's background, so not everything is clear.

For today: power and family ties can give us positions, but they do not guarantee wisdom or success. Before deciding something important, let us seek God's guidance and not only our own convenience.
exp.16:26:
This verse tells that when David arrived at Mahanaim, three men came out to meet him: Shobi, from the Ammonite city of Rabbah; Machir, from Lo-debar; and Barzillai, a man of Gilead who lived in Rogelim. The explanation of the original wording is not included here, since the phrase is not part of this verse. The verse goes on in the next one, where it says what they brought him.

The passage has no speaker; it is the narrator telling the story. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled and taken the throne from him. David was tired, with little support, in a faraway land. These three men, from different places, arrived just when he needed them most.

Today, when someone goes through a hard time, we do not need to wait for them to ask for help. We can notice who is worn out and offer something concrete: food, company, or simply our time. God often cares for his people through generous people.
exp.16:28:
This verse ends the list of what was brought to David and his people. Besides beds, wheat and beans, they brought honey, butter (here meaning cream from milk), sheep, and cheese made from cow's milk. All of it was so they could eat. Those who helped thought: "These people are hungry, tired, and thirsty in the wilderness."

The one telling the story is the author of the book. David was fleeing from his son Absalom and had arrived at Mahanaim, on the other side of the Jordan. Three men, Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai, provided supplies for him. The text does not explain all their reasons, but it does show that they saw the need and acted.

Today we can notice who is exhausted or going without, and help them with something concrete. A meal, a visit, or a little money can be the way God cares for someone through us.
exp.17:4:
King David gave an order to his three military commanders: Joab, Abishai, and Ittai. He asked them to deal gently with Absalom, the young man, that is, the young man himself. Gently here means with kindness and gentleness. The whole army heard that order.

David was about to send his troops out to fight against the followers of his son Absalom, who had rebelled and wanted to take the throne from him. The soldiers would not let him go into battle, so he stayed by the city gate. Even so, as a father, he publicly asked that his rebellious son be cared for. The text does not explain all his reasons, but it shows his love, and also his difficulty in separating his role as a father from his role as king.

Today it reminds us that love can remain alive even when someone has hurt us. But it also teaches us to ask for wisdom, so that affection does not keep us from acting with justice and clarity.
exp.17:5:
The verse tells us that David's soldiers went out into the open country to fight against the army of Israel, which was following Absalom. The battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Absalom, David's son, had rebelled against his father to take away his throne. David, although he was the king, does not go to the battle; he stays near the gate and asks his commanders to deal gently with Absalom. His grief as a father shows through in the middle of the war. Where that forest was located exactly is not known for certain.

For today: even when someone has hurt us, we can seek justice without losing compassion. David reminds us that love can remain alive in the midst of conflict, and that we should ask God for wisdom to act with firmness and with mercy.
exp.17:9:
This verse tells of a soldier who saw Absalom hanging from a holm oak, a kind of large evergreen oak, and went at once to inform Joab, the commander of David's army.

The setting is the battle between David's army and the followers of Absalom, his rebellious son. Absalom was riding a mule, which passed under a thick tree, and his head became caught. The soldier speaks with Joab, but he does not attack Absalom, because David had ordered that he be looked after. Later, Joab did act against that order.

For today: God sees what we do and the trouble we cause. This passage invites us to reflect on rebellion, and also to value obedience and respect for a given word, even when others pressure us to act differently.
exp.17:10:
Joab challenges the soldier who had told him: if you saw Absalom hanging from the tree, why didn't you strike him down and kill him right there? Joab says he would have given him ten shekels of silver (an amount of money in weighed coins) and a girdle, which was a soldier's belt, as a reward.

It is Joab, the commander of David's army, who speaks. Absalom had rebelled against his father, the king. But David had ordered that the young man be treated with care. Joab wants to end the rebellion and, according to the text, does not hold back because of the king's order. The soldier refuses to obey him.

For today: having good reasons is not enough to justify a wrong act. Before following someone who pressures us or offers us a reward, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are being faithful to what is just and to what God asks of us.
exp.17:12:
This soldier tells Joab that if he had killed Absalom in secret, he would have put his own life at risk. He thinks King David would find out about everything, because nothing is hidden from the king. He adds that Joab himself would not defend him but would turn against him. Doing something that would cost him his life is what he means by acting against his own life.

A man from David's army is speaking. Joab, the military commander, reproaches him for not having killed Absalom, who was caught in a tree. The soldier defends himself: he heard the king's command not to harm the young man. Joab disregarded that command shortly afterward.

For today: doing what is right does not always feel easy, but it gives firmness. This soldier acted with integrity, even though others pressed him. Before acting, ask yourself whether your decision would hold up in the light, for nothing is hidden from God.
exp.17:13:
Joab replies that he will not waste time arguing with that man. He takes three darts (small spears or short arrows) and drives them into Absalom's heart while Absalom is still alive, hanging in the middle of an oak tree (a large kind of oak).

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and had tried to take the throne from him. His hair had become tangled in the tree during the battle. Joab, the commander of David's army, is speaking here. A soldier had refused to kill Absalom because David had ordered that he be looked after. Joab openly disobeys that order from the king.

Today this reminds us that acting on our own, even with good reasons or justified anger, can break trust and hurt others. It is better to obey, to seek wisdom, and to trust God before making drastic decisions.
exp.17:16:
The explanation says that Joab's men took Absalom's body and threw it into a large pit in the forest. On top of it they piled a huge heap of stones. Then all Israel, that is, those who had followed Absalom, fled, each man to his own home.

This is part of the account of Absalom's rebellion against his father David. Joab had killed Absalom and stopped the pursuit. The narrator tells the ending without any honor: a pit in the forest and a heap of stones. Many understand that the heap of stones was a sign of shame, as happens in other cases in the Bible. The following text speaks of the pillar Absalom had set up for himself so that he would be remembered.

For today: seeking fame or recognition can leave us empty. It is better to live with humility, honoring God and our family, for only what we do in obedience to Him endures.
exp.17:18:
Ahimaaz, the son of the priest Zadok, asks Joab for permission to run and bring the news to King David. He wants to tell him that the Lord has avenged him of his enemies. The phrase about the Lord having avenged him means that God brought him justice, and the word "news" here simply means tidings.
