Ahimaaz speaks as a young messenger who is loyal to David. Absalom's rebellion has just ended with his death. Ahimaaz sees the victory as the work of God and wants to make it known. But Joab knows that David will grieve over the death of his son, and for that reason he holds Ahimaaz back. His zeal was sincere, though perhaps he did not take into account the king's pain.

For today: when we want to share something good, let us do it eagerly, but also with sensitivity. Good news needs the right moment and the right words, thinking about how the one who hears it will feel.
exp.17:19:
Joab tells Ahimaas that he will not be the messenger today. He may carry news another day, but not today, because the king's son has died.

Joab, the commander of David's army, had just killed Absalom, who had rebelled against his father. Ahimaas wanted to run and tell David about the victory. Joab knew that David, although he had won the battle, would suffer greatly over the death of his son. So he sent Cushi instead and tried to protect Ahimaas from receiving the force of the king's reaction. Interpreters explain Joab's reasons in different ways.

For today: not everything true is said in just any way. Before giving painful news, think about the moment, the person, and how to accompany it with care.
exp.17:23:
David sat between the two gates, probably the inner gate and the outer gate of Mahanaim. The watchman, the guard who keeps watch from a high place, climbed up to the flat roof over the gate. He looked far into the distance and saw a man running alone.

This is part of the account of the battle against Absalom, David's rebellious son. Ahimaaz insisted on bringing the news to the king, though Joab did not want him to. David is not narrating anything here. The text describes the scene while he waits anxiously to learn how his army fared and, above all, how his son fared.

For today: waiting for difficult news is distressing. We can learn to bring that waiting to God in prayer, without letting fear control us, and to be attentive to others when they wait anxiously.
exp.17:24:
The watchman, who was standing high on the wall, cried out and told King David that someone was running toward the city. David reasoned that if only one man was coming and not a group, he probably brought good news. The watchman is the one who looks out from the wall; the verse says he cried and told the king.

David was waiting for news about the battle against his son Absalom. He was sitting between the two gates of the city, waiting anxiously. His reasoning made sense: soldiers fleeing a defeat usually came in a group, not as a lone messenger. But the news would be more painful than he expected, for Absalom had died.

For today: when we wait for important news, it is natural to feel anxious and to draw hasty conclusions. It is better to hand the waiting over to God in prayer, for He sustains our hearts whatever the news may be.
exp.17:25:
He says that the watchman saw another man running alone and called out to the gatekeeper. King David replied that this one was also a messenger. The explanation's two source-language words, the watchman who keeps guard from a high place and the gatekeeper at the door, are simply the watchman and the gatekeeper of the verse, so no separate note is needed.

We are in the war between David and his son Absalom. David waits for news of the battle, sitting between the two gates of the city. The watchman speaks, reporting what he sees, and David speaks, interpreting it: if someone runs alone, he brings news, and David thinks it will be good news. Soon two messengers arrive: Ahimaaz and another man. Ahimaaz brings word of the victory, but David also wants to know whether his son is alive.

For today: when we are waiting for hard news, we can give our anxiety to God in prayer, while remaining watchful and patient. Sometimes the answer comes in parts, and we need to trust while the whole of it arrives.
exp.17:26:
What it says: The watchman standing in the tower recognizes the first runner by the way he runs. He says it looks like Ahimaaz, the son of Zadok. King David replies that Ahimaaz is a good man and that he surely brings good news.

Context: David is waiting for news of the battle against his son Absalom, who had rebelled. The watchman speaks from the wall, and David, anxious, interprets what he hears. He expects good news because of Ahimaaz's character. But what truly worries him is his son, and Ahimaaz's answer will be evasive. The Bible does not say why, but the text shows that the news is painful.

For today: It is easy to expect the news we want simply because we trust the one who brings it. Let us learn to wait with humility, asking God for strength to receive the truth, whatever it may be.
exp.17:30:
This verse tells how Cushi came before David with news he thought was good. Cushi says that the Lord has taken up the king's cause and freed him from all who rose against him. Notice that he does not yet mention Absalom.

Cushi is a messenger sent by Joab after the battle against Absalom's army. David was waiting to learn whether his son was alive. Cushi presents the victory as the work of God, but David asks about Absalom, and the answer breaks him. Here the Bible shows David as a king, but also as a wounded father.

For today: a victory can come mixed with pain. We can thank God for what is good and, at the same time, be sensitive to someone who is suffering, without rushing to celebrate.
exp.18:2:
The explanation says that David's soldiers, who had just won the battle, entered the city of Mahanaim quietly and as if hiding, just as an army that fled defeated does, feeling ashamed. The soldiers' secrecy means entering without being noticed.

The narrator tells what happened after the death of Absalom, David's son who had rebelled against him. Joab told the army that the king was mourning his son without comfort. Thus the victory celebration turned into mourning, because the soldiers felt as if they had done something wrong by defending the king.

Our emotions and words, though understandable, affect those around us. If we lead or care for others, let us make room both for pain and for recognizing those who have fought beside us.
exp.18:3:
David, with his face covered, cried out in a loud voice and with great grief for his son Absalom. He repeats "my son" again and again, like someone who cannot find comfort. Covering the face was a sign of deep mourning and sorrow.

It is the narrator who describes David. Absalom had rebelled against his father and was killed in battle by Joab. David's army had won, but the king wept so much that the victory turned into mourning. Afterward Joab rebukes him, because the soldiers who risked their lives felt ashamed.

For today: a father's grief is real and should not be despised, but we must also care for those who stand beside us. When we suffer, let us ask God for comfort and wisdom so that we do not neglect others, nor stop thanking those who have served us faithfully.
exp.18:4:
Joab enters the house of King David and tells him, firmly, that today he has put to shame all his servants. They had just saved the king's life, along with the lives of his sons and daughters, and the lives of his wives and concubines. The word "concubines" refers to secondary wives within the king's household, which was common in that time.

Joab is the commander of David's army. He speaks this way because the army won the battle against Absalom, the rebellious son, but David keeps weeping over him. The soldiers enter the city as if they had lost. Joab fears the kingdom will fall apart, so he confronts the king harshly.

For today: the grief is real and needs its time, but it should not make us forget those who stand beside us and have helped us. Even in mourning we can give thanks and care for those who accompany us.
exp.18:5:
Joab speaks harshly to King David. He tells him that he is loving those who hate him (Absalom, who rebelled) and hating those who love him (his loyal servants).

Joab, the commander of the army, speaks after the victory over Absalom's rebellion. The army returned in shame, as if it had done something wrong, because the king kept weeping over his dead son. Joab fears that the people will lose heart and abandon David. His words are harsh, but the text shows that David listened to them and went out.

For today: grief is real and deserves to be mourned, but we should not forget those beside us who need us. Even in sorrow, let us give them gratitude and attention.
exp.18:6:
Joab tells King David to get up, leave the place where he has shut himself away, and speak kindly to his servants, that is, to his soldiers and attendants. "Comfort" here means speaking to their hearts, encouraging them, and acknowledging them. Joab warns that if David does not come out tonight, all of them will abandon him, and that will hurt him more than any misfortune he has suffered in his life.

Joab, the commander of the army, speaks harshly. Absalom, David's son, had rebelled and died in the battle. David was grieving inconsolably, and the people, who had risked their lives for him, felt ashamed and scorned. Joab does not speak tenderly, but his warning was urgent.

For today: the pain is real, but it must not blind us to those who stand beside us. Even in mourning, we can be thankful for and care for those who sustain us.
exp.18:7:
He says David obeyed the advice he received: he got up and sat at the city gate, which was the public place where important matters were handled. There they told all the people that the king was sitting at the gate, and the people went to see him. On the other hand, "Israel" (those who had followed Absalom) had fled, each one to his own home.

Joab spoke harshly to David, because the king was mourning the death of his son Absalom, and this discouraged the soldiers who had saved his life. Joab warned him that if he did not go out to encourage them, he would lose all support. David responded and showed himself publicly before his people.

For today: grief is real and deserves to be felt, but we also have responsibilities toward those around us. With God's help, and sometimes with honest counsel, we can get up and serve.
exp.18:8:
This verse tells us that throughout all the tribes of Israel the people were arguing with one another. They remembered that David had saved them from their enemies, including the Philistines. But now the king had been forced to flee the land because of Absalom.

The people of Israel had followed Absalom in his rebellion, and Absalom died in battle. Then the people were confused and ashamed, not knowing what to do. That is why they began to remember the good that David had done and to ask why no one was bringing the king back. In this way David's return to Jerusalem is prepared.

Today we can learn to remember with gratitude the good that others have done for us, before we let ourselves be carried away by confusion or the fashion of the moment. And if we are wrong to follow someone, we can always set things right with humility.
exp.18:9:
It says that Absalom, whom the people had anointed as king, died in battle. So those who are speaking ask why they remain quiet and inactive, doing nothing to bring David back. "Anointed" means they had set him apart as king by pouring oil on him.

The speakers are the people of the tribes of Israel, who were divided and confused after the rebellion. They had followed Absalom, but he was no longer there. They remembered that David had rescued them from their enemies. So they urge one another to restore him. Soon David also speaks to the elders of Judah.

For today: when we recognize that we have been following a wrong path, it is not enough to lament or to stay still. God invites us to take concrete steps back, to ask forgiveness, and to restore what we have damaged.
exp.18:10:
Here King David sends the priests Zadok and Abiathar with a message for the elders of Judah, his own tribe. He asks them why they would be the last to bring the king back to his house, since all Israel had already spoken of his return.

David speaks after the death of Absalom, who had rebelled against him. The other tribes were already talking about bringing him back, but Judah, where David came from, had remained silent. David wants his return to be peaceful and wants his own people not to feel left out. Some think he also seeks to win their political support.

For today: when there is a break in a relationship, do not wait to be the last to take the step toward reconciliation. Sometimes those closest to us are the slowest to draw near, and a kind word spoken in time can open the way.
exp.18:14:
This verse tells how David, after Absalom's rebellion, returns toward Jerusalem and reaches the Jordan River. There, at a place called Gilgal, the people of Judah come out to meet him and help him cross the river. The phrase about helping him cross means bringing him over to the other side.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. David had fled because of his son's rebellion, and Absalom had already died. Then David sought to win back the loyalty of Judah, his own tribe, and sent them a message through the priests. Judah answered by calling him to return. Some scholars also see here a political move by David to unite the people again.

For today: when there are wounds or divisions, restoring a relationship calls for concrete steps from both sides. Take the first step yourself with humility, and receive with grace the one who wants to return.
exp.18:16:
This verse says that a thousand men of the tribe of Benjamin were accompanying Shimei. Ziba, the servant of the house of Saul, also came, with his fifteen sons and his twenty servants. All of them crossed the Jordan River before the king arrived.

This is the account of David's return to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. The men of Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, wanted to show loyalty to the king. Shimei and Ziba had earlier acted in questionable ways toward David, so their haste to arrive seems to be seeking the king's favor. Their true intentions are not stated here, and the text does not explain them.

For today: when we have failed or offended someone, it is good to approach them with humility and sincerity, not only with outward gestures. God looks at the heart, and true reconciliation begins with honest repentance.
exp.18:17:
They crossed at the ford to carry over the king's household and to do what was good in his sight. When Shimei son of Gera crossed the Jordan, he fell down before the king, that is, he bowed to the ground as a sign of humility.

This is part of David's return to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. Earlier, Shimei had cursed and humiliated him as he fled (2 Samuel 16). Now, with David victorious, Shimei comes with a thousand men from Benjamin and asks for forgiveness. We do not know whether his repentance was sincere or for convenience; the text does not make this clear.

When we have wronged someone, it is best to acknowledge it soon and with humility. Asking for forgiveness without excuses opens the door to reconciliation, even though we cannot control how the other person will respond.
exp.18:20:
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, asks whether Shimei should not be put to death for what he did. Shimei had cursed the Lord's anointed, that is, King David, whom God had chosen and set apart to rule. Abishai takes it for granted that the offense deserves the death penalty.

Shimei, of the tribe of Benjamin, had insulted and cursed David when the king was fleeing from his son Absalom (2 Samuel 16). Now Absalom is dead, David is returning, and Shimei is the first to come and ask for forgiveness. Abishai, a loyal soldier of a hard temper, wants to punish him. David restrains him and spares his life.

Today we can learn that justice and mercy must go together. When someone offends us and then repents, we do not always have to demand what they deserve. Let us ask God for a heart that knows how to forgive, as He forgives us.
exp.18:23:
It says that Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, went down to meet King David. He had deliberately left himself unkempt: he had not washed his feet, had not trimmed his beard, and had not washed his clothes. This was from the day David left Jerusalem until he returned safe and sound. Having feet that were washed and a beard that was trimmed were normal signs of personal care.

Context: The narrator tells of David's return after Absalom's rebellion. This follows his pardon of Shimei. Mephibosheth was lame and had been treated with kindness by David. His servant Ziba had accused him of disloyalty. Here his appearance seems to be a sign of mourning for David, although he himself will explain this in the next verse. The text does not fully resolve who was telling the truth.

For today: When someone is falsely accused, sincerity and humility speak louder. And whoever judges should listen calmly, without rushing to conclusions.
exp.18:25:
Mefiboset explains to King David why he did not go with him when David fled from Jerusalem. He says that his servant deceived him. According to him, he had ordered that a donkey be saddled for him so he could ride it and go with the king, because he is lame.

David was fleeing from Absalom's rebellion. Now he returns in victory, and Mefiboset, Saul's grandson, comes out to meet him showing signs of mourning. His servant Ziba had said earlier that Mefiboset hoped to keep the kingdom for himself (2 Samuel 16:3). Who is telling the truth is not certain: David divides the lands between the two of them and does not fully settle the matter.

For today: before judging someone by what others say, let us listen to both sides. And if we are slandered, let us trust that God knows the heart, even when no one else sees it.
exp.18:28:
King David cuts short the conversation with Mephibosheth. He asks why he should keep talking about it and announces his decision: Mephibosheth and Ziba will share the land.

David speaks after returning to Jerusalem following Absalom's rebellion. Ziba, a servant of Saul, had accused Mephibosheth of disloyalty, and David had given him all of Mephibosheth's land (2 Samuel 16). Now Mephibosheth says Ziba deceived him. We do not know for certain whether David fully believed him; some see in this decision a hasty arrangement or a political compromise. Mephibosheth replies that Ziba may keep everything, since what matters is that the king has returned in peace.

Today we can learn to value people more than possessions. It is also wise to listen calmly and seek the truth before deciding, so that we do not commit injustice.
exp.18:30:
It says that Barzillai, a man from the region of Gilead, came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan River together with King David. He wanted to accompany him to the river's edge, on the other side. The Gileadite in the verse means that he came from Gilead, and Rogelim was his town.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was returning to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. Barzillai had been loyal, since, as the following verse says, he provided food when David fled to Mahanaim. Now he was going along with him to see him off with respect and to honor him on his return.

For today: loyalty shows itself in difficult moments and also in moments of celebration. We can ask ourselves to whom we owe thanks, support, or companionship, and do so with generosity and without expecting anything in return, as Barzillai did.
exp.18:31:
The explanation says that Barzillai was an old man, eighty years old. He had supplied King David with food and necessities while David stayed in Mahanaim. He was able to do this because he was very wealthy. The word "provided" in the verse means food and the things needed to live.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, and Barzillai had helped him in that difficult time. Now the king returns to Jerusalem after the rebellion, and Barzillai accompanies him as far as the Jordan. This detail explains why David wants to honor him and offers him a place to live at the court.

For today: Barzillai used his wealth to serve in a time of need, without expecting anything in return. We can ask ourselves what we have, whether money, time, a home or help, and who needs that today. God often remembers and honors humble generosity.
exp.18:34:
Barzillai tells King David that he is already eighty years old and feels that his age has taken away his strength and his senses. He says that he can no longer discern between good and evil, that is, he can no longer taste what he eats or drinks, nor enjoy the voices of singing men and singing women. So he asks why he should be a burden to the king.

Barzillai was a wealthy man from Gilead who had helped David with food and supplies while David was fleeing from his son Absalom. Now David wants to reward him by taking him to live with him in Jerusalem. Barzillai is grateful, but he humbly declines the offer and suggests that Chimham, probably a young man from his household, go in his place, although the text gives no further details.

For today: let us learn to recognize our stages of life with humility and gratitude. We can serve with generosity without demanding rewards, and we can also help others receive opportunities that we no longer need ourselves.
exp.18:35:
Barzillai tells King David that he will go only a little further with him, as far as the Jordan River. "Servant" is a humble way of speaking about himself. "Reward" means a payment or a prize. He asks plainly why the king would want to give him such a great prize for something so small.

Barzillai was a wealthy man from Gilead who had supplied David and his people with food when they were fleeing from David's son Absalom. Now David is returning as king and offers to let Barzillai live with him in Jerusalem. Barzillai, who is eighty years old, humbly declines because he feels too old. He asks that his young Chimham go in his place.

For today: we can serve with generosity without expecting honors. It is also wise to recognize our stages and limits, and to open the way for younger people with gratitude and peace.
exp.18:38:
All the people crossed the Jordan River, and then King David crossed as well. When he reached the other side, David kissed Barzillai, an elderly man who had helped him, and blessed him. Then Barzillai went back to his home.

After Absalom's rebellion, David returns to Jerusalem. Barzillai had supported him with provisions when David fled, and he went with him as far as the Jordan. David offered to have him live with him at the court, but Barzillai, already very old, preferred to die in his own city and suggested that Chimham go in his place. The text does not make clear who Chimham is; many think he was Barzillai's son.

Today we can honor with affection those who have helped us in difficult times. A hug, a word of blessing, or a sincere thank you are worth a great deal, and it is also wise to recognize our own limits, as Barzillai did.
exp.18:39:
David crossed the Jordan River and arrived at Gilgal. Chimham, the man Barzilai had entrusted to him, went with him. All the people of Judah also escorted the king, along with half the people of Israel, that is, a part of the northern tribes.

Here the narrator speaks. David was returning to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. He had promised to look after Chimham as a gesture of gratitude toward Barzilai, who had supported him during his flight. But the verse ends by showing a tension: Judah and the other tribes were beginning to dispute who had more right to accompany the king.

For today: gratitude is shown through concrete actions. And when peace returns, care must be taken that pride or rivalry does not divide those who ought to celebrate together.
exp.19:2:
David returned to Jerusalem and set apart the ten concubines (secondary wives) whom he had left to look after the palace. He placed them under guard in a house, provided them with food, but never had relations with them again. They lived shut away, like widows, until their death.

The narrator tells this after Absalom's rebellion, in which Absalom had publicly shamed them (2 Samuel 16:21-22). Meanwhile, another revolt arises, that of Sheba. The text does not explain David's motives: it may have been protection, shame, or a legal measure. They were victims, and their lives were marked by the sins of others.

Today we see that sin wounds innocent people too. We can look on those who suffer because of others' mistakes with compassion, and help them receive care, dignity, and hope.
exp.19:6:
This verse says that an army went out from Jerusalem to pursue Sheba, son of Bichri. Joab's men went, along with the Cherethites and Pelethites (David's personal guard, as it is commonly understood), and all the mighty men. The phrase that describes them going after him means following behind him, pursuing.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sheba had led a rebellion against David, and the king feared it would be worse than Absalom's. Amasa had been slow to gather Judah, so David sent Abishai. Joab and his men went with him, and soon Joab would act violently against Amasa.

For today: when a problem arises, it is not wise to put off what is urgent. Delay, pride, or rivalry can do harm. Let us act responsibly and with a clean heart.
exp.19:7:
When Joab's men reached the great stone at Gibeon, Amasa came out to join them. Joab was dressed in his military clothing, and over it he wore a belt with a dagger strapped to it at his waist. As he stepped forward, the dagger slipped from its sheath.

This is part of the account of Sheba's rebellion. David had appointed Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab. The narrator points out the dagger because Joab is about to kill Amasa through deceit. The text does not say whether the dagger fell by accident or whether Joab let it fall on purpose; many read it as a move meant to make him look unarmed.

For today: violence is sometimes hidden behind friendly gestures. Let us distrust the ambition and jealousy in our hearts, and seek sincere relationships, without duplicity.
exp.19:12:
It says that when they had removed Amasa's body from the road, all the people who had stopped beside him went on after Joab to pursue Sheba, son of Bichri. The explanation then notes that the wording in the old text, which was written for readers of a different translation, is handled here: the source's own quoted words are not part of the verse you see, so no comment on them is carried over.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Sheba had led a rebellion against David. Joab, the commander of the army, had just killed Amasa, another commander, and the people stood still looking at the body. One of Joab's soldiers moved the corpse aside and covered it, and so the people resumed the march. The text does not approve of the crime; it only tells what happened.

For today: let us not be swept along by whoever leads with force or cunning without asking whether what they do is right. Before following anyone, let us consider their actions in the light of God's Word.
exp.19:13:
The verse says that Sheba, the son of Bichri, went through all the tribes of Israel until he reached the city of Abel of Beth-maachah, and all the Berites. There the people gathered together and went after him. It is likely that "Berites" is the name of a place or of a group of people, and scholars are not entirely sure of its exact meaning.

Sheba had led a rebellion against King David. Meanwhile, Joab, the commander of the army, had killed Amasa and pursued Sheba to stop the revolt. This verse shows the rebel's route before they caught up with him.

For today: words of anger and division can spread quickly. Before following someone, let us ask whether they lead us toward peace or toward a break.
exp.19:14:
They came and laid siege to Seba in Abel of Beth-maacah, where he had taken refuge. They surrounded the city, built a ramp of earth up against the wall (this is the "rampart"), and all the soldiers working alongside the wall were trying to pull it down. "Besieged" means surrounded.

The narrator tells how Joab pursued Seba, who had started a revolt against David. Seba fled through the tribes of Israel and shut himself up in this city. Joab wanted to end the uprising quickly. What follows shows that a wise woman intervened before the city was destroyed.

When there is conflict, force may seem like the only way forward, but sometimes a calm and wise voice prevents greater harm. Before acting harshly, it is good to stop, listen, and look for a solution that preserves life and peace.
exp.19:15:
A wise woman called out from inside the city of Abel. She urgently asked that she be heard and that Joab be called to come and speak with her.

Joab, commander of David's army, was pursuing Sheba, who had rebelled against the king and taken refuge in Abel. Joab and his men laid siege to the city and began to tear down its wall. Then this woman, whom the Bible calls wise, speaks up to prevent the destruction of her people. She takes the initiative and asks for a conversation before there is more violence.

For today: when there is a conflict, before letting everything be destroyed, seek to speak calmly and wisely. A well-spoken word, at the right time, can protect many people and open the way to peace.
exp.19:20:
Joab says that he does not want to destroy the city. His only demand is that they hand over Sheba, son of Bichri, a man from the region of Ephraim who lifted up his hand against David, that is, he rebelled. If they hand him over, Joab will leave. The woman answers that they will throw his head to him over the wall.

Joab, David's general, was pursuing Sheba in the city of Abel. A wise woman challenged him for wanting to destroy a peaceful city. Joab clarifies that he is only seeking the rebel, and she commits to resolving the matter.

For today: when there is a conflict, a wise person can keep many from paying for the guilt of one. Before reacting with violence, let us seek dialogue, the truth, and solutions that protect the innocent.
exp.19:21:
What the text says: A woman of the city spoke wisely to all her neighbors. They cut off the head of Sheba, the rebel, and threw it out to Joab. Then Joab blew a trumpet, the army withdrew, and each man went back to his tent. Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.

Context: Sheba had led a rebellion against David. Joab, the commander of the army, besieged the city of Abel. A wise woman negotiated with him: if they handed over only the guilty man, the city would be spared. In this way the conflict ended without destroying all the inhabitants.

For today: Wisdom and dialogue can prevent greater tragedies. Before reacting with anger in a conflict, look for solutions that protect the innocent and resolve the problem at its root.
exp.19:22:
This verse opens a list of David's chief officials. It says that Joab was placed in command of the whole army of Israel, and that Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was in charge of the Cherethites and the Pelethites. These were, as is commonly understood, the king's personal guard, though scholars are not entirely certain of their origin.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator who summarizes how David's government was organized. This comes after the rebellion of Sheba, which ended when a wise woman of the city of Abel persuaded the people to hand over his head. With peace restored, the account shows the order of the kingdom, although Joab remained in charge despite his violent deeds.

For today: clear order and responsibilities help us care for people. Serve where God has placed you, with honesty, and remember that holding a position does not excuse doing wrong.
exp.20:0:
This verse tells that in David's time there was a famine that lasted three years in a row. David sought God to learn the cause, and God answered that the trouble came from Saul and from his household, which carried a guilt of blood, because Saul had killed the Gibeonites. Asking the Lord for guidance means David inquired of God, looking for his direction.

The narrator explains in the following verses that the Gibeonites were not Israelites. Israel had made them a covenant of peace (Joshua 9). Saul had attacked them, and God took that injustice seriously. The Bible does not say here when this happened, so we do not know more details.

For today: when there are problems, it is good to ask God with humility, and to be willing to acknowledge and repair injustices, even past ones, and to keep what we have promised.
exp.20:3:
The Gibeonites tell David that they do not want money or gold from Saul or from his family. They also do not want any Israelite to be put to death. David answers them that he will do whatever they ask.

There is a famine in the land, and David seeks God, who points to a bloodguilt that Saul brought upon the Gibeonites. They were a people with whom Israel had made an oath (Joshua 9), but Saul tried to wipe them out. David wants to repair the harm. What they ask for afterward is hard to understand, and readers interpret it in different ways.

For today: when we have hurt someone, repairing the harm begins by listening humbly to what the injured person needs, not to what is comfortable for us. Promises and agreements matter to God.
exp.20:6:
The explanation says that King David did not hand over Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, to be put to death. The word "spared" means that he protected him and kept him safe. The reason was the oath made before the Lord between David and Jonathan. Be careful: this Mephibosheth is different from another man with the same name, the son of Rizpah, who was indeed handed over.

There was famine in Israel, and David sought God. The Gibeonites, whom Saul had mistreated, asked for seven of Saul's descendants. David chose others, but he took care of Mephibosheth because of the promise he had made to his friend. How to understand this ancient justice is a matter of debate among scholars.

For today: keep our word, especially promises made before God, even when years pass or circumstances change. Our faithfulness can bless and protect others.
exp.20:8:
It says that David handed seven of Saul's descendants over to the Gibeonites, and they hanged them "before the Lord" on a hill. "Hanged" here may mean hanging the bodies up or displaying them after death; the text gives no further detail. Everything happened at the beginning of the barley harvest, that is, the spring harvest.

The narrator tells what happened after a three-year famine in Israel. According to the chapter, God said that Saul had wronged the Gibeonites, with whom Israel had a covenant. David asked them what restitution they wanted, and they requested this. The passage is difficult, and readers understand it in different ways, since the Bible does not explain everything.

For today: promises and injustices matter to God, and their effects can last for years. If we have harmed someone, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and seek to make right what can be made right.
exp.20:9:
Rizpah took a sack of coarse cloth, the kind worn in mourning, and spread it out for herself on the rock. She stayed there from the start of the barley harvest until the rain fell from heaven. She watched over the bodies of her two sons and the five others who had been hanged. She did not let the birds of the air touch them by day, or the wild animals by night.

The account is told by the narrator of Samuel. There was famine in David's time, and the Gibeonites asked for justice because of the violence Saul had done against them. David handed over seven of Saul's descendants. Leaving a body without burial was a great dishonor. Rizpah, grieved, protects her own. The text does not explain everything, and this episode has been much debated.

For today: faithful love can show itself in quiet perseverance. Staying close to someone who suffers, without abandoning them, is a real way of honoring their dignity. God also sees such acts.
exp.20:11:
This verse tells how David went to collect the bones of King Saul and of his son Jonathan. The men of Jabesh-gilead had taken them away secretly, from the street of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them after defeating Saul on Mount Gilboa.

This happens after a three-year famine in Israel. David sought God and understood that Saul had done harm to the Gibeonites. The sons of Rizpah had been executed, and she had cared for them with great grief and steadfastness. When David learned of this, he acted to give everyone a proper burial.

For today: God values the dignity and the memory of people. We can honor those who have died and humbly repair the wounds of the past, rather than ignoring them.
exp.20:12:
This verse says that David ordered the bones of Saul and of his son Jonathan to be gathered up, and that the bones of those who were hanged were also collected. The word "hanged" refers to the seven descendants of Saul who had been executed shortly before and left hanging on the mountain.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. There was famine in the land because of an injustice Saul had committed against the Gibeonites. Rizpah, the mother of two of those executed, guarded the bodies with great devotion. When David learned of this, he acted to give all of them a proper burial. Afterward, the text says that God was moved to show favor to the land.

For today: honor those who have passed away, and humbly make amends for the wrongs of the past. If there is something we can correct or care for with love, we should not leave it for later.
exp.20:16:
Abishai, nephew of David and son of Zeruiah, came to help him just when a Philistine giant was about to kill him. Abishai struck down the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men bound themselves to him with an oath: he would never again go out with them to battle, so that he would not put out the light of Israel. The light stands as a picture of the king's life and guidance, which gave light and hope to the people.

The ones speaking are the group of soldiers loyal to David. David was already older, had grown weary in the fighting, and had been in mortal danger. His men understood that losing the king could leave the whole people in darkness, and so they decided to protect him.

For today: God helps us through other people. Let us acknowledge our limits, accept the support of others, and also care for those who serve as a light for others.
exp.20:18:
This tells of another battle against the Philistines, in a place called Gob. Elhanan of Bethlehem struck down (that is, defeated and killed) a warrior named Goliath of Gath. The shaft was the wooden pole of his spear, as thick as a weaver's beam, the great beam of a loom.

It is part of a list of victories over Philistine giants, at the end of David's reign. His men had just stopped him from fighting, to protect his life. This verse is difficult: 1 Chronicles 20:5 says that Elhanan killed the brother of Goliath. Some think there was an error in copying the text, and others that there was another warrior with that name. It is not known for certain.

God uses many people, not only the famous. Serve faithfully where you are, even when no one notices.
exp.21:1:
Here David says that the Lord is his rock, his fortress, and his deliverer. These are three images: the rock speaks of a firm place where one does not fall; the fortress, of a secure place against attack; and the deliverer, of someone who rescues.

David sings these words on the day God delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, who pursued him for years. It is a song of thanksgiving that looks back and acknowledges that God sustained him through real dangers. This same song appears, with small differences, in Psalm 18.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, remember how God has helped you before and make it known to him in prayer. Putting his faithfulness into words strengthens trust, and you can run to him as to a firm refuge.
exp.21:7:
When God answered the cry of his servant, all of creation was shaken. The earth moved and trembled, and even the foundations of heaven, that is, the firmest supports of the universe, were stirred. The reason is that God was angry: his wrath rose against what threatened his son. This is poetic language, not a literal description.

David sings this psalm when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He had felt that death surrounded him, he cried out to the LORD, and God heard him from his temple. Here David uses images of earthquake and storm to show how powerful that help was.

For today: when you feel surrounded by anguish, cry out to God. He hears you and is not indifferent to your pain. Perhaps you will not see the earth tremble, but you can trust that the God who moves the heavens is concerned for you and acts in his own time.
exp.21:12:
This verse says that, before the brightness of God's presence, burning coals were kindled. It is a poetic image: the light that comes from God is so intense that it seems to set things on fire. The burning coals are glowing embers, pieces of charcoal at red-hot heat.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. To describe how God came to his aid, he uses the language of a storm: clouds, thunder, lightning and fire. This is not a literal description, but a way of expressing the power and holiness of God, and that He does hear the one who cries out to Him.

For today: when you find yourself surrounded by problems that overwhelm you, remember that God is greater than they are. Cry out to Him with confidence, and also with reverence, because His presence is holy and powerful.
exp.21:15:
It says that the bottom of the sea was laid bare and the very foundations of the earth were uncovered, when God rebuked with force. "The channels of the sea" are the currents or depths of the sea. "The foundations of the world" are the base of the earth. "The blast of the breath of his nostrils" is a poetic image of God's anger, like a powerful gust of wind.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving at the end of his life, after God had delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He uses images of storm, thunder, and earthquake to describe how great God's power is in rescuing him. It is poetic language, not necessarily a literal account of a physical event.

For today: when your troubles feel like deep waters that threaten to swallow you, remember that God is more powerful than any force. You can pray with confidence and give him thanks, knowing that he cares for you.
exp.21:17:
It says that God rescued the speaker from powerful enemies, people who hated him and who were stronger than he was.

David is speaking, in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul, as the text at the beginning of the chapter indicates. He uses grand images, such as seas and deep waters, to show that God intervened with power. He tells it as a testimony of gratitude.

Today, when you face something bigger than yourself, there is no need to pretend you are strong. You can admit your limit, ask God for help, and afterward remember and tell how he sustained you.
exp.21:21:
David says he took care to follow the way the Lord set before him, that is, his manner of life and his commands. The word "kept" here means that he obeyed them and watched over them carefully. "Have not wickedly departed" means that he did not turn away from God in a rebellious or malicious way.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, near the end of his life, after the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He does not claim he never failed; the Bible shows his serious sins. Here he speaks of the general direction of his life: he sought God and, when he fell, he returned to Him. Many understand this to refer to his underlying faithfulness, not to total perfection.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our direction is toward God. We do not need to be perfect, but we should return to Him promptly when we stray, with humility and sincerity.
exp.21:23:
He says that David was blameless before God, meaning sincere and whole in his loyalty, without living a double life. It also says that he kept himself from his wrongdoing, which means his tendency to do what is evil. The explanation adds nothing else about those words.

David speaks, at the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from Saul and from all his enemies. He does not say that he never sinned, since the Bible records his serious falls. Many understand that he is speaking of his general faithfulness to God, of not having abandoned him to follow other gods. Some think he is referring to his innocence in the face of the accusations of his enemies.

Today, we can ask God to help us be the same in public and in private. It is also wise to recognize what our most frequent weakness is and to set practical limits to guard against it, trusting in the grace of God.
exp.21:26:
This verse says that God acts according to the heart of each person. With the one who is clean, that is, sincere and pure, God shows himself pure and trustworthy. With the crooked, the one who twists the path on purpose, God shows himself opposed and unyielding toward his wickedness.

David speaks in this song of thanksgiving, toward the end of his life, after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He recounts how the Lord sustained him. He says that God was faithful to him, since David sought to walk with integrity, though he was not perfect. Some see here a general principle of how God deals with people.

For today: if you want to experience more of God's nearness, live with sincerity before him. Confess your faults, leave deception behind, and walk honestly, trusting in his mercy.
exp.21:27:
He says that God rescues the humble people, that is, those who recognize their need for Him. But His eyes are on the proud, the arrogant, to bring them down, that is, to humble them and pull them down from their haughtiness.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, which also appears in Psalm 18. He sings it when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. Earlier he said that God deals with each person according to their heart: kindly with the good, and with the wicked, He shows Himself as one who will not be deceived. This verse continues that idea. Then David says that God is his lamp and gives him strength.

Today we can examine our hearts honestly. If we have done wrong, it is better to admit it and ask forgiveness than to defend ourselves with pride. God draws near to whoever trusts in Him with humility.
exp.21:28:
This verse says that God is David's lamp. A "lamp" is a light that guides a person through the dark, and "darkness" refers to difficult, confusing, or dangerous times. David declares that the Lord himself gives him light when everything looks dark.

David speaks near the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. Shortly before, he says that God is just toward the humble and firm toward the proud. Then David speaks of the victories God gave him. This same song also appears in Psalm 18.

For today: when you do not know which path to take, do not despair. Pray, read the Bible, and trust that God will show you the next step, even if you cannot yet see the whole way.
exp.21:30:
This verse says that God's way, that is, his manner of acting, is perfect, without error or wickedness. His word has been tested like metal refined in the fire until it is clean and proven. And God is a shield to those who trust in him, which here means relying on him and taking refuge in him.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that appears at the end of his life, after God had delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that God was faithful in the midst of danger. This same song appears, with small variations, in Psalm 18.

For today: when you do not understand what is happening in your life, remember that God is trustworthy and his word is sure. Read it calmly and take refuge in him, even if you cannot yet see the answer.
exp.21:35:
He says that God gave David a shield that comes from his salvation, meaning a protection that springs from God's saving help. "Salvation" here means rescue or deliverance, not good physical health. Gentleness is kindness and a warm, considerate way of treating someone.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that appears near the end of his life, after God rescued him from Saul and his other enemies. Earlier he mentions his swift feet and his hands trained for battle. Now he acknowledges that his strength and his victories did not come from himself, but from God's protection and kindness.

For today: when something goes well for you, do not think only of your own effort. Take a moment to thank God for his care, and trust that his goodness also sustains you in what you still face.
exp.21:39:
It says that God gave David strength to fight, like someone who fastens a belt of power around him before battle. It also says that God brought down under his feet those who rose up against him. The phrase about fastening and the phrase about bringing down are the two images in the verse, and each is simply rendered here in ordinary words.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul (2 Samuel 22:1). The words about pursuing and destroying reflect the warfare of his time as king of Israel. What matters is that David acknowledges that the victory did not come from his own strength, but from God.

For today: we do not take this text as permission to harm others. We can apply it this way: when facing a difficult trial, ask God for strength, and after coming through it, thank him instead of boasting.
exp.21:41:
They looked around, but there was no one to save them. Even when they cried out to the Lord, he did not answer them. David speaks at the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from Saul and from his enemies. Here he describes the defeat of those who opposed him. The text does not explain why God did not answer those enemies; the context suggests they had risen up against the king whom God had anointed, though the passage does not spell this out.

For today: it is not healthy to seek God only when we are in trouble while living far from him. We can draw near to God sincerely every day, and not only in crises, trusting that he hears the heart that is humble and repentant.
exp.22:0:
Now these are the last words of David. This verse presents David's final message, the last thing he wants to leave behind. David describes himself with four traits: he is the son of Jesse, a man whom God raised up to a high place, the anointed one of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of Israel's songs, that is, the gentle psalmist of the psalms.

The speaker is King David, now an old man. He mentions that he is the son of Jesse, recalling his humble beginnings as a shepherd. He presents himself as one chosen by God, not by his own merit. What follows in the verses after this is an inspired word about how a just ruler should govern. Some scholars think these are not literally his last words in life, but rather his last recorded poem or prophetic message.

For today: if God has given you some place, whether in the home, at work, or in the church, remember that it comes from His grace. Use it with humility, justice, and gratitude.
exp.22:6:
It says that whoever wants to touch the thorns, that is, wicked people, must protect himself with iron and with the shaft of a spear. In the end, those thorns are burned right there on the spot.

Those are part of David's last words. He compares a righteous king to the morning light (earlier verses) and the wicked to dangerous thorns. Although his family is not perfect, God made an everlasting covenant with him. Some understand that God himself judges the wicked; others, that the king must confront them firmly.

For today: do not approach evil carelessly, nor trust in your own strength. Trust in God's covenant and justice, and let Him judge what you cannot put right.
exp.22:8:
This verse introduces Eleazar, son of Dodo, of the Ahohite family, as one of the most outstanding of David's three mighty men. He was with David when they stood against the Philistines, who had gathered to fight. At that moment, the men of Israel had withdrawn or gone up, leaving Eleazar almost alone at the front.

The writer of Samuel lists David's mighty men as a tribute to those who served him. The text that follows shows that Eleazar fought until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. It makes clear that the true source of the victory was God, and that the LORD brought about a great salvation. Commentators do not agree on the details of how Israel withdrew, but they do agree that Eleazar resisted with courage.

For today: sometimes we are called to stand firm even when others pull back. Let us do so with faithfulness and honest weariness, remembering that the final victory comes from God.
exp.22:12:
Three of David's thirty chief warriors went down to meet him at the cave of Adullam. It was harvest time. Meanwhile, the Philistine army had camped in the valley of Rephaim.

The author of the book is listing David's bravest men. Here it is the narrator speaking, not David. David was fleeing from Saul or hiding from the Philistines, and the cave was a refuge. Scholars debate exactly when this episode took place, and the text does not make it clear. What it does show is the loyalty of these men, who risked passing close to the enemy.

For today: loyalty is tested in difficult times. We can ask ourselves whom we stand with when there is risk, and how we can be faithful to God and to the people he has placed in our path, even when it costs us.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that David was in the stronghold, a protected place, while the Philistines, his enemies, had a garrison in Bethlehem. "Garrison" means a group of soldiers that occupies and guards a place. Bethlehem was David's hometown, so seeing his enemies there was painful.

Here the narrator describes the situation before telling the story of David's three mighty men. It is not known with certainty whether the "stronghold" is the cave of Adullam or some other refuge, and scholars interpret it in different ways. What matters is that David was living under pressure, and his longing for water from his homeland arises in that difficult moment.

For today: even when you are in a time of pressure or waiting, God sustains you. And when someone serves you with love and sacrifice, value it with humility and gratitude, as David did when he offered that gesture to God.
exp.22:15:
These three mighty men of David broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, took it, and brought it to David. David would not drink it, but poured it out before the Lord. The word "broke" here means they forced their way through by strength, and "well" refers to a pit where water is kept.

The narrator describes a moment in David's life, when he was in the stronghold and the Philistines were occupying Bethlehem, his hometown. David expressed a longing for home, and his brave men took him seriously and risked themselves to fulfill it. Then David, seeing the cost, declared that the water was like the blood of those men.

Today we can learn to value the sacrifice of others and not treat lightly what cost someone so much. We can also offer to God, with humility, what others give us with such love.
exp.22:19:
This verse presents Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, a brave man from Kabzeel, a town in the south of Judah. He is described as a valiant man, strong and courageous, and as one who had done many great deeds. He killed two lion-like men of Moab, or two warriors of Moab, depending on how the Hebrew is translated, since that wording is not entirely clear. He also went down into a pit and killed a lion in the midst of a pit in a time of snow, a difficult and slippery moment.

This passage is part of the list of David's mighty men at the end of the book. The narrator names the men who served the king with courage. Benaiah stands out as someone highly respected, although he did not become one of the first three.

For today: courage often shows itself in uncomfortable situations and without applause. We can ask God for strength to do what is right when it is hard, without expecting recognition.
exp.22:24:
This verse names two warriors from David's group of thirty mighty men: Shammah and Elika, both from a place called Harod. Harod was probably a town or a spring near where Gideon camped, though scholars do not fully agree on this. In 1 Chronicles 11:27 the name Shammoth appears, so some believe there are variations in the names across the lists.

Here the narrator of Samuel gathers the list of brave men who stood with David in his battles. It is a record of honor, written to remember those who served the king faithfully, even though their names are not famous.

God remembers ordinary people who serve with faithfulness. Perhaps no one applauds what you do in your family, your work, or your church, but your effort does not go unnoticed. Serve with steadiness, knowing that God sees and values every act of loyalty.
exp.22:28:
This verse continues a list of names. It mentions Heleb, son of Baanah, from the town of Netophah, and Ittai, son of Ribai, from Gibeah, a town in the tribe of Benjamin. They are two more among David's mighty men.

The text is told by the book's narrator, not by David. After the king's final words, the account lists the warriors who supported him. It is a record of honor: although their deeds are not told here, their names were kept. That Ittai was from Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, shows that David had support from different places, though the text does not explain more.

For today: God notices those who serve without being famous. Do your part faithfully, even when no one applauds it. And value those who serve beside you.
exp.22:29:
This verse names two more of David's mighty men. Benaiah was from Pirathon, a town in the territory of Ephraim. Hiddai came from the brooks of Gaash, that is, from a valley or stream near Mount Gaash. These are only names and places of origin.

It is part of the list of David's thirty, the outstanding warriors who accompanied David (2 Samuel 23:8-39). The list appears after David's last words. The text simply records them and does not explain why each one is included. This Benaiah of Pirathon should not be confused with Benaiah son of Jehoiada, mentioned earlier. The names in this list are written somewhat differently in 1 Chronicles 11.

God takes notice of people who seem ordinary. These men came from small towns, and we know almost nothing of their stories, yet they were recorded. Your faithful service, even if no one applauds it, does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.22:33:
This verse names two more of David's warriors. Eliphelet was the son of Ahasbai, and his family came from Maacah, a small region north of Israel. Eliam was the son of Ahithophel, from the town of Giloh (also called Gilo), in the hill country of Judah.

The narrator of the book lists the brave men who accompanied David. They came from different places, and some had foreign origins. Ahithophel, Eliam's father, was David's counselor and later joined Absalom's rebellion. Some think this Eliam is the same one who appears in 2 Samuel 11:3, but this is not certain.

God uses people from all kinds of families and places to carry out his work. Even if no one remembers them, their names matter. Today you can serve faithfully where you are, without seeking applause. God sees and remembers your work.
exp.22:35:
This verse names two more warriors from David's list of mighty men. Igal was the son of Nathan and came from Zobah, a region to the north of Israel. Bani was from Gad, one of the tribes. Notice that some of these heroes came from different places, and even from outside Israel.

The author of the book records here the elite men who accompanied David, known as the thirty. It is a kind of honor roll at the end of David's reign. About Igal, other ancient versions of the text give a slightly different name, and it cannot be known for certain which is the original.

God takes note of people whom almost no one remembers. Though only their names remain of these men, their faithfulness was written down. Serve wherever you are, without seeking applause; what you do with steadiness and loyalty does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.22:36:
It says that Zelek, a man of Ammon, and Naharai, from the city of Beeroth, were among David's mighty men. Of Naharai it adds that he was armourbearer to Joab, that is, the one who carried his weapons and accompanied him in battle. Joab was the son of Zeruiah, David's sister. That Zelek was an Ammonite shows that there were also foreigners among these warriors.

The author of the book presents a list of David's mighty men, the most outstanding soldiers of his army. There is no speech here, but a record. Its purpose is to honour each one for his service to the king. The list ends with 37 names.

For today: God notices those who serve, even when their task is quiet or supportive, like that of an armourbearer. Serve faithfully where you are; your work does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.22:38:
The verse names Uriah the Hittite as the last name on the list of David's mighty men. The total is given at the end as thirty and seven in all. The word "Hittite" means he came from the Hittite people, that is, he was a foreigner. The number thirty-seven is understood as the thirty well-known men plus some others, such as the three chief warriors, although scholars explain this in different ways.

The writer closes a list of the loyal men who fought alongside David. Uriah is the same husband of Bathsheba, whom David had put to death (2 Samuel 11). Placing him at the end of the list shows, sadly, how serious that sin was. He was a faithful soldier.

For today: value the simple and faithful people around you, regardless of their origin. And remember that our decisions can hurt those who trust us. Ask God for an upright and humble heart.
exp.23:0:
It says the anger of God was kindled again against Israel, and that David was moved to give an order: to count the people of Israel and Judah.

The narrator of 2 Samuel introduces the start of a difficult episode. He does not explain here why God was angry. The text does not fully clarify who moved David: this passage attributes it to God, while 1 Chronicles 21:1 mentions Satan. Scholars explain this in several ways. Joab, the general, is surprised by the order and asks why the king wants it.

Today we can ask ourselves what lies behind our plans. Counting can be normal, but doing it to trust in our numbers and not in God is dangerous. Let us ask for a humble heart that rests in Him.
exp.23:2:
Joab answers King David with respect but with concern. He tells him that God could multiply the people a hundredfold, and that he hopes the king will see it with his own eyes. But right away he asks: why does my lord the king want this? That is, he does not understand the reason for counting the people.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. The king had just ordered a census of all Israel. The text says God's anger was against Israel, and it does not explain the reason in detail. Joab suspects the motive is not good, perhaps pride or trust in the number of soldiers. Even so, David insists and does not listen to him.

For today: before making a decision, examine your motives. If a wise person questions you sincerely, listen to them, and do not place your security in your numbers or achievements, but in God.
exp.23:5:
This verse follows the route of Joab and the commanders as they travelled through the land to count the people. After crossing the Jordan and reaching Aroer, they passed on to Gilead and to the lowlands mentioned in the text. Then they came to Dan-jaan and to the area around Sidon, in the north. The name in the lowlands is a difficult one: the Hebrew text is uncertain, and some scholars interpret it in other ways.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had ordered the census, and Joab carried it out even though he thought it was a bad idea. The journey through so many regions shows that the order was carried out in full detail, from the east to the north, and that it took almost ten months.

For today: when a decision springs from pride or from distrust of God, it can move forward with great order and effort and still be a mistake. Before planning in detail, it is wise to ask ourselves whether what we are doing honours God and trusts in Him.
exp.23:6:
This verse describes the last stage of the route that Joab and the commanders took while counting the people. They reached the stronghold of Tyre and the cities of the Hivites and the Canaanites. Then they went out toward the south of Judah, as far as Beersheba. The phrase about the south is explained here: the route went from north to south, so they finished covering the land from north to south.

The narrator describes the census that King David ordered Joab, his military chief, to carry out. Joab traveled through the whole country, and the journey lasted almost ten months. Earlier, Joab had warned David not to do it, but the king insisted. The text says David acted out of pride or confidence in his own strength, and afterward he acknowledged that he had sinned (v. 10). Some scholars see here a sign of his lack of trust in God.

For today: it is easy to measure our security by numbers, such as money, achievements, or approval. Today you can remember that your confidence rests in God, not in what you have.
exp.23:7:
The explanation says that Joab and the commanders traveled through all the land of Israel and returned to Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days. The word "Jerusalem" refers to Jerusalem, and the phrase about having gone through the land means that they had covered the whole territory from one end to the other. It was a long and thorough journey.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had ordered a census of the people, although Joab tried to talk him out of it. This verse sums up how long the task took. The verses that follow show the result and David's remorse. The Bible does not fully explain why the census was a sin; it has been interpreted as pride or as trust in human strength rather than in God.

For today: be careful about measuring your security only by numbers, possessions, or achievements. God wants you to trust in Him. And if you make a mistake, do as David did: acknowledge it quickly and ask forgiveness sincerely.
exp.23:8:
This verse says that Joab, the commander of the army, handed King David the result of the census. Israel had eight hundred thousand strong men, ready to fight with the sword, and Judah had five hundred thousand. Gave up the sum means that he reported the total. Drew the sword means that they were soldiers.

The narrator tells us that David ordered this census, and Joab, though he questioned it, carried out the order. The text then shows that David felt guilty and acknowledged his sin. The Bible does not explain this in detail, but it seems that David trusted the size of his army more than God. The figures in 1 Chronicles 21 are different, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, strength, or plans. Trust God first, and if you fail, confess with humility as David did.
exp.23:10:
This verse says that in the morning, after David had already confessed his sin, God spoke to the prophet Gad.

The narrator is speaking here. David had ordered the people to be counted, and his conscience accused him. He had asked for forgiveness, yet God still sent Gad with a message about the consequences. Some think David trusted in his military strength instead of trusting in God, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when we fail, God forgives us if we repent from the heart, but sometimes he allows us to face the consequences. We can accept them with humility, trusting that his mercy remains with us.
exp.23:12:
Gad comes before David and presents him with three possible punishments from God: seven years of famine, three months of fleeing from his enemies, or three days of plague in the land. Gad asks David to think carefully about his answer, since he must bring it back to God.

Gad is the prophet who served alongside David. He speaks on behalf of the LORD, after David had taken a census of the people, something his own conscience later rebuked him for as sin. The text does not detail all the reasons here, but it shows that the king's sin had consequences for the whole nation.

Today we can learn that our decisions affect others, and that when we fail, it is best to place ourselves in the hands of God, who is merciful, as David later acknowledged.
exp.23:13:
Here David says that he is in great distress. Among three possible punishments, he prefers to fall into the hand of God, because God's mercies are many, rather than into the hands of people. That is, he trusts in God's goodness more than in human cruelty.

David speaks with the prophet Gad. He had taken a census of the people, and this displeased God. The text does not detail all the reasons, and it has been interpreted in several ways, perhaps out of pride or from trusting in his military strength. God offers him three options: famine, flight, or plague. David chooses to put himself in God's hands.

For today: when you face the consequences of a mistake, do not run away from God. Come to Him with humility, because His mercy is greater than any human judgment.
exp.23:17:
That same day the prophet Gad came to David and gave him a clear instruction: go up and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah, a Jebusite man. A threshing floor was a flat piece of ground where grain was beaten to separate it from the husks.

David had just acknowledged his sin in taking the census of the people, and the angel had stopped his hand at that threshing floor. Gad, who was a prophet and was with David, passed on God's direction to him. The altar would serve for offering sacrifices and seeking forgiveness. Many understand that this place was later connected with Jerusalem and the temple, although the text here does not say so.

For today: when we recognize our faults, God shows us a way to return to Him. Respond with humility and obedience, without delay.
exp.23:18:
David got up and went to the place the prophet Gad had pointed out to him. He did this because it was a command from God and not his own idea. The word for going up here means going to a higher place, and the word for the message means a spoken word or message.

Background: David had taken a census of the people and recognized that this was a sin. A plague was striking Israel. David asked that the punishment fall on him and his family, not on the people. Then God sent Gad with clear instructions: build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah. There David would offer sacrifices, and the dying would stop.

For today: when we acknowledge our failures with humility, God shows us the next step. Obeying Him promptly, even when it costs us, is part of returning to Him with a whole heart.
exp.23:19:
This verse tells how Araunah, when he looked up, saw King David coming toward him with his servants. He went out to meet them and bowed down with his face to the ground. Bowing down to the earth was a sign of respect before someone in authority.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David went up to Araunah's threshing floor, Araunah being a Jebusite, because the prophet Gad had told him to build an altar there to the LORD. This happens after a plague had fallen on the people, and David was seeking to have the deadly sickness stopped. Araunah did not know why the king had come, and that is why he received the king with humility.

For today: when God guides us to do something, we can obey with humility, and also treat with respect and kindness those we meet along the way. Araunah honored David, and David would later honor God with an offering that truly cost him something.
exp.23:20:
Araunah asks King David why he has come to visit his servant. David answers plainly: he wants to buy the threshing floor, that is, the flat place where grain was beaten out, in order to build an altar to the Lord there. His purpose is that the plague, the death that was killing the people, may be stopped.

David had sinned by taking a census of the people, and God sent a plague upon Israel. The prophet Gad told him to set up an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. Araunah, a respectful and generous man, is surprised to see the king arrive, and David explains his reason with sincerity.

For today: when we recognize our wrongs, it is good to respond with humility and concrete action. David does not stop at repentance; he seeks to worship God and to help others, and he is willing to pay a price for it.
exp.23:21:
Araunah tells David to take whatever he wishes and offer the sacrifice. He points to the oxen for the burnt offering, which was an offering burned completely for God. He also offers the threshing tools and the yokes of the oxen to be used as wood for the fire on the altar.

Araunah, the owner of the threshing floor, the place where grain was threshed, speaks here. David had sinned by counting the people, and a plague came. Now he goes up to buy the threshing floor to build an altar and ask that the dying stop. Araunah, with respect, wants to give everything for free. In the next verse, David refuses.

For today: Araunah's generosity is beautiful, but David reminds us that sincere worship costs us something. We can ask ourselves what we give to God with real effort: time, attention, money, or service, and not just what we have left over.
exp.23:23:
David tells Araunah that he does not want to take the land for free. He insists on paying for it, because he would not offer sacrifices to God that cost him nothing. He buys the threshing floor (the place where grain was separated from the chaff) and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver. A shekel was a unit of weight used as money.

David speaks after having sinned by counting the people. A plague was falling on Israel, and the prophet Gad had told him to build an altar on that threshing floor. Araunah, generously, offers him everything. But David wants to worship with a sacrifice of his own. In 1 Chronicles 21:25 another figure appears, and scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: God does not seek cheap gifts, but a willing heart. Ask yourself what you give to God that truly costs you: time, forgiveness, generosity, or obedience.
exp.6:27:
David answers God's promise with a prayer of praise. He says that the Lord is God, and that his words are true. David recognizes that the Lord has promised this good thing to his servant. Here the good thing is the promise of blessing that David has just heard through the prophet Nathan.

David is praying after the prophet Nathan told him that God would build him a "house," that is, a line of descendants and a dynasty. David had wanted to build a temple for God, but God promised him something greater: that his family would endure. This prayer springs from gratitude and humility. Christians often see in this promise a pointer to Jesus, a descendant of David, although each tradition explains it with different nuances.

Today we can pray as David did: remember what God has promised in his Word and rest in the fact that he is faithful. When you doubt, repeat his promises in prayer and trust.
exp.9:3:
This verse tells how Hanun, king of the Ammonites, seized David's servants, shaved off half of each man's beard, cut off their garments at the hips, and sent them away. The explanation of the words "shaved" and "sent away" is given in the wording above: to shave means to remove the beard with a razor, and to send away means to dismiss them back to where they came from.

The narrator describes what happened when King Nahash died. David wanted to show kindness and sent comforters. But the Ammonite princes planted suspicion, and Hanun believed the worst. In that culture, the beard was a sign of dignity, so this was a public humiliation. It ended in war.

For today: before judging someone's intentions, ask and listen. Suspicion without evidence, fed by bad advice, can turn a kind gesture into an offense and destroy relationships. Ask God for wisdom and humility.
exp.7:6:
It says that David took the gold shields that belonged to the officers of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and brought them to Jerusalem. "Officers" here means the men who served the king, such as commanders or soldiers in his service. Some translators understand these to be gold shields, while others think they could be quivers or weapons decorated with gold; the Hebrew allows for that uncertainty.

The account is from the biblical narrator, who summarizes David's victories. Hadadezer and his Syrian allies were defeated, and David took the spoils, as was the custom in the wars of that time. The text says that the LORD preserved David wherever he went, and so it presents these victories as part of God's care over the kingdom.

For today: what God gives us or entrusts to us is not only for our own benefit. David brought the shields to Jerusalem, the center of the kingdom. We can ask ourselves how to use our resources, talents, and achievements with gratitude, serving others and recognizing that God is the one who sustains us.
exp.21:24:
The explanation says that God rewarded David according to his righteousness and the cleanness of his hands before Him. The word "repaid" is the wording in your verse, and the phrase "according to" matches "according to" in your verse. "Cleanness" speaks of a life without guilt in the sight of God. It does not say that David was perfect, but that he sought to obey God with sincerity.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Earlier, he says that he kept God's laws in mind and guarded himself from wickedness. This same song also appears in Psalm 18. Some understand that David is speaking of his general faithfulness to the Lord, not of being without sin, since the Bible also records his serious failures.

Today, we can live with sincerity before God, without pretense. When we fail, let us confess and return to Him. God sees the heart and cares for those who seek Him with integrity.
exp.19:18:
A woman from the city of Abel comes before Joab and tells him that she and her people are among the peaceable and faithful in Israel. She accuses him of trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel, a city with standing and with many families under its care. Then she asks him why he would swallow up the LORD's inheritance, that is, the people and the land that belong to God.

A woman whom the text calls wise is speaking. Joab was pursuing the rebel Sheba, and he had laid siege to the city where Sheba had taken refuge. She tries to stop the violence through dialogue. In the end, the city hands over Sheba and a massacre is avoided.

For today: before reacting harshly, it is worth taking the time to speak calmly and to look for a way out that protects the innocent. A wise word can prevent a great deal of harm.
exp.21:50:
This verse says that God brings great salvation to his king and shows steadfast love to his anointed one.
