The phrase about great salvation means that God gives major victories and rescues to the one he has chosen. The phrase about loving devotion means that he acts with kindness and loyalty. His descendants means the people who come after David in his line. The words "forever" show that this kindness has no end.

David speaks at the end of a song of thanksgiving. He composed it when God delivered him from his enemies, including Saul. David speaks of himself in the third person, as "the anointed," that is, chosen by God. The promise about his descendants recalls God's covenant with him. Many Christians see its final fulfillment in Jesus Christ, a descendant of David.

For today: when God has helped you, do not keep it to yourself in silence. Write down one concrete help you received today and give thanks for it in prayer. Trust that his faithfulness remains firm.
exp.23:16:
Here David sees the angel striking down the people, and he speaks to the LORD. He admits his guilt: "Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly." He calls the people "these sheep," meaning innocent people whom he, as a shepherd, was supposed to care for. He asks that the punishment fall on him and on his father's house.

David speaks after having ordered a census of the people, something God regarded as a serious sin. The Bible does not fully explain why it was wrong; some think it was pride or trust in his military strength. A plague had already killed thousands. David, as king, takes responsibility and shows the heart of a shepherd.

For today: when we fail, let us not look for excuses or blame others. Honestly acknowledging our mistake, and caring for those who suffer because of it, is the first step toward asking forgiveness and beginning to repair the harm.
exp.11:25:
This verse tells us that Joab, the commander of David's army, kept up the fighting against Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. There he captured the royal fortress, which was probably the fortified part of the city where the palace stood. Some believe it is the same as the "city of waters" mentioned later.

The narrator tells this while David was in Jerusalem, after his sin with Bathsheba and the birth of Solomon. Joab did the hard work on the battlefield. Then, with humility and loyalty, he asks David to come and complete the victory, so that the honor belongs to the king.

For today: Joab did not keep the recognition for himself, but gave it to his leader. We can learn to work with honesty and not always seek applause, but to serve with humility wherever God places us.
exp.11:30:
David brought out the people of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and he made them work at the brick kilns, the furnaces where bricks were baked. He did the same to all the other Ammonite cities, and then he returned to Jerusalem.

This is part of the account of the war against Ammon. The narrator reports what happened without stating whether God approved of it. Scholars debate whether this was forced labor or something far harsher, involving torture and death, and the wording of the original text allows both readings.

For today: the Bible sometimes reports deeds without approving them, and the violence of power leaves its marks. May power never make us forget the dignity of the people who are under our authority. Let us treat them with justice and mercy.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that King Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, confronts Abner: "Why did you sleep with my father's concubine?" A concubine was a secondary wife, and sleeping with her means having a sexual relationship with her.

Ish-bosheth, who ruled over Israel with Abner's support, was speaking, and Abner was the commander of his army. At that time, taking the wives of the previous king was seen as a claim to the throne. Ish-bosheth suspects that Abner wants power. The Bible does not say whether the accusation was true, and Abner becomes angry and does not respond directly to it.

For today: before accusing someone, let us look for evidence and speak with respect. An accusation made lightly can break a relationship of trust and bring serious consequences, as happened here.
exp.16:6:
Hushai tells Absalom that the advice Ahithophel has just given is not sound, at least for this moment. The words "this time" show that Hushai is not condemning Ahithophel in general, but is saying that this particular plan is a mistake.

Hushai speaks because Absalom, who had rebelled against his father David, asked for his opinion. Ahithophel had proposed pursuing David at once. Hushai was a friend of David and, according to the account, was there to undermine Ahithophel's advice. That is why he speaks with great cunning, though the text does not say everything he was thinking.

For today: before deciding something important, listen to more than one opinion, and ask whether the counsel is wise, not just whether it sounds convincing. And ask God for discernment.
exp.1:5:
David wishes the men of Jabesh-gilead that the LORD will show them loving devotion and faithfulness. He also promises that he himself will show them the same favor, because they cared for the body of King Saul. The words "loving devotion and faithfulness" speak of loyal love and of a faithfulness that stays firm. "Show you the same favor" means that he will treat them with kindness in return.

David speaks as a king just anointed over Judah in Hebron. The men of Jabesh had buried Saul with honor, and David sends messengers to thank them. He may also have been seeking their friendship, since he later encourages them to be brave and tells them that Judah has anointed him. The Bible says nothing more about his intentions, so it is best not to claim more than the text states.

Today we can notice those who do acts of kindness that no one sees or that bring them no benefit. We should thank them with sincere words and, if possible, with a concrete gesture. In this way we reflect the loving devotion and faithfulness of God.
exp.20:4:
The Gibeonites answer King David. They speak of Saul as the man who consumed them and plotted against them to exterminate them from existing within any border of Israel. "Plotted" means that he schemed something in secret, and "exterminate" means to wipe something out completely, leaving nothing behind.

There is a famine in the land, and David seeks God, who explains that it is because of the blood Saul shed against the Gibeonites. They were a people with whom Israel had made a covenant (Joshua 9). The Bible does not recount the details of that slaughter here. David asks them how he can make amends for the wrong, and they explain their complaint.

For today: injustices of the past matter to God, even when time has passed. If we have harmed someone, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and seek to repair the damage, not to ignore it.
exp.14:25:
This verse shows David placing himself entirely in God's hands. If God were to say, "I do not delight in you," David answers, "Here I am." In other words, he is ready to accept whatever God decides. He asks that God do to him whatever seems good to Him.

David speaks with the priest Zadok as he flees from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. The Levites had carried God's ark out to go with him, but David asks that it be brought back to the city. He does not want to treat the ark as a charm that would secure God's favor. He prefers to trust in the Lord's will, whatever it may be.

For today: when you go through a crisis, you can pray with humility and entrust the outcome to God. Trusting does not mean doing nothing. It means acting wisely and accepting with peace whatever He decides.
exp.17:22:
Ahimaaz insists on running with the news, even though Joab had already said it was not worth it. Joab gives in and says to him, "Run." Ahimaaz takes the way of the plain, which was easier and faster, and he outran the Cushite.

Absalom, David's son, had rebelled and has just died in battle. Joab first sent the Cushite with the message. Ahimaaz, son of the priest Zadok, wanted to carry the news too. Joab hesitated because the message would be painful for David. The Bible does not fully explain Ahimaaz's reasons; some think it was eagerness.

Haste and good spirits are not enough; we also need to know what message we are carrying and how to deliver it with wisdom and love. Before speaking or acting in a hurry, let us ask God for discernment.
exp.14:3:
Absalom says that he wishes he were appointed judge in the land, so that everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to him, and he would give them justice. A "grievance" is a complaint about being wronged, and a "dispute" is a disagreement that needs to be settled.

Absalom, the son of King David, would stand each morning beside the gate of the city, where cases were heard. He would speak with the people who came to see the king, telling them that their claim was right and that no one would listen to them. In this way he criticized his father and won sympathy. The text says he "stole the hearts" of Israel, and this prepares the way for his rebellion.

Let us take care not to be carried away by fine words and by one who seeks to be admired. Let us ask God for sincerity to serve others without hidden motives.
exp.18:1:
The explanation says that the day of victory turned into sorrow for the whole army. The soldiers were told that the king was deeply grieving over the death of his son. Mourning is deep sorrow for someone who has died. Here the word "grieving" describes sorrow and anguish.

The account tells what happened after David's troops defeated the rebels led by Absalom, the king's son. Absalom died in the battle. David, as a father, wept inconsolably, and this discouraged those who had risked their lives for him. Joab, his commander, learned of it and soon afterward rebuked the king.

For today: grief is real and deserves to be mourned, but our emotions also affect those around us. We can ask God for comfort and wisdom to suffer without forgetting to give thanks and to care for those who stand beside us.
exp.7:17:
Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was in charge of the Cherethites and Pelethites, who were David's personal guard. Their exact origin is not certain; some think they were foreign soldiers. David's sons are described as priestly leaders, a word that here most often means priests, so it is understood in several ways. In this verse, these sons held important positions close to the king.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After recounting David's victories, he presents the list of his main helpers. In this way he shows that his kingdom was already well organized and firm.

For today: no one serves well alone. David had helpers with clear tasks. In your family, your church, or your work, share responsibilities and recognize the service of others. Order and teamwork can also honor God.
exp.10:21:
The messenger set out, arrived where David was, and reported to him everything Joab had sent him to say. The phrase "set out" means he left to make the journey, and "reported" here means he gave a full account of the message.

Here the narrator of the story is speaking. Joab, the commander of the army, was besieging the city of Rabbah. He had sent Uriah to the most dangerous part of the battle, just as David had ordered, and Uriah died. Joab expected the king to be angry about the defeat, so he prepared the message to soften the blow with the news of Uriah's death. The text does not say what Joab really thought deep down, but it does show that he knew what David wanted to hear.

For today: a hidden sin often drags other people into silence, manipulation, or cover-up. If we have done wrong, it is better to confess it soon, as David later did, and not keep covering it up.
exp.4:19:
It says that David came to Baal-perazim and there defeated the Philistines. He recognized that it was God who gave them the victory, and he compared the victory to a flood bursting out and rushing forward. The verse says "defeated," and it describes God as having burst out against his enemies, like a sudden rush of water breaking through. For this reason he named the place Baal-perazim, which is usually understood to mean "the Lord of the breakthrough" or "the one who bursts through."

The speaker is the narrator, and then David. The Philistines had invaded the valley of Rephaim, near Jerusalem, shortly after David was made king over all Israel. Before fighting, David consulted God and received a clear promise of victory. His response shows gratitude, not pride.

For today: before making important decisions, seek God's direction in prayer and in His Word. And when something goes well, give Him thanks instead of claiming the credit for yourself alone.
exp.19:9:
This verse tells us that Amasa was not on guard against the dagger in Joab's hand. Joab stabbed him in the stomach, and his intestines spilled out onto the ground. Joab did not need to strike him again, because Amasa was already dead. Then Joab and his brother Abishai went on pursuing Sheba, the son of Bichri.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had appointed Amasa as commander of the army in place of Joab, and Sheba had led a rebellion. Joab, perhaps moved by jealousy and ambition, greeted Amasa as a friend and killed him by treachery. The Bible recounts the event without approving of it.

For today: violence disguised as affection is deception. Let us guard our hearts so that we do not hide resentment behind kind words, and let us seek peace with sincerity.
exp.7:14:
This verse says that David was king over all Israel and that he administered justice and righteousness for all his people. Here "justice" and "righteousness" describe acting rightly and fairly toward everyone in the kingdom.

The narrator of the book speaks here, summarizing David's reign after describing his military victories. Just before this, the text says that the LORD gave David victory wherever he went. Then his chief officials are listed. In this way, the passage shows that his kingdom had not only strength but also order and good government. Even so, the book will later show that David also failed.

For today: if you have some authority, whether in your home, your work, or your church, try to treat everyone with fairness, without favoritism. Ask God to help you act justly and honestly in everyday life.
exp.12:23:
Absalom comes to King David and tells him that his servant has just hired shearers, the workers who cut the wool from the sheep. It was a busy time of work and celebration. Absalom invites the king and his servants to come along with him.

The phrase "your servant" is a respectful way for Absalom to speak about himself.

Absalom speaks politely, but the text has already told us that he had been nursing anger against Amnon for two years because of what Amnon did to Tamar, his sister. The invitation seems generous, yet it hides a plan. David refuses to go, and then Absalom manages to get Amnon to go. We will see the consequences later.

For today: resentment kept silently can grow and lead us to act with deceit. Bring your pain to God and seek justice and healing without revenge, before bitterness takes control of you.
exp.16:0:
Here Ahithophel proposes a military plan to Absalom. He asks to choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David.

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and David had fled from Jerusalem. Ahithophel was a highly respected counselor, and here he gives his advice for ending the rebellion quickly. According to the verses that follow, he wanted to attack David while David was tired and weak. Later, Hushai offers a different counsel, and Absalom prefers it. The text says that the Lord determined to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel (2 Samuel 17:14).

For today: a plan may seem very wise and quick, but it guarantees nothing if it goes against what God allows. Before acting, it is good to pray, seek advice, and look for God's will.
exp.14:19:
Here David asks Ittai whether it is fair that, having arrived only yesterday, he should now be made to wander around with them. David says, "I do not know where I am going," meaning he does not know where he will end up. He asks Ittai to go back and take his brothers with him, and he prays that the LORD will show him loving devotion and faithfulness.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. Ittai was a foreigner from Gath, and David, with generosity, offers him the freedom to stay in safety. He does not want to drag him into an uncertain and dangerous situation.

For today: true generosity thinks of the good of the other, even in the midst of our own pain. And Ittai's loyalty reminds us that accompanying someone in their difficult moment is worth more than staying comfortable.
exp.21:4:
David felt surrounded by deadly dangers, like waves that rise up and give no way of escape. The phrase "torrents of chaos" refers to rushing floods of disorder and destruction. The word "overwhelmed" here means that they swept over him and filled him with dread.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God, which the text places at the time when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and remembers how close he came to death. He does not hide his fear, and he tells it to show that God rescued him.

Today, when you feel that problems are sweeping you away like a current, do not pretend you have no fear. Tell God honestly, as David did, and cry out to Him. Then, when the trial has passed, remember with gratitude how He held you up.
exp.10:3:
David sent messengers to bring Bathsheba to him, and when she came to him, he slept with her. The text notes that she had just purified herself from her uncleanness, that is, from the ritual impurity caused by menstruation (Leviticus 15), and then she went back home.

This is part of the historical account in Samuel. David was supposed to be at war, but he stayed in Jerusalem. He saw Bathsheba, learned that she was married, and still acted. The text does not tell us what she felt, and it does not say she freely agreed; before a king, her room to refuse was minimal. That is why many read it as an abuse of power. The pregnancy that follows leads to the cover-up and the death of Uriah.

For today: sin usually advances step by step: a look, a question, an order. Stop early, recognize your limit, and never use your authority to take what does not belong to you.
exp.1:14:
Then twelve men from the tribe of Benjamin stood up for Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and twelve of David's servants came forward. They were two equal groups, ready to face each other. "Got up and were counted off" means they stepped forward and were numbered, so that each side had the same number of fighters, facing toward the middle, between the two sides.

The narrator describes the moment after Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army, proposed to Joab, David's commander, that some young men should "play" a contest, meaning they should stage a kind of combat. Israel was divided: some followed the house of Saul and others followed David. What seemed like a game ended in a slaughter, and the text does not say that God commanded it.

Today, this account warns us that pride and division turn a "test of strength" into tragedy. Before accepting a challenge or an argument, it is wise to ask where it may lead us and to seek peace.
exp.6:20:
Here David tells God that the great things he has done and promised were done for the sake of his own word and according to his own heart. "Great things" here means wonderful works and promises. "Servant" is David himself. God also revealed these things to him so that he would understand them.

David is praying after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: his family and his kingdom would be established forever. David sits before the Lord, amazed. He understands that he did not receive this on his own merit, but because God chose to give it out of pure goodness.

For today: when you see God's goodness in your life, do not think first about what you deserve, but about who God is. Give thanks with humility, remembering that his favors come from his love and his faithful word.
exp.23:1:
Here King David orders Joab, the commander of his army, to travel through the whole land, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, and to register the troops. David wants to know how many men there are in Israel. The words "go through" mean to cover the entire region, and the order is given to Joab, who is to carry it out with others under him.

Before this verse, the text says that the Lord was angry with Israel and that David was moved to take the count. The text does not explain the reason for the anger. Joab objects, but the king insists. Many readers understand that the problem was David's trust in the number of his soldiers rather than in God, although the passage does not say this in those words.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in numbers, money or resources, or in God. It is also wise to listen to those who warn us with good judgment, as Joab did.
exp.13:12:
Here the woman turns the king's argument back on him. She asks him: "Why have you devised a thing like this against the people of God?" She points out that when the king grants protection to her son, he condemns himself, because he has not brought back his own banished son. Being convicted means being shown to be at fault, and the one who has fled or been driven out is the banished son.

The speaker is a wise woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab. She tells an invented story about her son so that David will see his own situation with Absalom, who fled after killing Amnon. David had forgiven her son, but not Absalom.

For today: we are quick to show grace to others, but slow to extend it to those who hurt us most. Let us ask God for humility to examine whether our mercy is even-handed, and to seek reconciliation wherever it is possible.
exp.21:9:
God parted the heavens and came down to the earth, with dark clouds beneath his feet. The image is poetic: it pictures God coming with great power, like a massive storm, to act on behalf of his servant.

David sings this song of thanksgiving after the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. The images of trembling, smoke, fire, and dark clouds show that God is not distant: he steps in and intervenes. Many read these images as poetic language rather than a literal event seen in this way.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems, remember that God sees, draws near, and acts. Before asking for help, you can give thanks for the times he has already sustained you.
exp.12:12:
Tamar tells Amnon that if he forces himself on her, she will carry her shame wherever she goes, and he would be left looking like one of the fools, people who lack good sense and respect for God. Then she asks him to speak with the king, since the king would not refuse him.

Tamar, the daughter of King David, speaks to her half-brother Amnon, who already has her cornered. She tries to stop him with reasons. Her remark about asking the king's permission can be understood in several ways: some think she only wanted to buy time, since the Law forbade that marriage. The Bible does not make this clear.

Today: when someone says "no," that "no" must always be respected. If someone confides that they have suffered abuse, listen to them, believe them, and help them seek protection. Staying silent is never neutral.
exp.21:49:
David says he will praise the LORD openly, even before the nations that are not Israel. "I will praise You" here does not mean admitting sins, but recognizing and declaring with praise who God is. "Among the nations" refers to the foreign peoples. David also says he will sing praises to the name of the LORD.

David speaks, already in his old age, in a song of gratitude because God rescued him from his enemies, among them Saul. This same song appears almost word for word in Psalm 18. After telling how God rescued him and gave him victory, David responds with praise. According to the New Testament, Paul quotes this verse in Romans 15:9 to speak of the nations also praising God.

When God helps you through a difficulty, do not keep your thankfulness to yourself. Tell someone about it this week and praise Him with a song or a prayer aloud.
exp.2:26:
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab pulled him aside into the gateway, as if to speak with him privately. Joab was gentle and seemed friendly. There, right on the spot, he stabbed Abner in the stomach, and Abner died. The reason given is the death of Asahel, Joab's brother.

The narrator tells this after Abner made a peace agreement with David. Joab did not trust him, so he brought Abner back without David knowing. Earlier, Abner had killed Asahel in battle. Interpreters see in Joab a desire for revenge and perhaps also a fear of losing his position.

For today: revenge hides its anger behind kind words. Ask God to heal your wounds and to free you from repaying evil with evil.
exp.2:31:
This verse tells us that Abner was buried in Hebron. King David wept aloud at his tomb, and all the people wept with him. The words "wept aloud" mean that he mourned openly, without hiding his grief.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army. Joab and his brother Abishai had killed him to avenge the death of their brother Asahel. David had not ordered that crime, and with this public mourning he wanted to show that he had no part in it. Some believe he also sought to calm the people and keep peace among the tribes. The text says nothing more about his motives.

When someone dies unjustly, we should not stay silent or indifferent. To mourn sincerely and to reject violence and revenge is also a way of defending justice and peace.
exp.22:27:
This verse names two of King David's brave warriors: Zalmon, who came from Ahoh, and Maharai, who was from Netophah. In this list, each man's name is joined to his town or his family. In the Reina-Valera 1909 the names are written in an older form. Some modern versions write "Zalmon the Ahohite" and "Maharai the Netophathite."

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. He is closing the account of David's reign with the list of his thirty most outstanding warriors. We know almost nothing more about them, because the Bible records only their names. That shows that God and the people remembered their service.

For today: God sees and remembers faithful service, even when no one applauds it. Serve where you are, with steadiness and humility, without seeking fame.
exp.2:32:
Here David composes a lament for Abner and asks a question: "Should Abner die the death of a fool?" The word "lament" means a mourning song or speech for the dead. "Fool" here refers to a foolish or wicked man, someone who dies because of his own guilt or as a criminal.

David speaks in public during Abner's funeral. Abner was the commander of Saul's army, and Joab had killed him treacherously in Hebron. David wants everyone to see that he took no part in that crime. For this reason he orders mourning, walks behind the coffin, and weeps. The verses that follow explain that Abner fell in an ambush, not through a fair trial.

Today, this passage invites us to reject violence and injustice, and to weep sincerely when someone suffers harm. It also encourages us to act with integrity, so that our actions and our grief show what is truly in the heart.
exp.16:3:
This verse says that the proposal Ahitofel had just made seemed good to Absalom and to all the leaders of Israel. The word "elders" refers to the respected heads and authorities of the people. "Proposal" here means the plan or advice that was put forward.

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and Ahitofel was a highly respected counselor who was now supporting him. His plan was to attack David at night, when he would be exhausted, and to kill only him. Although everyone agreed, Absalom also wanted to hear Hushai, who in reality was loyal to David. In this way God was going to frustrate the counsel of Ahitofel.

That something seems good to many does not mean it is right. Before following advice, it is wise to pray, to listen to other wise voices, and to ask ourselves whether it honors God.
exp.3:5:
Two brothers entered Ish-bosheth's house pretending to be wheat merchants, as if they had come to do some business. The verse says they came in as if to get some wheat, which describes their disguise. They stabbed him in the stomach, near the ribs, and then slipped away. The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, so the exact wording is debated.

The narrator of the book tells how Ish-bosheth, son of Saul and David's rival, was treacherously murdered while taking an afternoon nap. Rechab and Baanah were his captains. They killed their own king, believing David would reward them. But later David punished them for this instead of rewarding them.

For today: do not use deceit or violence to achieve what seems good or convenient. God does not need our tricks, and gaining something through wickedness rarely ends well.
exp.13:15:
The woman trusts that the king will listen to her and rescue her from the man who wants to cut off her and her son from God's inheritance. In the original, the word behind "cut off" means to wipe out or eliminate, and "God's inheritance" refers to the land and people of Israel, the place where they had their home.

A woman from Tekoa speaks, sent by Joab with an invented story about two sons, one of whom killed the other. Through that story she seeks to make David reflect on his son Absalom, who was banished for killing Amnon. She asks that her son not be cut off from the family, and so she prepares the way for David to see his own situation.

For today: God teaches us to seek paths of restoration, not only of punishment. Before shutting the door on someone, ask yourself whether there is a fair and loving way to reconcile.
exp.9:7:
The explanation says that the men of Ammon came out of their city and lined up for battle at the entrance of the city gate. The Arameans they had hired, from Zobah, Rehob, Tob, and Maacah, did not join them but stayed apart, out in the open country. The word "companies" in the verse refers to groups of soldiers, and "by themselves" means separately.

The narrator tells of the war between Israel and Ammon. The Ammonites had shamed David's messengers and knew that this would bring consequences. That is why they paid foreign armies. With the Ammonites facing the gate and the Arameans in the open country, Joab was surrounded on two fronts, as the following context shows.

For today: when we act wrongly, it is tempting to look for support from any side before admitting the mistake. That kind of security is often fragile. It is better to make things right with humility and trust in God, not in compromised alliances.
exp.15:20:
Here Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with the concubines whom David has left behind to take care of the palace. The phrase "sleep with" refers to intimate relations with them. The words "a stench to your father" mean that Absalom would become a openly rejected enemy of his father, with no possibility of making peace. In this way, Absalom's followers would be encouraged, because they would see that there was no turning back.

Ahithophel was a highly respected counselor who had previously served David and now supported the rebellion. His plan was a public act of rupture and of seizing power. Years earlier, the prophet Nathan had announced that disgrace would come upon David's house (2 Samuel 12:11-12), although the Bible does not make this wickedness right.

For today: a counsel that is much admired can still be evil. Before following an idea, test it against the Word of God and with a humble heart, not only by who says it.
exp.11:26:
Joab sends word to David that he has already fought against Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and has captured the water supply of the city. The explanation notes that the words "sent" and "messengers" are plain, and that the word for "fought" carries the sense of struggling against an opponent. The water supply was probably the part of Rabbah that controlled the city's water, and some scholars take the phrase to point to the royal quarter. Scholars explain this in different ways.

Joab, David's general, is the one speaking. Israel was at war with the Ammonites, and David had stayed behind in Jerusalem. Joab had nearly conquered the city already, but he wants David to come and complete the victory, so that the honor belongs to the king and not to Joab. This comes right after David's sin and the word of Nathan.

For today: learn not to take credit that belongs to others. When you accomplish something, acknowledge those who gave you the opportunity, and work with humility and loyalty, without seeking your own fame.
exp.22:32:
Shammah the Hararite and Ahiam, son of Sharar the Hararite, were among David's brave men. Both came from Harar. They appear here only as names in a list, and no story is told of what they did. The parallel names in 1 Chronicles 11:34-35 are similar but not identical, so it is not certain whether these are the same men or differences that crept in while the text was copied.

The verse belongs to the list of David's most outstanding warriors, called "the thirty," which comes after the account of David's last words. The writer names them so that those who stood with David in battle and in his reign are remembered. That men with no recorded deeds are still named shows that their service mattered.

For today: God sees and remembers faithful service even when it goes unnoticed. You do not need to be famous or stand out to be important in his work. Serve steadily where you are, trusting that God values what you do.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated the entire army of Hadadezer. The verse is left unfinished, and the idea continues in the next one.

The narrator recounts David's victories over neighboring kingdoms. Hamath was north of Israel, and Toi was an enemy of Hadadezer. So when he learned of the defeat, he sent his son Joram with gifts and greetings of peace. In this way Toi acknowledged David's power and sought his friendship. David dedicated those gifts to the LORD.

For today: David did not keep the gifts or the fame for himself, but dedicated them to God. When we receive achievements, blessings, or recognition, we can do the same: thank God and put what we have at his service, rather than boasting.
exp.11:23:
Here it says that David comforted his wife Bathsheba, who was also grieving the death of their son. Later they had another son, and they named him Solomon. The text states that the LORD loved the child.

The phrase "he went to her and lay with her" refers to their marriage relationship, meaning they were intimate with each other. "So she gave birth to a son" simply means that she bore a child.

The narrator tells what happened after David and Bathsheba's first son died, a child born after the sin of both of them. David stopped fasting and accepted what had happened. Then the account shows that God did not abandon them. The name Solomon is related to a Hebrew word meaning "peace," though some explain it in other ways.

For today: when someone suffers a loss, we can accompany them with tenderness and patience. We can also trust that God, in his mercy, can bring new hope after pain and repentance.
exp.17:2:
The men of David tell him not to go with them into the battle. "You must not go out" means "you will not go." "If we have to flee" is their way of saying what might happen if the army runs. They say that the enemy would not care about them, even if half of them died. They also tell David that he is worth ten thousand of them, and they ask him instead to support them from the city.

David is fleeing from his son Absalom, who rebelled against him. He has organized his army into three groups and wants to go with them. The people speak out of love and out of reason: if the king is killed, everything is lost. David accepts their advice and stays at the gate.

For today: sometimes loving means accepting the advice of wise people who care for us, even when we want to do everything ourselves. Knowing how to listen is a form of humility and wisdom.
exp.22:3:
This verse compares the just ruler to the light of a cloudless morning at sunrise. It also compares him to the glistening grass that sprouts on the earth after rain. The word "ruler" here means the one who governs or has authority. The idea is that a leader who fears God brings clarity, freshness, and life to his people.

David speaks in what the Bible calls his final words. He says that God himself gave him this message by his Spirit. He describes what someone who governs should be like. In the verses that follow, he admits that his own house is not perfect, but he trusts in the covenant God made with him. Some also see here a look forward to the Messiah, the perfect King.

For today: if you have any authority, in your home, your work, or your church, try to exercise it with justice and respect for God. In this way your conduct can be like a clear dawn that brings encouragement and helps others to grow.
exp.8:1:
It says there was a servant from Saul's family named Ziba. He was summoned to David, and the king asked him, "Are you Ziba?" Ziba replied, "I am your servant," a humble way of saying "at your service."

David has just asked whether anyone is left from the house of Saul to show kindness to, remembering his promise of friendship with Jonathan. Since Saul had been his enemy, searching for his descendants was not the usual thing to do in that time. Ziba, who knew that family well, will be the one to give him the lead about Mephibosheth.

Today: David's kindness grew out of a fulfilled promise. Think of someone to whom you owe gratitude or a word you gave, and look today for a concrete way to show them care, even if a long time has passed.
exp.11:11:
He says that David sinned in secret, but God would bring the consequences into the open, in broad daylight, before all the people. "In broad daylight" means in full view, where everyone can see. "I will do this thing" refers to the punishment announced earlier: violence and dishonor within his own family.

The speaker is the prophet Nathan, sent by God to David. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and had Uriah killed to cover up his sin. Nathan tells him that God saw everything. Later, the story of his family shows serious conflicts, and many see this as part of these consequences.

For today: what is hidden is not hidden from God. Instead of covering up a wrong, it is better to confess it soon, as David did, and trust in God's forgiveness, even though some consequences may remain.
exp.22:31:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions Eliahba, from Shaalbon (a town or place), and Jonathan, described as one of "the sons of Jashen." No one knows for certain who Jashen was; some scholars believe the original text has a small variation, and the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 11 reads differently.

The writer is the narrator of the book, who presents David's mighty men, called "the thirty." He does not want only to recount battles, but to acknowledge the men who supported the king with loyalty and courage. They come from different places, united by a single purpose.

For today: God notices people whom sometimes no one remembers. Serve faithfully wherever you are, even if your name is not famous; God does not forget your work.
exp.10:4:
What it says: Bathsheba became pregnant after she had been with David. She sent word to the king with a short message: "I am pregnant." "Conceived" means that she became pregnant, and "sent word" means that she sent a message to him.

Context: The speaker is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, a soldier who was away at war. David, as king, had her brought to him and he lay with her. The text reports the event in few words and does not say what she felt. Because the king had so much power, many believe she could not refuse, although the Bible does not make this clear. This notice puts David face to face with the consequences of his sin, and it leads him to try to hide it.

For today: A hidden sin does not disappear; sooner or later its consequences come to light. It is better to confess in time and ask God for forgiveness, rather than cover up one wrong with more wrongs.
exp.22:9:
This verse speaks of Eleazar, one of David's mighty men. He stood his ground and struck down the Philistines until he was worn out; his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword, as if it had cramped. The LORD brought about a great victory that day, and afterward the troops came back to Eleazar, but only to plunder the dead left on the field.

These are among the last words of David, in which his bravest men are remembered. The account highlights Eleazar's courage, but it credits the victory to the LORD. The Bible does not explain why the others had withdrawn earlier; it only shows that Eleazar stayed firm when others pulled back.

For today: God can use our perseverance, even when we feel alone or tired. Keep doing what is right with faithfulness, and remember that the final result comes from God.
exp.14:27:
David tells Zadok and Abiathar that he will wait at the fords in the wilderness, that is, at the crossing places near the Jordan, until word comes from them. "You" and "your" refer to the priests and to their sons. The phrase "to inform me" means to let him know what is happening.

David speaks as he flees from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. He had asked that the ark of God be returned to the city, and he places his future in God's hands. The priests and their sons would serve as his messengers and would keep him informed of what happened. Some also see here a prudent strategy, not only faith.

For today: in times of crisis, trust God, but act with wisdom. Wait with patience and seek the counsel of faithful people, without rushing ahead.
exp.2:36:
On that day, all the troops and all Israel were convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner, son of Ner. In other words, Abner's death was not David's idea, and he had not ordered it.

The narrator is speaking here. Joab, the commander of David's army, had killed Abner, and many could have suspected David. But David wept publicly, fasted, and honored Abner at his burial. Through those actions, the people saw that he was sincere. The text does not say David proved this with words, but through his conduct.

For today: when someone doubts you, the best answer is usually to live with integrity and humility, not only to defend yourself with words. God sees the heart, and over time your actions speak.
exp.0:2:
David asks a man who has just arrived, "Where have you come from?" The man answers, "I have escaped from the Israelite camp."

David is speaking at Ziklag, where he is waiting for news after defeating the Amalekites. The man arrives with torn clothes and dirt on his head, signs of mourning and grief in that culture. Later he will say that Saul and Jonathan died. As the story goes on, we will see that his account of how Saul died includes details the Bible does not confirm, so it is wise to read it carefully.

For today: when strong news arrives, ask calmly and listen closely before you react. David asked for facts and then asked more questions. Doing the same helps us be prudent and keeps us from being carried away by rumors.
exp.22:11:
This verse tells how Shammah, one of David's mighty men, took his stand in the middle of a field full of lentils and defended it. He struck down the Philistines, and the LORD brought about a great victory.

The phrase "the middle of the field" refers to a plot of land in the middle of the action. "Victory" here means a decisive win in battle. "Struck down" means that he defeated them in combat.

The passage appears in a list of David's mighty men, near the end of Second Samuel. The narrator points out that the people had fled, but Shammah held his position. Although the field seemed like a small thing, he did not give it up, and the account credits the triumph to the LORD, not only to the warrior.

For today: sometimes we are called to defend something that seems small, such as honesty, family, or faith, when others give up. We can stand firm with humility, trusting that the LORD gives the victory.
exp.19:24:
This verse closes a list of King David's main officials. Sheva was the scribe, that is, the secretary who put the affairs of the kingdom in writing. Zadok and Abiathar were priests, in charge of religious service. Ira the Jairite was the chief minister near David; the term "chief minister" can be understood as an adviser or a high assistant. Some sources call him a priest, and it is not entirely clear what his exact role was.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator's account. After the rebellion of Sheva son of Bichri, the story shows that the kingdom was once again put in order. The list reveals an organized government, with military leaders, administrators, scribes and priests.

For today: God values order and steady service. Every task, even one that goes unnoticed, like that of the scribe, helps the community function. Serve faithfully wherever you are.
exp.18:36:
Barzilai asks King David to let him go back home so that he may die in his own city and be buried beside his father and mother. In his place he offers Chimham, his servant, to cross over with the king and receive his kindness. The phrase "do for him what is good in your sight" means: treat him however you think is right.

Barzilai, a man of eighty years and very wealthy, had provided food and shelter for David and his people when they were fleeing from Absalom. Now David wants to reward him by taking him to Jerusalem. Barzilai, because of his age, humbly declines. It is not known with certainty who Chimham was; many think he was Barzilai's son, but the text does not say so.

For today: we can recognize our limits and the stages of life. Barzilai did not cling to honors or comforts, but preferred to be in his own home and to bless someone younger. We can do the same: serve with generosity, accept with gratitude what no longer belongs to us, and make way for others.
exp.19:19:
Joab answers with force: "Far be it! Never!" He says that he does not want to swallow up or destroy the city. The phrase "Far be it from me" means something like "God forbid that I would do such a thing." And "destroy" means to ruin or tear down.

Joab, commander of David's army, was pursuing Sheba, who had rebelled against the king. Sheba took refuge in the city of Abel, and Joab besieged it. A wise woman called to him from the wall, and Joab made clear that his aim was not to level the city, but to capture the rebel. In this way a massacre was avoided.

For today: before reacting harshly, it is wise to listen and to clarify what we truly seek. Often a calm conversation prevents greater harm and makes it possible to solve the problem without hurting the innocent.
exp.4:24:
David did exactly what the LORD had commanded him. He defeated the Philistines, and he struck them down all the way from Gibeon to Gezer. Here "struck down" means that he defeated them in battle. Some versions name the starting place as Geba rather than Gibeon, so the place names can vary depending on the manuscript.

David was at war with the Philistines, who wanted to defeat him as soon as he became king over all of Israel. Before fighting, David inquired of God, and God gave him a strategy: surround the enemy and wait for a sign, the sound of marching in the tops of the trees. Then God himself would go out ahead of him.

Today, before important decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer and in his Word. Then obey with patience, waiting for his timing even when his plan does not look like yours.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that David was now settled in his palace. God had given him rest from all the enemies around him. The word "settled" means that he was established and secure in his home. The phrase "from all his enemies around him" means that the threats came from every side. "Rest" means peace and quiet.

The narrator of the book tells how David's life stood after many wars. With that peace, David begins to think about God and notices that he lives in a house of cedar, while the ark of the covenant still stays in a tent. For this reason he speaks with the prophet Nathan. Nathan opens a very important moment: God will respond with a promise about David's descendants.

For today: when God gives you a time of calm, do not use it only to rest or to get comfortable. Ask yourself how you can thank him and serve him better, with your time, your possessions, or your attention to others.
exp.0:15:
David tells the man who has just been condemned, "Your blood be on your own head," meaning that the guilt for his death rests on him, not on David. The man had said with his own mouth, "I killed the LORD's anointed." The word "anointed" refers to the king chosen by God.

David speaks after hearing news of Saul's death. A young Amalekite claimed to have killed him, hoping for a reward. According to 1 Samuel 31, Saul had taken his own life, so it is possible that the young man was lying or exaggerating. David did not reward him but judged him by his own words, since he respected Saul as the king God had set in place.

For today: our words carry weight and bind us. Let us speak with truth, without seeking advantage through lies, and respect what God considers sacred.
exp.22:16:
Here David says that he cannot drink the water that his three mighty men brought him. They risked their lives to get it, so David compares it to their blood. The words "Far be it from me" are a strong way of saying "I would never do such a thing." Then he poured it out before God as an offering, and the text stresses that these three mighty men performed this deed.

David speaks during a time of war against the Philistines. He had a passing longing for water from his town, Bethlehem, which at that moment was held by the enemy. Out of loyalty, his soldiers broke through the enemy lines to bring it to him. David understood that something so precious was not for his own pleasure, but to honor God.

For today: value the sacrifice of those who serve you, and do not use others to satisfy your whims. When someone gives themselves for you, respond with gratitude and with reverence toward God.
exp.22:37:
This verse continues the list of David's mighty men. It names two men, Ira and Gareb, and says that both were "the Ithrite." That probably means they came from the family of the Ithrites, a clan that lived in Kiriath-jearim, though some think it may have been a different group or place. The Bible tells us nothing more about them.

The text has no direct speaker. It is the narrator of Samuel who keeps the record of the warriors who helped David in his reign. The list ends with "thirty-seven," since it includes the famous "thirty" and other leaders. These names are mentioned to acknowledge their service, even though they did no deeds that are recounted.

For today: God sees and remembers those who serve faithfully, even when no one else notices. You do not need to be famous to be valuable in his work. Do your work with steadiness, because the Lord does not forget what you do out of love and loyalty (Hebrews 6:10).
exp.11:16:
It says that the elders of David's household stood beside him to help him up from the ground, where he was lying. But he was unwilling and would not eat anything with them. "Elders of his household" refers to the older men of his family or his court whom he trusted.

The narrator recounts what happened after David's sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. Nathan confronted him, and the child of the two of them fell ill. David, in grief and repentance, fasted and pleaded with God for the child's life. The elders did not want to see him suffer so much, but he kept crying out to God.

When pain crushes us, there is no single right way to react, but we can do what David did: bring our anguish to God with sincerity. And if someone is suffering, walking alongside them with tenderness is worth more than hurrying them to feel better.
exp.22:34:
This verse mentions two more of David's brave warriors: Hezro, who was from the area of Carmel, and Paarai, who was from Arbi. Some readers know the first name spelled differently, as Hezrai, and many write it Paarai as well. Both are places in the territory of Judah.

The text is not a speech but a list that forms part of the end of the book. Here the "thirty" warriors who accompanied and defended David are named. About these two men we know nothing more from this chapter: only their names and their origin. Some scholars think the list honors their loyalty, although the text gives no further details.

God notices those who serve faithfully, even when almost no one remembers their story. If your work goes unnoticed in your family, your church, or your job, keep going with perseverance. What is done faithfully is not lost before God.
exp.12:8:
Tamar brought the pan and set the food down in front of Amnon, but he would not eat it. Then he told everyone, "Send them all away," and everyone left the room.

Amnon, David's son, was pretending to be sick. Tamar, his half-sister, had come at her father's request to look after him. By refusing to eat and sending everyone away, Amnon left himself alone with her. The text does not say so here, but what follows shows that this was part of a plan to harm her.

For today: when someone insists on being alone with you in a strange way, or pressures you to be, do not ignore it. God cares for the vulnerable, and we too must protect them, believe them, and speak up in time.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that Abner, the commander of Saul's army, made Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, king. He set him up as king over Gilead, Asher, Jezreel, Ephraim, and Benjamin, and over all Israel. The word for "made him king" means "raised him up" or "proclaimed him."

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not one of the characters. Saul had died, and David was already king of Judah in Hebron. Abner, however, did not want to hand over power to David, so he put Ish-bosheth on the throne. Some think he did this out of loyalty to Saul's family, while others think he also wanted to keep his own influence. The text does not make this clear. In this way the people were divided.

For today: before supporting any leader, ask yourself whether they are seeking God's will or only human interests. Ask God for wisdom to act with humility and not out of pride.
exp.18:13:
This verse says that the hearts of all the men of Judah were swayed, as though they were one man, toward David. Then they sent him a message: "Return, you and all your servants." The verse's word "swayed" means that something moved them to change their attitude, and "servants" refers to his followers.

David, already king, had fled from Jerusalem when his son Absalom rebelled, and Absalom died. Now the people hesitated to bring him back. David sent messengers to the elders of Judah, reminding them that they were his own family, and offered Amasa, Absalom's former commander, the command of the army. The text says that something "swayed" the hearts, and it does not make clear whether this refers to David, to his message, or to God at work.

Today, after a conflict, humility and kind words can open the way to reconciliation. We can take the first step, even when others hesitate.
exp.4:14:
This verse is part of a list of sons born to David in Jerusalem. Three names appear here: Ibhar, Elishua, and Nepheg. The word "and" is not in this verse, so the names are simply listed one after another. The list continues in the next verse.

The author of the book, whom Jewish tradition associates with Samuel and other writers, tells how David established himself as king in Jerusalem. After mentioning that he took more wives, the account lists his children. This shows that his kingdom was growing and becoming secure. Nothing more is said about these three sons here. Moreover, the Bible does not hide the fact that this practice of having many wives would bring trouble to his household.

For today: God pays attention to every person, even to names that are barely mentioned. Remember that your life matters to Him, even when others do not notice it. Also think about how our decisions at home leave a mark on our children.
exp.0:22:
The explanation says that Saul and Jonathan were beloved and delightful in life, and that in death they were not divided. They were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions. The phrases about being beloved and about not being divided are explained as meaning dear to others and joined together, respectively.

David speaks in a song of mourning, sometimes called "the song of the bow." He has just learned that Saul and Jonathan died in battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. Although Saul had pursued him to kill him, David does not rejoice: he honors both of them and weeps openly. Some think that "were not divided" refers only to dying together in battle, although their relationship as father and son was not always harmonious.

Today we can learn to remember the good in people, even in those who hurt us. In the face of a loss, instead of holding on to resentment, we can thank God for what was valuable in them and honor with respect the one who has passed away.
exp.16:1:
Here Ahithophel proposes attacking David by surprise. "Weak and weary" means without strength, worn out and discouraged. "Attack him" means to fall on him suddenly. His plan is to throw David into a panic so that the people with him will flee, and so strike down only the king.

Ahithophel had been David's counselor, but he joined the rebellion of Absalom, the king's son. David was fleeing from Jerusalem, exhausted and saddened by the betrayal of his son. Ahithophel takes advantage of that moment of weakness and proposes acting that very night, before David can regroup.

For today: a piece of advice can sound very logical and still be unjust or harmful. Before following an idea, it is good to ask whether it is right before God, not only whether it is convenient. And if you are weary today, remember that God cares for the weak.
exp.17:28:
The explanation says that King David, anxious, does not ask about the battle but about his son: "Is the young man Absalom all right?" In other words, he wants to know whether Absalom is well. Ahimaaz answers that when Joab sent them, he saw a great tumult, but he does not know what it was.

After Absalom's rebellion, his army was defeated. Ahimaaz ran with the news of the victory, but Joab knew that Absalom had died. Many understand that Ahimaaz avoids telling the hard truth, perhaps because he did not know it well or because he did not dare. David, as a father, still loves his rebellious son.

Today we can learn to speak the truth with love and honesty, without hiding it out of fear. And we can also remember that, even when someone fails us, a parent's love can continue to ache and ask for prayer and God's comfort.
exp.19:10:
One of Joab's young soldiers stood near Amasa and called out: "Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, follow Joab!" Here "young soldiers" refers to men serving under Joab's command. "Stood near" means he stopped and stayed beside the body.

Joab had just treacherously killed Amasa, his rival, by pretending to greet him as a friend. David had appointed Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab, and now Sheba, who had rebelled, had to be pursued. The soldiers were stopping by the body, and this young man wanted them to keep moving. His words mix loyalty to Joab with loyalty to the king, even though Joab had just committed a crime.

Today, loyalty to a person must not blind us to injustice. Let us be faithful to God first, and not excuse wrongdoing out of affection or the pressure of the group.
exp.8:3:
Here David asks where Jonathan's son is, and Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, tells him that he is staying at the house of Machir, son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar. The phrase "that one" in the earlier wording points to the son who was lame in his feet, whom Ziba had just mentioned.

David wanted to show kindness, a goodness that reflects the faithful love of God, because of the promise he had made to his friend Jonathan. Ziba is the one who provides the information. Little is known about Lo-debar, which lies east of the Jordan. The text does not explain why Mephibosheth was there, though it may have been a place of refuge and little visibility.

For today: God and his people seek out those who have been forgotten or hidden away. Think of someone who is alone or set aside, and look for a concrete way to show them kindness this week, with a visit, a phone call, or some help.
exp.1:1:
This verse tells us that David went to Hebron, as God had directed him. He went with his two wives: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, who had been the wife of Nabal of Carmel before Nabal died. Hebron sits on higher ground, which is why the text says David "went up" there.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not David himself. Saul had died, and David did not simply act on his own initiative. He first asked God where to go. By naming his wives, the account shows that David was not traveling alone but with his household. Afterward, in Hebron, the people of Judah anointed him as king.

For today: before making an important decision, bring it to God in prayer and seek his direction. And remember that your decisions also affect your family, so move forward with them in mind.
exp.15:7:
Shimei tells David that the LORD is paying him back for all the blood spilled from Saul's family. In his view, David has ruled in Saul's place, and now the kingdom is going to Absalom. He says David has come to ruin and calls him "a man of bloodshed" (a violent man, guilty of killings).

Shimei, a relative of Saul, speaks while David is fleeing Jerusalem because of Absalom's rebellion. He insults David and throws stones at him. His accusation is doubtful, because the Bible does not say that David killed Saul's family in order to reign. Even so, David does not respond with revenge; he considers that the LORD may be using this insult.

When someone criticizes us harshly, even if the criticism is unfair or ill-intentioned, we can pause our reaction and ask ourselves with humility: Is there something here that God wants to teach me?
exp.22:14:
David expresses a wish out loud: he longed for a drink of fresh water from the well near the gate of his hometown, Bethlehem. A "well" is a pit or reservoir that holds water, and "Oh, that someone would get me a drink" is a simple way of saying "I wish someone would bring me a drink."

David speaks in a difficult moment. He is hiding in a stronghold while the Philistines occupy Bethlehem, his town. It was probably a sigh of homesickness rather than a command. Even so, three of his mighty men risked their lives to bring him the water, and David, moved by it, did not drink it but poured it out before God.

For today: value the sacrifices others make for you and respond with humility and gratitude. Also, be careful with your words, because a simple wish can lead others to take risks. Honor God above your own desires.
exp.16:5:
This verse tells of Hushai coming to Absalom. Absalom repeated to him what Ahithophel had proposed and asked whether they should carry it out or not. He asked for his opinion, saying, "What do you say?"

Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and Ahithophel was his chief counselor. Hushai, on the other hand, was a friend of David and pretended to support Absalom in order to hold back Ahithophel's plan. The Bible says afterward that the Lord determined to defeat the good advice of Ahithophel (17:14).

For today: before making an important decision, do not rely on just one voice. Seek advice, but pray and examine who is giving it and with what intention. God can guide you even through people who act with wisdom.
exp.21:45:
This verse says that foreigners, or people who were not part of the nation of Israel, lost their courage and were filled with fear. "Lose heart" means they grew weak from dread. The "strongholds" are the fortified places where they had taken cover, and the verse pictures them coming out of those places trembling.

David, now an older man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God for rescuing him from Saul and his enemies. He acknowledges that his victory and his kingdom came not by his own strength alone, but by the help of the Lord, whom he calls his rock.

For today: when problems or people make you feel intimidated, remember that God is your firmest refuge. Instead of relying only on your own resources, pray and give thanks for the times He has sustained you, and walk with courage and humility.
exp.6:11:
When David dies (the phrase "rest with your fathers" is a way of speaking of death), God will raise up one of his descendants. The word "descendant" means offspring, and "who will come from your own body" means that this will be a son of his own. God promises that he "will establish his kingdom," that is, he will make it firm and secure.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple for God, but God answers that he himself will make David a "house," meaning a dynasty. The promise was first fulfilled in Solomon, and many Christians see its full fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we do not see the result. David would not see everything that was promised, but he trusted. We can do the same and trust that God continues to work beyond our lives.
exp.11:12:
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan replied that the LORD has taken away his sin, meaning He has forgiven it, and that David will not die. Here "taken away" means that the guilt is lifted.

Nathan, a prophet of God, had confronted David over his adultery with Bathsheba and over having ordered the death of Uriah. God had announced serious consequences. When David breaks down and confesses, forgiveness comes. However, the text shows that forgiveness does not erase all the consequences: the child would die.

If we have failed, it is not wise to hide it or make excuses for ourselves. We can confess it honestly to God, trusting in his forgiveness. And, although some consequences may remain, God does not abandon us.
exp.14:0:
He says that, some time later, Absalom provided a chariot with horses for himself, along with fifty men to run ahead of him. The Berean wording makes clear that Absalom arranged these things for his own use. The fifty runners went before him like an escort that announced his coming and made him look important.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not one of the characters. Absalom was the son of King David. He had returned to Jerusalem after being exiled for killing his brother Amnon. This display of power seems to be the start of his plan to win over the people, and the verses that follow show how he gradually won the heart of Israel. Many see it as preparation for taking the throne from his father, though here the text only describes the events.

Today we can ask ourselves what we seek when we present ourselves before others. It is worth examining whether we serve with humility or whether we use our image and influence to make ourselves look great.
exp.19:5:
Here David tells Abishai, his nephew and military commander, that Sheba, the son of Bichri, will do more harm than Absalom did. He tells him to take the king's servants, that is, the loyal soldiers, and go after Sheba. The fear is that Sheba will reach fortified cities and get away from them.

Sheba had just stirred up a rebellion against David, right after Absalom's revolt. David had asked Amasa to gather the men of Judah within three days, but Amasa was slow. That is why David acts with urgency, before the problem grows. The Bible does not explain all his reasons, but his concern is clear.

For today: it is not wise to let a small problem grow through neglect. With prayer and wisdom, it is good to face it in time, before it causes more harm.
exp.15:16:
Absalom asks Hushai whether this is the loyalty he shows to his friend David. The verse uses "loyalty" for the word the older translation rendered as "kindness," meaning faithful devotion. Absalom is surprised that Hushai did not go with David when David fled from Jerusalem.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David and had just entered Jerusalem. Hushai, David's friend, came and greeted him as king. Absalom suspects him and tests him. Many understand that Hushai was acting in secret to help David, although the text does not say so in this verse; the account that follows shows it.

For today: when someone questions your loyalty, act with wisdom and sincerity before God. Ask Him to guide you to be faithful to people and to what is right, without being carried away by the pressure of the moment.
exp.10:13:
The text says that the next morning David wrote a letter to Joab, his general, and sent it with Uriah himself. The phrase "sent it with Uriah" means that Uriah was the one who carried it.

The passage follows the story of David, Bathsheba, and Uriah. David had sinned with Bathsheba, who was pregnant. He wanted Uriah to sleep with his wife to cover it up, but Uriah did not go home, not even when he was drunk. So David moved to a worse plan. Without knowing it, Uriah was carrying his own death sentence, as the following verses show.

For today: a hidden sin often leads to another, more serious one. If you have failed, do not cover it up with lies or manipulation. Confess to God and seek help in time, as David later did (Psalm 51).
exp.6:17:
David went in before God, sat before the LORD, and prayed. He asked, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my family, that You have brought me this far?" In plain terms, he was asking, "What am I worth, and what has my family done to deserve this?" He wanted to understand why God had raised him to a place of honor. The phrase about sitting before the LORD means that he came into God's presence and remained there in prayer, and the text allows for that idea of him settling in to pray.

David speaks as king now. He has just heard, through the prophet Nathan, God's promise that his family and his kingdom would be established forever. David does not answer with pride but with wonder and gratitude, acknowledging that everything he has is a gift from God.

For today: when you receive blessings or achievements, follow David's example. Before taking credit, pause to give thanks, recognize that God has brought you this far, and pray with a humble heart.
exp.20:15:
During another battle against the Philistines, a warrior named Ishbi-benob resolved to kill David. He was a descendant of Rapha, a line of very tall and strong men. His bronze spear weighed about three hundred shekels, close to three and a half kilograms. He was also carrying a new sword.

Here the book's narrator speaks. He tells that David, already an older man, went out to fight and grew weary. At that moment he was left vulnerable. The Bible does not explain in detail where this line of giants came from; it only shows that they were fearsome enemies. Soon Abishai rescued David, and his men decided that he would no longer go out to battle.

No one can carry everything alone, not even a strong leader. Recognizing our weariness and letting others help us is not weakness but wisdom. God often cares for us through people close to us.
exp.0:17:
This verse is a short note before David's song. It says David ordered the people of Judah to be taught the Song of the Bow, and that it is written in the Book of Jashar. In Hebrew this book is called the Book of Jashar, which means "the upright" or "the just." It was an ancient collection of songs that we no longer have. The word "bow" may be the name of the song, or it may mean that the song was to be learned with a bow in hand. It is not certain.

The narrator explains why David composed this lament, a funeral song, after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. David wanted Judah to learn it and remember it.

Today we too can honor those who have passed away, even those who hurt us, by remembering what was good with respect. Turning grief into prayer or into a song helps us heal and not forget.
exp.6:12:
God says that a son of David will build a temple to honor his name. In return, God himself will establish the throne of that kingdom forever. The word "forever" is part of the verse's wording, so its meaning is simply that the throne will last without end. The temple is the house in this passage, though the word "house" can also mean a family or a royal line.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a house for God, but God answers that he will build a house for David, meaning a royal line of descendants. Many understand that the first fulfillment was Solomon, who built the temple. Christians also see a fuller fulfillment in Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: God keeps his promises even when we do not see the full result. We can serve him faithfully and trust that he keeps working beyond our lifetime.
exp.11:5:
David says the rich man must pay back the little ewe lamb four times over. The word "tantos," meaning "times," would mean paying four times its value. He gives the reason: the man has done this thing and has shown no pity, that is, he felt no compassion for the poor man.

Here David speaks as king and judge. The prophet Nathan had told him a story about a rich man who took away a poor man's only little ewe lamb. David did not know the story was about himself, because of his sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah. The law of Moses required paying four sheep for a stolen and slaughtered sheep (Exodus 22:1). Without knowing it, David pronounced his own sentence.

For today: it is easy to see clearly the sin of others and to soften our own. Let us ask God for a humble heart that examines itself first and acts with mercy.
exp.21:46:
David says that the LORD lives, and he blesses his Rock with strength and joy. He calls God "my Rock," meaning a firm place where he is safe. Since the verse reads "blessed be my Rock," the phrase can be understood as the Rock that holds him up. "May God, the Rock of my salvation, be exalted" means that God be lifted up and honored. "The Rock of my salvation" means the firm place from which my rescue comes. David wants everyone to recognize the greatness of God.

David, the king of Israel, speaks in a song of thanksgiving near the end of his life. He wrote it when the LORD delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, as the beginning of the chapter indicates. The verses before it tell how foreigners submitted to him in fear. David does not claim the victory for himself; he gives it to God.

For today: when you get through a difficulty, don't stop at relief alone. Take a moment to thank God out loud, acknowledging that he was your firm refuge.
exp.15:5:
Shimei, while cursing David, threw stones at him and at all of King David's servants. Even so, the troops and all the mighty men stayed close to the king, on his right and on his left. In other words, David was surrounded and protected.

The narrator tells this moment while David is fleeing from Jerusalem because of the rebellion of his son Absalom. Shimei, of the family of Saul, takes advantage of the king's fall to insult him and blame him for the blood of Saul's house. The Bible does not say here that David was guilty of that, and interpreters see it in different ways.

For today: when we are attacked or humiliated, we do not always need to respond with anger. David bore the insult calmly and left his case in God's hands. We can ask God for self-control and humility.
exp.12:38:
It says that King David was longing to go to Absalom, his son. Time had eased the grief over Amnon's death. "Longed to go" means he was eager to see Absalom. "Had been consoled" means he had already found some peace after the loss.

The narrator tells this after Absalom killed Amnon, his half-brother, and fled to Geshur. He stayed there three years. David was a king and also a wounded father. Some scholars point out that the Hebrew can be understood in more than one way, but the most common idea is that David missed Absalom.

Today, time can ease pain, but it does not always mend broken relationships. If there is a family member who has become distant, it is not enough to miss them in silence. Ask God for wisdom and humility, and take a concrete step toward reconciliation, with truth and with love.
exp.21:31:
This verse asks two questions to make a point: there is no other God besides the Lord, and no rock is like our God. The word "except" here means the same thing as "besides."

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. He has just said that God gives him victory and that his word is pure and protects those who trust in him. Here David acknowledges that his strength was not his own, but came from God.

For today: when you feel weak or face a great problem, do not rely only on your own abilities. Before you act, take a moment to tell God, "You are my strength," and ask him for wisdom and courage for the next step.
exp.10:6:
The explanation says that when Uriah came before David, the king asked him questions about how Joab was doing, how the troops were doing, and how the war was going. The phrase "how they are doing" here refers to their well-being. "The troops" are the soldiers. The exchange sounds like an ordinary conversation between a king and a soldier.

The narrator tells us that David had already gotten Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, pregnant, and now he is trying to hide it. That is why he has Uriah called back from the front. The questions seem kind, but they are a smokescreen: David wants Uriah to go home to his house so that everyone will believe the child is his.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, when we try to cover up a mistake, we use kind words that hide bad intentions. God sees the heart. It is better to confess in time than to pretend everything is normal and make the damage worse.
exp.13:30:
This verse tells how Joab, the commander of David's army, went to Absalom's house and asked him angrily, "Why did your servants set my field on fire?" The word "field" refers to his land, where he grew crops, and Absalom's servants had set it alight.

Joab speaks here, annoyed because Absalom had burned his barley. Absalom had returned to Jerusalem after years in exile, but King David still would not receive him. Absalom wanted Joab to plead on his behalf and, since Joab was not coming, he turned to pressure. Commentators see here a man who is impatient and manipulative, though his pain at being kept apart from his father seems genuine.

For today: the desire to be reconciled is good, but the methods matter. Forcing others or harming them to get what we want usually makes everything worse. Let us seek peace with patience, honest dialogue and respect.
exp.23:24:
It says that David built an altar to the LORD in that place and offered two kinds of sacrifices: burnt offerings, which were burned completely as a full surrender, and peace offerings, which expressed gratitude and fellowship with God. The verse then says that the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and that the plague upon Israel was halted.

The background is David's decision to count the people, which brought a plague as its consequence.
