David bought the threshing floor of Araunah, the place where the angel had stopped, and he did not want to receive it for free. He wanted his offering to cost him something. Many believe that this place was later connected with the temple, although the text of this verse does not say so.

For today: our worship should not be cheap or only words. Think of something concrete, such as your time, your money, or your forgiveness, and give it to God with humility, grateful for his mercy.
exp.6:8:
God says that he was with David everywhere he went, and that he cleared away all of David's enemies from in front of him. God also promised to make a great name for him, a reputation and honor like that of the greatest people in the land.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, but God reminds him that it was He who took him from tending sheep and made him king. Before speaking about what David would do for God, God shows what He had already done for David. Then He promises him a house, meaning a lasting family and kingdom.

For today: before we worry about what we must do for God, let us remember what He has already done for us. Looking back and giving thanks gives us humility and confidence for the future.
exp.18:33:
Barzillai answers the king with a question: "How many years of my life remain, that I should go up to Jerusalem with you?" He means that he has little time left and that the journey is not worth making. The verse speaks of his remaining years and of going up to Jerusalem, which sits on high ground.

Barzillai, a wealthy man of eighty years, had supplied David with food in Mahanaim during his flight. David, grateful, offers to let him live with him at court. Barzillai, humbly, turns down the honor and acknowledges his limits because of his age.

For today: know how to be thankful for what you receive, but also to recognize with humility your seasons and your limits. Not every honor must be accepted; sometimes serving well and stepping aside is the wisest course.
exp.17:29:
What it says: King David tells Ahimaaz to move aside and stand here. Ahimaaz steps aside and waits.

Context: David was waiting for news of the battle against his son Absalom. Ahimaaz arrived first and gave a report of victory, but when David asked about Absalom, he did not answer clearly. So David made him wait until Cushi arrived. It is likely that Ahimaaz did not want to give the painful news of Absalom's death, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: Sometimes we have to wait to receive the full truth. And when it falls to us to speak, let us not hide what is hard; let us tell the truth with respect and compassion.
exp.11:10:
God says he will bring punishment on David through a disaster that will come from his own household. His wives will be taken before his eyes and given to another, someone close to him. That man will lie with them in broad daylight, so the whole world will see it. "Lie with" means to have sexual relations.

The prophet Nathan speaks, sent by God, after David abused Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed. David did this in secret, but God responds with a punishment visible to everyone. Later, the Bible tells of his son Absalom doing something similar (2 Samuel 16:22). Afterward David acknowledges his sin and receives forgiveness, though the consequences remain.

For today: God forgives the one who truly repents, but our decisions can leave marks. For that reason it is wise to act with integrity, even when no one sees us.
exp.6:13:
God says that he will be a father to David's son, and that this son will be his son. When he does wrong, God will discipline him "with the rod of men" and "with the blows of the sons of men," that is, with human punishments, measured and real, like those a father would use to correct a child.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God promises him that his descendants will reign and that his son will build the house. Many understand that this refers first to Solomon, and the New Testament also applies this promise to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5). The discipline in this verse fits the kings who failed.

For today: God corrects us because He loves us as a Father, not to destroy us. When you feel correction, do not run away; listen, acknowledge your mistake, and return to Him, knowing that His mercy remains with you.
exp.0:6:
In this verse, Saul, wounded and leaning on his spear, turned around, saw the young man, and called out to him. The young man answered, "Here I am!"

The speaker is a young Amalekite who comes to David with news of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan. David asks him how he knows, and he tells his version of what happened on Mount Gilboa. We do not know whether he is telling the truth: the account in 1 Samuel 31 is different, and many think he embellished the story to win David's favor.

Today we can learn to be honest, especially when we believe a lie would benefit us. It also invites us to answer "Here I am!" with willingness when someone needs us, but always with sincerity and good intentions.
exp.9:16:
When David was told that the Arameans were gathering again, he brought all Israel together, crossed the Jordan River, and went to a place called Helam. There the Arameans lined up against him in battle and fought.

The verse says the news was "reported" to David, so it was someone who brought him word. The Arameans are the same people as the Syrians.

This is a historical account, not a speech. The Arameans had been defeated before, but Hadadezer brought reinforcements from across the Euphrates River, led by his commander Shobach. David acts quickly and gathers the people to defend Israel. The chapter describes how this war, which began with the conflict involving the Ammonites, came to an end. Locating Helam precisely is difficult, because it is not known for certain where it was.

For today: when a problem arrives, do not let it grow or ignore it. David heard the warning and acted with resolve and in unity with his people. Face difficulties with prayer, good counsel, and responsible action, trusting that God sustains the one who does what is right.
exp.22:2:
God himself spoke to David, and this is what he said: the one who rules over people must rule fairly and with reverence toward God. The phrase "the God of Israel" and the title "the Rock of Israel" are names for God that point to his power and his protection.

Here David speaks, now an old man, in what the Bible calls his "last words." He says that the Spirit of God spoke through him. David, who was a king, leaves a teaching about what a good ruler should be like. Then he compares such a ruler to the light of the morning, and he also acknowledges that his own family was not perfect.

For today: if you have authority over others, at home, at work, or in the church, try to act with justice and remember that you are accountable to God.
exp.17:3:
David accepts the counsel of his people. He says, "I will do whatever seems best to you." Then he stands beside the gate of the city while all the troops march out by hundreds and by thousands.

David is fleeing from his son Absalom, who rebelled against him and tried to take away his kingdom. The army is divided into three parts, and David wanted to go into battle with them. The men stop him, because if he is killed, everything would be lost. He yields and stays at the gate, and from there he watches his troops march out. Later he will ask that they deal gently with Absalom.

For today: knowing how to listen to good advice is a sign of humility. Even when we are leaders, we do not always have to impose our own desire. Let us ask God for wisdom to accept the help of others.
exp.16:17:
A young man saw them and told Absalom. Even so, the two left quickly and came to the house of a man in Bahurim. That man had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it to hide.

This is part of Absalom's rebellion against his father David. Jonathan and Ahimaaz were secretly carrying a warning to David, sent by Hushai, so that he would cross the Jordan. The narrator tells how they came close to being caught, but they were protected.

God often cares for his work through simple and brave people, like this family who hid the messengers. Today we can ask ourselves: what can I offer, even if it seems small, to help others with faithfulness and courage when it is needed?
exp.3:7:
It says that Rechab and Baanah brought the head of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, to David at Hebron. They presented the killing as an act of justice from the LORD against Saul and his family, whom they call "your enemy." "Offspring" means descendants, and "sought your life" means he was looking to kill David.

The two brothers are speaking; they had just killed Ish-bosheth while he slept. They expected a reward from David. They invoke the LORD to justify their crime, but David had not asked them for anything like this, and in the next verse he firmly rejects them.

Today: let us be careful not to invoke the LORD to cover personal interests or unjust acts. God does not need our schemes to carry out his plans. Before saying "God willed it so," it is worth asking whether what we did truly reflects his justice and his character.
exp.17:7:
The battle spread across the whole countryside, and the forest claimed more lives that day than the sword did. The phrase "the whole countryside" means the entire surrounding land, the full stretch of the terrain. "Sword" here stands for the fighting itself. The text does not say how the forest killed people; some think of swamps, ravines, wild animals, or people who got lost or fell while fleeing.

This is part of the account of Absalom's rebellion against his father David. The narrator describes the battle in the forest of Ephraim, east of the Jordan, between David's men and Absalom's followers. What follows is Absalom's death, when his head became caught in a tree.

For today: disasters do not always come from where we expect them. When life is thrown into disorder by conflict, even what seems harmless can harm us. That is why it is wise to seek peace, ask God for direction, and avoid unnecessary quarrels.
exp.13:3:
The woman from Tekoa came before King David. She fell facedown in homage and cried out, "Help me, O king!" That is, she was asking the king directly for his help.

Joab, the commander of the army, wanted David to be reconciled with his son Absalom, who had been banished for killing his brother Amnon. Joab coached this woman on what to say, and she pretended to be a widow in mourning with a story similar to David's own. In this way, the king would see his own situation from the outside. Interpreters debate whether Joab acted with good intentions or for convenience, and the Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: Before asking for help or advice, approach with humility and sincerity. And when someone speaks to you the truth, even indirectly, listen with an open heart, without becoming defensive.
exp.6:6:
God reminds David that, throughout all the time He journeyed with Israel, He never asked any of the leaders He appointed, "Why haven't you built Me a house of cedar?" To "shepherd" means to care for and guide, the way a shepherd looks after his sheep. A "house of cedar" refers to a fine, costly palace built of cedar wood.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers that He had never asked for one, since He had been with His people while they lived in a tent. Some see here a call to humility; others see God himself deciding the timing and the form. Then He promises to build David's house, that is, his descendants.

For today: our good intentions do not replace God's guidance. Before doing something great for Him, ask Him what He desires, and remember that He always acts first on your behalf.
exp.1:16:
That day the battle was intense, and Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David. The narrator of the book tells of the war between two sides after the death of Saul. Abner supported Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, while David was recognized as king in Judah. Before the general battle, twelve men from each side fought and died together, which was very tragic. Then the fighting spread. David's men won, and soon Joab, Abishai, and Asahel appear, whose actions will bring further consequences.

For today: conflicts between brothers or families leave deep wounds, even when someone "wins." Seek peace and resolve disagreements in time, before they grow and cost lives, relationships, or trust.
exp.18:40:
Here the men of Israel, the northern tribes, come to King David and complain with irritation. They ask why their brothers, the men of Judah, took the king away and brought him, his household, and all of David's men across the Jordan River without including them. Their question shows they felt left out and passed over.

After Absalom's rebellion, David returns to Jerusalem. Judah was quick to welcome him back, while Israel felt ignored at a moment of honor. It is the people of Israel speaking, wounded in their pride. This tension shows divisions that would later grow within the kingdom.

For today: when there is reconciliation, let us take care that no one feels excluded. Before speaking in anger, it is wise to speak with humility and seek peace, for wounded pride can break what God wants to heal.
exp.6:4:
God tells the prophet Nathan to go to David, his servant, and ask him a question: "Are you the one to build for Me a house to dwell in?" The words "Go and tell" are a command, and "this is what the LORD says" shows that this is a message from God. "House" here means a temple.

David was already living in his palace and wanted to build a worthy place for God. Nathan, without consulting God, had told him to do what was in his heart. That same night God corrects Nathan and speaks. The question is not a simple refusal; God shows that he had never asked for a house, since he had walked with his people in a tent. Later, God promises David that he himself will build David a house, that is, a dynasty.

We may have good desires to serve God, but it is wise to ask him first and listen to his answer. God does not need our works to be great; he invites us to obey him with humility.
exp.14:2:
Absalom tells each person who arrives with a legal problem: "Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy to hear you." The phrase "has no deputy" means that the king has no representative to attend to their case.

Absalom, David's son, speaks at the city gate, where legal cases were settled. Little by little he wins the hearts of the people, criticizing his father's administration without evidence. Then he offers himself as the ideal judge. His goal was to prepare a rebellion against David.

Today, beware of the one who agrees with you only to win your trust. Sweet words can hide personal interests. Let us ask for wisdom to tell sincere care apart from manipulation, and let us seek out those who serve with integrity.
exp.0:0:
This verse tells us that Saul had already died. David had just returned from defeating the Amalekites, and he stayed in Ziklag, his home town, for two days. The phrase "after the death of Saul" places the story at a point after the king's death, and "defeated" here means that David won the battle against them.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who picks up the account from 1 Samuel. David did not yet know what had happened on Mount Gilboa. In the meantime, he had recovered the families whom the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag (1 Samuel 30). This verse marks a pause before he receives the news of the king's death.

For today: sometimes there is a time of waiting between a victory and the next change in life. We can use those quiet days to rest, to give thanks to God, and to trust that He directs what is coming, even when we do not yet know it.
exp.7:2:
David defeated Hadadezer, king of Zobah, an Aramean kingdom north of Israel. "Defeated" means he won the battle against him, and "dominion" refers to the land and rule the king held. The verse says Hadadezer had marched out to restore his dominion along the Euphrates River. It is not stated whether he was trying to restore his own control there or whether David was pushing toward that region. Some believe it was David expanding his kingdom, others that it was the king of Zobah.

The narrator of the book recounts David's victories over several neighboring peoples. He shows how the kingdom of Israel grew stronger. Many connect this with God's promise to give land to Israel, which named the Euphrates as its limit.

Today we can learn to trust that God keeps his promises in his own time. It is also worth reviewing our goals: growing is not wrong, but we should ask God for direction and not depend only on our own strength.
exp.8:5:
It says that Mephibosheth, grandson of King Saul and son of Jonathan, came before David and fell facedown in reverence. David called his name, and Mephibosheth answered, "I am your servant," meaning, "Here I am, ready to do what you ask." Falling facedown was a deep sign of respect, as he knelt or lay down on the ground before the king.

David had promised his friend Jonathan to show kindness to his family. Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, told him where Mephibosheth was, and David sent for him. Mephibosheth probably feared David, since many kings of that time eliminated the descendants of the previous king.

For today: David's kindness reminds us that we can keep our promises and treat with grace those who have no way to repay us. Think of someone to whom you can show that kindness this week.
exp.21:13:
The LORD thundered from heaven, and his voice resounded as the voice of the Most High. This verse says that God made his voice heard like thunder coming from the heavens. The word "thundered" means it sounded like thunder, and "the Most High" is a name for God that stresses he is above all things. The phrase "the voice of the Most High resounded" means he spoke with force, so that everyone could hear him.

David, now older, speaks in a song of gratitude. He writes it after God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He uses images of storm, fire, and trembling to describe God's power when he comes to deliver his servant. These are poetic images, not necessarily a literal account of an event.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems or fear, remember that God is neither far away nor silent. You can cry out to him with confidence, believing that he has the power to act on your behalf. And when he helps you, do not forget to give him thanks, as David did.
exp.15:8:
Abishai, one of David's warriors, is outraged when he sees Shimei insulting the king. He calls Shimei a "dead dog," an expression of contempt meaning someone of no worth or power. He asks permission to go over and cut off Shimei's head. The phrase "cut off his head" simply means that he would kill Shimei by beheading him. "Let me go over" means he asks for permission to cross over to where Shimei is.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled against him. Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, takes advantage of the moment to curse him and throw in his face the blood of that house. Abishai reacts violently to defend David, but David stops him and decides to bear the insult with humility, leaving everything in God's hands.

When someone attacks us, our quick reaction is usually to take revenge. David teaches us to stop, to listen for whether there is some truth in the criticism, and to trust that God is the one who brings justice.
exp.6:24:
David asks God to carry out the promise he made about him and his family. The phrase "confirm forever" shows that David wants the promise to last. He also asks God to do what he has promised, just as God said he would.

David, the king of Israel, is the one speaking. God had just promised him through the prophet Nathan that he would build a "house," meaning a lasting line of descendants and a firm kingdom for him. David answers with humility, remembering how God redeemed Israel from Egypt. He demands nothing; he relies on what God has already said. Many Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of Jesus, a descendant of David.

When we pray, we can rely on the promises of the Bible. Praying with God's Word gives us confidence and reminds us that God is faithful.
exp.16:8:
Husai tells Absalom that David is surely hiding in a cave or some other location. If some of your troops fall first, whoever hears of it will say, "There has been a slaughter among the troops who follow Absalom."

Husai speaks as David's friend, though he pretends to be loyal to Absalom. His true purpose was to defeat Ahithophel's counsel, which proposed pursuing David at once. Husai wanted to buy time so that David could organize himself. Many understand that God used this to accomplish his purpose, as the text says shortly after.

For today: A well-considered word can change the course of a situation. Before acting in haste, it is wise to pause, weigh the consequences, and ask God for wisdom to speak and to decide.
exp.6:3:
That same night, God spoke to Nathan. The phrase "the word of the LORD came" means that God gave him a direct message.

David, now settled in his cedar palace, was troubled that the ark of God was still kept in a tent. Nathan, without consulting God, answered him encouragingly: "Do whatever is in your heart." His intention was good, but he spoke on his own. Now God sets the course right and speaks to him again, for He has His own plan and His own timing.

For today: good desires are not enough; we must pray and wait for God's direction before acting. Even good advice from a respected leader should be brought before the Lord.
exp.2:24:
Joab tells David that Abner did not come with good intentions. In his view, Abner came to deceive him, to track his movements, and to learn everything he was doing. "Track your movements" means keeping close watch on where you go and what you do day to day, and "deceive you" means to make you believe something false.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. Abner had come to offer that all Israel would join David, and David sent him away in peace. Joab may have had sincere suspicions, but he also had a personal motive: Abner had killed his brother Asahel. That is why the text then shows Joab killing Abner in secret. Some see political concern here; others see plain revenge.

For today: when we accuse someone, let us examine our hearts. Sometimes suspicion dresses itself up as caution, yet it hides resentment. Let us ask God for wisdom and a clean heart before we judge.
exp.21:2:
This verse says that David trusts in God as his rock, a firm and secure place to stand. He calls God his shield, who protects him from danger. He speaks of the horn of his salvation, meaning a power that saves, since a horn was a symbol of strength. He also calls God his stronghold, his refuge, and his Savior. The word "violence" refers to the attacks and the wickedness of his enemies.

David sings this song on the day God delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, who pursued him to kill him. He speaks from gratitude, looking back and recognizing that God was his defense in very difficult years.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure, do not look first to your own strength. Tell God in prayer, "You are my refuge." Remembering how he helped you before strengthens your trust for what comes next.
exp.18:12:
David tells Amasa to say that he is a close relative: "Aren't you my flesh and blood?" This means they share the same family line. Then David makes a solemn oath: "May God punish me, and ever so severely, if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab." He is saying that if he does not keep his word, he calls down God's judgment on himself.

David speaks after the death of Absalom, when he wants to return to Jerusalem. Amasa had commanded Absalom's army, and Joab, David's general, had killed Absalom. With this offer, David seeks to reconcile Judah and win Amasa over. Many also see here a political desire to set Joab aside.

Today we can learn to seek reconciliation and to extend a hand to those who have failed us. But it is wise to do so without letting pride or convenience direct our decisions.
exp.5:2:
This verse tells that David and his people set the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David wanted to bring the ark, the symbol of God's presence, to Jerusalem. They were doing it with celebration and great enthusiasm. But the law said that the ark was to be carried with poles on the shoulders of the Levites, not on a cart. The text of this verse does not point this out, but the account that follows shows that something went wrong.

For today: good intentions and great enthusiasm in serving God are not enough. It is also important to seek how He wants to be honored, by knowing His Word and obeying it with humility.
exp.17:17:
This verse tells that Absalom, during his lifetime, had a pillar set up for himself in the King's Valley. He said he had no son to preserve the memory of his name, so he gave the pillar his own name. The phrase "to this day" means that when this was written, the place was still known as Absalom's Monument.

The narrator tells this right after Absalom's death, since he rebelled against his father David. He was buried in a pit under a heap of stones, without honor. The contrast is strong: he wanted a monument, and he ended up with a heap of stones. The Bible also says that Absalom had three sons (2 Samuel 14:27), so perhaps they died young; the text does not explain this.

For today: seeking fame or being remembered can be empty. It is better to live with humility and faithfulness to God, because He is the one who gives a remembrance that lasts.
exp.11:8:
Here God asks David why he despised the command of the LORD and did what is evil in His sight. The word "despised" in the verse means to look down on something and treat it as unimportant, so David treated the LORD's command as if it did not matter. He put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took Uriah's wife as his own. The verse shows that Uriah was killed by the sword of the Ammonites, which means he died in battle at the hand of the enemy.

The prophet Nathan speaks in God's name. He has just told David a parable, and now he says to him, "You are the man." David had taken Bathsheba and arranged the death of her husband, Uriah. God reminds him of everything He had given him and shows him the seriousness of his sin.

For today: do not minimize your faults or hide them. God sees everything and has given us much. Instead of justifying ourselves, we can acknowledge the wrong honestly and ask Him for forgiveness.
exp.6:2:
Nathan tells King David to go and do all that is in his heart, because the LORD is with him. "Go" simply means "go ahead and do it." "Is with you" means the LORD is present and supporting him.

David had just been given rest from his enemies. Living in a house of cedar, he was troubled that the ark of God was still kept in a tent. Nathan, the prophet, answered right away by encouraging his good desire. But that same night God spoke to Nathan and corrected the answer: it would not be David who built the temple. Nathan spoke with good intentions, but without first consulting God.

For today: a good desire is not always God's plan or his timing. Before we act, and before we give advice, let us pray and seek God's guidance, and be willing to be corrected.
exp.20:21:
These four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his soldiers. This verse closes the account of the battles against the descendants of the Philistine giants. It describes four huge warriors from Gath, the family line of the giant Rapha, who were killed by David and his men. The word "giant" here stands for a term that can also be a family or clan name.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who summarizes Israel's wars against the Philistines in the last years of David's reign. Earlier, it is told how Jonathan killed a man who had six fingers on his hands and six toes on his feet. It is not known with certainty how these four are related to the giant of Gath, or exactly how the family of Rapha is connected to them. What is clear is that the victory came through the effort of the whole group.

For today: great challenges are rarely overcome alone. God often works through the unity of his people. Value the work of others and serve alongside them.
exp.1:4:
David sent messengers to the people of Jabesh-gilead to bless them. He tells them that the LORD should bless them because they showed kindness by burying Saul, whom David calls "your lord."

David had just been anointed king over Judah, in Hebron, and he learns what the people of Jabesh did. Saul had been his persecutor, but David recognizes the value of honoring a fallen king. According to 1 Samuel 31, these men recovered the bodies of Saul and his sons. Perhaps David was also seeking their support, although the text does not say this directly.

Today we can learn to recognize and be grateful for the good that others do, even when it involves someone with whom we have had conflicts. A gesture of respect and gratitude can open doors to peace.
exp.11:4:
David became furious when he heard the story of the rich man who took the poor man's one little ewe lamb. His anger burned hot against the man. David then swears, "As surely as the LORD lives," a solemn way of affirming something, and declares that the man who did this deserves to die, meaning he deserves a severe punishment.

The prophet Nathan tells this story to David at God's direction. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah put to death. Nathan does not accuse him directly, but with a parable. David, without realizing it, condemns himself. A few verses later Nathan will say to him, "You are the man." It is worth noting that the law did not call for death for stealing a sheep; David's reaction shows his indignation, and also how blind he was to his own sin.

We often see the wrongs of others clearly and find it hard to see our own. Let us ask God for humility to examine ourselves with the same justice with which we judge others, and to receive correction without excuses.
exp.21:32:
God is the one who gives me strength to keep going, and he himself clears the obstacles from my path. The word "fortress" here means a place of safety and protection. When the verse says he makes my way clear, it means he removes what stands in the way and keeps the road open before me.

King David is the speaker. This song of thanksgiving was written when God delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul, as the opening of the chapter explains. David looks back and recognizes that he did not triumph by his own ability, but because God protected and guided him in the midst of battles and dangers.

For today: when you face a difficult task, do not rely on your own strength alone. Before taking the step, ask God for protection and direction, and then thank him for every advance, large or small.
exp.9:15:
Hadadezer, the king of the Arameans, sent messengers to bring more Arameans from beyond the Euphrates River. They came to Helam, with Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, leading them.

This is part of the historical account of the war between Israel and the Ammonites, who had allied themselves with the Arameans. The Arameans had been defeated by Joab and Abishai, but they did not accept that defeat and gathered more troops. Here no one is speaking; the narrator tells what Hadadezer did to fight against Israel again.

For today: stubbornness and pride can lead us to insist on a path that has already failed. Instead, we can stop, acknowledge our mistakes, and seek God's guidance before moving forward.
exp.14:8:
King David gave his son Absalom permission to go to Hebron. "Go in peace" was a common way of saying goodbye and giving a blessing. So Absalom got up and went.

David speaks here with a father's confidence, believing that Absalom was going to keep a promise made to God. But the verses that follow show that Absalom had another plan: to prepare a rebellion and proclaim himself king in Hebron.

Today we can learn that using religious words does not always show a sincere heart. It is wise to ask God for wisdom to discern, and to make sure that our own promises to Him are true and not a pretext for other purposes.
exp.13:10:
In this passage the woman asks King David to invoke the LORD your God and to prevent the avenger of blood from increasing the devastation, so that her son is not destroyed. "Those close to the blood" were the family members who were expected to take revenge for a death. David vows by the LORD that not a hair of her son's head will fall to the ground, meaning that he will be completely protected.

A woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab, speaks here while pretending to be a widow whose son is in danger. It is an invented story meant to lead David to reflect on his own son Absalom, who was banished for having killed his brother Amnon. David does not yet see that he himself is at the center of the matter.

For today: sometimes we judge other people's situations easily, but we find it hard to show the same mercy at home. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our own need for forgiveness and reconciliation.
exp.0:21:
They say that the weapons of Jonathan and of Saul never came back without having struck their enemies. "Blood of the slain" and "fat of the mighty" speak of enemies fallen in battle; the "fat" is a poetic image for the strength of the warriors. Jonathan's bow did not retreat, and Saul's sword did not return "empty," that is, without achieving its purpose.

David sings this lament after the deaths of Saul and Jonathan on Mount Gilboa. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not mock him. He honors the good that was in both of them and mourns the defeat of Israel, without letting the Philistines rejoice.

Today we can learn to remember with respect the good that was in others, even in those who wounded us. In grief, gratitude and honesty heal more than resentment.
exp.11:18:
This verse tells of the moment David realizes that his son has died. Seeing that his servants were whispering to one another, he understood what had happened. He asked them directly, "Is the child dead?" and they answered, "He is dead." The servants are his attendants, the household staff who worked for him.

The child was the son of David and Bathsheba, who became ill as a consequence of David's sin. For seven days, David fasted and pleaded with God for the child's life, lying on the ground. His servants were afraid to give him the news, thinking it might harm him. Here the narrator describes how David came to know it without being told.

For today: when painful news arrives, it is better to face the truth honestly than to hide it. David asked plainly and then worshiped God. We can bring our pain to God and go on trusting in Him.
exp.9:5:
What it says: The Ammonites recognized that they had become a stench to David. Rather than make peace, they hired soldiers from other Aramean peoples: twenty thousand foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zoba, a thousand men from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand men from Tob.

Context: The book's narrator tells the story. David had sent messengers to comfort Hanun over the death of his father, but Hanun's advisers suspected them of being spies and humiliated them. The Ammonites knew this would bring war, so they prepared to fight.

For today: When we have done wrong, it is better to acknowledge it and seek reconciliation than to reinforce our pride. Asking forgiveness in time can prevent greater conflicts.
exp.21:48:
God brought David out from among his enemies and set him in a safe, high place, far above those who rose up against him. The BSB says God "exalts" David above his foes and "rescues" him from violent men, which is the same idea as being lifted to safety and taken out of danger.

David speaks here, near the end of his life, in a song of thanks to God for rescuing him from many dangers. Many think the "violent men" refers to Saul, although the text does not give the name, and it could also speak of enemies in general. David acknowledges that his victory came from God, not from his own strength.

For today: when you go through an unjust or difficult situation, tell God what you feel and trust that he can take care of you. And when you come through it, do not forget to thank him sincerely.
exp.21:14:
God shot out His arrows, which are like darts, and with them scattered and confused the enemies. He also hurled lightning, and the lightning routed them. The phrase "scattered the foes" means that God broke up the enemies and threw them into disorder. The lightning routed them, meaning it drove them into flight and defeat.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, near the end of his life, after the LORD had rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He uses poetic images of storm, thunder, and trembling to describe how God acted on his behalf. These are not details of a literal weather event but language that expresses the power of God.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, remember that God sees and is able to act. Cry out to Him with confidence, and then give thanks, as David did, for every deliverance.
exp.21:5:
He says that David felt entangled by the place of the dead and facing mortal danger. "Sheol" here is the Hebrew word for the realm of the dead, the grave. The "cords of Sheol" are like ropes that wrap around a person and pull them down, and "confronted" means that the snares of death met him suddenly, when he did not expect them.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and describes how close he came to dying. This same song appears, nearly word for word, in Psalm 18. It is poetic language, with strong images to express a real anguish.

For today: when you feel trapped or caught off guard by a trial, do what David did: cry out to God with honesty. He hears those who seek him, even in the darkest moments.
exp.12:32:
Jonadab tells King David not to be overwhelmed by believing the false report that all his sons have been killed. According to him, only Amnon died. The phrase "do not take to heart" means "don't dwell on it" or "don't accept it as true." "The report" here refers to the rumor that was going around.

News reached David that Absalom had killed his sons, and the king tore his clothes in grief. Jonadab, David's nephew and the adviser of Amnon, speaks calmly. He says Absalom had planned this since Amnon violated Tamar. The text does not explain how Jonadab knew this, and there is no way to know for certain.

For today: when faced with bad news, it is wise to wait and verify before reacting. But we also see that grief without justice or forgiveness can end in violence. Let us place our wounds in God's hands.
exp.15:6:
Shimei shouts at David to leave. He calls him "you worthless man of bloodshed", that is, a violent man guilty of killing. "Worthless man" describes someone with no regard for God or for what is right.

Shimei was of the family of King Saul. David was fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom had rebelled. Shimei takes advantage of this moment of weakness to accuse him, throwing stones at him and cursing him. He was convinced that God was punishing David for the fall of Saul's house. The Bible does not show that David had killed Saul or his family, so the accusation was very doubtful. Even so, David did not respond with violence.

For today: when someone attacks us with injustice, we can keep silent, examine our hearts, and trust that God is the righteous judge, instead of responding with revenge.
exp.18:15:
This verse tells us that Shimei, son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin and from the town of Bahurim, hurried down to meet King David. The word "hurried" means that he moved quickly. He came down together with the men of Judah to welcome the king who was returning.

The narrator describes David's return after Absalom's rebellion. Shimei was the same man who had earlier cursed David and thrown stones at him as he fled (2 Samuel 16). Now, seeing that the king was coming back with power, he rushes to show himself a friend. The Bible does not say how sincere his heart was; the text only shows his speed, and then he falls down and asks for forgiveness.

We can ask for forgiveness truly and in time when we have failed. But we also learn to examine our motives: are we seeking reconciliation out of love and repentance, or only out of convenience? God looks at the heart.
exp.16:2:
Here Ahitophel says that if only King David is killed, he will bring all the people back to Absalom, the way a bride returns to her husband. You seek the life of only one man, he says, and then all the people will be at peace. The phrase "the man you seek" shows that David is the only one Absalom wants to eliminate.

Ahitophel, once David's counselor, now supports Absalom's rebellion. He proposes a quick, surprise attack while David is exhausted. His plan sounds logical, and everyone likes it. However, Absalom decides to also listen to Hushai, who was in fact loyal to David. What follows shows that God would work through that second counsel.

For today: a piece of advice can sound wise and still not be good. Before following a plan, let us ask God for discernment and compare what we hear with his Word, not only with what suits us.
exp.6:23:
This verse says that God has made Israel his own people in a way that is firm and lasting. It also says that the Lord himself has become their God. The first phrase, "you have established," means that God has set this relationship in place with certainty. The second phrase, "you have become their God," means that he has claimed them as his own.

David speaks this prayer after the prophet Nathan delivered God's promise about his house and his descendants. David feels humble and thankful. He remembers how God rescued Israel from Egypt and chose them. His prayer rests on what God has already done and promised.

For today: when you doubt whether God sustains you, remember that his faithfulness does not depend on your strength but on his character and his promises. Pray as David did: give thanks for what God has already done, and trust in what he has promised.
exp.7:11:
This verse finishes the list of what David set apart for the LORD: the silver and gold taken from the Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites, Philistines and Amalekites, along with the plunder he won from Hadadezer, king of Zobah. "Plunder" means whatever is taken from a defeated enemy.

The account is a narrative, told by the author of the book rather than by David himself. It describes how, after several victories, David did not keep everything for himself. When Toi sent him gifts of silver, gold and bronze, David set them apart for the LORD along with the rest. The text shows that he recognized God as the one who gave him the victory, and it confirms this at the end: "The LORD preserved David wherever he went."

For today: when you receive achievements or possessions, acknowledge that they come from God. Set aside a part of them with gratitude, whether as an offering, your time, or help to others, instead of keeping it all for yourself.
exp.2:10:
Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul who was ruling over Israel, did not dare to speak against Abner. He had no reply to give him. The phrase "did not dare to say another word" means that he chose to say nothing at all, and "for fear of Abner" shows that he was afraid of him.

Abner was the commander of the army and Ish-bosheth's main support. He had become angry because Ish-bosheth accused him of something related to one of Saul's concubines. Abner answered with force and swore to help David. The king stayed silent because he depended on Abner's power.

For today: when fear makes us silent in the face of what is unjust, it is wise to ask God for courage and wisdom. We should also take care that our leadership does not depend only on the power of other people, but on acting with integrity.
exp.18:32:
It says that King David invites Barzillai to cross the Jordan with him and to live in Jerusalem. David promises to provide for him and to keep him at his side at the royal court. The phrase "at my side" means that Barzillai would be close to the king, sharing his company and household.

David is speaking as he returns to Jerusalem after the rebellion of his son Absalom. Barzillai, an elderly wealthy man from Gilead, had supported him with food when David was in Mahanaim. David wants to thank him for his kindness and to honor him. Barzillai, however, humbly answers that because of his age he would no longer enjoy the court, and he does not want to be a burden.

For today: let us learn to thank generously those who have helped us. Also, like Barzillai, let us be simple and realistic about the stages of our lives, without envying honors we do not need.
exp.18:37:
Here King David accepts Barzillai's proposal. He says that Chimham will cross the Jordan with him, and he promises to do for Chimham whatever is good in Barzillai's sight. He also says he will do for Barzillai whatever he desires. The phrase "what is good in your sight" means "whatever you prefer."

Barzillai was a wealthy old man from Gilead who had helped David with supplies when he was fleeing from Absalom. Now David was returning to Jerusalem and wanted to reward him. Barzillai, because of his age, turned down the honor and offered Chimham in his place. The Bible does not make clear who Chimham was; some think he was his son, but the text does not say so.

For today: gratitude is shown through deeds. And, like Barzillai, we can learn to bless others by generously sharing the honors we receive, without clinging to them.
exp.2:16:
Abner speaks to the elders of Israel, the leaders of the tribes. He reminds them that for a long time they had wanted David as their king. The words "for a long time now" point to a desire that had lasted for years, and "sought" means they had been looking to David and wishing for him.

Abner was the commander of the army of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, but he had fallen out with him and wanted to switch sides to David. He had already brought Michal back to David, and now he is preparing the ground among the leaders. We do not know with certainty all of his motives; the text shows both his personal interest and the recognition that God had promised the kingdom to David.

For today: sometimes we know what God wants, but we let time pass without obeying. Let us ask for the courage to act with sincerity and not only out of convenience.
exp.14:23:
Zadok was also there, along with all the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of God, which was the symbol of God's presence. They set the ark down on the ground. Abiathar offered sacrifices while all the people finished leaving the city. The sentence about the ark being set down can stay as it is, but the detail about Abiathar offering sacrifices is less certain: the text does not say where or when those sacrifices were made, so readers should take this as a general description of his role.

The narrator tells of David's flight from Jerusalem because of the rebellion of his son Absalom. The priests want to accompany him and bring the ark, believing that this way God would be with the king. David will answer that the ark must return to the city.

Today we can learn that the presence of God is not controlled or carried along as a guarantee. In moments of crisis, let us trust in his will and leave the outcome to him, as David did.
exp.14:6:
Absalom asks King David for permission to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow he has made to the LORD.

Many ancient manuscripts read "forty years" here, but the Berean Standard Bible reads "four years," and the number is uncertain.

Absalom is David's son, and he is winning the people's affection with flattery and embraces. Hebron was the place where David was crowned, and there Absalom would begin a rebellion. The text suggests that the vow was an excuse to disguise his plans, though it does not say so in those words.

Today: speaking about God does not make our intentions pure. Let us ask Him to examine our hearts, so that our faith is not a mask for ambition, but a sincere surrender.
exp.4:0:
It says that all the tribes of Israel went to David at Hebron. They said to him, "Here we are, your own flesh and blood," a way of saying that they were part of the same family and people as him. Hebron was a city in Judah, where David was already reigning.

The speakers are the representatives of the northern tribes. Saul and his son had died, and David had been reigning alone over Judah for about seven years. Now they acknowledge his leadership, remembering that he had already led them in battle and that God had chosen him as shepherd of the people. For that reason they make a covenant with him and anoint him king.

For today: to recognize and respect those whom God has placed as guides, and to seek unity, especially when we go through times of change. Unity grows when we remember that we are one people under God.
exp.13:20:
Here King David tells Joab that he grants the request: Joab is to go and bring back his son Absalom. The phrase "young man" refers to Absalom, and "bring back" means returning him to Jerusalem.

David speaks with Joab, the commander of his army. Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled to Geshur, where he had lived in exile for years. Joab wanted him to return, so he sent a woman from Tekoa with an invented story to move the king's heart. David discovered that Joab was behind it, yet he still gave in. Scholars do not agree on whether this was David's wisdom, his tenderness, or his weakness.

For today: forgiving and seeking reconciliation is good, but it is wise to do so with truth and repentance, not only out of emotion. Let us ask God for wisdom to join love and justice in our relationships.
exp.4:21:
This verse says that the Philistines attacked again. The phrases used in the source are rendered here in the verse's own terms: "Once again" and "spread out" describe their returning with their troops to the Valley of Rephaim, a valley near Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had already defeated the Philistines at Baal-perazim and had burned their idols. Even so, they came back. What matters comes next: David did not trust in the earlier victory, but went back to inquire of the LORD, and God gave him a different strategy.

For today: a past victory does not excuse us from praying again. When a problem returns, do not face it with the formula that worked before, out of habit. Ask God, listen to his guidance, and move forward with patience, trusting that he goes before you.
exp.22:7:
Here begins the list of David's mighty men. The verse speaks of a warrior named Josheb-basshebeth, who was chief of the Three, the foremost of David's champions. He fought against eight hundred men and killed them in a single battle. The text is part of the history of Israel, which honors the heroes of David's kingdom.

There are doubts about the exact name and the number. In 1 Chronicles 11:11 the name appears as "Jashobeam" and the number as three hundred slain. There may have been an error in copying, or these may be separate accounts. No one knows for certain. After speaking of the wicked, the text shows those who served faithfully.

Today we can value and thank those who serve with courage and steadfastness, often without many people noticing. We can also ask God for the courage to faithfully do what is ours to do, knowing that He sees and remembers our service.
exp.9:8:
This verse tells how Joab, the commander of David's army, saw that the enemy was closing in on him from two sides, with battle lines both in front of him and behind him. Then he selected some of the best soldiers of Israel and arranged them in battle formation against the Arameans.

The passage is narrative, so it is the narrator speaking rather than a character. David had sent Joab because the Ammonites had humiliated David's messengers, and the Ammonites hired Aramean soldiers to fight for them. Joab found himself between two fronts, so he divided his forces. He put his brother Abishai in charge against the Ammonites, while he himself faced the Arameans, who posed the greater threat.

For today: when you feel pressed from several sides, do not freeze. Think calmly, put your priorities in order, and ask for help from those who are with you. Joab planned with wisdom and, as you will see in the following verses, he also trusted in God.
exp.9:14:
It says that the Arameans, when they saw that they had been defeated by Israel, did not give up but regrouped. The word "Arameans" here is the name for the people also called Syrians in some older texts. The phrase about regrouping means they came together again to gather their forces.

This is the account of the writer of Samuel, not a speech. It tells of the war between David and the Ammonites, who had humiliated David's messengers and then allied themselves with the Arameans. Joab had won the first battle, but the Arameans did not accept their defeat and called on Hadadezer to fight again.

A victory does not always end the struggle. What seemed settled yesterday, whether a temptation, a problem, or a tension, can return with force. For this reason it is wise to stay alert, to pray, and not to become overconfident, like David, who mobilized all of Israel and continued to depend on God.
exp.19:16:
When he had come near to her, the woman asked, "Are you Joab?" "I am," he replied. "Listen to the words of your servant," she said. "I am listening," he answered. Words that need a note: "servant" is the woman herself, spoken with humility; "listen" means pay attention and hear what is said.

Joab, David's commander, was pursuing the rebel Sheba, and he had the city of Abel under siege. They were about to bring down the wall. A wise woman, who spoke for the people of the city, asked to speak with him to seek a peaceful way out and prevent destruction.

For today: before acting harshly, it is worth stopping to listen. Joab could have continued the attack, but he listened. Listening calmly can prevent great harm and open the way to peace.
exp.2:11:
Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf with a message. First he asks, "To whom does the land belong?", a question meant to make David think about who should rule. Then he proposes, "Make your covenant with me, and surely my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you."

Abner was the commander of Saul's army and had supported Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, as king. But he had become angry with him and decided to switch sides. Interpreters debate whether he was thinking of the good of the people or of his own advantage; the Bible does not fully make this clear.

Today, when we seek peace or unity, let us examine our motives. Even good results can come from mixed intentions, and God invites us to pursue what is good with a sincere heart.
exp.21:29:
It says that David, with God's help, can defeat enemy armies and scale walls that seemed impossible to cross. "I can charge an army" means defeating forces; "I can scale a wall" speaks of crossing strong defenses. The strength does not come from him alone, but from You and from my God.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, when God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul. It rests on the confession that God is his lamp and his light in the darkness. Then he affirms that God's way is perfect and that He is a shield for those who take refuge in Him.

For today: when you face a problem that looks like an enormous wall, do not trust only in your own strength. Pray, seek God's guidance, and take the next step in faith, remembering that He is with you and sustains you.
exp.19:3:
King David says to Amasa, "Summon the men of Judah to come to me within three days, and be here yourself." Here "the men of Judah" means men able to go to war.

David speaks as king, after the rebellion of Absalom. Now Sheba, son of Bichri, is stirring up Israel against him. David gives this task to Amasa, who had been commander of Absalom's army and to whom David had promised a place of command (2 Samuel 19:13). In this way he was seeking to win the people back. The text does not explain why Amasa was later slow.

For today: when we receive a responsibility, timing matters. Carrying out what has been entrusted to us on time shows faithfulness and prevents bigger problems.
exp.15:0:
David had just gone a little beyond the summit (the Mount of Olives, on his flight), and there Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, was waiting to meet him. He had a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ziba, who had served in Saul's household, appears with provisions just when David is weary and in need. Afterward he accuses Mephibosheth of treason. We cannot be certain whether Ziba was telling the truth or was seeking his own gain; the later account leaves doubts.

Today we can be thankful for timely help, but it is also wise to discern. Before believing what someone says about another, especially when it benefits the one speaking, it is wise to investigate, to pray, and not to judge in a hurry.
exp.2:12:
David agrees to make a covenant with Abner, the commander of Ish-bosheth's army. But he sets a condition: Abner will not be allowed to see David unless he first brings Michal, Saul's daughter, with him.

David speaks as king of Judah at Hebron. Abner, who had been supporting the reign of Ish-bosheth, offers to switch sides to David and unite Israel. Michal had been David's wife, but Saul had given her to another man. Scholars often see here both a legitimate claim and a political move, since being Saul's son-in-law strengthened his right to the throne. We cannot be certain which motive weighed more.

For today: important agreements call for clear and honest conditions. But it is also wise to examine our motives, so that what is right is not mixed with self-interest, and to think about how our decisions affect other people.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that David was thirty years old when he became king, and that he reigned forty years in total. The reader's wording "became king" replaces the older phrasing, so the explanation uses it throughout.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not David. After years of conflict with the house of Saul, the elders of Israel come to Hebron and recognize David as king. The author summarizes the length of his reign: seven years and a half in Hebron over Judah, and thirty-three in Jerusalem over all Israel. The figure of forty is a round number, and the text presents it as a summary.

For today: God can bring a person to his purpose with patience. David waited years from the time he was anointed until he reigned over everyone. Trust God's timing and be faithful while you wait.
exp.5:21:
Here David says he is willing to humble himself even further to honor God. "Humiliate" and "humble" describe lowering yourself, becoming small and of little standing in the eyes of others. The "maidservants" are the female servants. David states that he will be fine being low in his own sight, and that these same servants, the ones Michal mocked, will honor him.

David speaks with Michal, Saul's daughter and his wife. He had just brought the ark of God to Jerusalem, dancing with joy before the Lord. Michal despised him in her heart and criticized him with sarcasm. David answers that his praise was for God, who chose him as king. The text does not clearly say whether Michal's lack of children was a punishment or a circumstance; it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: do not let the opinion of others hinder your sincere worship. Praising God with humility is worth more than guarding your image.
exp.23:11:
God tells the prophet Gad to say to David: "I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you." The words "Go and tell" are a command to carry a message. "Offering" means that God sets before David three options of punishment, and the king must choose one.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Gad. David had ordered the people to be counted, and then his conscience accused him. He acknowledged his sin and asked for forgiveness, but the consequences came all the same. The Bible does not explain in detail why counting the people was so serious; some believe David trusted in his military strength instead of trusting in God.

For today: when we fail, it is good to confess quickly, as David did. God's forgiveness is real, but some consequences may remain. Even so, we can place our lives in the hands of a compassionate God, not in the hands of fear or of other people.
exp.1:6:
What it says: David encourages the men of Jabesh-gilead to be strong and courageous. He tells them that Saul, their lord, is dead, and that the house of Judah has anointed him as their king.

Context: David speaks through messengers. He wants to thank the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul with respect. At the same time, he lets them know about his new reign in Judah, perhaps seeking their support. Later Abner set Ish-bosheth up as king over the rest of Israel, so the country was divided. David's motives may have been both gratitude and politics.

For today: Recognizing and thanking others for the good they do, even someone difficult, is a form of mercy. We can also encourage those living through uncertain times, telling them in concrete words that they are not alone.
exp.22:21:
This verse sums up what Benaiah did: he killed lions, defeated a giant Egyptian, and took away his spear. "Won a name" means that he became famous, that his reputation was great among David's brave warriors. "Along with the three mighty men" refers to a group of outstanding fighters.

The passage is a list of the bravest men in David's army. The narrator remembers them to honor their loyalty and courage. The next verse makes clear that Benaiah did not become one of the first three, although he was highly respected. Some think that his fame brought him close to them.

For today: God notices those who act with courage and faithfulness, even if they are not the first. Do what is right today with firmness, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.7:0:
It says that David defeated the Philistines, an enemy people of Israel, and subdued them. He also took a place called Metheg-ammah from them. "Defeated" means that he beat them in battle, and "subdued" means that he brought them under his control. It is not known for certain what Metheg-ammah is. Many think it refers to Gath and its villages, according to a parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 18:1.

The author of the book tells the story of Israel. This comes some time after God promised David a house and a lasting kingdom (chapter 7). The account shows how David strengthened his kingdom and gave security to the people.

For today: God keeps what He promises, though sometimes He does it step by step. Trust Him in your struggles, and do not lose heart if progress is slow.
exp.20:19:
There was another battle against the Philistines, this time at Gath. A man of great height lived there, with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four digits in all. He too was descended from Rapha, which likely points to a family line of unusually tall men.

The author of the book is not identified with certainty. He is summarizing the final wars of David's reign against the Philistines. The next verse tells how this man challenged Israel, and Jonathan, David's nephew, killed him. The passage shows that the fearsome enemies fell before David and his servants.

For today: problems that seem enormous are not bigger than God. David did not fight alone, and his team also had a part to play. Face your own "giants" by trusting in God and leaning on other believers.
exp.7:9:
Toi, king of Hamath, sent his son Joram to visit King David. He sent him to greet David and to bless him, because David had defeated Hadadezer, Toi's enemy. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold and bronze. The reader should know that the gifts are described simply as articles of metal, and the reference to bronze fits the Hebrew wording here. Another passage (1 Chronicles 18:10) gives the son's name as Hadoram, so it is either the same person under another name or a different person, and this is not known for certain.

The narrator describes how David's kingdom grew. By defeating Hadadezer, David gained great fame, and other kings sought his friendship. Toi was glad, because he now had one fewer enemy. Then David dedicated these gifts to the LORD.

For today: when God gives us a victory or a blessing, we can receive it with gratitude and hand it back to Him. What we have is not only for our own pride, but to honor God and to serve others.
exp.16:27:
This verse lists what three men brought to David and his people: beds, basins, clay vessels, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, and lentils. The word "basins" refers to bowls, and "roasted grain" was grain ready to eat without much cooking. The phrase "brought beds" simply means they brought beds to David.

The speaker here is not a character but the narrator of the book. David was fleeing his son Absalom, who had rebelled, and he arrived weary at Mahanaim. There Shobi, Machir, and Barzilai, three men of good standing, brought him provisions. The next verse explains why: they knew the people were hungry, tired, and thirsty.

For today: concrete help is a form of love. Notice who is going through a hard time and offer something practical, such as food, rest, or company, without waiting to be asked.
exp.22:18:
It speaks of Abishai. It says he was more honored than the Three, a group of three, and that he became their commander. Yet even so, he was not included among the Three, David's most famous heroes.

The narrator of Second Samuel lists David's mighty warriors and their deeds. Abishai, brother of Joab, raised his spear against three hundred men. Scholars disagree about how to understand the two groups of "three": most likely they are two different trios, but the text does not fully clarify this.

Today: you can give your best and be recognized, and still not be "the first." The Bible records Abishai with honor all the same. Serve with devotion without comparing yourself, trusting that God values your faithfulness, not your place on the list.
exp.2:22:
This verse tells how Joab returned with his troops and, when he arrived, was told that Abner, the son of Ner, had come to see King David. He was informed that David had sent Abner on his way and that Abner had left in peace, meaning without being held or harmed. The phrase "he was informed" means that someone let him know.

The one speaking here is the narrator, who reports the news that Joab receives. Abner had been commander of Saul's army and came to make an agreement with David to unite Israel under his rule. Joab, David's general, was not present when everything happened. The text that follows shows that Joab distrusted Abner and confronted David for having let him go.

For today: when we do not know the whole story, it is easy to react with suspicion or anger. Before judging, it is wise to listen, seek the truth, and seek peace.
exp.5:7:
Then David became angry because the LORD had burst forth against Uzzah, and he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem, but they were carrying it on a cart, and not as God had directed, by carrying it with poles. Uzzah reached out and touched it, and God struck him down. The text tells us that David was angry, and it names the place after what happened there.

For today: God is loving, but he is also holy. Let us draw near to him with reverence and obedience, not only with good intentions.
exp.19:17:
Here the wise woman says that long ago people used to say, "Seek counsel at Abel," and that disputes were settled that way. The phrase she quotes is the wording your verse uses, so there is no need to explain any old words here.

Joab had laid siege to the city of Abel of Beth-maacah, because Sheba, who had rebelled against David, had taken refuge there. The woman speaks to stop the destruction. She appeals to Abel's reputation as a place where disputes were settled wisely and peacefully. Some believe the saying shows that people sought wisdom there; the text gives no further details about its origin.

For today: A wise word spoken with respect can prevent great harm. Before acting in anger, let us learn to listen and to talk things through, as Joab did, and always seek peace.
exp.2:8:
Abner makes a strong oath: "May God punish me severely if I do not do for David what the LORD promised him." The words call down punishment on oneself if one fails to keep one's word.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army and was supporting Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, as king. Ish-bosheth accused him of sleeping with Rizpah, one of Saul's concubines, and Abner became extremely angry. So he decided to switch sides to David and transfer the kingdom. His motive seems more anger and wounded pride than obedience to God, although the promise to David was real.

Today, God can carry out his plans even when people act from mixed motives. Let us ask him to cleanse our intentions, so that we obey by faith and not out of pride or resentment.
exp.14:13:
David said to all the servants with him in Jerusalem, "Get up and let us flee, or we will not escape from Absalom!" He tells them they must leave quickly, because if they stay, Absalom will soon catch up with them, bring disaster on them, and put the city to the sword. "Leave quickly" means "hurry," and "put the city to the sword" means "kill the people of the city with violence."

David is speaking here as the king of Israel. His son Absalom had plotted against him and was winning the hearts of the people. When David learns that Israel is following Absalom, he decides to leave the city. It seems he wants to spare Jerusalem from fighting within its walls, and also to save his own people.

For today: sometimes acting wisely means withdrawing rather than fighting out of pride. When a conflict could hurt others, thinking first about their well-being can be an act of humility and love.
exp.13:9:
In this verse, King David promises to protect the woman. He tells her that if anyone speaks against her or threatens her over what she asked for, she should bring that person to him, and that person will no longer trouble her. "Trouble" here means harm or bother.

David, the king, is speaking with a woman from Tekoa. She tells a story about her son, who had killed his brother, and her relatives want to kill him. Many understand that Joab sent her so that David would reflect on his own son Absalom, who had been banished for a similar crime. David does not yet see the comparison, and he promises to protect her.

For today: Those who hold authority can use it to protect the vulnerable. But we also need humility to listen, and to see whether what we advise others we should also apply in our own lives.
exp.17:0:
This verse tells how David reviewed and organized the people who were with him. The word for "reviewed" here means he examined them carefully, looking over the troops. Then he appointed leaders: the commanders of a thousand soldiers and the commanders of a hundred. In this way he divided the army into groups, each with a clear leader.

The account is told by the author of the book of Samuel. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled and taken the kingdom. They were at Mahanaim, on the other side of the Jordan. Before the battle, David prepared the army in an orderly way, placing Joab, Abishai, and Ittai in charge of the troops.

For today: Before facing a great challenge, it is wise to pray and also to plan in an orderly way. God does not despise preparation; He shares out responsibilities, asks for help, and trusts that He guides the outcome.
exp.2:23:
Joab comes before King David and confronts him with a sharp question: "What have you done?" He tells the king that Abner had come to him, and asks why he would dismiss him and let him get away.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had come to Hebron to make an agreement with David and unite Israel, and David had sent him away in peace. Joab had just returned from a raid. He distrusts Abner, and the Bible also reminds us that Abner had killed Asahel, Joab's brother. So there may be personal reasons behind his words, along with his concern for the kingdom.

Before we accuse or act against someone, it is wise to examine our own hearts. Joab says he is protecting the king, but perhaps resentment is what moves him. Let us ask God for sincerity, so that we can tell the difference between a just concern and a vengeance wearing a disguise.
exp.1:24:
The explanation says that the Benjamites rallied around Abner, formed a single unit, and took their stand on top of a hill. The word "unit" here refers to an organized group of soldiers, and the hill is a small rise of ground.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After the death of Saul, there is war between the followers of Ish-bosheth, who are from Israel, and the followers of David. Abner, commander of Ish-bosheth's army, had killed Asahel, brother of Joab, and Joab and Abishai were pursuing him. The Benjamites, the tribe of Saul and of Abner, gathered to defend themselves from a high place.

Today we can see how much harm violence between brothers causes. When there is conflict, seeking peace in time prevents more pain. Let us ask God for humility to speak and to forgive before the wound grows.
exp.18:22:
David tells Shimei, "You shall not die," and confirms it with an oath. The phrase "swore an oath" means that he made a solemn promise, calling on God as witness.

David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Shimei had cursed him as he fled (2 Samuel 16), and now he comes to ask for forgiveness. Abishai, who wanted to defend the king, asked that Shimei be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed. David rejected this and chose to show mercy on the day of his return. Later, before his death, David gave his son Solomon instructions about Shimei (1 Kings 2), and readers debate how to understand that.

Today we can learn that forgiveness opens the door to peace. When someone has offended us and repents, we can respond with grace instead of revenge, and keep the word we have given.
exp.12:0:
This verse introduces three sons of David. Absalom has a very beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon, another son of David, fell in love with her. Here the word "love" sounds like affection, but what follows in the account shows that it was a selfish and harmful desire. Tamar and Absalom were full brother and sister, both children of the same mother and father; Amnon was a half-brother to both, from a different mother.

This is the beginning of a very painful episode. The narrator is the author of the book of Samuel, who recounts without embellishment the troubles within David's family. This happens after David sinned with Bathsheba, and many readers see a connection with the consequences God had announced for his household, although the text does not say so directly here.

Today it reminds us that not every strong feeling is true love. It is wise to examine our desires in the light of God and set boundaries in time, before they hurt others.
exp.12:6:
This verse tells how King David sends word to his daughter Tamar at the palace, asking her to go to the house of her brother Amnon and prepare a meal for him. The request is simple and familiar: a father asks a daughter to cook for a sick son. The small fried cakes mentioned earlier were little flat breads fried in oil. David does this believing that his son is truly sick.

Amnon pretended to be ill following the advice of his cousin Jonadab, and so he deceived his father. His real purpose was to be alone with Tamar, and what follows in the account is a terrible assault against her. David acts with trust and good intentions, but without realizing the deception.

For today: It is wise to be attentive and not to trust blindly, even within the family. Those who care for others, such as parents or leaders, should ask, observe, and protect the most vulnerable. And if someone suffers abuse, they deserve to be heard and protected.
exp.9:1:
David decides to show kindness to Hanun, the son of Nahash, because his father had shown kindness to him. Hanun has become king, and David wants to honor his father's memory. "Show kindness" means acting with goodness and loyalty. Sending servants "to console" Hanun means offering sympathy over the loss of his father. David sends his servants with that message of support, but when they arrive in the land of the Ammonites, the story takes a troubling turn.

The text does not explain how Nahash showed kindness to David. It only says that David wants to repay that favor. That is why he sends a formal delegation, as was customary between kings. What follows shows that Hanun's advisers suspected bad intentions, and the king humiliated the messengers.

For today: practice gratitude through concrete actions. If someone helped you, look for ways to honor them or their family in their grief. And even when others misread your good intentions, keep acting with kindness and without malice.
exp.17:6:
This verse tells us that the army of Israel, the one that followed Absalom, was defeated by David's men. The slaughter that day was great: twenty thousand men died. "David's servants" refers to his loyal soldiers. "Slaughter" in the verse refers to a great number of deaths in battle.

The narrator describes the battle in the forest of Ephraim, when Absalom rebelled against his father David. Shortly before, David had asked his captains to deal gently with his son. Even so, the fighting was fierce. The text says the forest devoured more people than the sword did, though it does not explain in detail how. The figure of twenty thousand may be understood literally or as an approximate number.

For today: decisions of rebellion and pride leave deep wounds that reach many people. Before following a path of division, it is wise to stop, seek God, and consider the harm we might cause to others.
exp.5:19:
David returned home to bless his household after the great celebration when he brought the ark into Jerusalem. There Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, came out to meet him with mockery. She said the king had distinguished himself, but she spoke with sarcasm, saying he had uncovered himself in front of the maidservants like a vulgar person would do. Her "distinguished" likely means that he had made himself look very impressive, and her words were meant to shame him. The phrase "uncovered himself" probably refers to David taking off his royal robes and dancing in light linen clothing, not necessarily to being without any clothing at all. A "vulgar person" is a crude man who acts out foolish antics.
