Michal speaks with contempt because she watched David dance with all his strength before the Lord. To her, a king should keep his dignity. David answers that he was worshiping God, who chose him over her father and his house.

Today, let us not allow the fear of other people's opinions to keep us from worshiping God with sincerity and joy. And let us take care not to despise the devotion of others simply because it is expressed differently from our own.
exp.13:27:
This verse says that Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two years without being able to see the face of King David, his father. The phrase "see the king's face" means to be received by him, to stand in his presence. So Absalom was close by, in the same city, yet he remained kept apart from his father.

The account has no one speaking. Instead, the narrator tells what happened. Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled. Later Joab arranged for him to return to Jerusalem, but David would not receive him. The reconciliation was left unfinished. The Bible does not fully explain David's reasons, and the silence between the two prepared tensions that would come later.

For today: a broken relationship is not healed simply by being near. If there is a wound in your family, seek sincere dialogue, forgiveness, and honesty in time, before silence and resentment grow.
exp.20:17:
Some time later at Gob, there was another battle with the Philistines. At that time, a warrior of David named Sibbecai, from the Hushathite clan, killed Saph, a descendant of Rapha. Here "descendant of Rapha" refers to one of the giant-born people of the region.

The narrator of the book recounts several wars against the Philistines at the end of David's reign. After David nearly died at the hands of another giant, his men protect him and point out that other brave men were also fighting. The account shows that the victory did not depend on a single hero.

Today we can learn that God often carries out his work through a team. Some people are not very well known, like Sibbecai, but their faithfulness matters. Serve wherever you are, without waiting for applause, and rejoice when others also contribute.
exp.11:20:
David's servants are shocked by his behavior. While the child was alive, David fasted and wept; but when the child died, David got up and ate. The phrase "got up" matches the wording of the verse, and "ate" here refers to eating food in general.

The servants speak. The child was the son born from David's relationship with Bathsheba, and he became sick as a result of David's sin. While the boy lived, David pleaded with God for his life. When the child died, David worshiped in the house of the LORD and then ate again. The servants expected more mourning, not less, and that is why they ask.

For today: there is a time to plead with God with all your heart, and another time to accept his answer with humility. When sorrow comes, we can worship, rest in God, and move forward, without ceasing to feel sadness.
exp.1:26:
Joab swears by God: "As surely as God lives." He says that if Abner had not spoken up, his troops would have kept pursuing their Israelite brothers until morning. The words are difficult, and they can be understood in two ways: that the fight would have ended sooner if Abner had not stirred up the battle, or that the pursuit would have continued until the next day.

Joab, the commander of David's army, is speaking. Abner, the commander of Saul's army, has just asked him to stop the pursuit and prevent more deaths among brothers. Joab answers firmly, but he agrees to stop and blows the trumpet.

For today: when a conflict harms people who should be united, it is wise to stop in time. You do not need to win the argument; sometimes the bravest thing is to seek peace before bitterness grows.
exp.22:26:
This verse names two warriors from David's army: Abiezer, from the town of Anathoth, and Mebunnai, from Hushah. "From Anathoth" and "from Hushah" show where each man came from. They are only names, with no details about their deeds.

The narrator of the book of Samuel presents the list of the thirty, David's most outstanding warriors. Anathoth was a town in the tribe of Benjamin, near Jerusalem. In 1 Chronicles 11:29 a warrior from Hushah named Sibbecai appears, and some think he could be the same person under another name, but this is not certain.

God remembers those who serve, even though almost no one knows them. Today, your faithful and quiet work in your family, your church, or your job also counts. You do not need applause to be valuable in God's work.
exp.10:1:
One evening David got up from his bed and strolled around on the roof of the palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the Bible describes her as very beautiful. The verse opens with "One evening," and the word "bathing" shows that she was washing herself.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book, not David. He points out that it was the season when kings went out to war, but David stayed in Jerusalem while Joab and the army fought. The text does not say this in so many words, but it shows that David was not where he should have been, and that prepares the sin that follows.

For today: many falls begin with carelessness, not with a great evil. Looking was not the greatest sin; what was serious came afterward, when he let desire take charge. When something tempts you, move away quickly, busy yourself with what is rightly yours to do, and ask God for strength.
exp.16:11:
It says that Israel's army will attack David wherever they find him, coming down on him like dew settling over the ground. "Descend on him like dew" suggests a sudden, widespread attack that covers everything. "Not even one will remain" means that no one will be left alive, neither David nor any of his men.

The speaker is Hushai, David's friend, who pretends to be loyal to Absalom. His real purpose is to give David time to flee and regroup. With grand and stirring words, he persuades Absalom not to follow Ahithophel's advice. The verses that follow say that God allowed Ahithophel's good counsel to fail.

For today: even when other people's plans seem convincing and powerful, God remains in control. We can trust that he knows how to guide events, and we should be wary of speeches that flatter our pride.
exp.22:10:
After him was Shammah, son of Agee, the Hararite. When the Philistines had banded together near a field full of lentils, Israel's troops fled from them. Shammah is a reminder that not every man ran. The passage simply recalls what happened, and it is the narrator, not any speaker in the scene, who tells it.

This passage is part of the list of David's mighty men, at the end of the book of 2 Samuel. The purpose is to show that, even when the people gave way out of fear, God worked through people who did not turn back. The next verse makes clear that it was the Lord who gave the victory.

For today: sometimes everyone around you gives in to something that seems small or worthless, like a field of lentils. Ask God for the courage to stand firm in what is right, trusting that the victory comes from Him.
exp.6:21:
This verse is a song of praise. David declares that God is great because there is no one like him, and that there is no God but him. He grounds this in what Israel had heard, generation after generation, about God's works. The idea that God makes himself great means that he shows himself to be great and worthy of honor by what he does.

David speaks in prayer, sitting before the Lord. God had just promised him, through the prophet Nathan, that his family would reign for a long time. David had wanted to build a temple, but God promised him something greater: to establish his house, that is, his descendants. David responds with amazement and gratitude, remembering how God had rescued Israel from Egypt.

For today: before asking for anything, take a moment to remember what God has already done in your life and in the history of his people. Thanking him and acknowledging his greatness helps you trust him more.
exp.2:27:
In this verse, David, on hearing that Abner had been killed, declared that neither he nor his kingdom bore any guilt for that bloodshed. The statement "I and my kingdom are guiltless" makes the same claim, and "before the LORD" points to the same meaning. "Forever" shows that David wanted his innocence to be clear to everyone.

David speaks as king of Judah. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had just made a peace agreement with him. Joab, commander of David's army, killed him in secret, partly to avenge the death of his brother Asahel. David did not know this beforehand and feared that people would think he had ordered it, which would have ruined the peace.

For today: when others do something wrong in our name or near us, silence is not enough. It is wise to clearly reject injustice, to ask God to guide us, and to keep our witness honest.
exp.1:20:
Abner, who is fleeing in the middle of the battle, tells Asahel to turn to his right or left and seize one of the other young soldiers, taking that man's equipment instead of chasing him. The young men are the young soldiers, the equipment is what is taken from a defeated enemy, and "chasing" means running after him from behind. But Asahel refused to stop the pursuit.

This happens after the battle between the men of David and those of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul. Abner was the commander of Saul's army, and Asahel, brother of Joab, was a very swift warrior. Abner did not want to kill him, because he knew that this would bring enmity with Joab. The verses that follow show that Asahel ended up dead.

For today: when someone wise warns us and offers a way out, it is wise to listen. Stubbornness or pride can lead us to fight battles that are not ours and to pay a very high price.
exp.19:8:
Joab approaches Amasa and asks him, "Are you well, my brother?", a common greeting. With his right hand he grabs Amasa by the beard to kiss him, the way relatives and friends greeted one another. The verse names the right hand, and the rest of the account shows that Joab's left hand already held the dagger.

Joab was David's general. David had appointed Amasa in place of Joab, and Joab and Amasa were cousins. The Bible does not say in detail everything Joab was thinking, but the account shows that he used a friendly greeting to kill Amasa by surprise. The narrator speaks, and Joab speaks.

For today: let us be careful not to use kind words or gestures of affection to hide bad intentions. May our greeting and our heart say the same thing, and may we be sincere with those we deal with.
exp.21:47:
It is God who defends David and brings about justice for him. "He avenges me" means that God vindicated David against his enemies and acted on his behalf. "Brings down nations beneath me" means that God placed the nations under David's authority.

David, now an old man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving that recalls how God delivered him from Saul and from other enemies (2 Samuel 22:1). He does not claim the victory for himself; he praises it as the work of God, whom he calls his rock, that is, his firm refuge. Some understand this as a song that also carries a prophetic tone about the Messiah, although the text speaks first of David.

For today: when you are wounded or treated unfairly, avoid taking revenge on your own. Hand the situation over to God in prayer, trust that He does justice in his own time, and give thanks for every help received.
exp.22:25:
This verse continues the list of David's mighty warriors. It names Helez the Paltite and Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite. Tekoa was a town in Judah, south of Bethlehem. The names appear with almost no details.

The author of the book records the final events of David's reign and honors his "thirty" trusted men. Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator. Each one is named because his loyalty helped David and Israel. No deed is told of Helez or Ira; the Bible gives no further information, and it is not right to invent any.

For today: God sees and remembers those who serve without anyone applauding them. If your work is quiet, do it faithfully. Your name may be little known among people, but God knows it.
exp.14:32:
David answers Husai: if you go with me, you will be a burden to me. The verse reads, "David said to him, 'If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me.'"

David speaks while he is fleeing from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Husai, his faithful friend, arrives with torn clothes and dust on his head, signs of mourning. David has just prayed that God would make the counsel of Ahithophel fail. Then, instead of accepting Husai's company, he asks him to return and serve Absalom in order to help him from within. In this way David does not reject Husai; he gives him a different task that is more useful.

For today: serving God and others does not always mean doing what we most desire or what seems closest to us. Sometimes loyal love shows itself by accepting the place where God puts us, even when it is difficult or not easily seen.
exp.17:27:
Ahimaaz runs up to King David and calls out, "All is well!" This was a common greeting, and it also meant that he was bringing good news. He bows facedown before the king to show respect, and then he praises the LORD your God, because he has handed over the men who raised their hands against the king. In other words, God gave David the victory over those who had risen up against him.

Ahimaaz, the son of the priest Zadok, runs to report the outcome of the battle against Absalom, David's son, who had rebelled. He speaks of the victory but avoids saying the most painful thing: that Absalom had died. Then David asks about his son, and Ahimaaz answers evasively. He perhaps wanted to give only the happy part of the news.

For today: let us give thanks to God for his victories, but let us be honest and sensitive when we share difficult news. Telling the whole truth, with love and care, is better than showing only what is pleasant.
exp.8:7:
Mephibosheth bows down again before David and says, "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?" It is a very humble way of speaking. "Show regard for" here means to notice someone with favor and care. Calling himself a "dead dog" meant calling himself worthless, someone not deserving of attention.

He speaks as Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul. David has just promised him kindness for the sake of Jonathan, his friend, and restored to him his family's lands. Mephibosheth was lame in his feet (2 Samuel 9:3, 4:4), and came from a fallen family. His reaction shows astonishment, not pride.

For today: God treats us with grace that we have not earned. We can receive his kindness with humility and gratitude, and share that same kindness with those who seem to have nothing to offer.
exp.16:21:
This verse tells how David and all the people with him got up during the night and crossed the Jordan River before daybreak. No one was left on the far side or behind; everyone made it across. The phrase "by daybreak" refers to the time just before the sun rose.

The account is narrated by the writer of Samuel. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled. Ahimaaz and Jonathan, hiding in a well, had warned him of the plan of Ahithophel, the counselor who wanted to attack him quickly. David acted on the warning without delay and crossed the river. In this way he gained time and moved away from danger.

For today: when God gives us a clear warning, it is wise to act promptly and not put off until tomorrow what we can do today. Also, let us take care of all who depend on us, so that no one is left behind.
exp.18:0:
This verse tells us that someone reported to Joab, the commander of the army, that King David was weeping and mourning over his son Absalom. The word "reported" means "informed him," and "mourning" refers to David's deep grief over a loss.

David's army had just won a battle against Absalom, who had rebelled against his father. Absalom died in that fight. The narrator is describing how the news reached Joab. The verses that follow show that the king's weeping dampened the joy of the soldiers, and they entered the city ashamed, as though they had lost.

For today: grief and duty can clash. David loved his son even though Absalom had betrayed him. We can learn to mourn honestly, but also to consider how our sorrow affects those around us who have served us faithfully.
exp.10:14:
This verse tells what David wrote in the letter that Uriah himself carried to Joab. The order was to put Uriah at the front, where the fiercest fighting was, and then withdraw from him, so that he would be struck down and killed. The instruction to withdraw means pulling back and leaving him without support.

The narrator explains that David had already sinned with Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and she was pregnant. David tried to get Uriah to spend time with his wife so that the truth would be hidden, but Uriah would not go home while his companions were in battle. So David decided to have him killed, using the war as a cover.

For today: a hidden sin often leads to another, worse one. Instead of covering up our failings, it is wise to confess them to God soon and seek the forgiveness and help that He gives.
exp.19:4:
The explanation says that Amasa went out to gather the men of Judah, as the king had commanded him, but he took longer than the three days David had set for him. The word "took longer" in the verse means he delayed or was late. The explanation does not give the reason for the delay.

The one telling the story is the narrator. David had just returned to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion, and Amasa was the commander David had put in place of Joab. Another uprising had broken out, the revolt of Sheba, and quick action was needed. Amasa's delay caused David to send others after Sheba. The Bible does not say why it took so long; some think he had difficulty winning the trust of Judah, but that is only one possibility.

For today: when you are given something important, carry it out on time, or let the right person know if you will be late. Responsibility and honesty in small things care for others and show faithfulness.
exp.21:22:
David says that he always kept all of God's ordinances in view. God's commands are his instructions, and his statutes are his righteous rules or standards. The word "ordinances" here refers to rules God has set, and David says he has not disregarded God's statutes. This means he kept them in mind and did not set them aside.

David speaks this at the end of his life, in a song of thanks because God rescued him from Saul and from all his enemies. When he speaks of "my righteousness," he is not claiming to be perfect, since the Bible records his serious sins. Many understand that he is speaking of his general faithfulness to God and his desire to obey him. Others see here a contrast with his enemies.

For today: keep God's Word in view. Read a passage each day and put one concrete teaching into practice, so that obedience becomes a habit and not something occasional.
exp.12:16:
Amnon calls his attendant, the young man who served him, and orders him: "Throw this woman out and bolt the door behind her!" In the verse, the command is to throw her out, and "this woman" is Tamar, his half-sister.

Amnon is the speaker, the son of King David. He had just abused Tamar, and suddenly his supposed love had turned into hatred. She begged him not to send her away, because that would be one more wrong added to the first, but he would not listen. He treats her like an object he no longer wants, taking no responsibility at all. The Bible tells this plainly and does not approve of it.

For today: when someone suffers an injustice, let us not leave them alone. Let us listen, protect, and stand with them in compassion, instead of staying silent or looking the other way.
exp.19:0:
This verse tells us that a worthless man named Sheba, son of Bichri, from the tribe of Benjamin, was there at that moment. He blew a ram's horn and shouted that Israel had no share in David and no inheritance in Jesse's son. Then he told the people to go back, every man to his tent, meaning to their homes.

The narrator calls Sheba a worthless man because he took advantage of a moment of tension. David had just returned after Absalom's rebellion, and the tribes of the north and Judah were arguing over who had done more for the king (2 Samuel 19). Sheba used that anger to divide Israel.

Today, when there are conflicts between people, it is easy for someone to stir up anger with words that drive people apart. We can choose to be peacemakers: to think before we speak, not to repeat complaints that divide, and to seek reconciliation.
exp.15:18:
Husai says: "Whom should I serve? Shouldn't I serve his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you." Here "whom should I serve" asks whom he ought to serve. Husai implies that his loyalty belongs to the king's family.

Husai is speaking with Absalom, who rebelled against his father David and took Jerusalem. Earlier, David had asked Husai, his friend, to return to the city and pretend to support Absalom in order to frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15:32-37). For this reason his words are clever and have a double meaning. The text does not comment on whether that was right, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: loyalty and wisdom matter, but not everything is what it seems. Ask God for discernment to act with integrity in complicated situations.
exp.13:0:
Joab, son of Zeruiah and commander of David's army, saw that the king longed for Absalom. The word "saw" here means he noticed or understood what was going on. Interpreters read the king's longing in slightly different ways: some take it as a deep desire to see his son again, while others take it as a movement of the heart toward reconciliation.

Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled into exile. David longed for him, but he did not act on that longing. Joab, a practical and clever man, decided to step in with the story of a woman from Tekoa. Interpreters debate whether he did this out of sincere compassion, for political reasons, or for both.

For today: when a broken relationship hurts us, feelings alone are not enough; we must seek paths of truth and justice that bring real healing. Let us ask God for wisdom to be reconciled without ignoring sin.
exp.4:18:
Before David went into battle against the Philistines, he asked God two questions: should he go up against them, and would God hand them over to him? God answered him directly: "Go up," because He would surely give the Philistines into David's hand. To "inquire" of the LORD means to seek His direction, and "into your hand" means giving David the victory over them.

The Philistines had heard that David was now king over all Israel, and they came out to attack him, spreading out across the valley of Rephaim. David did not rush ahead on his own impulse. He turned to God first, because he knew the outcome of the war depended on the LORD and not only on his own strength or skill as a warrior.

Before making important decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer and in His Word. Even if you already have experience or feel capable, ask Him first. Then act with confidence in what He shows you.
exp.2:35:
What it says: All the people noticed how David honored Abner, and they were pleased by it. Whatever the king did pleased them.

Context: It is the narrator who speaks. Abner, commander of Saul's army, had been killed by Joab, and David mourned him publicly, fasted, and composed a lament. In this way he showed that he had no part in that death. The people, who could have suspected David, saw his sincere grief and accepted it. The verses that follow confirm this: they understood that the king had not caused that death.

For today: Our conduct speaks louder than our defenses. When we act with integrity, humility, and compassion, even in difficult moments, we naturally gain trust. Let us strive to live openly and sincerely.
exp.13:19:
Joab, the king's servant, is the one who brought about this change of affairs. "This change of affairs" means he gave the matter a new direction, presenting it in a different way so that it would reach the outcome he wanted. The woman adds that King David has wisdom like the wisdom of an angel of God, and that he knows everything that happens in the land.

The woman of Tekoa is speaking. Joab had asked her to tell David an invented story about a son who had been banished. Through this, he hoped to lead the king to bring his son Absalom back. David discovers that Joab is behind it, and she admits the plan. Her praise may be sincere, but it also sounds like flattery meant to soften the moment.

We may seek reconciliation, but with honesty. If we speak with truth and humility, we avoid manipulating others, even when our intentions are good.
exp.10:23:
Here the messenger tells David how the battle at Rabbah went. He says that the archers shot at David's soldiers from the wall, and that some of the king's soldiers were killed. At the end he adds, almost in passing, that Uriah the Hittite is dead as well. The "archers" are the men shooting from the wall, and "your servants" are David's soldiers.

The messenger repeats Joab's report. Joab had ordered Uriah to go to a dangerous place, as David had requested in a letter, and that is why other soldiers were lost. Joab knew the king might become angry at the approach to the wall, so he mentioned Uriah's death to calm him. David, however, responds coldly.

For today: a hidden sin never stays small; it drags others along and leaves victims. If we have failed, the best thing is to confess early and seek God's forgiveness, not to cover it up.
exp.13:14:
She says that she came to speak with the king because the people had made her afraid. By "the people have made me afraid," she refers to the threat from her relatives, who wanted to take away her son. She tells how she resolved to speak, thinking: "Perhaps he will grant the request of his maidservant." Calling herself "maidservant" is a humble way of addressing the king.

The one speaking is the woman of Tekoa, sent by Joab. She tells a made-up story about her son in order to move David's heart and lead him to think about his son Absalom, who was banished. Many understand that the whole thing was a strategy. Here she explains her courage in coming before the king.

For today: when something frightens us, we can take a step of courage and speak with humility. It is also good to ask for wisdom to tell the truth honestly and not with deception.
exp.18:27:
Mephibosheth tells King David that his whole family deserved death from the king, yet David has seated him at his own table among those who eat with the king. So he feels he has no further right to keep appealing for help. The guests are the people invited to eat at the king's table, and the phrase "deserves death" means that he and his family deserved to die.

He speaks as Saul's grandson when David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Ziba, his servant, had accused him of disloyalty, and Mephibosheth says that Ziba deceived him. The Bible does not fully make clear who was telling the truth. What stands out is his humility and his gratitude toward David, who had earlier shown him kindness.

For today: when we remember that we have received favors we did not deserve, such as forgiveness and God's care, it is easier to live with gratitude and let go of our complaints. We might ask ourselves today: what am I complaining about, and what kindness of God am I forgetting?
exp.2:38:
Here David says that he is still weak, though he has already been anointed as king. He recognizes that the sons of Zeruiah, Joab and Abishai, are too fierce for him, meaning he cannot restrain them. For that reason he does not carry out justice himself, but asks the LORD to repay the evildoer according to his evil.

David speaks after Joab killed Abner treacherously. Abner was going to help him unite all Israel under his reign. David wants to make clear that he did not order that death, and he shows this through public mourning. Some think he also admits that he did not have enough strength to punish Joab at that time.

For today: when you come across an injustice that you cannot correct, do not fold your arms or take revenge. Act with honesty, do what is within your reach, and leave the rest to God, who judges with justice.
exp.7:1:
David defeated the Moabites and made them lie down on the ground. Then he measured them off with a cord: two lengths were for those to be put to death, and one length was for those to be spared. The survivors became subject to David and paid him tribute, that is, compulsory taxes. The word "defeated" is the verse's own, and "measured them off" refers to the cord mentioned in the verse.

It is a historical account, not a speech. It tells how David extended his kingdom after defeating the Philistines. The passage does not explain why he treated Moab this way, and scholars do not agree on the details. Some think it refers to prisoners of war in a very violent era.

For today: this passage reminds us that the Bible honestly recounts the harshness of human history. It invites us to be thankful for the mercy of Christ and to seek peace, treating with compassion even those who have been our adversaries.
exp.13:23:
In this verse, King David decides that his son Absalom may return to Jerusalem, but he does not want to see him. "He may return to his house" means that Absalom is allowed to go home. "He must not see my face" means that he is not permitted to come into the king's presence. Absalom obeys and spends a period of time without seeing his father.

It is David who speaks. Absalom had killed his brother Amnon and fled to Geshur. Joab, the commander of the army, managed to get David to allow his return. But David did not receive him fully: there was a return, but not a reconciliation. The Bible does not explain all of David's reasons; they could be grief, doubt or indecision.

For today: a partial forgiveness leaves open wounds. If there is a broken relationship in your family, seek with prayer and humility a true reconciliation, with truth, justice and love, not merely a peace that only looks like peace.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that David, when he heard that the Ammonites were preparing for war with the help of Syrian soldiers, sent Joab, his military commander, together with the entire army of mighty men. "Sent" means that he gave the order to go out; "the mighty men" were the strongest and best-prepared warriors of Israel.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Samuel. David's messengers had been humiliated by the Ammonites, and they, knowing that they had made themselves hateful to David, hired foreign armies. David did not wait to be attacked, but responded with his whole army under the command of Joab.

For today: when we face a serious problem, it is good to act with responsibility and preparation, without ignoring it. Even so, we do well to trust God while we do what is ours to do.
exp.20:13:
They buried the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan in Zela, in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Saul's father Kish. This verse tells how their remains were laid to rest with honor in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. "Buried" means they were placed in the grave, and "answered their prayers" means that God responded favorably to the requests made for the land. Everything was done as King David had commanded, and afterward God answered the prayers made for the land.

The narrator is the author of the book, who recounts events from David's reign. Before this there had been three years of famine, and David sought God. The cause was a wrong that Saul had committed against the Gibeonites, whom he had mistreated. David addressed that matter and also gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan, which the Philistines had exposed.

For today: God cares about justice and about making right what was done wrongly. If there is something we can correct or restore, it is good to do so with humility and honor.
exp.1:30:
It says that David's men struck down the Benjamites who were with Abner, and that 360 of them died. They also picked up the body of Asahel, Joab's brother who had died earlier, and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. "Struck down" means they defeated them in battle, and "buried him" means they laid him to rest.

Here the narrator of the book is summarizing the outcome of a battle. Israel was divided: David ruled over Judah, and Abner supported the house of Saul. The Benjamites were Saul's tribe. This struggle between brothers of the same people left many dead, and the account sadly records the cost of that division.

For today: conflicts among those who should be united leave deep wounds. Before letting a quarrel grow within the family, the church, or the workplace, seek peace and reconciliation while it is still possible.
exp.17:20:
Joab tells the Cushite to go and report to King David what he has seen. The Cushite bows low before Joab, showing respect, and then takes off running.

The Cushite bowing to Joab shows respect toward the commander of David's army.

"A Cushite" refers to a man from Cush, that is, an Ethiopian or Nubian, and he was probably a servant of Joab.

Joab speaks as the commander of David's army. Absalom, the king's son, had rebelled and has just died. Joab knows the news will deeply grieve David, so he does not want Ahimaaz to carry it, since Ahimaaz had brought a message of victory. He chooses the Cushite, who had seen what happened. The Bible does not explain all of Joab's reasons, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: Some news must be given with honesty and with care. Before speaking in painful moments, let us think about who should say it, how, and with how much compassion.
exp.15:22:
In those days, the advice of Ahithophel was regarded so highly that it was like seeking an answer from God's own word. Both David and Absalom valued his counsel. The verse uses the name Ahithophel, and to consult the word of God means to ask God for an answer.

The narrator makes this comment right after Ahithophel's terrible advice. Absalom had rebelled against his father David, and Ahithophel, who had formerly advised the king, switched sides to the son's cause. His counsel was highly respected, but here it was used for evil and to shame David publicly.

For today: a person can be very wise and have great standing, but that does not guarantee that their advice is right. Before following any advice, let us compare it with the Word of God, and ask God to give us wisdom with humility and a good heart.
exp.8:2:
Here King David asks whether anyone is still left of Saul's family to whom he can show the kindness of God, that is, a generous goodness like the goodness God shows. Ziba answers that there is still a son of Jonathan, who is lame in both feet, meaning he has great difficulty walking.

David speaks as king, but he does so remembering the promise of friendship he made with Jonathan. Ziba, a former servant of Saul, is the one who knows where the young man is. Later the text tells us his name is Mephibosheth. In that time, new kings usually eliminated the descendants of the previous king, so David's intention is surprising.

Today we can ask ourselves: to whom can I show kindness without expecting anything in return? Think of someone weak or forgotten, and generously keep a promise or a debt of affection.
exp.21:38:
The explanation says that David finished off his enemies completely: he "devoured" them and "crushed" them, so that they could not rise again. The phrase about them having fallen under his feet is an image of total victory, like a victor standing over the defeated.

It is David the king speaking, in a song of thanks to God, written when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He does not claim the victory for himself: in the verses that follow he says that God clothed him with strength and gave him the triumph. The language of war was typical of his time and of his role as king of Israel.

For today: we do not use this verse against people, but to trust that God gives us strength in the struggles, sin, and fear we face. In the face of whatever threatens you now, ask God to sustain you, and thank him afterward.
exp.4:5:
David and his men marched on Jerusalem to attack the Jebusites, the people who lived there. The Jebusites mocked David and told him he would never get in, saying that even the blind and the lame could hold him off. Their words were meant to show how sure they were that the city could not be taken.

The ones speaking are the Jebusites, confident that their city was impossible to take. David had just been acknowledged as king over all Israel and was looking for a central capital. Scholars read the mention of "the blind and the lame" in several ways: it may be a taunt, or a reference to defenders or symbolic figures. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not lose heart when others mock what God has placed in your heart. What seems impossible is not impossible for one who trusts in the Lord. Act with faith and with perseverance.
exp.16:13:
What it says: Absalom and all the men of Israel decided that the advice of Hushai the Archite was better than that of Ahithophel. The text explains that the LORD had purposed to thwart Ahithophel's good advice, in order to bring disaster on Absalom. The word "thwart" here means to block or frustrate a plan so that it cannot succeed.

Context: Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David. Ahithophel proposed pursuing David at once, but Hushai, who was secretly loyal to David, advised waiting and gathering all of Israel. His plan gave David time to escape. The narrator tells us that behind that decision was the hand of God.

For today: When things seem to go wrong or the plans of others seem stronger, we can trust that God is still at work. Let us pray and do what is right, resting in the knowledge that He governs even what we cannot see.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that David composed and sang a lament for the death of Saul and of his son Jonathan. The word "lament" means that he mourned, weeping and expressing his grief. A lament is a sad song sung when someone dies.

The account tells that a young man from the Amalekites came before David saying that he had killed Saul, hoping for a reward. David did not celebrate; instead he condemned him for daring to lay hands on the LORD's anointed. After that, David expressed his sorrow in the form of a song. It is remarkable that he mourned even Saul, who had hunted him to kill him. The text does not say that David hid his suffering, but that he turned it into poetry.

For today: when someone who wronged us suffers a loss, we can choose respect and compassion instead of gladness or resentment. Weeping honestly before God is also healthy.
exp.11:29:
David took the crown from the head of the king of Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites. It weighed a talent of gold (about 30 kilograms) and was set with precious stones. They placed it on David's head. David carried away a great amount of plunder from the city.

The narrator tells what happened after Joab, the commander of the army, attacked Rabbah. Joab asked David to come and finish the victory, so that the honor would go to the king. Some read "their king" as the king himself, while others understand "Milcom," the Ammonite god; the Hebrew allows both readings.

For today: triumphs and honors can puff up the heart. David received a crown right after his serious sin, and he still needed humility. May our successes lead us to thank God and to acknowledge our faults, not to feel superior.
exp.12:28:
It says that Absalom's young men did to Amnon just as Absalom had ordered. When the other sons of the king saw this, they got up, each one climbed onto his mule, and fled. "Young men" here refers to Absalom's attendants or helpers, and "mules" were riding animals, widely used by the king's sons.

The narrator tells the outcome of a plan of revenge. Two years earlier, Amnon had violated Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David did not punish him. Absalom held on to his resentment, arranged a feast, waited until Amnon was merry with wine, and ordered him killed. The brothers fled out of fear, not knowing what would happen next.

For today: unaddressed pain and injustice can turn into resentment and end in violence. Instead of keeping the wound hidden, let us seek justice, counsel, and healing, and leave vengeance in God's hands.
exp.2:17:
Abner calls Israel's leaders to act now: "Take action," that is, make David king. He reminds them that the LORD has said to David, "Through My servant David I will save My people Israel from the hands of the Philistines and of all their enemies."

Abner, commander of Saul's army, had quarreled with Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, and now he switches sides. He speaks with the elders of Israel and with the tribe of Benjamin to persuade them to recognize David. The Bible does not detail in this passage where the LORD made that promise; it presents it only as a word already known. Abner may also have had interests of his own, and the text does not hide this.

For today: God keeps his promises, but he sometimes expects us to act with obedience. Let us not put off until tomorrow what God has already shown us clearly.
exp.12:33:
Absalom fled at once after killing his brother Amnon. Meanwhile, the young man on watch looked up and saw many people coming down the road to the west of him, along the side of the hill. The watchman went and reported to the king that he saw men approaching from the direction of Horonaim, along the hillside.

Here the narrator continues the story. Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom had ordered that Amnon be killed at a feast. First came the rumor that all the king's sons had been killed, but Jonadab said that only Amnon had died. The watchman saw the king's sons returning, which confirmed what Jonadab had said.

For today: unaddressed pain and revenge only bring more pain. When someone suffers an injustice, it is wise to seek justice and healing without taking matters into one's own hands. And before repeating alarming news, it is good to verify it first.
exp.11:22:
The explanation says that when David's little son died, he stopped fasting and weeping. He asks sincerely: "Why should I fast now that he is dead? Can I bring him back again?" And he concludes: "I will go to him, but he will not return to me."

David, the king of Israel, speaks here. His son with Bathsheba was sick as a consequence of David's sin, and he pleaded with God for the child's life with fasting and weeping. When the child died, he accepted God's will, worshiped, and went back to eating. Some think "I will go to him" expresses hope of being reunited; others think it only says that he too will die. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: cry out to God with your whole heart while there is hope, and when He has already answered, rest in His care, grieve honestly, and keep going forward in faith.
exp.1:19:
Abner glances back and asks Asahel whether it is really him chasing him. Asahel replies, "It is." The phrase "glanced back" means that Abner turned around to see who was following him so closely.

We are in the war between the army of Judah, under David, and the army of Israel, under Abner, after the death of Saul. Asahel, brother of Joab, was very swift and ran after Abner without turning aside. Abner speaks to him, and the verses that follow show that he wanted to avoid killing him and wanted him to stop.

For today: sometimes we rush after something with such eagerness that we do not listen to warnings. Being quick and brave is not enough; wisdom is needed to know when to stop. Let us ask God for discernment before we follow a path.
exp.18:18:
Here Shimei asks King David not to hold his wrongdoing against him. "Do not hold me guilty" means not to treat him as guilty, and "do not remember your servant's wrongdoing" means not to recall it or hold a grudge over what he did when David left Jerusalem.

Shimei belongs to Saul's family. When David was escaping from his son Absalom, Shimei cursed him and threw stones at him (2 Samuel 16). Now Absalom is dead, David is returning as king, and Shimei, fearing for his life, immediately humbles himself and admits his sin. Abishai asks that he be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed. Some think his repentance was more fear than a true change of heart; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you have failed, do not make excuses or hide. Acknowledge your mistake with humility and ask forgiveness from the person you offended. And when it falls to you to forgive, remember the mercy you have received.
exp.0:25:
David says he is deeply grieved over the death of Jonathan, whom he calls "my brother." He says Jonathan was delightful to him, meaning very dear and pleasant company. He affirms that Jonathan's love was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women.

David sings this lament after learning of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan in the battle against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David honors him publicly. Jonathan, Saul's son, had made a covenant of loyalty with David and defended him. Some see here a comparison with faithfulness and sacrifice; the text says no more than that, and it is not fitting to add details it does not mention.

Today we can value faithful friends, tell them how much they mean to us while they are alive, and be that kind of friend to others.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that David sang a song of thanksgiving to the LORD. He sang it on the day the LORD rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul. The phrase "sang this song to the LORD" means he directed these words to God himself, as a sung prayer. "The LORD" is the name of God.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who introduces David's song. David was hunted for years by King Saul and also faced other wars. This song appears almost word for word in Psalm 18. The text does not say exactly when he composed it, only that it was the day the LORD delivered him. Looking back, David recognizes that his victory came from God.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, don't wait until you have forgotten it. Take a moment to thank God, either in writing or aloud, remembering how he sustained you.
exp.21:44:
The explanation says that people from other nations, the foreigners, drew near to David either in fear or with feigned submission. The verse you have says "Foreigners cower before me," so the "foreigners" here are the people from other nations. The text describes them as coming to him in fear and then obeying him as soon as they hear, so their obedience is described as immediate, with no need for David to press them. Some readers understand that this obedience was sincere, and others that it was forced, and the text leaves room for both ideas.

David sings this hymn of gratitude at the end of his life, after God delivered him from Saul and from his enemies. He acknowledges that God made him king and gave him victory over peoples he did not even know. The explanation notes that the wording "when they hear me, they obey me" means that, as soon as they heard about him, they were already obeying him.

For today: when a responsibility or an achievement comes your way, do not credit it only to your own effort. Give thanks to God, as David did, and use your influence with humility and justice.
exp.17:8:
As Absalom was riding on his mule, he came face to face with David's servants. The mule carried him under the thick branches of a large oak, and his head became fast caught in the tree. The mule kept going, and Absalom was left hanging in midair. The tree is described as a large oak with thick branches, and the verse gives no further detail about its kind.

The narrator is telling the story. Absalom had rebelled against his father David, and his army had just been defeated in the forest of Ephraim. The text does not explain exactly how he was caught; it says only that his head was caught fast in the tree.

For today: whoever turns away from authority and from the love of their family out of pride or ambition will, sooner or later, be caught by their own decisions. Today we can ask God for humility and seek reconciliation before pride leaves us with no way out.
exp.22:20:
He struck down an Egyptian who was a huge man and was carrying a spear. Benaiah went against him with only a club. He snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear. "Struck down" here means "killed" or "overcame," and "huge man" means a man of great size.

This passage is part of "the last words of David," where the account lists his mighty men. The narrator wants to show the deeds of Benaiah, who was famous among the thirty, though he did not reach the first three. David placed him on his council, that is, he gave him trust and responsibility. The text does not explain every detail of the fight.

For today: courage does not depend on having the best tools, but on acting with faith, determination and wisdom in the face of what we confront. God can use the little we have, and He also calls us to be faithful in difficult times.
exp.2:34:
The verse says that all the people came and urged David to eat something while it was still daylight. David made a solemn vow instead: he called on God to punish him, and severely, if he tasted bread or anything else before the sun set.

Joab had killed Abner, the commander of Saul's army, who had been coming to make a covenant with David. David wept publicly and fasted to show his grief. In this way he made it clear before all Israel that he had not ordered that death, as the following verse says.

For today: when there is injustice, it is not enough to say that we disagree. Our conduct must also show sincerity, humility, and respect for life. We must take care that our actions match our words.
exp.14:7:
Absalom tells King David that, while he was living at Geshur in Syria, he made a promise to the LORD: if the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem, he would worship the LORD in Hebron. Now he says he wants to go and keep it. A "vow" is a solemn promise made to God. "Geshur" was a neighboring region where Absalom took refuge after fleeing for having killed his brother Amnon.

Absalom, David's son, is the one speaking. It seems like a pious request, but the following text shows it was a pretext: Hebron would serve him as a starting point to proclaim himself king and rebel. Some commentators doubt that the vow really existed; the text does not make this clear.

Using religious words to cover selfish intentions is dangerous. Let us examine our motives: may our devotion to God be sincere and not a facade to get what we want.
exp.1:7:
Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul's army, took Saul's son Ish-bosheth and moved him to Mahanaim. In this verse, the army is the group Abner leads, and he is the military commander who makes this move.

Saul had died, and David had already been anointed king by the house of Judah. Abner, however, would not accept David as king, and he sought to keep the kingship within Saul's family. Scholars agree that Abner held much power and that Ish-bosheth depended on him, although the text does not spell out all of his reasons.

For today: God carries out his purposes even when others resist with their own decisions. We can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God's will or only defending our comfort or our power.
exp.12:35:
This verse tells us that, as soon as the messenger finished speaking, the sons of King David came in, wailing loudly. Then the king and all his servants also wept very bitterly. The verse describes intense grief, and "servants" means the people who served the king.

Amnon, David's son, had been killed on the orders of his brother Absalom, who did it to avenge their sister Tamar. At first a false report spread that all the king's sons had been killed. Jonadab, a cousin, calmed David by saying that only Amnon had died. When the sons arrived, the truth was confirmed and everyone wept. Absalom fled.

God allows us to weep when sin and violence break apart a family. If you are living through a wound like this, do not hide it: bring it honestly before God, seek comfort from trusted people, and ask for wisdom to act with justice and mercy.
exp.19:25:
A quick note on the text: the passage I was given for 2 Samuel 20:26 comes out empty. In the verse, the text reads: "and Ira the Jairite was David's priest." What I was given as earlier context belongs to verse 25 and part of verse 24.

The verse says that Ira the Jairite served as a priest to David. Scholars do not agree on his exact role, so the meaning of his office is not fully clear.

This verse closes the list of the main officials of David's kingdom. It is not about a single character speaking; it is the narrator recording who helped the king govern, after the rebellion of Sheba had come to an end.

For today: God uses little-known people, like Ira, to sustain important things. Serve faithfully where you are, even when few notice.
exp.1:0:
David asked God what to do after Saul's death. First he wanted to know whether he should go up to one of the towns of Judah, and God told him to go. Then he asked where, and God answered: to Hebron.

The account follows the death of Saul, which is described earlier in the book. David had spent years running away from Saul, and now the way was open. Yet he did not act on his own or seize the moment. The text shows him seeking the LORD first, and then Hebron becomes the place where his reign over Judah begins.

Before taking an important step, it is wise to pray and ask God humbly. Even when a door seems open, it is wise to ask for direction and not rush ahead. God can guide step by step, as here: first a general direction and then a more specific one.
exp.18:19:
Shimei admits before King David that he has sinned. He says he has come "the first of all the house of Joseph," that is, before the other tribes of the north, to go down to the Jordan and meet the king. "Servant" is a humble way of addressing him.

Shimei is the man who had cursed and insulted David when the king was fleeing from Jerusalem because of Absalom's rebellion. Now David returns as king, and Shimei, fearing punishment, comes forward humbly and asks for forgiveness. Some think he also hoped to protect himself with this gesture, and the text does not say whether his repentance was sincere. Even so, David spares his life.

Acknowledging our sin simply and without excuses is the first step in asking for forgiveness. God invites us to return to him, and we too can show mercy to those who have offended us.
exp.11:24:
The explanation says that God sent a message through the prophet Nathan, and that the child was to be named Jedidiah. This name means "beloved of the Lord." Your verse says the name was given because the LORD loved him, so the explanation follows that wording and reads the name as a sign of God's love for the child.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David had sinned grievously with Bathsheba and lost the first child. After that sorrow, Solomon is born. God sends Nathan, the same prophet who had earlier confronted David, now with a sign of grace. The Bible does not explain in detail how the message was delivered.

For today: God can restore and bless after repentance and sorrow. If you have failed, return to Him with sincerity, trust in His forgiveness, and walk with hope.
exp.17:11:
This man answers Joab that he would not harm Absalom even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed out into his hands, which was a very large sum of money. He refers to Absalom as "the son of the king," and recalls that everyone heard David's order to Joab, Abishai, and Ittai: "Protect the young man Absalom for my sake."

The speaker is a soldier of David who found Absalom hanging from a tree during the battle against the rebels. Joab, the commander of the army, rebukes him for not killing Absalom. The soldier refuses out of respect for the king's command. Joab, however, later kills Absalom anyway.

For today: this soldier teaches us to remain faithful to what is right even when we are offered a great reward or when someone in power pressures us. Obeying God and acting with integrity is worth more than any reward.
exp.3:0:
When Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, learned that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost all his courage. The words "he lost courage" describe a man whose strength drained away, leaving him weak and unable to act, like someone who has given up hope. "Dismayed" means that all Israel was filled with fear and distress.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abner was the general who held up Ish-bosheth's kingdom against David. He had been killed by Joab, the commander of David's army. Without Abner, Ish-bosheth was left without support, and the people, who depended on that leadership, felt that everything was falling apart. The text says nothing more about how each person felt; it only shows the great shock.

When we lose the thing on which all our security rested, fear paralyzes us. It is wise to place our trust not only in people or positions, but in God, who does not die or change. He holds our weary hands.
exp.10:20:
Here Joab gives instructions to a messenger. If David became angry because the soldiers went so close to the city wall, the messenger was to ask him, "Who struck Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth?" and remind him that a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech from the wall, so that he died in Thebez. After that, the messenger was to say, "Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well."

Joab speaks after David, wanting to hide his sin with Bathsheba, had ordered that Uriah be placed at the front of the battle. Joab carries out that order and prepares the report to soften the king's anger. The sentence about Uriah reveals what really mattered.

For today: when an unjust decision is hidden behind good explanations, the death of a person remains serious. Let us be honest, acknowledge our faults in time, and not let others pay for them.
exp.4:6:
David captured the fortress of Zion, a well-defended place in Jerusalem, and from then on that site was known as the City of David. The word "Nevertheless" at the start of the verse means "but" or "however," and with it the text stresses that, even though the Jebusites felt secure, David succeeded in taking the place.

The narrator explains that David, already king over all Israel, went to Jerusalem, which was inhabited by the Jebusites. They mocked him, saying that even the blind and the lame could defend the city. Scholars debate the exact meaning of that taunt, but it clearly expressed great confidence in their walls. David took the city and made it his capital.

For today: sometimes we face obstacles that seem impossible and voices that mock our faith. This passage encourages us to keep moving forward with confidence in God, who gives strength and direction to accomplish what He has entrusted to us.
exp.1:15:
Each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his opponent's side, and all twenty-four of them fell down dead together. That is why the place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which means something like "the field of sharp edges" or "the field of swords"; the exact meaning of the name is debated. It was in Gibeon.

Abner, the commander of Ish-bosheth's army, proposed a contest of combat with twelve men from each side, and Joab, David's general, agreed. What seemed like a practice duel ended in a slaughter that ignited a larger battle. The text does not say who started it; it only shows how divided and violent Israel had become.

For today: what is treated lightly, like a game of pride or rivalry, can end in real harm. Before we pit ourselves against someone, let us ask God for humility and seek peace.
exp.15:19:
Here Absalom asks Ahithophel for advice, saying, "Give me counsel. What should we do?" That is, he asks what the next step should be. The explanation keeps to the wording of the verse, so the question is translated directly.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David and had taken Jerusalem. Ahithophel, who had once been David's counselor, now stands on Absalom's side. Hushai had just offered his loyalty, although the Bible shows that he was in fact loyal to David. Ahithophel will give an evil and shameful piece of advice, which will make reconciliation between Absalom and David impossible.

For today: asking for advice is wise, but it matters a great deal whom we ask. Let us seek voices that draw us closer to God, to truth, and to peace, not voices that feed our pride or our bad decisions.
exp.21:18:
They confronted David in his day of disaster, but the LORD was his support. "Confronted" means they came against him directly, and "day of calamity" is a time of disaster or distress. A "support" is someone who holds you up so you do not fall.

David is the one speaking. This song of thanksgiving appears at the end of his life, after God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul, as the text indicates. David looks back and recognizes that God held him up in the most difficult moments, when his adversaries were stronger than he was.

For today: when a hard day comes, do not wait until you feel strong before you draw near to God. Say to Him simply, "Lord, hold me up." Then, like David, remember and give thanks for the times He has already held you up.
exp.3:8:
David answers Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite. Before giving his reply, David makes a solemn oath: "As surely as the LORD lives," meaning that he swears by the living God. He then says that the LORD has redeemed or rescued his life from all distress, meaning that the LORD has delivered him from every danger and trouble.

David is speaking as king in Hebron. The two brothers had just murdered Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, while he was sleeping, and they brought his head to David expecting a reward. They presented the killing as the work of God. David, on the other hand, recalls that God had looked after him without any need for betrayal or unjust violence.

For today: when God has sustained you through difficult moments, you do not need to achieve your goals through deception or injustice. Trust that He can carry out His plans in a clean and righteous way.
exp.14:16:
King David left Jerusalem together with all the people who were with him, and they stopped at the last house of the city, at its outermost edge. The verse describes the group pausing at the edge of the city, and this is the place where they gathered before continuing on.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled and gained the support of many in Israel. The narrator tells us that the king leaves with his family and his servants. They stop to organize the march and to see who will go with him. There the loyalty of people such as the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and the men of Gath becomes visible.

For today: when a crisis forces you to leave what is familiar, pause for a moment to see who walks with you, and be grateful for their loyalty. Take care of faithful relationships, and trust God while you walk through uncertainty.
exp.4:13:
This verse begins a list of the sons who were born to David in Jerusalem. The first four names are Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. The phrase "born to him in Jerusalem" tells us these were David's sons, and Jerusalem is the city we now spell Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not David. After David was recognized as king over all Israel and set up his capital in Jerusalem, the text mentions his growing family. The list shows the expansion of his kingdom, though it also reveals that he took more wives, something the Bible later shows with painful consequences. Solomon would later be the king who followed David.

For today: God cares for people, not just for great events. Every name matters. Value your family, pray for it, and do not neglect it for your goals or responsibilities.
exp.23:22:
This verse says that Araunah gave everything to King David, and he did so with the generosity of a king. Then he offered a blessing: "May the LORD your God accept you," that is, that God would receive you with favor and show you his kindness. The phrase "Araunah gives all these to the king" can be understood in two ways: that Araunah gave as a king would give, or that he himself was of royal descent. Scholars do not agree.

David had sinned by counting the people, and a plague was striking Israel. A prophet told him to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. Araunah, with good will, wanted to give him the land, the oxen, and the wood for the sacrifice.

Araunah was generous, but David replied that he would not offer to God something that cost him nothing. Today we can ask ourselves: does my service to God cost me anything, or do I give only what I have left over? Sincere devotion has value before Him.
exp.10:8:
Here it says that Uriah, instead of going home, spent the night at the entrance of the king's palace, alongside all the servants of his master. The phrase "slept at the door" means that he lay down at the entrance of the palace; "servants of his master" refers to the king's officials and attendants; and "did not go down to his house" means that he did not go home.

David had sent for Uriah from the front line of battle. He had already slept with Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, and she was pregnant. David hoped that Uriah would go home and sleep with her, in order to cover up his sin. The narrator tells us that Uriah did not do this. Later he will explain that it did not seem right to him to enjoy comforts while the ark and his companions were in the field.

Today, Uriah's integrity challenges us not to seek comfort when others are suffering. It also reminds us that hiding a sin almost never works; the better course is to acknowledge it before God with sincerity.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that the prophet Nathan told David everything God had revealed to him, leaving nothing out and adding nothing. The phrase "all the words of this entire revelation" is the key idea here: Nathan passed along the whole message he had been given, exactly as he had received it, and the word "revelation" refers to the message God had made known to Nathan.

God had just promised David that his house and his kingdom would be made secure forever. David wanted to build a temple for God, but God answered through Nathan that He Himself would build a house for David, meaning a line of descendants. Many Christians see in this promise a sign that points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

Today we can learn from Nathan's faithfulness: when we share what God says in His Word, we should do so with honesty, without changing it to please others or to make it fit our own tastes.
exp.10:0:
It says that in the spring, when kings march out to war, David sent Joab, his servants, and the whole army of Israel. They defeated the Ammonites and besieged Rabbah, but David remained in Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, telling David's story without embellishment. The Ammonites had insulted David's messengers, and that is why there was war. The detail that the king stayed at home prepares what follows: his fall with Bathsheba. The text does not say why he stayed, so it is best not to invent reasons.

For today: when we stop doing what we are responsible for, we become more exposed to temptation. Ask yourself whether there is some responsibility you are avoiding, and ask God for the strength to carry it out faithfully.
exp.21:16:
God reached down from heaven and took hold of David, pulling him out of deep waters. The words "took hold of me" and "drew me out" describe God acting with strength to rescue him. The waters stand for danger, like a flood that threatens to drown a person.

David, now an old man, sings this song of thanks for being saved from his enemies and from Saul. The verses just before this describe God as a power who shakes the earth and the heavens to help him. Here the water is not literal. It is figurative language for troubles that overwhelmed him. The verses that follow explain that his enemies were stronger than he was.

For today: when you feel problems pulling you under, call out to God with confidence. He can help you, sometimes in unexpected ways. Afterward, do not forget to give thanks, as David did.
exp.21:34:
It is God who trains David for battle. "He trains my hands for battle" means that God gives him skill in fighting. "My arms can bend a bow of bronze" speaks of a strength greater than what David has by nature. The exact metal of the Hebrew is understood in more than one way, so the wording can vary, but in any case it was a very hard bow to bend.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and recognizes that his victories did not come from his skill alone. Everything he knew how to do and the strength he had came from God.

For today: what you can do in your work, your family, or your studies is also a gift. Thank God for your abilities and ask him to help you use them with humility and to face your struggles with confidence in him.
exp.20:7:
Here it says that David took seven descendants of Saul. Two were sons of Rizpah, a woman who had been with Saul: Armoni and Mephibosheth (not the son of Jonathan). The other five were sons of Merab, Saul's daughter, who were raised by Michal, another of Saul's daughters, after Merab's children were given to Adriel the son of Barzillai the Meholathite. "Raised" means "brought up" or "cared for as a child".

The context is a famine lasting three years. God connected it with Saul's violence against the Gibeonites, with whom Israel had made a covenant. The Gibeonites asked for justice, and David, the king, agreed. He spared Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, because of his promise. Some manuscripts name Michal here while others name Merab, and this difference is explained in several ways.

Today: Unjust decisions leave wounds that reach other people, even years later. Keeping one's given word and repairing the harm with humility, rather than ignoring it, honors God and protects others.
exp.17:15:
Then Joab blew the ram's horn, a horn used to give orders in battle. At that signal, David's troops stopped chasing the soldiers of Israel who had followed Absalom. The verse says Joab restrained them, meaning he stopped the pursuit.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Absalom had rebelled against his father, King David, and had just died. Joab, the commander of David's army, brought the fighting to an end. Some understand that he did this to prevent more deaths among brothers; the text does not explain his reasons in detail.

For today: knowing when to stop is wisdom. When a conflict has reached its end, continuing to strike only adds pain. Let us ask God for self-control to seek peace and not prolong the fighting.
exp.13:11:
The explanation says the woman asks King David for permission to say something more. Her request is phrased as "Please, may your servant speak a word," and she calls herself "your servant," speaking with humility. David grants her the freedom to speak with the word "Speak."

This woman is from Tekoa, and Joab sent her to persuade David with an invented story about a son in danger. David has just promised her that her supposed son will be safe. Now she uses that promise to show him that he himself has a banished son, Absalom, and that he should bring him back.

For today: when we have to say a hard truth, let us do it with humility and respect, asking for the chance to speak. And listening with patience, as David did, helps us see what we did not want to see.
exp.20:2:
Here David asks the Gibeonites what he can do for them and how he can make amends for the harm that was done to them. To make amends means doing something to repair a wrong and set things right. "The inheritance of the LORD" refers to the people of Israel and their land. David wants the Gibeonites to bless Israel again, that is, to speak well of the nation and seek its good.

Here King David is speaking. There had been famine for three years, and God told him that the cause was the blood Saul had shed when he killed the Gibeonites. Israel had made a covenant of peace with them, and Saul broke it. David seeks justice for those who were wronged.

For today: when we have hurt someone, it is not enough to hope they will forget. We can follow David's example: approach with humility, listen to the one we have wronged, and ask how to repair the damage, without excuses.
exp.21:40:
God caused David to see his enemies retreat before him. The image of "the necks" of enemies, meaning that they turned their backs in defeat, is not in your reading, so the explanation focuses on what the verse does say: the enemies fled, and David destroyed those who hated him. In this way David was able to overcome his opponents. The victory is presented as something God made possible.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, written when the Lord delivered him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. It is a poem of praise, and it also appears in Psalm 18. The imagery of war is strong and typical of its time. David insists that the triumph was not his own but God's, who strengthened him.

For today: when you overcome a difficulty, do not take all the credit for yourself. Pause to thank God. And in the face of your struggles, remember that He can give you strength and a way through, not in order to hate people, but to overcome evil with His help.
exp.21:36:
You broaden the path beneath me, so that my ankles do not give way. This means that God gave David a wide and firm path to walk on, so that his ankles would not give way beneath him. The image is of someone who moves forward with steadiness, never wavering.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. Before this verse he acknowledges that God trained him for battle and protected him like a shield. Afterward he speaks of pursuing his enemies. David credits God for his firmness, not his own strength.

For today: when you face a hard season and feel your strength failing, ask God for steadiness instead of trusting only in yourself. Give thanks for the times he held you up without your noticing.
exp.11:6:
Nathan says to David, "You are that man!" In other words, you are the rich, unjust man in the story. Then Nathan speaks on behalf of the LORD, the God of Israel, and reminds David of what God had done for him: he anointed him (chose him and set him apart with oil) as king over Israel, and he delivered him from the hand of Saul, who was hunting him down.

Nathan is a prophet sent by God. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah put to death. Nathan told the parable of a rich man who took the only little ewe lamb from a poor man, and David, outraged, condemned himself without realizing it.

It is easy to see the sins of others and excuse our own. Today we can ask God to show us our hearts with honesty, and to remember his goodness before we harden ourselves. His correction seeks to lead us to repentance and to his forgiveness.
exp.13:8:
The woman from Tekoa asks King David to rule in her favor, and she is willing to take the blame herself. Here "iniquity" means the guilt, or the punishment owed, for failing to keep the law as it was expected to be kept. She says: if there is any blame, let it fall on me and my father's house, and let the king and his throne be free of guilt.

The woman speaks as someone sent by Joab, according to the chapter, and she tells an invented story about two sons and a killing. Her real aim was for David, as he decided to forgive her supposed son, to see that he should also bring back Absalom, his son who had been sent away. She takes care that the king is not left exposed by his decision.

For today: sometimes helping others means taking on risk and responsibility, instead of placing it on someone else. But we also learn to be sincere, without manipulating others, even for good causes.
exp.21:43:
It says that God rescued David from the strife of his own people and preserved him as the head of nations. Even peoples David had not known came to serve him. "Strife" means conflicts or struggles.

David sings this song of thanksgiving near the end of his life, after being delivered from his enemies and from Saul. Before he became king over all Israel, he faced internal divisions, and later his victories extended his influence over other peoples. David attributes all of this to God, not to his own strength. Some also see in these words a look ahead to the reign of the Messiah, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you look back and see conflicts overcome and doors that opened, give thanks to God out loud. Recognizing that He sustained you keeps you humble and confident for what lies ahead.
exp.18:42:
The men of Israel tell the men of Judah that they have ten shares in the king, meaning ten of the twelve tribes, so they have a greater claim on David. They complain that they were looked down on, since they were the first to speak about bringing the king back. But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.

David was returning to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Judah escorted him first across the Jordan, and Israel felt ignored. Judah answered that the king was their relative. The argument was about honor and pride, and it grew heated. This clash sets the stage for the rebellion of Sheba, which comes next.

For today: when we feel overlooked, it is easy to answer with harsh words. That quarrel between brothers shows how quickly pride divides. Before you make a complaint, ask yourself whether you are seeking justice or only honor, and speak with humility.
exp.6:14:
He says that God will never take away his loving devotion from David's son, even when he corrects him for doing wrong. With Saul it was different: God removed him from his place as king. "But" means "but," and "loving devotion" here is a faithful, steadfast love that does not abandon.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God promises him something greater: to establish his dynasty forever. This promise is directed first to Solomon, who would build the temple, and Christians also see it fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David. Interpreters debate how some of the details apply, but the promise of faithfulness is clear.

God corrects his children without ceasing to love them. If you fail today, do not think that God has rejected you. His discipline seeks to restore you, not to destroy you. Return to him with confidence and humility.
exp.3:9:
Here David recalls something that had already happened. A man came to him with the news that Saul was dead, believing he was bringing good news. David had him seized and put to death at Ziklag. That was his reward for his news.

David speaks to Rechab and Baanah, who had just murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, hoping for a reward. David reminds them that he did not reward the one who came to him announcing Saul's death. If that man was punished in this way, then all the more would he punish those who killed an innocent man in his own bed.
