Today we learn that the end does not justify the means. God is not pleased when we seek gain through wickedness, even when we call it "help." Let us ask him to guide us to act with justice and honesty.
exp.13:7:
The king tells the woman to go home, and he promises that he himself will issue an order in her favor. The words "I will give orders on your behalf" mean he will make a decision about her case.

King David is speaking. A woman from Tekoa has come before him with a story about two sons who fought, and one killed the other. Now her family wants to put the surviving son to death. Most scholars understand that Joab sent her with this story to lead David to think about his own son Absalom, who had been sent away for killing his brother. David does not yet know this. He responds with compassion, but he still does not give a full decision.

For today: Those in authority should listen carefully to people who are suffering. But it is also wise to act with justice and good judgment, not only with kind words.
exp.14:15:
This verse tells us that David left Jerusalem together with his entire household. He left behind only ten of his concubines, secondary wives of the king, to take care of the palace. The phrase "followed him" shows that the household went along with him.

David flees because his son Absalom had rebelled and was coming to take the throne. The king wants to avoid a battle inside the city that would harm the people. The text does not explain why he chose to leave those women behind. Later in the story, they suffer the consequences of that rebellion (2 Samuel 16:21-22).

Today we can learn that the decisions of those who hold authority affect others, sometimes in painful ways. Before deciding, let us think about those who will be left exposed or vulnerable, and ask God for wisdom to care for others.
exp.10:5:
This verse tells how David sends orders to Joab, his commander, asking him to send Uriah the Hittite to him. Joab obeys and sends him to the king. The word "Hittite" in the verse names Uriah's people, a man of foreign origin who lived in Israel.

David gives this order after learning that Bathsheba is pregnant from having been with him. Uriah, her husband, was at war. David calls him back to try to hide what he has done, by having Uriah spend time with his wife. Joab only carries out the order, without knowing, according to the text, the reason behind it.

For today: when we commit a wrong, the temptation is to cover it with another deception, and that makes everything worse. It is better to confess soon and seek God's forgiveness sincerely.
exp.15:21:
This verse tells us that they set up a tent for Absalom on the roof of the palace. There Absalom slept with his father David's concubines, and he did it in the sight of all Israel. A roof here means the flat top of the house, and the phrase "slept with" refers to sexual relations.

Absalom had rebelled against his father David, who fled from Jerusalem and left ten concubines behind to look after the palace. Following the advice of Ahithophel, Absalom did this public act to show that the break with David was final. It also fulfilled what God had announced through Nathan (2 Samuel 12:11-12), although that does not make Absalom's action good.

Good advice can sometimes lead to a destructive path. Before following an opinion, even one that comes from someone very respected, let us compare it with the Word of God and with a humble heart.
exp.16:14:
Hushai tells the priests Zadok and Abiathar what took place at Absalom's council. He explains that Ahithophel gave one piece of advice, and that he himself gave a different one. The word "advised" in this verse means that he offered his opinion or plan. "The elders of Israel" were the leaders of the people.

Hushai was a friend of David, and he had presented himself to Absalom as one of his advisers. His mission was to make Ahithophel's plan fail. Now he informs the priests, who were David's secret allies, so that they can warn David to cross the Jordan. The text says that the LORD allowed the good advice of Ahithophel to be defeated.

For today: God can work in the middle of confusing or unjust situations, even through people who act with wisdom and courage. When you face a difficult situation, pray, act with prudence, and trust that God is still in control, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.22:30:
This verse names two of David's men: Abi-albon, who came from Arbath, and Azmaveth, from Barhum. The place names "from Arbath" and "from Barhum" tell us where they came from. They were probably towns near Judah and Benjamin, although some of the names are spelled differently in other texts, such as 1 Chronicles 11.

The author of the book, who is not identified, gives a list of David's mighty men. They were soldiers who supported him in his battles. After mentioning the deeds of the most famous ones, the text goes on with individual names without saying what they did. Even so, they were recorded.

God notices faithful people, even when no one applauds them. Today you can serve steadily in your family, your work, or your church, without seeking fame. What you do together with others, with loyalty, has value before God.
exp.2:25:
He says that Joab left David's presence and, on his own, sent messengers after Abner. They caught up with him at the well of Sirah and brought him back. David was unaware of it. Being unaware of it means the king gave no approval and did not know what was happening.

Joab was the commander of David's army. Abner, formerly commander of Saul's army, had come to make a peace agreement with David, and David let him go in peace. Joab, who wanted to avenge the death of his brother Asahel, accused Abner of spying and acted in secret. His plan ended in murder.

For today: when we feel resentment, it is easy to justify decisions made in secret. If we cannot do something openly, or with the knowledge of those who lead us, it is better to place it in God's hands before we act.
exp.21:37:
David says he will chase his enemies and destroy them, and he will not turn back until they are finished. Some of the wording is worth a closer look. The phrase about breaking them means he will destroy or crush them, and the phrase about finishing them off means he will put an end to them and wipe them out.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving to God, when the Lord rescued him from his enemies and from the hand of Saul. The verses around it show that David does not rely on himself: God gave him a shield, strength, and firm footing. It is the language of war, typical of a king in his time, and the victory is credited to God.

For today: let us not take this as permission to hate people. We can apply it to our struggles against sin, resentment, or bad habits: with the strength of God, we should not stop halfway, but persevere until we win.
exp.21:20:
David says here that God dealt with him according to his righteousness, and that the cleanness of his hands was the basis of his reward. The phrase "He has repaid me" in the verse above means God paid him back, and "according to the cleanness of my hands" describes the honest conduct on which that repayment rested. "Clean hands" speak of conduct that was honest, without violence or deceit.

David sings this psalm of thanksgiving after God delivered him from his enemies, among them Saul. The nearby verses say that God brought him out into a large place, a place of freedom, because God delighted in him. David does not claim to be perfect, since the Bible also records his serious sins. He speaks of his general faithfulness to God, and some understand it to refer mainly to his innocence before those who were pursuing him.

For today: live with integrity, even when no one sees you or recognizes you. And trust that God sees your faithfulness and knows how to care for you and to respond in his time.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that Hushai advises Absalom to gather all Israel, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, a multitude as countless as the sand on the seashore. He also urges that Absalom himself lead them into battle. The word "advise" in this verse corresponds to "recommend" in the source, and "seashore" corresponds to "shore of the sea."

Hushai, David's friend, speaks before Absalom and his advisers during the rebellion. Ahithophel had proposed attacking David at once. Hushai, who had presented himself as loyal to Absalom, seeks to gain time so that David can organize. His counsel appeals to Absalom's pride. The Bible later shows that the Lord allowed this advice to be accepted (2 Samuel 17:14).

For today: a piece of advice can sound very convincing and still have a hidden purpose. Before deciding, let us ask God for wisdom, examine the motives of the one advising us, and take care that our pride does not make us listen only to what flatters us.
exp.19:23:
This verse is part of a list of the chief officials of David's kingdom. Adoram was in charge of the forced labor, the work the people were required to do for the government. Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the recorder, a term for someone who kept track of the affairs of the kingdom and reminded the king of them; some understand him as a chronicler or secretary of state.

The narrator presents this list after the rebellion of Sheba, which Joab brought to an end. With order restored, it shows who helped David govern. The list seems to come from a later period in his reign. About Adoram's work the text says nothing more, so it is best not to assume details.

For today: God uses unglamorous tasks, such as managing, recording, and organizing. If your work is of that kind, do it with honesty and order, because it also serves others and God.
exp.13:4:
Here King David asks the woman, "What troubles you?" She answers that she is a widow, for her husband is dead. With those words she begins to present her case.

The woman is from Tekoa, and she comes before David. Joab, the commander of the army, put these words in her mouth so that she would tell a story to the king. According to the account, Joab wanted David to reconsider his position toward his son Absalom. She pretends to be a widow in trouble, and the text does not say that everything she tells is true.

Today we can learn to listen with compassion, but also with wisdom. Before judging a case, it is good to ask God for discernment and to look at everything with humility.
exp.6:9:
God promises that he will provide a secure place for Israel. He says he will "plant" them, like someone who plants a tree so that it takes root and is not easily pulled up. The "sons of wickedness" are evil people, and to "oppress" means to treat others cruelly and unjustly. He promises that they will no longer be oppressed as they were in the past.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan and gives a message to David. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers by reminding him of what he has already done for him: he took him from tending sheep and made him king. He then promises peace for the people and a lasting house for David. Some believe this promise was partly fulfilled in Solomon and also points to Jesus, a descendant of David.

God is the one who gives stability and rest. When you feel that your life is unsteady, remember that he can plant you and give you roots. Trust in his faithfulness and seek to put down roots in him each day.
exp.7:7:
This verse tells us that David took a large amount of bronze from Betah and Berothai, two cities that belonged to Hadadezer. Bronze is a metal made by combining copper with other metals, and a large amount means a great deal of it.

The narrator of the book recounts David's victories over the neighboring kings. After defeating Hadadezer, David receives spoils and tribute. The text notes that the LORD was with David wherever he went. Later, in 1 Chronicles 18:8, it is said that this bronze was used for the temple, although it is not mentioned here. It is not known with certainty where those cities were located exactly.

For today: everything we have, whether much or little, comes from the protecting hand of God. We can ask ourselves how we use our resources, and whether we put them at the service of something greater than ourselves.
exp.0:18:
This verse opens David's funeral song. It says that the glory of Israel, meaning its honor and its pride, has been struck down on its heights. The word "glory" is the one the verse uses, and the "mighty" are the warriors who have fallen, especially Saul and Jonathan. The song itself is a lament, a mourning song.

David speaks after learning of the deaths of Saul and Jonathan in the battle against the Philistines, on the mountains of Gilboa. Although Saul had pursued him in order to kill him, David does not celebrate his death but mourns. He also orders that this song be taught to the people of Judah. Some understand "the bow" to name the song itself; others, a military training exercise. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: learn to grieve sincerely, even the loss of someone who harmed you. Honoring the good that was in a person keeps the heart healthy and keeps bitterness away.
exp.5:4:
David and all the house of Israel celebrated with joy before the LORD as they brought the ark. They played many kinds of instruments made of wood: harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, sistrums (rattle-like instruments), and cymbals (metal plates).

The writer tells how David moves the ark of God toward Jerusalem. It was a time of festivity and honor to God. However, the account goes on to the death of Uzzah, because the ark was not being transported as God had commanded. This shows us that sincere joy must be accompanied by obedience and reverence.

For today: worshiping God with gladness is good, but we must also seek to do so with respect and according to his Word. May your joy and your obedience walk together.
exp.21:19:
He spoke of how God brought David out of a narrow, cramped place into an open one, that is, into freedom and safety. He rescued him because God took pleasure in him. The phrases "brought me out" and "rescued me" are the verse's own wording, and "into the open" describes a space free of pressure. "He delighted in me" means that God was pleased with him and wanted to show him favor.

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. He looks back and acknowledges that enemies stronger than he was attacked him in his day of distress, but God was his support. The verses that follow speak of his faithfulness, and some understand this as his sincerity toward God rather than perfection.

For today: when you feel trapped, remember that God can open a way for you. Thank him for the times he has already done so, and trust that he cares for you because he loves you.
exp.9:11:
Joab encourages his brother Abishai to be strong. "Be strong" means keep up your courage and resolve. He says they should fight bravely for their people and for the cities of God, and that the Lord should do what is good in His sight.

The one speaking is Joab, the commander of David's army. Israel was surrounded: the Ammonites on one side and the Syrians who supported them on the other. Joab divided the troops and promised mutual help. Then he did his part with courage, and he left the outcome to God. The text tells how the Syrians fled and then the Ammonites as well.

For today: do what is yours to do with dedication and courage, without waiting for others to do it, and lean on those around you. Then leave the result in God's hands with humility, trusting that He works for good.
exp.5:22:
This verse says that Michal, the daughter of King Saul, had no children for the rest of her life. The name appears here as "Michal" in the Berean Standard Bible as well, and the explanation below refers to her by that name.

Here the narrator closes the scene of 2 Samuel 6. Michal had scornfully criticized David because he danced with joy before God when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. David answered that he was doing it for the Lord. The text does not explain the reason she had no children. Some think it was a punishment from God for her attitude; others say the fact is simply recorded, perhaps because of the distance between her and David. There is no certainty.

For today: let us guard our hearts so that we do not despise the sincere worship of others. A proud or critical attitude can draw us away from joy and from the relationships God wants to give us.
exp.23:9:
After David had taken the count of the troops, his conscience troubled him deeply. The phrase "his heart struck him" means his conscience hit him, like a thorn pricking the heart. He then spoke to the LORD, admitting that he had sinned greatly in what he had done, asking God to take away his guilt, and confessing that he had acted very foolishly, meaning he had acted without wisdom.

David speaks with God after the count of the troops has been reported to him. The text does not explain here in detail why the counting was a sin. The chapter begins by saying that the LORD had been angry with Israel, and Joab had tried to talk David out of it. Many think David trusted in the strength of his army more than in the LORD, but the passage does not state this clearly.

When our conscience troubles us, we should not silence it or make excuses. We can be honest with God, admit that we have acted very foolishly, and ask for his forgiveness. He welcomes anyone who humbles themselves sincerely.
exp.15:2:
Here King David asks about Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, and Ziba, his servant, answers that he stayed behind in Jerusalem. According to Ziba, Mephibosheth thinks the people of Israel will give him back his grandfather's kingdom today. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "the master's grandson" refers to Mephibosheth.

David flees Jerusalem because of the rebellion of his son Absalom. Ziba arrives with supplies and, very conveniently, accuses his master of treason. The Bible does not confirm in this passage whether it is true. Later, Mephibosheth gives a different version (2 Samuel 19), so Ziba may have been lying to keep the property. David decides quickly, without listening to Mephibosheth.

For today: before believing an accusation against someone, especially when the person making it stands to gain, it is wise to stop, ask questions, and listen to both sides. Being fair requires patience, even when we are tired or under pressure.
exp.22:4:
David admits that his household has not always stood right with God, yet he holds on to the fact that God has made an everlasting covenant with him, well arranged in every part and secure. Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part. David trusts that God will bring about his full salvation and fulfill every desire he has in this covenant.

These words come near the end of David's life, as his last words. He speaks of the righteous ruler who rules in the fear of God, and he looks back honestly at his own family, which has not been entirely like that. His mind goes back to the promise God gave him in 2 Samuel 7 about his dynasty. Many Christians see in this a sign pointing forward to Jesus, the perfect King.

For us today, you do not have to be perfect to trust God. He keeps his promises because of his faithfulness, not because of our merit. Rest in his grace, and keep obeying him with humility.
exp.1:17:
The passage says that the three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Zeruiah was David's sister, so these three were his nephews. Of Asahel it is said that he was fleet of foot, very swift, "like a wild gazelle," a graceful animal known for its quickness and agility.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After the battle at Gibeon, where David's men defeated Abner's men, he introduces those who take part in the pursuit. He highlights Asahel's speed because it explains why he runs after Abner, the commander of Israel's army. What follows shows that speed alone was not enough to make his decision wise.

For today: the gifts God gives us, such as talent, strength, or speed, need good judgment. Before we rush after something, let us ask for wisdom.
exp.22:22:
This verse speaks of Benaiah. It says he was most honored among the Thirty, a group of David's outstanding warriors, but that he did not become one of the Three, the top three among them. The explanation about the terms is simple: "the Thirty" refers to the group of warriors, "the Three" refers to the top three, and the verse says David appointed Benaiah over his guard.

These words are part of the "last words of David," a list of his brave men. The text wants to acknowledge and remember those who served the king with courage. Benaiah is presented as someone of great worth, though not the first of them all. Scholars understand the exact sense of being "appointed over his guard" in different ways.

For today: you do not need to be number one to be valuable. God sees the faithfulness and courage of those who serve steadily. Do your part with bravery and honesty, without comparing yourself too much to others, and trust that your service will be remembered.
exp.7:12:
It says that David made a name for himself when he came back from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The word "striking down" here means that he defeated them in battle and killed many of them.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who sums up David's victories. The verses around it show that David dedicated what he won to God, and that "the LORD preserved David wherever he went." Other passages (1 Chronicles 18:12 and the heading of Psalm 60) mention Edom and other army commanders, so scholars explain that difference in several ways.

For today: if God gives you success or recognition, do not keep it to show off. Give thanks for it, use it justly, and offer God the best of what you have received.
exp.5:0:
David again assembled the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand in all. The word "again" points back to an earlier gathering, and "chosen" refers to select men, probably warriors or representatives of the people. The text does not make clear whether they were soldiers or a broader assembly.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David was already king over all Israel and had taken Jerusalem. Now he wants to bring the ark of God, a symbol of the Lord's presence, to his new capital. Gathering so many people shows that he wanted to do this as a matter for the whole nation. The verses that follow tell how the move went wrong, because they did not carefully follow what God had commanded.

For today: good intentions and great enthusiasm are valuable, but they are not enough. Before we undertake anything to honor God, let us look in his Word for how he wants it done, and not only for how it seems best to us.
exp.2:15:
Paltiel, Michal's husband at that time, followed her, weeping all the way to a place called Bahurim. There Abner, commander of the army of Ish-bosheth, told him to go back, and he returned home.

Abner is the one speaking. He was taking Michal to David, who claimed her as his first wife. Abner was seeking an agreement with David, and returning Michal to him was part of that deal. The text does not explain everything Paltiel felt, but his weeping shows real grief. The Bible tells us nothing more about him.

For today: God asks us to see the pain of people, even when decisions made by those in power affect them. If you are in a position of authority, treat with compassion those who lose something. And if you suffer a loss you cannot control, remember that God sees your tears.
exp.21:33:
He makes my feet like a deer's feet, so I can run and leap over rough ground without stumbling. He also stations me on the heights, that is, on high and secure ground, far from danger.

David, now an older man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving because the Lord rescued him from Saul and from all his enemies (2 Samuel 22:1). He looks back and recognizes that his victories and his steadiness did not come from his own strength alone, but from the Lord. The heights can be understood as secure places on the battlefield, or also as his position as king; interpreters see it both ways.

Today, when you go through difficult roads, ask God for firmness with every step. And when things go well, remember to thank Him.
exp.8:12:
So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table, and he was lame in both feet. It says that Mephibosheth stayed to live in Jerusalem, because he had a fixed place at King David's table. It also makes clear that he was lame in both feet. "Lived" tells us he made his home there, and "always" shows that this was something constant, not a one-day invitation.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He closes the story in which David seeks out someone from Saul's family to show kindness, because of the promise he made to Jonathan, his friend. Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson. David gave him back the lands and treated him like a son of the king. Mentioning his lameness underlines that he had nothing to offer.

For today: God welcomes us by grace, not for what we are worth. We can imitate that kindness by inviting into our table, our church, or our life someone who feels small or rejected.
exp.19:1:
This verse tells how nearly all the people of Israel stopped following David and began following Sheba, son of Bichri. By contrast, the men of Judah stayed by their king, remaining with him all the way from the Jordan River to Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sheba, a man from Benjamin, blew a trumpet and cried out that they had no share in David. This happens shortly after Absalom's rebellion, when the tribes were still divided and resentful over how David would return to the throne. Sheba took advantage of that discontent to stir up another rebellion.

For today: when there is division and shouts that sweep the crowd along, it is easy to be carried away. Let us ask God for firmness to be loyal to what is just and true, even when most people take another path.
exp.20:1:
This verse tells us that King David summoned the Gibeonites to speak with them. The text explains who they were: they were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan. Israel had made a binding oath of peace with them (Joshua 9). Saul, however, tried to kill them, and the Bible says he did it in his zeal for Israel and Judah. The word "remnant" here means "survivors."

After three years of famine, God explained to David that the trouble came from Saul's wrong against the Gibeonites. David acts as a responsible king and seeks to make things right by listening directly to those who were harmed.

Today we learn that a promise made, even to those who are different from us, matters greatly to God. When there is injustice, the way forward is to acknowledge it, listen to the one who was wronged, and seek to repair it.
exp.6:19:
This verse says that David is left without words before God. He asks what more he could say, because God already knows him completely. The word "servant" refers to someone who serves his master, and "Lord GOD" is a way of addressing God with respect and reverence.

David speaks in prayer, sitting before the ark, after God promised him, through the prophet Nathan, a lasting descendant and an enduring house. David wanted to build a temple, but God answered that He would make a "house" for David, that is, a royal family. David responds with wonder and humility before such kindness, which he had not earned.

For today: sometimes, instead of saying much, it is enough to rest in the fact that God truly knows us, with our struggles and desires. You can pray simply, give thanks, and trust that He understands what you cannot put into words.
exp.13:25:
It says that Absalom cut his hair once a year, because it was heavy and bothered him. When he weighed it, it came to about two hundred shekels, "according to the royal standard." A shekel was an ancient unit of weight, and "the royal standard" was probably an official measure set by the king, though it is not known exactly. For that reason, the modern equivalent is uncertain, but it was a very abundant head of hair.

The narrator of the book describes Absalom, son of David, while he lives in Jerusalem without being able to see the king. First his beauty is highlighted, and then his children are mentioned. The text seems to show how much people admired his appearance. But it also lets us see that, although he looked perfect on the outside, there was an unresolved conflict with his father.

For today: let us not confuse a good image with a healthy heart. Let us ask God to help us seek reconciliation in our relationships, rather than caring only for what others see of us.
exp.12:11:
Tamar tells Amnón not to violate her. "Violate" here means abusing someone against her will. She explains that such a thing should never be done in Israel, meaning that God's people do not act that way. "Disgraceful" describes a serious evil, a wickedness.

Tamar, daughter of King David and half-sister of Amnón, speaks. He pretended to be sick so that he could be alone with her. Tamar resists with courage, appeals to what is right in Israel, and tries to stop him with her words. Even so, Amnón abuses her. The guilt is his alone.

Today, this text teaches us to take every person's "no" seriously and to believe those who report abuse. If anyone is in danger, let us seek help and protection without delay. God has compassion on victims and does not blame them.
exp.10:22:
This verse gives the messenger's report to David about the battle. It says that the men of Rabbah overpowered the Israelites and came out against them in the field, but that the Israelites drove them back to the entrance of the city gate.

The messenger speaks following Joab's instructions. Joab had been reckless in approaching the wall, and he feared David's anger. Moreover, that attack cost the life of Uriah, whom David had ordered killed to hide his sin. The messenger gives the details of the battle first, as Joab had instructed him.

For today: when we have done something wrong, it is easy to hide it behind well-arranged words. God prefers that we live in truth and confess in time, for He forgives those who repent with sincerity.
exp.16:16:
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying at En-rogel, a spring outside Jerusalem, because they could not be seen entering the city. A servant girl would come to them and pass along information, and they would then go and inform King David of what they had learned.

David was fleeing from his son Absalom, who had rebelled against him. Hushai, David's trusted friend, had given advice meant to buy time, and David needed to know the danger quickly. The priests Zadok and Abiathar could not leave the city without drawing attention, so they used their sons and a servant girl as secret messengers. The Bible does not give her name.

God can use ordinary people who go unnoticed to carry out an important role. Today, a timely message, a prayer, or a quiet act of service can help others a great deal. Let us faithfully do what is ours to do.
exp.18:24:
This verse tells how King David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Mephibosheth comes from Jerusalem to meet him, and the king asks him a direct question: "Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?"

David speaks with Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul. When David fled, Mephibosheth stayed in the city. He appears neglected, as if in mourning. His servant Ziba had accused him of treason (2 Samuel 16), and it is not easy to know for certain who was telling the truth. David wants to hear his side.

For today: before judging someone by appearances or by what others say, let us give them the chance to explain themselves. Listening with patience helps us seek justice and care for our relationships.
exp.10:10:
Uriah tells David that the ark of the covenant, Israel and Judah are living in tents, and that Joab, his commander, and his soldiers are camped out in the open field. Because of this, he says, he cannot go home to eat, drink and sleep with his wife. He swears this with strong emphasis: "As surely as you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do such a thing!" The phrase "the open field" refers to open country outside the town.

Uriah is a Hittite soldier loyal to Israel. David had him return from the war expecting that he would spend the night with his wife Bathsheba, so that everyone would think the child she was carrying was Uriah's. Uriah, knowing nothing of this, refuses that comfort out of solidarity with his fellow soldiers. His integrity stands in sharp contrast to David's deception.

For today: true loyalty is shown in sacrifice. Let us ask God for an upright heart, and if we have failed, let us not cover up sin, but confess it with humility.
exp.6:15:
God promises David that his family and his kingdom will endure forever in God's presence. "House" means his descendants, his dynasty. "Before Me" means under God's care, and "forever" means without end. His throne will be "established," that is, secure.

God speaks through the prophet Nathan. David wanted to build a temple, but God answers that He will build David a "house," a dynasty. The promise includes Solomon, although many Christians see it fully fulfilled in Jesus, a descendant of David. Jews understand it in other ways.

Today we can trust that God keeps His promises even when we fail. If you feel insecure today, remember that His faithfulness does not depend on your perfection. Rest in His word and respond with gratitude, as David did.
exp.5:8:
This verse says that David feared the LORD that day. The word "feared" here means he had a deep respect for God mixed with alarm. So he asked, "How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?" That is, he wondered how something so holy could ever come near him.

David speaks after Uzza died when he touched the ark while it was being carried to Jerusalem. The law said the ark was to be carried by the Levites with poles, not on a cart (Numbers 4:15). David was saddened and frightened, and so he left the ark at the house of Obed-edom, where it became a blessing.

For today: God is loving, but He is also holy. Let us come to Him with reverence and obedience, seeking to do things as He directs, not only as seems good to us.
exp.0:8:
He asks the young man to stand over him and kill him, which means to come close and put an end to his life. He says that agony has seized him, meaning severe pain and distress, but that his life still lingers, meaning he is still alive.

The one speaking is a young Amalekite who comes before David after the battle in which Saul died. He tells how the king died and presents his crown and armband, hoping for a reward. His account does not match 1 Samuel 31, where Saul falls on his own sword. Many believe he lied to gain David's favor, although the text does not state this directly.

Today it reminds us that we should not take advantage of others' pain or shape the truth to gain an advantage. God values honesty and compassion.
exp.12:37:
He says that Absalom escaped after killing his brother Amnon and went to Geshur, a region northeast of Israel. He stayed there three years. The words "had fled" and "gone" show that he moved away in order to hide.

The account is told by the narrator of the book. Amnon had dishonored Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom took revenge by killing him. Then he took refuge with his maternal grandfather, King Talmai, since his mother was that king's daughter. Meanwhile, David was grieving the loss of one son and the absence of the other.

For today: revenge and wounds left unhealed can separate families for years. If there is conflict in your home, do not wait for three years to pass; seek to speak with humility, to ask for forgiveness or to forgive, and let God guide the reconciliation.
exp.18:41:
The men of Judah answered the men of Israel that they had brought the king across the Jordan because he is their relative, one of their own. They ask why the Israelites are angry, since they have not eaten at the king's expense and have received nothing from him for themselves.

David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Judah was the first tribe to welcome him back and escorted him when he crossed the Jordan. The other tribes of Israel felt overlooked and voice their complaint. Judah defends itself by pointing to its family bond. The argument grows so heated that soon another rebellion breaks out, although the text shows that both sides spoke with pride and with wounds.

When someone feels set aside, it is easy to respond defensively. Before arguing, let us listen with humility and seek peace, remembering that we are brothers.
exp.20:14:
The explanation says that the Philistines went to war against Israel once again. David went down with his servants to face them, and in the middle of the battle David became exhausted. The word "servants" here means his fighting men, his soldiers.

The narrator tells this after the story of the famine and how the bones of Saul were buried. God had already been moved to act on behalf of the land. But the war with the Philistines was still going on. David was no longer the young man who defeated Goliath, and his exhaustion sets up what follows: a giant nearly kills him, and his men protect him. Some think David was older; the text does not give his exact age.

Even strong leaders grow tired and need help. You do not have to carry everything alone. Accept the support of others and rest in time, trusting that God sustains your life.
exp.16:25:
This verse says that the Israelite army, together with Absalom, camped in the region of Gilead. The word "camped" describes setting up a military camp. Gilead was an area east of the Jordan River.

Here no character speaks; this is the narrator's account. Absalom had rebelled against his father David, and David had fled to Mahanaim, also in that area. Absalom crossed the Jordan with his troops and prepared for battle. The text also mentions that he placed Amasa, a relative of Joab, in command of the army. In this way we see that the family and the kingdom were divided.

For today: when there are family conflicts, pride and anger can grow until they become opposing sides. We should not wait for everything to explode; let us seek reconciliation and wise counsel in time, before the wounds grow deeper.
exp.4:20:
The explanation says that the Philistines, fleeing in defeat, abandoned their idols there, that is, the images of their gods. David and his men carried them away. The word "idols" refers to figures that people worshiped or trusted for their protection.

It is part of the historical account of when David was already king of Israel. The Philistines came up to attack him, and David first inquired of God. After the victory at Baal-perazim, it is clear that the idols could not save those who worshiped them. Carrying them away shows that David trusted only in the LORD.

For today: ask yourself what things you have relied on for "protection" instead of trusting God. Consult the Lord first in prayer and, if anything has taken his place in your heart, let it go with resolve.
exp.21:11:
He says that God surrounded himself with darkness, like a canopy spread around him. That darkness is made of a gathering of water, that is, clouds heavy with rain, and of thick clouds. A canopy is a covering hung over a space, and "as though" means "as if it were."

David speaks in a song of thanksgiving, near the end of his life, after God delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies. He uses storm imagery to describe how God came to rescue him. It is poetic language, not a literal account of what could be seen.

For today: God is greater than we can see or understand. When your life feels dark or confusing, remember that God may be at work even among the clouds. Trust in Him and ask Him for help with sincerity.
exp.9:13:
When the Ammonites saw that the Arameans had fled, they too fled before Abishai and went inside their city. The Arameans were the hired allies the Ammonites had counted on, and once those allies ran, the Ammonites gave up the fight and retreated behind their walls. So Joab, who had been fighting against the Ammonites, returned to Jerusalem.

This verse closes a stretch of the war between Israel and the Ammonites, who had shamed David's messengers. Earlier in the chapter, Joab split his army into two fronts and urged his brother Abishai to be strong and to trust that the LORD would decide what seemed good in his sight. When the Arameans fled, the Ammonites lost both their support and their nerve. The text does not say the war was over for good, since the Arameans gathered again later in the chapter.

For today: do faithfully your part, with courage and teamwork, and leave the outcome in God's hands. Also, do not place your security only in human support, because such support can fail you when you need it most.
exp.23:3:
This verse says that King David insisted on his order, even though Joab and the army commanders did not agree. The phrase "the king's word prevailed against" means that the king's order won out. So Joab and the commanders left the king's presence to register the troops of Israel, that is, to count the people of Israel.

David is the one giving the orders, and Joab, his general, had already asked him respectfully why he wanted to count the people. Joab seemed to see a danger. The text does not explain all the reasons, but later the account shows that this census displeased God (v. 10).

For today: when we have authority or influence, let us listen to the wise advice of others. Not everything we are able to do is wise to do. Let us ask God for humility to stop and examine our intentions.
exp.14:21:
David agrees that Ittai the Gittite should go with him. "March on then" means "all right, come with us." Ittai crosses over together with all his men and their families, including the little ones. "Gittite" means that he came from Gath, a Philistine city.

David is fleeing from Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Ittai was a foreigner who had arrived only recently. David had offered to let him go back to a safe place, but Ittai vowed his loyalty to the king, whatever might happen. So David answers him with these words. The crossing of the brook Kidron marks the beginning of the road toward the wilderness.

Today we can learn from Ittai's loyalty: remaining faithful to someone in difficult times, not only when everything is going well. It also invites us to value those who stand with us in trials and to be that kind of support for others.
exp.6:22:
Verse 23 says that no nation on earth is like Israel. God himself went out to redeem them as his own people, made a name for himself through them, and did great and awesome wonders on their behalf. He drove out the nations and their gods from before his people, and he redeemed them for himself from Egypt.

The one speaking is King David, in prayer. God had just promised him, through the prophet Nathan, that his family would have an enduring kingdom. David responds with humility and gratitude, remembering how God had acted before in the history of his people. That gives him confidence that God will keep what he has promised.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember what God has already done for you and for his people. Thanking him for the past strengthens confidence that he will remain faithful.
exp.20:20:
This giant taunted and insulted Israel, and Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimei, killed him. "Taunted" means that he mocked the people and dared them to fight.

The narrator of 2 Samuel summarizes Israel's last wars against the Philistines. He concludes by saying that four descendants of the giant of Gath fell by the hand of David and his servants. The text shows that the victory was not the work of a single hero, but of a whole team. Some scholars see difficulties when comparing the names with other passages, such as 1 Chronicles 20.

Today: you do not have to face your "giants" alone. God often gives us victory through family and brothers and sisters in the faith. Ask for help, and help others too.
exp.15:15:
Hushai, David's friend, went to Absalom and cried out, "Long live the king! Long live the king!" The name "Archite" tells us he came from a clan called the Archites.

Context: Absalom had rebelled against his father David, who fled from Jerusalem. David had asked Hushai to return and frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15:32-34). That is why Hushai speaks in words that Absalom takes as loyalty, but which can carry a double meaning. Scholars debate how much of this was cunning and how much a careful response.

For today: when you have to act in confusing situations, ask God for wisdom and prudence, and be faithful to what is right, even when you cannot say everything.
exp.14:26:
David speaks here to Zadok the priest and asks him, "Are you not a seer?" Then he tells him to return in peace to the city, together with his son Ahimaaz, and Abiathar with his son Jonathan. The word "seer" refers to someone who perceives or sees what God wants to reveal. Some think David is also asking him to be his eyes in the city.

David is fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. Zadok and Abiathar had gone out with the ark of God, but David decides that it should return to the city. He does not want to use the ark as a charm; he places his future in God's hands. Moreover, those priests and their sons could send him news.

For today: in moments of crisis, entrust your situation to God with humility, without manipulating things. At the same time, act with wisdom, relying on faithful people.
exp.12:21:
It says that Absalom did not say a single word to Amnon, either good or bad. But inwardly he hated him, because Amnon had violated Tamar, his sister.

The account tells what happened after Amnon assaulted Tamar. Absalom told his sister to keep quiet and took her into his house. David was very angry, but the text does not say that he punished Amnon. Absalom's silence was not peace: the verse that follows shows that he waited two years and planned his revenge.

For today: silent resentment does not disappear; it grows and can lead to more pain. If someone has hurt you or has hurt someone you love, seek justice and help in healthy ways, and ask God to heal your heart before hatred makes the decisions for you.
exp.14:18:
Here King David asks Ittai, a man from Gath: "Why should you also go with us?" He tells him to go back and stay with the new king, since he is both a foreigner and an exile from his homeland. The word "exile" means a person who has been forced to live far from the place he calls home. "Go back" means return to where you came from.

David is fleeing Jerusalem because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. In that hard moment, David speaks with kindness. He does not want Ittai, who has only recently arrived, to suffer for a problem that is not his own. He offers to release him from the duty of accompanying him. Some understand that the "new king" Ittai was to return to is Absalom, although the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: true loyalty does not depend on comfort. Ittai reminds us that we can stand beside those we love in difficult times. And David teaches us to care for others, even when we ourselves are suffering.
exp.9:4:
When David heard what had happened, he sent someone to meet the men, because they had been deeply humiliated. He told them to stay in Jericho until their beards had grown back, and then to come home.

Here the narrator speaks first, and then David, who was king of Israel. David had sent these men to comfort Hanun over the death of his father, but the Ammonite leaders suspected them. Hanun shamed them by shaving off half of each man's beard and cutting away part of their clothing. In that culture, a man's beard was a sign of his dignity, so this was a serious insult.

For today: when someone is hurt or humiliated, we can approach them with compassion, respect their dignity, and give them time to recover, without expecting them to act as if nothing happened.
exp.17:14:
It says that ten young men who carried Joab's armor surrounded Absalom, who was already wounded, and struck him until he died. The words "young men" and "carried" are the terms the verse above uses, so they are used here as well.

The narrator tells the end of Absalom's rebellion against his father, King David. Absalom had been caught hanging from a tree in the forest. David had asked that he be treated gently, but Joab, the commander of the army, chose to disregard that order. Some see in this a political decision to end the war; the Bible does not explain all of his reasons.

Today we see that pride and rebellion lead to a sad end. We also learn to value obedience and mercy, since Joab ignored David's request. Let us ask God for humility to honor those in authority and to be reconciled before it is too late.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells us that the king of the Ammonites, the people living next to Israel, died, and that his son Hanun became the new king. The phrase "some time later" simply points to a time after the events that came before in David's reign.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book, who presents the change of rule in Ammon. The verses that follow say that David wanted to show kindness to Hanun, because Hanun's father had shown kindness to him earlier. The Bible does not spell out here what that kindness was. But the Ammonite leaders became suspicious of David and misread his gesture, which set the stage for a conflict.

Today we can learn not to draw hasty conclusions about other people's intentions. Before distrusting a kind gesture, it is wise to ask, to listen, and to seek wisdom from God, so that we do not damage a relationship over mere suspicion.
exp.6:5:
God reminds David that, since the day he brought Israel out of Egypt, he has not lived in a house. Instead, he has moved about with a tent as his dwelling. The portable sanctuary that traveled with the people was his home, not a building made of stone or wood. The word "dwelling" here means the place where someone lives. God wants to show that he was not tied to a building.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Nathan. David was living in a palace of cedar and wanted to build a temple for God. His desire was good, but God makes clear that he had never asked for it and that he is the one who takes the initiative. He will soon remind David how he took him from tending sheep to make him a leader.

Today we can serve God with good intentions, but it is wise to remember that he does not depend on our works to be with us. Before we rush to do something for God, let us first listen to what he wants, and serve with humility, grateful for what he has already done for us.
exp.22:23:
This verse begins the list of the "Thirty," a group of brave soldiers who served David. It names Asahel, the brother of Joab, and Elhanan, son of Dodo of Bethlehem.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recording the names of the most outstanding men in David's army. After telling of the deeds of the first three and of Benaiah, the text lists the rest. Asahel died young, in a battle against Abner (2 Samuel 2), so his name appears as a memorial. Some scholars think the list gathers men from different periods of David's reign.

For today: God does not forget those who serve, even when their name is little known. Faithfully doing your part, without seeking applause, also has value before Him. Simple names were written down in the Bible.
exp.16:15:
Hushai tells the messengers to hurry with an urgent message for David: he must not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness, but must cross over at once. If he does not, the king and everyone with him could be swallowed up, which means destroyed or wiped out. "Send quickly" means to send word without delay.

It is Hushai, David's friend, who speaks, pretending to be an adviser to Absalom. After Absalom chose his counsel over that of Ahithophel, Hushai passes the report on to the priests Zadok and Abiathar so that they can warn David. He feared that Ahithophel might still find a way to attack David, even though his advice had been rejected.

For today: when God gives you an opportunity or a warning, act promptly. Do not leave obedience and wise action for tomorrow. God also cares for us by using ordinary people who faithfully do their part.
exp.12:2:
This verse introduces a new character: Jonadab, Amnon's friend. He was the son of Shimeah, David's brother, so he was Amnon's cousin. The Berean Standard Bible describes him as a very shrewd man, which means clever and sharp in his thinking.

The narrator tells the story of Amnon, David's son, who desired his half-sister Tamar and suffered because of it. At that moment Jonadab appears, sees his sorrow, and in the verses that follow gives him a deceptive piece of advice that leads to a grave sin. The text does not say that God approved of this; the Bible shows it as a tragedy within David's family.

For today: let us be careful about whom we listen to. A clever friend is not always a good counselor. Let us seek voices that bring us closer to God and to what is right, not voices that feed our wrong desires.
exp.0:26:
This verse closes a song of mourning. It repeats the lament: the mighty have fallen, and even their weapons have been destroyed. "Perished" means that they came to an end or were lost. The "weapons of war" stand for the strength and the glory of those warriors, who are no longer here.

David is the speaker, and he composes this elegy, known as "the song of the bow," after the death of King Saul and his friend Jonathan in battle against the Philistines. Although Saul had pursued him, David does not celebrate Saul's death; he mourns him with respect. Some understand that "weapons of war" also refers to the warriors themselves, as a poetic way of speaking about them.

For today: learn to grieve honestly and to honor what is good in others, even in those who hurt you. Do not be in a hurry to skip past sorrow; God receives your sincere sadness.
exp.22:17:
Abishai, brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was the chief of the Three, a group of mighty warriors. The phrase "wielded his spear" describes him fighting with it, and "won a name along with the Three" means that he gained lasting fame. The verse says he struck down three hundred men in one encounter.

The author of the book lists David's most outstanding warriors. This comes right after the account of three brave men who risked their lives to bring David water from Bethlehem. Abishai appears as another example of loyalty and courage. Some scholars note that the text distinguishes between "the Three" and "the Thirty," and the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God can use our courage and our strength to serve others with loyalty. Ask yourself what ability you have and how you could put it at the service of someone this week, without seeking fame.
exp.12:17:
This verse says that Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, because that is what the king's virgin daughters wore. Amnon's attendant threw her out and bolted the door behind her. The word "attendant" refers to someone who serves in a household.

The narrator tells what follows Amnon's rape of his half-brother's sister Tamar. She had begged him not to send her away like that, because it would add to her shame. He despised her and ordered his servant to throw her out. The robe shows her position and her purity, which Amnon destroyed. Bolting the door shows his coldness and his rejection.

God sees the pain of those who have been wounded and rejected. Today we can stand with someone who suffers abuse, believe them, listen to them, and help them seek protection, without staying silent or minimizing what happened.
exp.14:4:
The verse tells us that when anyone came near to bow down before him, Absalom would not let them complete the gesture. He would reach out his hand, take hold of them, and kiss them, as though he were their equal. Bowing down was a sign of respect before someone in authority, and Absalom turned that custom to his own purposes.

Absalom was the son of King David. He would stand near the city gate, where disputes were brought, and speak with the people who came seeking justice from the king. Through these warm, personal gestures and his words, he sought to win the affection of the people. The text says that in this way he won the hearts of the men of Israel, but his real aim was to take the throne from his father, so his kindness was a form of deceit.

Today we can learn to tell the difference between sincere kindness and kindness used to get something. Let us examine our own motives when we treat others well, and ask God for an honest heart.
exp.8:9:
David tells Ziba, Saul's former servant, to work the ground for Mephibosheth along with his sons and servants, and to bring in the harvest. This way, Saul's grandson will have food to eat. In addition, Mephibosheth will always eat at the king's table. The text adds that Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.

David speaks with Ziba after speaking with Mephibosheth, who was crippled and called himself a "dead dog." David had promised kindness to Saul's family because of his covenant with Jonathan, and for that reason he returns the land and gives him a place at his table.

For today: God's grace reminds us that we should treat with kindness those who cannot provide for themselves, and faithfully keep the promises we make, even when we receive nothing in return.
exp.8:4:
The explanation says that King David sent for Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, and he was brought from the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar. The phrase "had him brought" means that David had him taken to the king. Lo-debar was a remote place, and the text gives no further details about it.

The one acting here is the narrator, telling what David does. Shortly before, David had asked whether anyone was left of Saul's house to whom he could show kindness. He was doing this because of the covenant of friendship he had made with Jonathan. Ziba, a servant from Saul's household, told him about this son who was lame in his feet, and David did not stop at words: he had him brought.

For today: true kindness moves and seeks people out. God sought us out when we were far away. We can think of someone who has been forgotten, alone or cut off, and do something concrete for them this week, such as a visit or a phone call.
exp.17:32:
The explanation says that King David, on learning that his son Absalom had died, was filled with grief. He went up to the room over the gate of the city and wept. He kept calling out his son's name and wished he had died in his place. "Was shaken" means that he was deeply stirred and shaken inside. "The chamber over the gate" was a room above the entrance of the city.

Here David speaks. Absalom had rebelled against him and tried to take away his kingdom. Joab and the soldiers defeated the rebellion, and Absalom died in the battle. Cushi brought the news as a victory, but David only asked about his son. His response shows a father's love that remains in place despite the betrayal.

For today: grief over someone we love, even if they hurt us, is real and should not be hidden. Bring it honestly to God, and ask him to give you comfort and mercy.
exp.15:9:
David answers Abishai, who wanted to kill Shimei for cursing the king. "Sons of Zeruiah" refers to Abishai and his brother Joab. The words "What have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah?" mean something like "we don't agree, don't pressure me." David says that if Shimei curses him because the LORD told him to, then no one can ask why he did it.

David flees from Jerusalem because his son Absalom rebelled. On the way, Shimei, a man from the family of Saul, curses him and accuses him of being violent. David does not know whether there is any truth in the accusation, and he decides not to take revenge. Commentators debate whether the LORD really told Shimei to curse David or whether David only recognizes that God allows it to happen.

For today: when you are criticized or treated badly, before responding in anger, stop and ask yourself whether God wants to teach you something. Trusting God helps us respond with humility.
exp.10:7:
He says David tells Uriah to go down to his house and wash his feet, which means to rest after the journey. When Uriah leaves the palace, a gift from the king follows him, a portion of food from the royal table.

David speaks after he has gotten Bathsheba, Uriah's wife, pregnant while Uriah is away at war. He calls him back from the front with a pretended kindness. Many understand that the real purpose was for Uriah to sleep with his wife, so that the pregnancy would seem to be his. The text does not say this directly here, but the context strongly suggests it.

For today: a kind gesture can hide a crooked intention. If we have done something wrong, let us not cover it with appearances; it is better to confess to God and seek the truth with humility, as David did afterward in Psalm 51.
exp.5:11:
It was reported to King David that the LORD had blessed the household of Obed-edom and everything that belonged to him, because of the ark of God. So David went and had the ark of God brought up from the house of Obed-edom into the City of David with rejoicing. The City of David is Jerusalem. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The narrator describes what happened after David became frightened. Shortly before, Uzzah died when he touched the ark while it was being carried (2 Samuel 6:6-9). David left it for three months at the house of Obed-edom. On learning that blessing was found there, he understood that drawing near to God was possible, and he resumed moving the ark. The Bible does not describe how that blessing appeared.

For today: God deserves respect, but he also wants to bless those who receive him. We can draw near to him with reverence and joy, making room for his presence in our homes.
exp.20:10:
When David was told what Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah and Saul's concubine, had done, the story returns to a woman who had been part of Saul's household. In plain terms, "was told" means David received news of her actions. A concubine was a woman who lived with a man as a secondary wife, a practice that was common in that time.

The account describes a time of famine in Israel, and David sought the Lord about it. Seven of Saul's descendants were handed over to the Gibeonites and hanged. Rizpah, who had lost two of her sons among them, stayed by the bodies for months, guarding them from the birds of the air and the wild animals of the field. When David heard about her devotion, he moved to honor the dead, and he also gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan for burial.

For today: faithful, steady love does not go unnoticed. Caring tenderly for those who suffer, even when no one else does, can move other hearts to act with compassion.
exp.17:1:
David divided his troops into three groups. He put one group under Joab, another under Abishai, Joab's brother, and the third under Ittai the Gittite, a man from Gath. The explanation's point about the word for "consigned" is that David handed the groups over to these men, placing them in charge. Then David announced that he himself would also march out with them.

David is fleeing from his son Absalom, who has rebelled against him. He is in Mahanaim, on the other side of the Jordan, and is preparing for battle. Ittai was a foreigner who had remained loyal to David. As is seen later, the people will not let the king go into battle, because his life was too valuable. David accepts their counsel.

For today: a good leader shares responsibilities and trusts others, but is also willing to share the risk. He also knows how to listen with humility when wise people give him advice different from his own.
exp.12:24:
Here King David answers Absalom's invitation to the sheep-shearing feast. He tells him that they should not all go, or they would be a burden to him. Absalom keeps urging him, but David is not willing to go; even so, he gives Absalom his blessing when they part.

Here David speaks as Absalom's father. Two years have passed since Amnon dishonored Tamar, Absalom's sister, and David did not bring about justice. The Bible does not yet say that Absalom is planning anything, but the account that follows shows that the invitation hid a plan of revenge. David did not know this.

Often friendly appearances can hide crooked intentions, and unresolved wounds can grow in silence. Today we can seek justice and reconciliation in good time, with honesty and prayer, instead of letting resentment ripen. It is also wise to ask for wisdom to discern.
exp.12:13:
He says that Amnon did not listen to Tamar. She begged him not to do her harm, but he, being stronger, violated her and forced himself on her. "Being stronger" means he had greater physical strength. "Lay with her" is a plain way of saying that he sexually assaulted her. It is an act of violence, not of love.

Context: Amnon was the son of King David, and Tamar was his half-sister. He pretended to be sick so that he could be alone with her. Tamar pleaded with him using reasons: she spoke of her shame, of what is right in Israel, and of a lawful way out. He would not listen. The Bible presents this act as a serious wrong, and it shows that she was the innocent victim.

For today: The Bible takes seriously the pain of those who suffer abuse and does not blame them. If someone tells you that they were hurt, listen to them with respect, believe them, and help them seek protection and support. And if you have lived through something like this, it is not your fault; seek help from people you trust.
exp.12:25:
Absalom asks his father David that, if he cannot go to the sheep-shearing feast, at least let his brother Amnon go with them. David answers with a question: "Why should he go with you?" that is, "why him in particular?" Shearers are the men who cut the wool from the sheep.

Absalom speaks with deceit. Two years earlier Amnon had abused Tamar, Absalom's sister, and Absalom had held onto his hatred. David's question shows that he may have suspected something, but the Bible does not say what he was thinking. In the end he gives way under the pressure, and Absalom uses the feast for his revenge.

For today: let us be wary of kindness that hides resentment, and let us not allow an unhealed wound to lead us into wrongdoing. Let us bring our pain before God and seek justice and forgiveness, not revenge.
exp.17:21:
Ahimaaz, son of the priest Zadok, keeps insisting that he be allowed to run after the Cushite to bring the news to the king, no matter what happens. Joab asks him what good it does to run if he will not receive a reward for the news.

Joab is the commander of David's army. He has just killed Absalom, the king's rebellious son, and he sends Cushi, a Cushite, to tell the king. Joab wants to protect Ahimaaz, because the news is painful and the king might react badly. Ahimaaz, however, is very determined. The Bible does not fully explain his reasons, so we do not know what moved him.

For today: before carrying a message, it is wise to examine our motives and listen to wise advice. Eagerness to be first is not enough; the timing, the manner, and the love with which we speak also matter.
exp.16:18:
This verse tells how the woman of the house took a cloth and spread it over the mouth of the well where Jonathan and Ahimaaz were hiding. Then she scattered grain over the cloth, as if she were drying it out in the open, so that nobody would suspect a thing.

"So nobody would know a thing" means that no one discovered the secret.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was fleeing from his son Absalom, and these two young men were carrying a secret message to warn him of Ahithophel's plan. They were seen and took refuge in Bahurim. The woman protected them with cleverness, and the pursuers left without finding them.

For today: God often uses simple people who are little known to accomplish his purposes. An act of courage and quiet help, such as protecting or supporting someone in danger, can have great value before God, even though no one notices it.
exp.18:26:
He says that Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, "has slandered" him, that is, he spoke falsely about him and spoke ill of him before King David. Mephibosheth calls the king "like the angel of God," meaning someone wise and able to judge rightly. For that reason he leaves the decision to him: "so do what is good in your eyes."

Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, is speaking when David returns to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Ziba had made David believe that Mephibosheth stayed behind to take advantage of the situation. Mephibosheth says that Ziba deceived him and left him behind. His neglected appearance and humble attitude support his account, though the text does not fully settle who was telling the truth.

For today: when you are falsely accused, do not despair or seek revenge. Speak the truth with humility and entrust the outcome to God, who sees the heart.
exp.6:1:
Here King David speaks with the prophet Nathan. He says that he is living in a house of cedar, a fine and costly wood, while the ark of God still remains in a tent.

David was already settled in his palace, because God had given him rest from his enemies. The ark was the symbol of God's presence among his people. David feels uneasy about that difference and thinks of building a house for God. Nathan encourages him at first, but that same night God speaks to him and gives him a different message, as seen in what follows.

When God gives us rest and blessing, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are giving him first place. Even so, it is wise to seek God before acting, even when our desire is good.
exp.22:1:
Here David says that the Spirit of God spoke through him, and that the words he uttered were not his alone, but God himself placed his message on his tongue. The name of God is the LORD, and "tongue" refers to the way he spoke.

These are David's "last words," that is, one of his final messages, spoken when he was already old. He was a king, but also a poet and singer, called "the sweet psalmist of Israel." Before speaking of the righteous ruler, he wants to make clear that what he will say comes from God. Many of his psalms reflect that same conviction.

For today: when you speak with others, ask God to let his words guide yours. Before you counsel, correct, or encourage, pray and seek his Word, so that what you say builds up and reflects his truth.
exp.10:26:
After the period of mourning for Bathsheba's husband was over, David had her brought to his palace. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD. The word "evil" here means that his actions were wrong and went against God's will; they grieved him deeply.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and then had Uriah killed in battle to cover up his sin. People could see an ordinary marriage, but the narrator shows us what God saw. Later, in chapter 12, God sends the prophet Nathan to confront him.

For today: even if we manage to hide a fault or make it look good, God sees everything. It is better to acknowledge sin quickly and come to Him with humility, for He offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.22:5:
The explanation says that wicked people, here called "the worthless," will be like thorns that are pulled up and thrown away. No one picks them up by hand, because they wound the one who touches them. The word "worthless" points to people who are corrupt and rebellious, as the verse describes them.

These words are part of the final words of David, a poem he spoke at the end of his life. Before that, the poem speaks of the righteous ruler who governs in the fear of God and is like the light of the morning. It then contrasts that rule with the ungodly, who are dangerous and end up burned. David also trusts that God made an everlasting covenant with him.

For today: do not lose heart in the face of evil that seems to be advancing. God sees it and has the last word. Try to live with justice, and trust God's promises, which are firm even when you do not yet see everything.
exp.3:2:
The verse explains a detail about the people of Beeroth. "Fled" means they ran away, and "lived there as foreigners" means they settled in Gittaim as outsiders, not as people from that place. Gittaim was the place where they took refuge, and they have lived there to this day, the time when this is being written.

The narrator tells the story of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and of Baanah and Rechab, two of his captains. He notes that they were from Beeroth, a town assigned to Benjamin. The Bible does not explain here why the Beerothites fled; some think it was because of some war or violence, but that is only a guess. This detail prepares the account of the betrayal by these two men.

For today: God sees those who have been displaced and those who live as strangers. We can treat with respect and help those who have had to leave their land. Also, being a captain or holding a good position does not guarantee a good heart; let us guard our loyalty and our decisions.
exp.12:31:
Jonadab tells King David not to believe the report that Absalom had killed all the king's sons. In his view, only Amnon has died. He says Absalom had been planning this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.

Jonadab is David's nephew, the shrewd friend who had earlier advised Amnon on the scheme to get Tamar alone. David is shattered by the false news, and Jonadab speaks with a calm and confident tone. The Bible does not explain how he knew these things; it only shows that he was well informed. It is worth noticing that he now speaks like someone who knows exactly what happened.

For today: an injustice not addressed in time can grow until it becomes a tragedy. Let us seek justice and healing soon, and let us be careful whose counsel we receive.
exp.6:7:
God tells the prophet Nathan to say this to David: "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to make you ruler over my people Israel." The word "pasture" in the verse refers to the open grassland where the flock grazes, and "ruler" here means a chosen leader or governor.

David wanted to build a house for God, a temple. God speaks through Nathan and, before talking about plans, reminds David who raised him up. God had never asked for a house of cedar; he had walked with his people in a tent. The point is that God is the one who gives and sustains, not the one who needs to be given things.

For today: remember where God took you from. Everything you have, your opportunities and your place, comes from his goodness and not only from your own effort. That keeps us humble and grateful, and it helps us serve God without thinking we are doing him a favor.
exp.5:15:
As the ark of the LORD entered the City of David, Saul's daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD. She despised him in her heart. "LORD" is the name of God, and "despised" means looking down on someone with scorn.

The narrator describes how the ark returns to Jerusalem amid celebration, trumpets and worship. David, wearing a linen ephod (a simple linen garment), joins in with joy. Michal was the daughter of Saul, the previous king, and her gaze from the window shows that she watches from a distance, without taking part. The text does not explain all her reasons; it only says that she despised him in her heart.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we look at the worship of others with criticism or whether we join in with humility. God looks at the heart, and sincere joy toward Him should not embarrass us.
exp.23:4:
They crossed the Jordan and camped near Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the valley, and then moved on toward Gad and Jazer. The source-language details that once appeared here are left out, since the verse's own wording already makes the meaning clear.

This is the narrator speaking. David had ordered the census, and Joab, although he warned him it was not a good idea, carried it out. The places named mark the route through the territory of Israel. The text does not explain all of David's reasons here, but the account shows that the census displeased God.

For today: when a decision troubles us, simply going ahead out of habit is not enough. It is wise to stop, pray, and listen to sound counsel before moving forward.
exp.1:13:
Abner proposes to Joab that some young soldiers get up and compete before them, that is, that they put on a kind of combat or contest in front of them. "Young men" here means young warriors. Joab agrees and replies, "Let them get up."

The speakers are the leaders of two rival armies. Abner serves Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and Joab serves David. They meet beside the pool of Gibeon, in the midst of a division among the tribes. The Hebrew word can suggest a game or a tournament, but what follows shows that it ended in a slaughter. The text does not say with certainty what Abner intended.

Today, this invites us to be careful with provocations that look like games but stir up pride and violence. Let us seek peace and think before challenging others.
exp.14:33:
Husai is told to go back to Jerusalem and present himself to Absalom as his new servant. Just as he served David before, he will now say that he will serve the new king. To "thwart" means to block or make fail, so the wording here is about undoing Ahithophel's plans. Ahithophel is Absalom's counselor.

David speaks with his friend Husai as he flees from Jerusalem, because his son Absalom has rebelled against him. David is climbing the mountain, worshiping God in the midst of his pain. Ahithophel, formerly David's counselor, has joined Absalom. David does not want Husai to come with him as a burden, but to help him from within, pretending loyalty to Absalom in order to frustrate Ahithophel's advice.

For today: in times of crisis, David prays, worships, and also acts wisely. We can trust God and, at the same time, take prudent steps, asking for help from faithful and honest people.
exp.21:25:
This verse says that God deals with each person according to their faithfulness. "Faithful" means loyal, steadfast and trusting toward God. "Blameless" means whole and sincere, without deceit. In other words, the one who stays loyal to God finds God faithful in return, and the one who lives with integrity finds Him true and open.

David speaks this, near the end of his life, in a song of thanksgiving because the LORD delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies. He does not claim to have been perfect, but says that he sought to follow God with sincerity and turned away from wickedness. He acknowledges that God shows Himself faithful to those who are faithful to Him.

For today: if you want to experience God's faithfulness up close, come to Him with sincerity. Today, without pretending, confess to Him what weighs on you and ask Him for help to live honestly at home and at work.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that David decided not to bring the ark of the Lord to the City of David, which was Jerusalem. Instead, he took it aside to the house of Obed-edom, a man from Gath. The word "Gittite" means a native of Gath.
