It is part of the narrator's account. David had just seen Uzzah die for touching the ark, and he felt sorrow and fear before the holiness of God. So he stopped. Later, when he saw that God blessed the household of Obed-edom, David resumed the move with joy. Some think Obed-edom was a Levite; the text does not make this clear.

Today we can learn that drawing near to God calls for reverence and humility. If we feel confused or afraid, we can pause, seek God, and return to obeying Him as He directs.
exp.16:9:
This verse says that if Absalom attacks David and his men, even the most valiant soldier, with the heart of a lion, will be overcome with fear. The phrase "with the heart of a lion" describes a man of great courage, and "will melt with fear" means his courage will drain away. The men who are with David are valiant warriors. All Israel knows that David is a mighty man, and that he has brave soldiers with him.

The speaker is Hushai, David's friend, who pretends to be loyal to Absalom. Absalom had rebelled, and David was fleeing. Hushai gives advice different from Ahithophel's, in order to buy time so that David could prepare. He praises David's bravery to instill fear and hold back an immediate attack. It is a strategy, and the Bible later shows that God was at work in this.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by hasty decisions or by fear. Ask God for wisdom, listen calmly to counsel, and remember that He can work even in the middle of difficult situations.
exp.19:11:
It says that Amasa lay in the middle of the road, covered in his own blood. A man saw that all the troops were stopping there, so he dragged the body off the road into a field and threw a garment over it, because everyone who came near him stopped in place. The phrase "wallowed in his blood" in the verse above describes a wounded body lying in its own blood.

The narrator tells what happened after Joab, David's commander, treacherously killed Amasa while they were pursuing Sheba, who had rebelled against David. The troops kept stopping, and this slowed the pursuit. Moving the body off the road allowed the army to move on. The account does not justify Joab; it only describes the events.

For today: violence and betrayal leave wounds that stop others and make us pause to look. This invites us to seek justice with integrity, without deceit, and to treat others' pain with respect.
exp.2:19:
This verse tells that Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty of his men. David held a feast for Abner and his men. The word "feast" means a special meal of welcome.

Abner had been the commander of Saul's army and had backed Saul's house against David. Now, after a falling-out with Ish-bosheth, he decides to approach David and help bring all Israel under David's rule. David receives him with hospitality, which opens the door to an agreement. The text does not say everything David was thinking, so it is best not to assume too much.

For today: when there is a broken relationship or a disagreement, sharing a meal and receiving someone kindly can open the way to peace. A simple gesture of hospitality can help people listen to one another.
exp.23:15:
The explanation says that the angel was already reaching out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, but the LORD relented from the calamity and had compassion, deciding to hold back the punishment. He told the angel who was destroying the people, "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" The threshing floor mentioned at the end of the verse was the flat, open place where wheat was beaten out to separate the grain. The angel stopped by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, a man who lived in Jerusalem before Israel took the city.

David had counted the people, and this brought a plague upon Israel. He chose to fall into the hand of God rather than into the hand of men, trusting in his great mercy. The narrator tells here of the moment when the punishment is stopped. Some understand that the LORD "relented" speaks of God's compassion, not of any mistake on his part.

When we fail, we can come to God with humility, because his mercy is greater than our error and he knows how to stop judgment in time.
exp.21:42:
David says he ground his enemies to dust like the dirt of the earth, and he crushed and trampled them like mud in the streets. These are vivid pictures of total victory, meaning nothing was left standing.

David sings this song of thanksgiving when God rescued him from Saul and other enemies. He speaks in poetic, war-filled language. But notice that he credits the victory to God: "You gave me." The enemies called on the LORD for help, and He did not answer them. After this, the text shows David as the head of nations.

For today: do not use this verse to justify violence or revenge against people. Instead, trust that God is the one who delivers and sustains. When you face a struggle, pray, act with justice, and give God the glory for every victory.
exp.17:31:
The explanation says that King David asks Cushi whether the young man Absalom is all right. The word "all right" here means in good health or unharmed. Cushi does not say directly that Absalom died, but he suggests it: he wishes that the enemies of the king, and all who rise up against him to harm him, would end up the same way as that young man.

Cushi is speaking, a messenger who brings news from the battle against Absalom's army, since Absalom had rebelled against his father. Cushi announces the victory, but David thinks only of his son. So when he understands the answer, he breaks down and weeps, as the following text shows.

For today: sometimes a victory brings pain, especially when family is involved. We can be honest with God in our weeping and also be careful when we bring bad news, with respect and compassion.
exp.12:15:
She says that Tamar answers Amnon: "No. Sending me away is worse than the great wrong you have already done to me." Her words make clear that she is not agreeing to be dismissed.

It is Tamar, daughter of King David and half-sister of Amnon, who speaks. He had just abused her with violence, and then, filled with hatred, he sent her out. Tamar, already wounded, defends her dignity: to be cast out in this way, in shame and without protection, made the injustice worse. The Bible does not present her as guilty.

For today: when someone suffers abuse, we should listen to her seriously, believe her, and protect her, not silence her or rush to hide the problem. God sees the pain of the wounded, and we can be instruments of his care and of justice.
exp.18:21:
Here David rebukes Abishai and Joab, the sons of Zeruiah, because they want to kill Shimei. "Adversaries" means people who oppose you, and David asks whether they are now acting as his opponents. He asks whether anyone should be put to death in Israel today, and he declares that he is aware that today he is king over Israel once again and wants to begin with peace.

Shimei had cursed David when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. Now David returns to Jerusalem, and Shimei, frightened, asks David for forgiveness. Abishai asks for Shimei's death because he cursed the Lord's anointed. David decides to use his authority to forgive, although the Bible later shows that this story had other chapters.

For today: when we have power or reason to repay evil with evil, we can choose mercy. Forgiving does not erase what happened, but it opens the way to peace and reflects the heart of God.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that Abner is going to take the kingdom away from the house of Saul and establish David's throne over all the people. "Transfer" means to move something from one place to another. "Establish" means to make something firm and secure. "From Dan to Beersheba" was a way of naming the whole territory, from north to south.

Abner, commander of Saul's army, speaks very angrily. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, had rebuked him over a matter involving a woman named Rizpah. Abner feels insulted after having been loyal, and he decides to switch sides. He says that God had sworn to give the kingdom to David. His motive mixes personal anger with the recognition of what God had promised.

For today: God carries out his plans even when people act from mixed motives. Let us ask God to cleanse our intentions, so that we obey his will with a sincere heart and not out of pride or anger.
exp.21:10:
He mounted a cherub and flew, and he soared on the wings of the wind. A cherub is a heavenly being that in the Bible accompanies the presence of God. The image is poetic: it describes God moving with speed and power, coming to help his people.

David speaks here, at the end of his life, in a song of gratitude. He dedicates it to God because God delivered him from Saul and from all his enemies. David uses images of storm, fire and trembling to show that God heard his cry and came to rescue him. It is not a literal description, but a way of expressing that God intervened with great power.

For today: when you feel alone or cornered, remember that God is not distant or indifferent. Cry out to Him with confidence and wait for His help, even if it does not arrive the way you imagine. He knows when and how to act.
exp.21:8:
This verse describes God with images of powerful fire: smoke rises from his nostrils, and consuming fire comes from his mouth, so intense that glowing coals blaze forth. It is poetic language. The word "consuming" means that the fire burns up and destroys whatever it touches. The verse's image of God's fierce response shows his opposition to evil.

David, already an old man, speaks in a song of thanksgiving because God rescued him from Saul and from his enemies. He was in distress, he cried out, and God answered. These images are not a literal scene, but a way of saying that God acted with strength to deliver his servant. Scholars understand these figures as poetry about divine intervention.

For today: when you feel that no one is listening, cry out to God. He is not indifferent to injustice or to your pain. Trust that his opposition to evil is part of his love for his own people.
exp.18:11:
Here David tells the elders of Judah: "You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood." He asks them why they would be the last to bring the king back. The phrase "my own flesh and blood" means that they are close family. "The last" means those who come at the end.

David speaks after the death of Absalom, who had rebelled against him. The other tribes of Israel already wanted David to return, but Judah, his own tribe, had stayed silent. David sends the priests Zadok and Abiathar to speak to them. He seeks reconciliation and appeals to family ties, not to force. The text shows that the heart of Judah turned toward him.

For today: when a relationship is broken, it is sometimes wise to take the first step with humility and to remember what unites us. A kind gesture can open the door to reconciliation.
exp.13:16:
The woman says she hopes the king's answer will bring her rest, that is, peace and relief. She praises him by saying he is like an angel of God because he is able to tell good from evil when he hears a case. She ends with a blessing: that the LORD her God will be with him.

It was a woman from Tekoa, sent by Joab, who pretended to be a widow with a family problem. Her story aims to make David reflect on his own son Absalom, who was exiled. Her compliments are part of a strategy, and afterward the king discovers that Joab was behind it.

Today we can learn to listen carefully and with discernment before we judge. We should also be cautious with flattery: it can be sincere, but sometimes it seeks to influence us. Let us ask God for wisdom to distinguish good from evil.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that during the war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner kept strengthening his position within the house of Saul. "Continued to strengthen his position" here means more than working hard. It means gaining power and influence.

The narrator is speaking. After the list of the sons born to David in Hebron, we are reminded that the kingdom was still divided. Abner, commander of Saul's army, was supporting Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. What follows shows that his growing power would soon clash with the king he was supporting.

For today: power and influence can grow without our noticing, and they can also change the heart. Let us ask God for humility, to use whatever position we have with integrity and to serve others, not to exalt ourselves.
exp.3:6:
They say that the two brothers entered the house of Ish-bosheth while he was lying on his bed. They stabbed and killed him, then cut off his head. They took his head and traveled all night by way of the Arabah, the low desert valley along the Jordan. The bed was simply where he was sleeping.

The narrator tells how Rechab and Baanah, captains of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, murdered him treacherously. They hoped to win David's favor by bringing him the head. But the account goes on to show that David did not reward them; instead he condemned the crime (verses 9 to 12).

For today: God is not pleased when we seek gain by unjust means, even when it seems they serve a good cause. David rejected that path. We can ask God to help us wait for his timing and to act with honesty, never betraying anyone to come out ahead.
exp.23:14:
God sent a deadly plague on Israel, from that morning until "the appointed time," which was probably the limit God had set, and which some understand to mean three days. Seventy thousand men died, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south; that is, across the whole nation.

The narrator tells the consequences of David taking a census of the people, which the text presents as a sin. Gad, God's prophet, gave him three possible punishments. David chose to fall into the hands of God, trusting in his mercy. Afterward, God stopped the angel, and David confessed his guilt and prayed for the people.

Today we see that our decisions, especially those of people who lead, affect others. When we fail, the best thing is to acknowledge it honestly and turn to God's mercy, not to excuses.
exp.5:18:
Here it is said that David, after bringing the ark to Jerusalem, gave every Israelite, men and women alike, a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake. Then everyone went back to their own homes.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Samuel. David rejoices that the ark of God, the sign of his presence, has at last arrived at its place. After offering sacrifices and blessing the people, he holds a shared feast. Everyone receives the same, regardless of rank. Right after this comes the clash with Michal, who scorns David's joy.

For today: when God blesses us, our joy grows when we share it. Think of someone you could invite to your table or help generously this week.
exp.6:28:
David asks God to bless his family, that is, his descendants, so that they may continue always before Him. He opens with "may it please You," which is how David humbly asks God to accept his request. David leans on what God has already promised: if God has spoken it, then with His blessing the house of His servant will be blessed forever.

David, the king, speaks after the prophet Nathan brought him God's promise: that God would build him a house, that is, a lasting dynasty. David had wanted to build a temple, but God promised him something greater. This prayer is his humble and grateful response. Christians see in this promise a foreshadowing of the Messiah, a descendant of David.

For today: when you pray, rest on what God has already promised in His Word. Ask Him with humility and confidence, knowing that He is faithful to fulfill what He says.
exp.13:29:
Absalom speaks to his servants and points out that Joab's field of barley is right next to his. He tells them to go and set it on fire, and they do it. "Set fire" means to burn, and "field" refers to land that is planted and farmed.

Absalom had been in Jerusalem for two years without being able to see King David. He had asked Joab, a leader close to the king, to speak on his behalf, but Joab ignored him twice. So Absalom turns to violence to get his attention. Afterward, Joab comes, and Absalom explains that he wants to see the king. The Bible does not approve of his act here; it only shows his impulsive character.

When someone ignores us, we may feel tempted to force a response through anger or pressure. It is better to speak with clarity and patience, seeking reconciliation without harming others or letting resentment take control of us.
exp.21:6:
David says that in great distress he called upon the LORD and cried out to his God, and that God heard him. "Called upon" means calling out to ask for help. "From His temple" here probably refers to God's heavenly dwelling, since in David's time the temple in Jerusalem did not yet exist. "My cry for help reached His ears" expresses that God attended to his plea closely and truly.

He speaks in a song of thanksgiving that he composed when God rescued him from his enemies and from Saul. Earlier he describes feeling surrounded by death and danger. Afterward, the song shows God acting with power, with the trembling of the earth and fire, in response to his cry.

For today: when you feel distress, you don't need to have the perfect words. Cry out to God with sincerity, trusting that he listens to you. Then remember and give thanks each time he helps you.
exp.6:26:
For You, O LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, have revealed this to Your servant when You said, "I will build a house for you." Therefore Your servant has found the courage to offer this prayer to You.

This verse says that God himself made David aware of a promise: "I will build a house for you." The phrase "have revealed this to Your servant" means that God told him this personally. "House" here means family and descendants, not a building. "Has found the courage to offer this prayer" means that David took courage to pray in this way. A prayer like this is a humble plea in which someone asks for something.

David speaks in prayer after the prophet Nathan brought him God's message. David wanted to build a temple, but God promised instead to establish a dynasty of kings from his family. David does not ask for something new: he rests on what God has already said. Many Christians see in this promise an announcement of Jesus, a descendant of David.

For today: when we pray, we can rest on the promises God has already given in his Word. Praying with confidence is not demanding, but responding in faith to what God has said.
exp.11:13:
Nathan, sent by God, speaks to David. David had taken Bathsheba and had her husband Uriah killed. David confessed, and God forgave his sin, so David would not die. But forgiveness did not remove every consequence. Some understand that the child's death shows how serious a king's sin was; the text does not explain more details.

For today: God truly forgives those who repent, but our actions can affect others and the way God is seen by those who watch us. Let us live with humility, confess quickly, and take care of our witness.
exp.4:7:
David says that whoever goes up through the gutter (most likely a water channel or tunnel, though its exact nature is not known for certain) will strike the Jebusites. He calls the people who mocked him "the lame and the blind," and says that David despises them. From this came a saying that the blind and the lame will never enter the palace.

David is the new king and attacks Jerusalem. The Jebusites, confident in their walls, mocked him, saying that even the blind and the lame could stop him. David responds with anger. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the saying. What is clear is that David takes the stronghold, and that the LORD was with him.

For today: do not lose heart at mockery or at obstacles that seem impossible. Trust in God, act with courage, and remember that Jesus did welcome the blind and the lame with compassion.
exp.16:12:
It says that, if David retreats into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city and drag it down to the valley, until not even a pebble can be found there. This is an exaggeration meant to show an overwhelming force.

The speaker is Hushai, David's friend, who pretends to be an advisor to Absalom. His real purpose is to counter Ahithophel's plan, which called for attacking David at once. Hushai wants to buy time so that David can organize. The text says that God allowed his advice to seem better.

For today: sometimes words full of grandeur and confidence sound convincing, but they are not wise. Before following a piece of advice, it is good to ask whether it is true and whether it pleases God. And we can trust that He works even when we do not see how.
exp.21:3:
David says that he will call upon the LORD, who deserves to be praised, and that in this way he will be saved from his enemies. "Call upon" means to cry out to him in trust. "Worthy to be praised" means he deserves to be praised. "Saved" means rescued or kept safe.

David speaks at the end of his life, in a song of thanks because God delivered him from his enemies and from Saul (2 Samuel 22:1). Before this, he called God his rock, shield, and refuge. Then he describes the mortal danger he faced. This song appears almost word for word in Psalm 18.

For today: when you are afraid or under pressure, do not wait for the storm to pass before you pray. Call upon God now, and praise him while you do, remembering how he has cared for you before. Praise strengthens trust, even when you do not yet know how he will help you.
exp.11:7:
God reminds David of everything he had given him: the house of Saul, his former master, and Saul's wives, whom God placed into David's arms and under his authority. He also gave him the house of Israel and Judah. And if that had not been enough, God says he would have given him even more.

Here God speaks through the prophet Nathan. He has just told David a parable about a rich man who took the only little ewe lamb of a poor man. David became angry, and Nathan answered him: "You are the man." God shows his kindness so that David may see the seriousness of his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah.

For today: when we are tempted, let us remember how much God has given us. Gratitude helps us not to seek what is forbidden and to live with humility.
exp.20:5:
The Gibeonites ask that seven male descendants of Saul be handed over to them so that they can be hanged before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, which they call "the chosen of the LORD." David answers: "I will give them to you."

There was a famine in the land, and the text explains that Saul had mistreated and killed Gibeonites, even though Israel had made an oath to them long before. David asks how the wrong can be made right, and the Gibeonites ask for this kind of justice. The text does not say that God commanded this method, and it is a difficult passage that is interpreted in several ways.

Today we learn that injustices and broken promises matter to God and leave consequences. If we have harmed someone, it is good to acknowledge it and seek to make amends with humility, without hiding it.
exp.18:29:
Mephibosheth tells King David that Ziba may take all the lands, not just half. For him, what matters most is that the king has come home safely. "Let him take all" means exactly that: let Ziba take everything. The king's safe return to his own house is the thing that counts most to him.

David was returning to Jerusalem after Absalom's rebellion. Mephibosheth, grandson of Saul and son of Jonathan, had been treated with kindness by David. Ziba had accused him of disloyalty, and Mephibosheth maintained that he had been deceived. David decided to divide the lands. Some think Mephibosheth spoke with sincerity and gratitude; others see resignation in the face of an unfair decision. The text does not make this entirely clear.

Today we can learn to value relationships and peace more than material gain. When something does not turn out the way we want, we can ask ourselves: what is truly most important? Being thankful for what we have received helps us let go of resentment.

sum.22: Near the end of his life, David says that God spoke through him: a just ruler who fears God is like the morning light. He admits that his household is not perfect, yet God made an everlasting covenant with him. Then his mighty warriors are named, and David refuses to drink the water that his men risked their lives to get for him, and he pours it out to God.
sum.7: David won many battles against the Philistines, Moab, Syria, and Edom, and those peoples came under his control. The text repeats that Jehovah kept him safe wherever he went, and David dedicated the silver and gold of the defeated nations to God. He ruled with justice and organized his government with his officials.
sum.17: David sends his army out against the rebels and asks them to deal gently with his son Absalom. But Joab kills him when he is caught hanging from a tree, and David wins the battle. When the king receives the news, he does not celebrate; he weeps with grief for his son, and he wishes he had died in his place.
sum.18: David weeps so deeply for Absalom that his people are ashamed, until Joab confronts him and the king encourages his servants again. Then he returns to Jerusalem, forgives Shimei, listens to Mephibosheth, honors Barzilai, and Judah and Israel argue over who has the greater claim on him. We see a wounded kingdom seeking to be reconciled.
sum.14: Absalom slowly won the hearts of the people through deception, and he had himself proclaimed king in Hebron. David fled Jerusalem in tears, and his loyal followers went with him, including Ittai. David left the ark in the city, trusting in God's will. He also asked Hushai to return to Jerusalem so that he could thwart the counsel of Ahithophel.
sum.12: Amnon, son of David, deceives his sister Tamar and rapes her, and then he cruelly rejects her. Her brother Absalom holds a grudge and, two years later, has Amnon killed, and then he flees to Geshur. This chapter shows how unaddressed sin brings more pain and violence to a family.
sum.10: David stayed behind in Jerusalem while his army was fighting, and he abused his power by taking Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, who became pregnant. To cover up his sin, David tried to trick Uriah, and when that failed, he ordered that Uriah be left to die in battle. Afterward he married Bathsheba, but this displeased the LORD.
sum.9: David wanted to show kindness to Hanun, the new king of Ammon, so he sent messengers to comfort him over the death of his father. But Hanun grew suspicious, humiliated David's messengers, and prepared for war with the help of the Syrians. Joab and David defeated them, and the Syrians made peace with Israel.
sum.16: Absalom preferred the advice of Hushai to that of Ahithophel, because the Lord had determined to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel. Hushai secretly warned David, who crossed the Jordan safely, and Ahithophel took his own life. In Mahanaim, David received generous help.
sum.13: Joab, seeing that David longed for Absalom, sent for a wise woman from Tekoa to tell David a made-up story about two sons and a revenge killing, so that he would be moved to forgive. David agreed that Absalom could return, but he did not receive him for two years. After a dispute with Joab, Absalom finally got to see the king, and David kissed him.
sum.15: While David is fleeing from Absalom, Ziba brings provisions and accuses Mephibosheth, and David gives him everything that belonged to Mephibosheth. Shimei curses and throws stones at David, but David endures the insult and hopes that God will look upon his affliction. Meanwhile, Hushai pretends to be loyal to Absalom, and Ahithophel gives him shameful advice.
sum.0: David learns at Ziklag that Saul and Jonathan have died. The news comes from a young Amalekite man, who claims that he killed Saul at Saul's own request and brings Saul's crown to David. David and his men mourn and fast. David orders the young man put to death for having said that he killed the Lord's anointed. Afterward, David composes a lament that honors Saul and Jonathan.
sum.1: David, guided by God, goes up to Hebron, and there the men of Judah anoint him king. He thanks the people of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul. Meanwhile, Abner makes Ish-bosheth king, and the rivalry ends in a cruel battle in which Asahel dies. The chapter shows that David seeks God's direction, and that division brings sorrow.
sum.3: When Abner dies, Ish-bosheth and all Israel are filled with fear. Two captains, Baanah and Rechab, kill Ish-bosheth while he sleeps and bring his head to David, expecting a reward. David condemns them for killing a righteous man in his own bed, orders them executed, and they bury Ish-bosheth's head in Abner's tomb.
sum.4: The tribes of Israel went to Hebron and anointed David as king over all the people. He captured Jerusalem, made it his city, and grew stronger because God was with him. Then he defeated the Philistines twice, always asking God for guidance and obeying it.
sum.6: David wanted to build a house for God, but God answered him through Nathan that He would instead build a house for David. He promised to establish the throne of David's descendants forever and to be a father to his son. David responded with humility, praising God and asking Him to keep the promise He had made.
sum.19: Sheba, a man from Benjamin, stirred up a rebellion, and almost all of Israel abandoned David, but Judah remained loyal to him. Joab treacherously killed Amasa and then pursued Sheba as far as the city of Abel. A wise woman persuaded her people to hand over Sheba's head, and in this way the city was spared from destruction.
sum.5: David wanted to bring the ark of God up to Jerusalem, but Uzzah died when he touched it. David then left the ark for three months at the house of Obed-edom, and God blessed Obed-edom. Later they brought the ark up with great joy, and David danced with all his strength. His wife Michal despised him for it, but David answered that his joy was for God.
sum.21: David sings a song of thanks to God for rescuing him from Saul and from all his enemies. He calls God his rock, his shield, and his savior, and he describes how God heard his cry and came down with power to save him. David praises God for being faithful to the humble and promises to sing to his name.
sum.8: David asks whether anyone is still left from the house of Saul so that he can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan. Ziba, a servant of Saul's household, tells him about Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, who is lame in both feet. David has him brought in, gives back to him all the land of Saul, and invites him to eat at the king's table regularly, just like one of the king's sons. Here we see a mercy that keeps its promise and gives honor to someone who feels unworthy.
sum.2: David grew stronger while the house of Saul grew weaker. Abner, offended by Ish-bosheth, switched sides to David and tried to unite Israel under him. But Joab killed him through deception to avenge the death of his brother Asahel. David publicly mourned him, fasted, and left the punishment in God's hands.
sum.20: There was a famine for three years, and God told David that it was because of the blood Saul had shed when he killed the Gibeonites. David handed over seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, and Rizpah kept watch over the bodies. David then buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan, and after that God was moved to show mercy to the land. Later, Israel defeated Philistine giants.
sum.11: God sends the prophet Nathan, who uses a parable to show David how serious his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah was. David admits, "I have sinned against the Lord," and God forgives him, but He announces painful consequences, including the death of the child. Later, Solomon is born, and Joab and David capture Rabbah.
sum.23: David ordered a census of the people, even though Joab warned him against it. Afterward David's conscience struck him, and he confessed his sin. God gave him a choice of punishment. David chose to fall into the hands of God, a plague came, and God stopped it. David bought the threshing floor of Araunah, built an altar there, and the plague ended.
